V1-001.topic: Lactate in sepsis: meaning, types and SSC 2026 use
V1-001.q: What is the role of lactate in sepsis, and is a high lactate always hypoperfusion?
a: Septic shock: a vasopressor is needed to keep MAP ≥65 mmHg **and** lactate is >2 mmol/L despite adequate fluid.
Type A = hypoxic: oxygen delivery fails. Type B = not hypoxic: adrenaline (β2-driven aerobic glycolysis), poor liver clearance, metformin.
Why it rises in sepsis: largely **β2-driven aerobic glycolysis** from endogenous and infused catecholamines, plus reduced hepatic clearance. Anaerobic glycolysis is only one part.
So a high lactate is not always hypoperfusion. Read it with CRT, mottling, urine output and the CO2 gap.
SSC 2026: measure serially, about **every 2 hours**. Aim for a fall of **≥10% per 2 h**, not normalisation.
Do not give fluid just to normalise lactate. If clearance is slow (liver disease, metformin, linezolid), lean on CRT.
V1-001.src: Singer M et al., JAMA 2016 (Sepsis-3); SSC 2026 (Prescott et al., Intensive Care Med / Crit Care Med 2026); Levy B et al., Lancet 2005;365:871; Garcia-Alvarez M et al., Crit Care 2014;18:503

V1-002.topic: CRT trials: ANDROMEDA-SHOCK 1 and 2, and how to measure CRT
V1-002.q: What did the capillary refill time trials show, and how do you measure CRT correctly?
a: ANDROMEDA-SHOCK (JAMA 2019): CRT-targeted vs lactate-targeted resuscitation in septic shock. 28-day mortality **34.9% vs 43.4%**, p = 0.06: not significant, but less organ dysfunction.
ANDROMEDA-SHOCK-2 (JAMA 2025): **1467** patients, 86 ICUs, 19 countries. 6 hours of CRT-targeted, phenotype-based resuscitation vs usual care.
Result: **win ratio 1.16** (95% CI 1.02–1.33, p = 0.04) on a hierarchy of mortality, duration of organ support and length of stay.
28-day mortality **26.5% vs 26.6%**: no difference. The win came from less organ support.
So CRT-targeted resuscitation now has RCT support, positive on a composite outcome, not on mortality. SSC 2026 suggests CRT as an adjunct target (conditional).
How: index finger distal phalanx, hand not dependent. Firm pressure for **10 s**, then time the return of colour. Normal **≤3 s**.
Pitfall: inter-rater variability. Standardise pressure, time and site, and repeat.
V1-002.src: Hernandez G et al., JAMA 2019;321:654 (ANDROMEDA-SHOCK); ANDROMEDA-SHOCK-2 Investigators, JAMA 2025;334(22):1988-1999; SSC 2026 (Prescott et al., Intensive Care Med / Crit Care Med 2026)

V1-003.topic: Microcirculation in shock: coherence and SDF/IDF metrics
V1-003.q: What are the microcirculatory parameters in shock, and what is haemodynamic coherence?
a: Haemodynamic coherence: when MAP and cardiac output are restored, microcirculatory flow should recover too.
Loss of coherence: macro fixed, micro still failing. Common in sepsis; a normal MAP does not mean the tissues are perfused.
Direct look: sublingual videomicroscopy with sidestream dark-field (SDF) or incident dark-field (IDF) imaging.
Metrics (2018 consensus): **TVD**, **perfused vessel density (PVD)**, **proportion of perfused vessels (PPV, not pulse pressure variation)**, **MFI**, and the heterogeneity index.
Bedside surrogates: capillary refill time, mottling score, Pv–aCO2 gap **>6 mmHg**, lactate.
Videomicroscopy is still mainly a research and teaching tool: special device, cohort-level evidence only.
V1-003.src: Ince C, Crit Care 2015;19 Suppl 3:S8 (haemodynamic coherence); Ince C et al., Intensive Care Med 2018;44:281 (second consensus on sublingual microcirculation)

V1-004.topic: Shock index and modified shock index
V1-004.q: What are the shock index and the modified shock index, and how do you use them?
a: Shock index (SI) = heart rate ÷ systolic BP.
SI **over 1** flags occult shock in trauma, even while systolic BP still looks acceptable.
Modified shock index (MSI) = heart rate ÷ mean arterial pressure. Using MAP brings diastolic pressure, and so vascular tone, into the ratio.
Normal SI **0.5–0.7**. Normal MSI **0.7–1.3**; MSI above 1.3 is linked to higher mortality (Liu 2012).
Why it works: heart rate rises before BP falls, so the ratio climbs early in compensated haemorrhage.
Worked example: HR 120, SBP 100 → SI 1.2. Same patient with MAP 75 → MSI 1.6.
Limits: beta-blockers, pacing, pain and pregnancy physiology all shift HR or BP. Trend it, and pair it with lactate or base deficit.
V1-004.src: Allgöwer M, Burri C, Dtsch Med Wochenschr 1967 (shock index); Liu YC et al., World J Emerg Med 2012 (modified shock index)

V1-005.topic: Undifferentiated shock on POCUS: pump, tank, pipes
V1-005.q: How do you approach undifferentiated shock with POCUS, and which finding changes your first drug?
a: Framework (RUSH): **pump, tank, pipes**, scanned in that order at the bedside.
Pump: pericardial effusion with RA systolic collapse or RV diastolic collapse = tamponade. LV: hyperdynamic, normal or poor. RV as big as LV, McConnell's sign = acute RV pressure overload, likely PE.
Tank: IVC size and collapse; lung sliding, B-lines and pleural fluid; free fluid in the abdomen.
Pipes: abdominal aorta for aneurysm, aortic root for dissection; femoral and popliteal veins for DVT.

Finding → first move: tamponade → drain, fluid as a bridge. Dilated RV with suspected PE **and shock** → systemic thrombolysis (ESC high-risk PE). Poor LV → noradrenaline for MAP, then an inotrope; no more fluid if congested.

Small collapsing IVC with hyperdynamic LV → fluid. Hyperdynamic LV with full tank → vasopressor (distributive). Absent lung sliding with a lung point (or no B-lines and no lung pulse) in shock → decompress. Aneurysm or dissection → surgery.
Caution: the IVC only suggests fluid response. Confirm with a dynamic test once the patient is stable.
V1-005.src: Perera P et al., Emerg Med Clin North Am 2010;28:29 (RUSH exam); Jensen MB et al., Eur J Anaesthesiol 2004;21:700 (FATE)

V1-006.topic: IVC: collapsibility vs distensibility, and the limits
V1-006.q: How does IVC ultrasound help, how do collapsibility and distensibility differ, and what are its limits?
a: Collapsibility index (spontaneous breathing) = (Dmax − Dmin) ÷ Dmax. Distensibility index (passive, ventilated) = (Dmax − Dmin) ÷ Dmin.
Why two: spontaneous inspiration lowers intrathoracic pressure and the IVC narrows; a positive-pressure breath raises it and the IVC widens.
Ventilated, passive, Vt ≥8 mL/kg: distensibility **>18%** suggests fluid responsiveness.
Spontaneous: IVC ≤2.1 cm with **>50%** collapse on sniff means a low RA pressure. It only suggests responsiveness, because effort varies breath to breath.
Performance: pooled performance is moderate (sensitivity about 0.6–0.7, specificity about 0.7–0.8); poor inter-observer reliability. Confirm with PLR or a VTI change.
False readings: raised intra-abdominal pressure squeezes the IVC; RV failure, severe TR and high PEEP keep it full; active expiration narrows it.
V1-006.src: Rudski LG et al., J Am Soc Echocardiogr 2010 (ASE right heart guideline); Barbier C et al., Intensive Care Med 2004;30:1740 (distensibility index); Long E et al., Shock 2017;47:550 (IVC meta-analysis)

V1-007.topic: Fluid tolerance: definition, markers, responsive but intolerant
V1-007.q: What is fluid tolerance, and what do you do in a patient who is fluid responsive but intolerant?
a: Fluid tolerance: the ability to take more fluid without harm from congestion.
Three separate questions: does he need it (hypoperfusion)? Will he respond (stroke volume rises)? Can he tolerate it? Responsive is not need, and not tolerance.
Markers of intolerance: rising VExUS grade, new B-lines on lung ultrasound, a rising CVP, raised EVLWI on PiCCO, worsening oxygenation.
Why it matters: in capillary leak or RV failure a responder still gains oedema with each bolus.
Responsive but intolerant: do not give fluid. Use a vasopressor for lost tone, or an inotrope for a weak pump.
Once perfusion is restored and he is stable: de-resuscitation, diuretics first, ultrafiltration if needed.
V1-007.src: Kattan E et al., J Crit Care 2022 (fluid tolerance position paper); Malbrain MLNG et al., Ann Intensive Care 2018 (ROSE phases); SSC 2026 (Prescott et al., Intensive Care Med / Crit Care Med 2026)

V1-008.topic: VExUS: protocol, grading and the congested kidney
V1-008.q: What is VExUS, and how does venous congestion damage the kidney?
a: VExUS (venous excess ultrasound) grades systemic venous congestion at the bedside.
Step 1, IVC: 2 cm or less = grade 0, no significant congestion. Stop.
Step 2, if IVC >2 cm: hepatic vein Doppler. Normal S > D; S < D = mild; S reversal = severe.
Portal vein: pulsatility **≥30%** = mild, **≥50%** = severe. Intrarenal venous Doppler: continuous = normal; pulsatile with separate S and D = mild; D-only (monophasic) = severe.

Grade 0: IVC <2 cm. Grade 1: IVC >2 cm with normal or only mild patterns. Grade 2: one severe pattern. Grade 3: two or more severe. Derived in cardiac surgery, where grade 3 predicted AKI; ICU validation is limited.
Kidney: renal perfusion pressure = **MAP − CVP**. Venous congestion raises the back-pressure and lowers it, so AKI follows even with a good MAP.
V1-008.src: Beaubien-Souligny W et al., Ultrasound J 2020;12:16 (VExUS grading system)

V1-009.topic: Hepatic vein Doppler: patterns and place in VExUS
V1-009.q: Spotter: hepatic vein Doppler. What does it tell you, and how does it fit with VExUS?
a: Where: pulsed-wave Doppler in a hepatic vein close to the IVC, from a subcostal or right intercostal window, with ECG.
Normal: retrograde a wave, then S and D both towards the heart, with **S > D**. In AF the a wave is lost and S is blunted, so S < D can occur without congestion.
**S < D**: mild congestion. Raised RA pressure blunts systolic filling.
**S reversal**, flow away from the heart in systole: severe congestion, as with severe TR.
In VExUS: one of three Doppler sites, with portal vein and intrarenal vein. Scored only once the IVC is >2 cm.
Same scan: look for ascites, and check portal flow (pulsatility ≥30% mild, ≥50% severe).
V1-009.src: Beaubien-Souligny W et al., Ultrasound J 2020;12:16 (VExUS); Scheinfeld MH et al., RadioGraphics 2009;29:2081 (hepatic vein Doppler waveforms)

V1-010.topic: What CVP is still good for
V1-010.q: What is the advantage of CVP in fluid management, and is CVP useless?
a: Poor predictor of fluid responsiveness: ROC area **0.56**. A single value should not decide a bolus.
Tolerance and safety limit: a CVP that rises with fluid while cardiac output does not says stop.
Back-pressure: organ perfusion pressure = **MAP − CVP**. A high CVP lowers renal perfusion pressure even with a good MAP.
Trend: the change with fluid or inotropes means more than one number. A rising CVP in RV dysfunction is ominous.
Waveform and comparison: large v wave in TR; CVP > PCWP suggests acute RV failure.
The line itself: ScvO2 sampling and the venous half of the CO2 gap.
V1-010.src: Marik PE, Cavallazzi R, Crit Care Med 2013;41:1774 (CVP meta-analysis); De Backer D, Vincent JL, Crit Care 2018;22:43 (CVP: ten answers); SSC 2026 (Prescott et al., Intensive Care Med / Crit Care Med 2026)

V1-011.topic: Arterial trace in aortic stenosis and aortic regurgitation
V1-011.q: Spotter: arterial trace in aortic stenosis and aortic regurgitation. How do you tell them from damping?
a: Aortic stenosis: **pulsus parvus et tardus**: a small, slow-rising upstroke with an anacrotic notch, a late peak and an indistinct dicrotic notch.
Aortic regurgitation: **wide pulse pressure** with a low diastolic pressure, a brisk upstroke and fast diastolic run-off. It may be bisferiens.
Why: in AS the narrow valve limits the rate of ejection. In AR blood falls back into the LV in diastole, so diastolic pressure drops.
Trap: a slow, rounded AS trace looks over-damped. Do a fast flush first; an optimal flush response means the shape is real.
Other patterns: alternans in LV failure, paradoxus in tamponade, spike and dome in HOCM, a swing with each breath in PPV.
V1-011.src: Esper SA, Pinsky MR, Best Pract Res Clin Anaesthesiol 2014;28:363 (arterial waveform analysis); Miller's Anesthesia, 9th ed. 2020 (cardiovascular monitoring)

V1-012.topic: Septic shock fluids: grades, CLOVERS and CLASSIC, when to stop
V1-012.q: Septic shock fluids: give the grade of each step, the restrictive-versus-liberal evidence, and when you stop.
a: Phase 1: at least **30 mL/kg** crystalloid in the first 3 h: **conditional, low** certainty. A starting point, individualised and reassessed (passive leg raise), not a fixed dose.
Fluid: **balanced over saline** (conditional, moderate). Exception: **saline in traumatic brain injury**, because balanced fluids are hypotonic.
After the first bolus: **CLOVERS** and **CLASSIC** both found restrictive = liberal for mortality. SSC 2026: **either strategy is acceptable**.
Persistent hypotension: start **noradrenaline peripherally**; do not wait for a central line.
Further fluid: guided by **dynamic measures** over static values or CVP; capillary refill time and serial lactate as adjuncts.
**Stop** when the patient is no longer fluid-responsive, or no longer fluid-tolerant (for example rising B-lines or worsening oxygenation).
After resuscitation: **active fluid removal** (new in 2026) once stable without hypoperfusion; diuretics first.
V1-012.src: Surviving Sepsis Campaign adult guideline 2026; CLOVERS (NEJM 2023); CLASSIC (Meyhoff, NEJM 2022)

V1-013.topic: Restrictive vs liberal fluids: CLASSIC, CLOVERS, ROSE model
V1-013.q: Restrictive versus liberal fluid in septic shock: the trials, the ROSE model and de-resuscitation targets.
a: **CLOVERS** (sepsis-induced hypotension, after 1–3 L): restrictive with earlier vasopressors vs liberal; about **2.1 L less** fluid in 24 h, no difference in 90-day mortality (14.0% vs 14.9%).
**CLASSIC** (ICU septic shock, after initial resuscitation): restricted vs standard IV fluid; no difference in 90-day mortality. Both trials: restrictive = liberal.
SSC 2026: after the first 30 mL/kg, **either strategy is acceptable**; give more only if fluid-responsive and fluid-tolerant.
**ROSE** model: **R**esuscitation (rescue, minutes) → **O**ptimisation (titrate to perfusion, hours) → **S**tabilisation (maintenance only, days) → **E**vacuation (remove the excess).
Evacuation = de-resuscitation, now an SSC 2026 statement: active fluid removal once stable without hypoperfusion; diuretics first, ultrafiltration if not enough.
De-resuscitation targets: neutral then negative fluid balance, falling weight, fewer B-lines and better oxygenation, while perfusion (capillary refill, lactate) stays normal.
Stop removal if hypoperfusion returns: rising lactate, slow capillary refill, falling urine output or hypotension.
Missing from the trial table: **ANDROMEDA-SHOCK-2** (2025): capillary-refill-targeted resuscitation beat usual care on a hierarchical outcome (win ratio **1.16**), with no mortality difference.
V1-013.src: CLOVERS (NEJM 2023); CLASSIC (Meyhoff, NEJM 2022); Malbrain, Ann Intensive Care 2018 (ROSE phases); ANDROMEDA-SHOCK-2 (JAMA 2025); Surviving Sepsis Campaign 2026

V1-014.topic: Balanced crystalloid vs saline: mechanism, trials, TBI
V1-014.q: Balanced crystalloid or 0.9% saline in the ICU: the mechanism of harm, the trials, and who should get saline.
a: Saline has far more chloride than plasma, so large volumes cause **hyperchloraemic metabolic acidosis**.
Proposed kidney harm: high chloride at the macula densa triggers tubuloglomerular feedback, renal vasoconstriction and a lower GFR, which may raise AKI.
**SMART** (2018, 15,802 ICU adults, cluster crossover, open label): MAKE30 **14.3% vs 15.4%** (OR 0.91) favouring balanced fluid.
**SPLIT** (2015), **BaSICS** (2021) and **PLUS** (2022): no significant difference in AKI or mortality.
Pooled (Hammond meta-analysis 2022): mortality RR about **0.96**, a probable small benefit. SSC 2026: **balanced over saline** (conditional, moderate).
**TBI**: balanced solutions are slightly **hypotonic** (Ringer's lactate most), so they may lower osmolality and worsen cerebral oedema; a BaSICS subgroup suggested harm. Use **saline**.
Ringer's lactate in large volumes: watch for hyponatraemia.
V1-014.src: SMART (Semler, NEJM 2018); SPLIT (Young, JAMA 2015); BaSICS (Zampieri, JAMA 2021); PLUS (Finfer, NEJM 2022); Surviving Sepsis Campaign 2026; Hammond, NEJM Evidence 2022 (balanced vs saline meta-analysis)

V1-015.topic: Albumin: SAFE, ALBIOS, SSC 2026 and indications
V1-015.q: Albumin in the ICU: what did SAFE and ALBIOS show, what does SSC 2026 say, and where is it indicated?
a: **SAFE** (2004, ICU): 4% albumin vs saline; 28-day mortality the same. Albumin is safe but not better.
**SAFE-TBI**: albumin **raised 24-month mortality** in TBI (33% vs 20%; GCS 3–8: 42% vs 22%), possibly because hypotonic 4% albumin raises ICP.
**ALBIOS** (2014, severe sepsis): albumin added to crystalloid; **no mortality benefit**; only a post-hoc signal of benefit in septic shock.

SSC 2026: **crystalloids alone** over crystalloid plus supplemental albumin (**conditional, moderate**). Case by case after large crystalloid volumes or in cirrhosis. 2021 had suggested albumin with large volumes.
**Avoid albumin in TBI.**
Indications with evidence: spontaneous bacterial peritonitis; large-volume paracentesis over **5 L**; hepatorenal syndrome (with terlipressin).
V1-015.src: SAFE (Finfer, NEJM 2004); SAFE-TBI (NEJM 2007); ALBIOS (Caironi, NEJM 2014); Surviving Sepsis Campaign 2026

V1-016.topic: Albumin in cirrhosis: SBP, paracentesis, HRS, ATTIRE
V1-016.q: Albumin in cirrhosis: the indications, the doses, and what ATTIRE showed.
a: Why: cirrhosis has a low effective arterial volume; albumin expands plasma volume and protects renal perfusion.
**Spontaneous bacterial peritonitis**: albumin **1.5 g/kg on day 1** and **1 g/kg on day 3**, with antibiotics, to prevent renal failure.
**Large-volume paracentesis** (over **5 L**): **6–8 g per litre removed**, to prevent post-paracentesis circulatory dysfunction.
**AKI / hepatorenal syndrome**: stop diuretics, albumin **1 g/kg/day for 2 days** as a volume challenge; if HRS-AKI, **terlipressin** plus albumin 20–40 g/day.
**ATTIRE**: targeting serum albumin **above 3.5 g/dL** in decompensated cirrhosis gave **no benefit** and **more pulmonary oedema**.
So: give albumin for an indication, not to correct a low level.
V1-016.src: Sort, NEJM 1999 (albumin in SBP); EASL clinical practice guideline on decompensated cirrhosis, J Hepatol 2018; ATTIRE (China, NEJM 2021); International Club of Ascites AKI criteria (Angeli, J Hepatol 2015)

V1-017.topic: Noradrenaline: receptor profile and why output rises in sepsis
V1-017.q: Is noradrenaline an inotrope or a vasopressor, and why does cardiac output rise with it in early septic shock?
a: Receptors: **α1-dominant** vasopressor with a smaller **β1** effect and little β2. Mainly a vasopressor, with some inotropy.
Status: **first line** in septic shock (strong recommendation).
Why output rises (1), **venous recruitment**: venoconstriction moves blood from unstressed to stressed volume, raising mean systemic filling pressure and venous return.
Why output rises (2): the **β1** effect adds contractility, and a higher diastolic pressure restores coronary perfusion.
So in early septic shock it acts like an internal fluid bolus plus mild inotropy; preload-dependent patients raise their output.
Caution: at high doses arterial constriction raises afterload; output can fall and tissue perfusion worsen.
V1-017.src: Surviving Sepsis Campaign 2026; Persichini, Crit Care Med 2012 (norepinephrine and venous return); Hamzaoui, Crit Care 2010 (early norepinephrine and preload)

V1-018.topic: MAP target: SEPSISPAM, the 65 trial, who needs more or less
V1-018.q: MAP target in septic shock: what did SEPSISPAM and the 65 trial show, and whom do you treat differently?
a: SSC 2026: initial **MAP 65 mmHg** over higher targets (**strong**, moderate certainty).
**SEPSISPAM** (NEJM 2014): higher vs standard MAP target; no mortality difference, more atrial fibrillation with the higher target.
SEPSISPAM, chronic hypertension subgroup: the higher target gave **less renal replacement therapy**, but no survival benefit.
**65 trial** (JAMA 2020, age 65 or over): permissive lower target vs usual care; no harm, with less vasopressor exposure.
SSC 2026: **60–65 mmHg** for age **65 or older** (conditional, new).
Individualise: consider a higher target in chronic hypertension with worsening kidneys; judge adequacy by perfusion (lactate, capillary refill, urine, mentation).
V1-018.src: SEPSISPAM (Asfar, NEJM 2014); 65 trial (Lamontagne, JAMA 2020); Surviving Sepsis Campaign 2026

V1-019.q: Peripheral noradrenaline: how do you give it safely, for how long, and how do you manage extravasation?
a: SSC 2026: **start peripherally**; do not delay for central access (conditional). Maximum duration and vein choice: insufficient evidence.
Solution: a **dilute** concentration through the peripheral line, as per the local protocol.
Site: a **large proximal vein** (antecubital or upper arm, ideally ultrasound-guided), not hand or wrist; a well-working cannula used only for the pressor.
Duration: no evidence-based limit; protocols vary, typically **24–72 h** (Cardenas-Garcia: 72 h cap, mean 49 h, extravasation about 2%). Move to a central line earlier if the dose escalates.
Monitoring: inspect the site frequently for blanching, swelling or pain.

Extravasation: stop, aspirate, remove the cannula, elevate, infiltrate **phentolamine** 5–10 mg in 10 mL saline around the site; alternatives topical nitroglycerin or terbutaline; warm compresses (low-quality evidence).
Then: central access, document, and watch for tissue necrosis.
V1-019.src: Surviving Sepsis Campaign 2026; Loubani and Green, J Crit Care 2015 (extravasation from peripheral vasopressors); Cardenas-Garcia, J Hosp Med 2015 (peripheral vasopressor safety)

V1-020.topic: Inotropes in septic shock: SSC 2026 statements and grades
V1-020.q: Inotropes in septic shock: what exactly does SSC 2026 say, with grades, and where does vasopressin fit?
a: Indication: persistent hypoperfusion with cardiac dysfunction despite adequate fluid and vasopressor.
SSC 2026: add an inotrope (**conditional, very low** certainty): **dobutamine added to noradrenaline**, or **adrenaline alone**.
New in 2026: with cardiac dysfunction, **noradrenaline OR adrenaline** is acceptable as the first-line agent.
**Levosimendan**: suggest against.
Vasopressin **0.03 U/min** added on escalating noradrenaline rather than raising noradrenaline; no fixed threshold in 2026 (2021 said 0.25–0.5 µg/kg/min).
Adrenaline is the third-line vasopressor if MAP is still inadequate.
Caution: dobutamine alone lowers MAP (β2 vasodilation); confirm cardiac dysfunction on echo, and stop if output does not improve.
V1-020.src: Surviving Sepsis Campaign 2026; Evans, Crit Care Med 2021 (Surviving Sepsis Campaign 2021)

V1-021.topic: Steroids in septic shock: grade, trials, fludrocortisone, stopping
V1-021.q: Steroids in septic shock: grade, evidence, hydrocortisone alone or with fludrocortisone, and when to stop.
a: SSC 2026: IV corticosteroids for septic shock with an ongoing vasopressor need (**conditional, low** certainty).
Drug: **hydrocortisone 200 mg/day** (50 mg 6-hourly or infusion). 2021 trigger: noradrenaline or adrenaline **≥0.25 µg/kg/min for at least 4 h**.

**Annane 2002** (hydrocortisone + **fludrocortisone**): lower 28-day mortality in ACTH non-responders (53% vs 63%). **CORTICUS 2008** (hydrocortisone alone): no mortality benefit, faster reversal, more superinfection; ACTH response did not predict benefit.
**ADRENAL**: hydrocortisone, no 90-day mortality difference, faster shock reversal. **APROCCHSS**: plus fludrocortisone, 90-day mortality **43.0% vs 49.1%**.
Fludrocortisone **50 µg/day** enterally is optional: patient-level data suggest added benefit, but absorption is unreliable on high-dose pressors.
**HYPRESS**: hydrocortisone in sepsis without shock did not prevent shock. No steroids for sepsis without shock.
When to stop: **once vasopressors are off**. No trial supports a particular taper, so stop or taper by local practice.
An ACTH stimulation test is not recommended to select patients: CORTICUS showed the response did not predict benefit.
V1-021.src: Surviving Sepsis Campaign 2026; ADRENAL (Venkatesh, NEJM 2018); APROCCHSS (Annane, NEJM 2018); CORTICUS (Sprung, NEJM 2008); HYPRESS (Keh, JAMA 2016)

V1-022.topic: Vitamin C in sepsis: LOVIT, VITAMINS, CITRIS-ALI
V1-022.q: Vitamin C in sepsis: the rationale, the trials, and why LOVIT showed harm.
a: Rationale: vitamin C is an antioxidant and a cofactor for endogenous catecholamine and vasopressin synthesis; levels are low in sepsis.
**VITAMINS** (2020): vitamin C + hydrocortisone + thiamine vs hydrocortisone; no improvement in vasopressor-free time.
**CITRIS-ALI** (2019): IV vitamin C in sepsis with ARDS; no change in SOFA or inflammatory markers (mortality only a secondary signal).
**LOVIT** (NEJM 2022, 872 patients on vasopressors): death or persistent organ dysfunction at day 28 **44.5% vs 38.5%** (RR 1.21).
Why harm (proposed): high doses may act as a pro-oxidant or blunt adaptive responses; stopping it may withdraw oxidative-stress protection (rebound).
Glucose meter interference: vitamin C falsely raises point-of-care glucose readings, risking missed hypoglycaemia or wrong insulin doses.
SSC 2026: **suggest against** IV vitamin C (unchanged).
V1-022.src: LOVIT (Lamontagne, NEJM 2022); VITAMINS (Fujii, JAMA 2020); CITRIS-ALI (Fowler, JAMA 2019); Surviving Sepsis Campaign 2026

V1-023.topic: Sepsis-3: why SIRS was dropped, and the shock criteria
V1-023.q: Sepsis-3: define sepsis and septic shock, explain why SIRS was dropped, and why lactate is in the shock definition.
a: Sepsis: life-threatening organ dysfunction from a dysregulated host response to infection; organ dysfunction = acute **SOFA rise ≥2**.
Septic shock: sepsis needing a **vasopressor for MAP ≥65** AND **lactate >2 mmol/L**, despite adequate fluid.
Why SIRS was dropped: **not specific** (present in many non-infected or uncomplicated patients) and **not sensitive** (some infected patients with organ failure are SIRS-negative).
SIRS describes an appropriate response to infection, not the dysregulated response that damages organs.
Why lactate is in shock: vasopressor plus raised lactate picked out the group with the highest mortality; it marks cellular and metabolic failure, not hypotension alone.
Lactate in sepsis rises mainly from adrenergic (β2) aerobic glycolysis and reduced liver clearance; tissue hypoxia is only one contributor.
V1-023.src: Singer, JAMA 2016 (Sepsis-3); Shankar-Hari, JAMA 2016 (septic shock criteria); Kaukonen, NEJM 2015 (SIRS-negative sepsis)

V1-024.topic: SSC 2026: changes missing from the lists, and a practice change
V1-024.q: SSC 2026: which changes are missing from the lists, and which one changed your practice?
a: Scale: **129 statements, 46 new**.
Antimicrobials: against empiric **anaerobic** or **antifungal** cover unless risk factors; **selective digestive decontamination** suggested in ventilated patients in low-resistance units (new).

**Procalcitonin**: not to decide starting antibiotics; use it to help stop them. Prolonged β-lactam infusion after a loading dose: now **strong**, on BLING III plus the 2024 meta-analysis (BLING III alone narrowly missed significance).
Vasopressors: with cardiac dysfunction, **noradrenaline OR adrenaline** first line (new). Vasopressin on escalating noradrenaline, no fixed threshold.
Against: **vitamin D** (new), plus vitamin C, β-blockers, probiotics and routine antipyretics. Bicarbonate only if pH ≤7.2 with AKI stage 2–3.
Systems: **ICU admission within 6 h**, code-sepsis teams, post-discharge rehabilitation (new).
Screening: NEWS, NEWS2, MEWS or SIRS over qSOFA (strong). The guideline does not single out NEWS2 as preferred.
Practice-change line: "I now start noradrenaline peripherally without waiting for a central line, and give β-lactams as prolonged infusions after a loading dose."
V1-024.src: Surviving Sepsis Campaign adult guideline 2026; BLING III (Dulhunty, JAMA 2024); SuDDICU (Myburgh, JAMA 2022); Abdul-Aziz, JAMA 2024 (prolonged β-lactam infusion meta-analysis)

V1-025.topic: Procalcitonin and NT-proBNP: how to use them in the ICU
V1-025.q: Procalcitonin and NT-proBNP: how do you use each, and would you start antibiotics on procalcitonin?
a: Procalcitonin rises in bacterial infection; interferon-γ from a viral response suppresses it.
**Not to start** antibiotics: sepsis is a clinical diagnosis, and a low procalcitonin does not exclude it (SSC 2026).
**To stop**: stop when procalcitonin falls by **≥80%** from its peak or to **<0.5 ng/mL**, with clinical improvement.
Evidence: **PRORATA**: fewer antibiotic days, mortality non-inferior. **SAPS**: fewer antibiotic days and *lower* 28-day mortality (about 20% vs 25%).
NT-proBNP: a low value helps **rule out heart failure**; a high value supports cardiac strain.
Caution: NT-proBNP is raised in **sepsis and AKI**, so a high value in a septic patient does not prove heart failure; echo decides.
V1-025.src: PRORATA (Bouadma, Lancet 2010); SAPS (de Jong, Lancet Infect Dis 2016); Surviving Sepsis Campaign 2026

V1-026.topic: Obstetric SOFA, and why normal values mislead in pregnancy
V1-026.q: Sepsis in pregnancy: why do normal values mislead, and what are omqSOFA and obstetric SOFA?
a: Why scores need adapting: pregnancy raises HR and cardiac output, lowers BP, gives a compensated respiratory alkalosis with low PaCO2, and lowers creatinine.
So non-pregnant normal values mislead: a "normal" creatinine or PaCO2 may already be abnormal, and tachycardia or low BP may be dismissed as physiology.
**omqSOFA**: RR **≥25**, SBP **≤90**, altered mentation (anything other than alert).

**Obstetric SOFA**: the same organ systems as SOFA, adjusted for pregnancy: modified PaO2/FiO2 bands, a lower creatinine threshold (scores from **≥90 µmol/L**), and a simple alert/voice/pain CNS score. Each system scores only **0–2** (not 0–4); CVS uses MAP <70 or vasopressors.
Use: omqSOFA at the bedside to flag risk; obstetric SOFA in the ICU to quantify organ dysfunction.
Pregnancy-specific sources: chorioamnionitis, endometritis, pyelonephritis; always consider the fetus and the timing of delivery.
V1-026.src: Bowyer, Aust N Z J Obstet Gynaecol 2017 (SOMANZ sepsis in pregnancy guideline); RCOG Green-top Guidelines 64a and 64b (bacterial sepsis in and after pregnancy)

V1-027.topic: TAPSE and MAPSE at the bedside: low TAPSE on the ventilator
V1-027.q: What do TAPSE and MAPSE tell you, and what does a low TAPSE mean in a ventilated patient?
a: TAPSE: tricuspid annulus long-axis movement on M-mode in apical 4-chamber. **TAPSE <17 mm = RV systolic dysfunction** (normal ≥17 mm, no upper cap).
MAPSE: mitral annulus long-axis movement in the same view. **MAPSE <~10 mm = LV long-axis dysfunction**, and in sepsis a low MAPSE carries prognostic weight.
Both are **load and angle dependent**: they measure shortening against the current load, not pure contractility.
On the ventilator, PEEP and plateau pressure compress the alveolar vessels and **raise RV afterload (PVR)**. A low TAPSE may be the ventilator, not the myocardium.

So I look for **acute cor pulmonale**: RV/LV end-diastolic area >0.6 (severe ≥1) with septal flattening or dyskinesia, and a plethoric IVC. RV dysfunction occurs in 22–55% of ARDS and worsens survival.
Response is **RV-protective ventilation**: minimise plateau and driving pressures, correct PaO2 and PaCO2 to lower PVR, and prone to unload the RV.
V1-027.src: Lang RM et al., ASE/EACVI chamber quantification, J Am Soc Echocardiogr 2015;28:1; Mekontso Dessap A et al., Intensive Care Med 2016 (acute cor pulmonale in ARDS); Bergenzaun L et al., Cardiovasc Ultrasound 2013 (MAPSE in shock)

V1-028.topic: Mechanical circulatory support in cardiogenic shock: who and which
V1-028.q: Is there a role for mechanical circulatory support in cardiogenic shock? Give the trial evidence.
a: **IABP-SHOCK II**: no 30-day mortality benefit in AMI shock, so IABP is not routine.

**ECLS-SHOCK (NEJM 2023)**: routine early VA-ECMO in infarct shock, 30-day mortality 47.8% vs 49.0%, with more bleeding and vascular complications needing intervention (limb ischaemia). ECMO raises LV afterload.
**DanGer Shock (NEJM 2024)**: Impella CP in STEMI shock, lactate ≥2.5, LVEF <45%, comatose out-of-hospital arrests excluded; n=360.
Result: 180-day mortality **45.8% vs 58.5%** (HR 0.74, **NNT 8**). The pump unloads the LV.
Price: composite complications **24% vs 6%** (bleeding, limb ischaemia, haemolysis) and renal replacement **42% vs 27%**.
My answer: yes, for a selected patient (STEMI shock, low EF, not comatose) in a hub centre, as rung three after drugs and reperfusion. Not routine for all.
2025 ACC/AHA ACS guideline: microaxial flow pump **2a** for selected STEMI-CS; routine IABP and routine VA-ECMO **3 (no benefit)**.
V1-028.src: Møller JE et al., DanGer Shock, NEJM 2024;390:1382; Thiele H et al., ECLS-SHOCK, NEJM 2023;389:1286; Thiele H et al., IABP-SHOCK II, NEJM 2012;367:1287

V1-029.topic: VA-ECMO: indications, complications, LV distension and venting
V1-029.q: VA-ECMO: give the indications, the complications, and how you recognise and vent LV distension.
a: Indication: refractory cardiogenic shock of any cause (stage beyond drugs) as a bridge to recovery, decision, durable VAD or transplant; also post-cardiotomy, massive PE and arrest (ECPR).
It gives **full biventricular support plus gas exchange**, the only device that does both.

Complications: **bleeding** and **vascular complications, mainly limb ischaemia** (ECLS-SHOCK: 23.4% vs 9.6% and 11.0% vs 3.8%), stroke, haemolysis, infection, and **differential hypoxia (Harlequin)** on femoral cannulation.

Contraindications: unrecoverable heart with no VAD or transplant option, **severe aortic regurgitation**, aortic dissection, inability to anticoagulate, severe peripheral arterial disease for femoral access.
LV distension: retrograde arterial flow raises afterload. A weak LV cannot open the aortic valve, so the LV dilates, LA pressure rises, and pulmonary oedema and LV thrombus follow.
Signs: aortic valve closed on echo, loss of arterial pulsatility, rising PA or wedge pressure, worsening pulmonary oedema.
Vent: first lower ECMO flow and add an inotrope; then **IABP** or **Impella** (ECPELLA) to unload; or **atrial septostomy** or a surgical LV vent to decompress the LA.
V1-029.src: Lorusso R et al., ELSO adult cardiac failure guideline, ASAIO J 2021; Thiele H et al., ECLS-SHOCK, NEJM 2023;389:1286

V1-030.topic: Peripartum cardiomyopathy: definition, drugs and bromocriptine
V1-030.q: Define peripartum cardiomyopathy, give the drug plan before and after delivery, and the role of bromocriptine.
a: Definition: heart failure with **LVEF <45%**, from late pregnancy to 5 months postpartum (mostly the month after delivery), with no other cause.
Before delivery: **beta-blocker (metoprolol)**, **hydralazine plus nitrate** for afterload, **loop diuretic** for congestion.
Avoid before delivery: ACE inhibitor, ARB, ARNI, MRA and SGLT2 inhibitor (fetal harm).
After delivery: full guideline-directed therapy. If breastfeeding, **enalapril or captopril** are acceptable.

Bromocriptine: blocks prolactin, whose 16-kDa fragment is thought to injure the myocardium. **2.5 mg once daily for 1 week** if uncomplicated; **2.5 mg twice daily for 2 weeks, then once daily for 6 weeks** if EF <25% or shock; always with at least prophylactic anticoagulation.
Evidence is limited: ESC 2018 class **IIb** (check ESC 2025). It also stops lactation, so discuss this first.
In shock: avoid dobutamine where possible, prefer **levosimendan**, go early to mechanical support, and plan urgent delivery with the heart team.
V1-030.src: Regitz-Zagrosek V et al., ESC Guidelines on cardiovascular disease in pregnancy, Eur Heart J 2018;39:3165; Bauersachs J et al., HFA/ESC position statement on PPCM, Eur J Heart Fail 2019; Hilfiker-Kleiner D et al., Eur Heart J 2017 (bromocriptine)

V1-031.topic: Tamponade: clinical diagnosis, echo confirmation, peri-drainage care
V1-031.q: Is tamponade a clinical or an echo diagnosis, and how do you keep the patient alive until it is drained?
a: Tamponade is a **clinical diagnosis confirmed by echo**: Beck's triad, tachycardia and pulsus paradoxus, in a patient with an effusion.
Echo confirms it: **RA systolic collapse**, **RV diastolic collapse** (more specific), **plethoric IVC**, and **mitral inflow variation >25%** with respiration.
An effusion alone is not tamponade; a small fast bleed can tamponade, a large slow effusion may not.
**Fluids only temporise**: a bolus props up filling pressure for a short time. Noradrenaline can support pressure. Neither treats the cause.
**Avoid positive pressure ventilation and induction before drainage** if possible: PPV cuts venous return and induction removes sympathetic tone, so the patient can arrest.
If intubation is unavoidable: have drainage ready first, keep vasopressor running, and use the lowest airway pressures.
Definitive treatment: **pericardiocentesis** or a surgical window.
V1-031.src: Adler Y et al., ESC Guidelines on pericardial diseases, Eur Heart J 2015;36:2921; Klein AL et al., ASE pericardial disease guideline, J Am Soc Echocardiogr 2013;26:965

V1-032.topic: Pericardial vs pleural effusion on PLAX, and what next
V1-032.q: Spotter: an echo-free space on PLAX. Pericardial or pleural, and what do you do next?
a: Find the **descending thoracic aorta** in cross-section behind the left atrium.
**Pericardial** fluid lies **anterior** to the descending aorta, tracking between it and the left atrium.
**Pleural** fluid lies **posterior** to the descending aorta and does not track in front of it.
Confirm in other windows: pericardial fluid wraps the heart in subcostal view; pleural fluid sits above the diaphragm in the mid-axillary view.

What next: size it at end-diastole (mild <10 mm, moderate 10–20 mm, large >20 mm), circumferential or loculated; an anterior-only space may be an epicardial fat pad. Then look for tamponade: RA and RV collapse, plethoric IVC, mitral inflow variation.

If tamponade or unstable: drain now. If stable: drain when symptomatic despite treatment, large (>20 mm) and chronic (>3 months), or suspected bacterial, TB or malignant; otherwise treat the cause and repeat echo.
V1-032.src: Klein AL et al., ASE pericardial disease guideline, J Am Soc Echocardiogr 2013;26:965; Adler Y et al., ESC Guidelines on pericardial diseases, Eur Heart J 2015;36:2921

V1-033.topic: Burns: ABLS fluid starting rule, targets, creep and feeding
V1-033.q: Give the current starting rule for burn fluids, the targets, fluid creep, and the feeding plan.
a: ABLS/ABA starting rate: **2 mL/kg/%TBSA** in adults, **3 mL/kg/%TBSA** in children, **4 mL/kg/%TBSA** in electrical injury. Parkland's 4 mL/kg is the historic upper figure.
Give **half in the first 8 h from the time of burn**, not from arrival; the rest over 16 h. Ringer's lactate.
Titrate hourly to urine output: **0.5 mL/kg/h** adults (about 30–50 mL/h); **1 mL/kg/h** children under 30 kg; **75–100 mL/h** in electrical injury until the urine clears.
Children ≤30 kg: add maintenance fluid with dextrose (D5LR) to the resuscitation rate; watch glucose.
Worked example: 70 kg, 40% TBSA adult: 2 × 70 × 40 = 5,600 mL in 24 h; 2,800 mL in the first 8 h = 350 mL/h.
**Fluid creep**: giving above the formula drives oedema, abdominal and limb compartment syndrome and pulmonary oedema. Cut the rate when urine is above target.
Feeding: **early enteral, ideally within 12 h**, protein **1.5–2 g/kg/day**. Blunt hypermetabolism with **propranolol** and **oxandrolone**.
V1-033.src: American Burn Association, ABLS Provider Manual 2018; Pham TN et al., ABA practice guideline on burn shock resuscitation, J Burn Care Res 2008; Rousseau AF et al., ESPEN burns nutrition guideline, Clin Nutr 2013

V1-034.topic: Inhalation injury: when to intubate, when to give hydroxocobalamin
V1-034.q: In a burn with suspected inhalation injury, when do you intubate, and when do you give hydroxocobalamin?
a: Intubate early, before swelling closes the airway: **stridor**, **hoarseness or voice change**, **full-thickness facial or neck burns**, **large TBSA burns**, falling consciousness or respiratory failure.
Soot, singed nasal hair and a closed-space fire raise suspicion; on their own they do not mandate intubation.
Expect a difficult airway. **Suxamethonium is safe in the first 24 h**; avoid it from 24–48 h after the burn until healed (hyperkalaemia).
Give 100% oxygen to all: it treats CO. Pulse oximetry reads falsely normal; check COHb on co-oximetry.

Give **hydroxocobalamin 5 g IV over 15 min** (repeat once) after a closed-space fire with soot or altered consciousness plus arrest, shock or lactate **≥10 mmol/L** (≥8 in pure cyanide poisoning). Do not wait for a cyanide level.
Watch: red skin and urine, interference with co-oximetry, colorimetric labs and dialysis blood-leak alarms, and an association with AKI (oxalate).
Avoid nitrites in smoke inhalation: methaemoglobin worsens oxygen delivery already cut by CO.
**Systemic corticosteroids and prophylactic antibiotics are not recommended** for inhalation injury.
V1-034.src: American Burn Association, ABLS Provider Manual 2018; ISBI Practice Guidelines for Burn Care, Burns 2016; Baud FJ et al., NEJM 1991;325:1761; Anseeuw K et al., Eur J Emerg Med 2013;20:2

V1-035.topic: Damage control: lethal diamond, SBP target and DCS timing
V1-035.q: What is damage control resuscitation and damage control surgery? What is the lethal triad, and what is the fourth limb?
a: Damage control resuscitation (DCR): restore perfusion and clotting before definitive repair.

**Permissive hypotension**: target **SBP 80–90 mmHg (MAP 50–60)** until bleeding is controlled (not 70–90). **Not in TBI** or spinal cord injury: in severe TBI (GCS 8 or less) keep **MAP 80 or more**.
**Haemostatic resuscitation**: blood products first, **1:1:1**; minimal crystalloid; **early TXA**; give **calcium**.
**Lethal triad**: hypothermia, acidosis, coagulopathy. Add **hypocalcaemia** and it becomes the **lethal diamond**: each worsens the others.
Damage control surgery (DCS): **abbreviated surgery** (control bleeding and contamination) → **ICU** resuscitation → **definitive repair at 24–48 h**.
Why stage it: a long operation in a cold, acidotic, coagulopathic patient deepens all four limbs; the ICU fixes physiology so the repair can be survived.
V1-035.src: Rossaint R et al., European guideline on management of major bleeding after trauma, 6th ed., Crit Care 2023;27:80; Holcomb JB et al., PROPPR, JAMA 2015; ATLS 11th ed., 2025

V1-036.topic: Hypocalcaemia in TIC: citrate, lethal diamond, calcium target
V1-036.q: Why is hypocalcaemia added to the lethal triad in trauma-induced coagulopathy, and what calcium target do you keep during a massive transfusion?
a: **Why calcium falls**: stored blood products contain **citrate**, which **chelates ionised calcium**. The more units given, the lower the ionised calcium.
**Why it matters**: calcium is a **cofactor for clotting**, and supports **cardiac contractility and vascular tone**. Low calcium worsens bleeding and shock.
**Lethal diamond**: hypothermia, acidosis, coagulopathy and **hypocalcaemia**; each worsens the others.
**Target**: keep **ionised calcium in the normal range (over 1.1–1.15 mmol/L)** during massive transfusion. Older notes give 0.9 mmol/L: that is too low.
**Monitor**: measure **ionised** calcium on the blood gas; total calcium can look normal while ionised calcium is low.
V1-036.src: Rossaint R et al., European guideline on management of major bleeding after trauma, 6th ed., Crit Care 2023;27:80

V1-037.topic: TEG/ROTEM trace: parameters and the product each one asks for
V1-037.q: Spotter: TEG/ROTEM trace. Name the parameters, and say which product you give for a prolonged R time versus a low MA/MCF.
a: Viscoelastic tests show the whole life of a clot in whole blood: **start** (time), **strength** (amplitude), **breakdown** (lysis).
**Start: R time (TEG) = CT (ROTEM)**. Long = low clotting factors → **FFP or PCC**. Long INTEM but normal HEPTEM = heparin → **protamine**.
**Speed of build-up: K time (TEG) = CFT (ROTEM); α-angle in both**. Long K/CFT or a low α = low fibrinogen → fibrinogen replacement.
**Strength: MA (TEG) = MCF (ROTEM)**; early amplitude A5/A10 in ROTEM. Low = weak clot, from low fibrinogen or low platelets.
Split the weak clot with **FIBTEM** (platelets blocked): low FIBTEM = low fibrinogen → **cryoprecipitate or fibrinogen concentrate**. Low EXTEM with normal FIBTEM = **platelets**.
**Breakdown: LY30 (TEG) ≈ LI30 (ROTEM); ROTEM also reports maximum lysis (ML)**. Hyperfibrinolysis = **ML over 15%** (ROTEM) or **LY30 over 3%** (TEG, trauma) → **tranexamic acid**.
Rule of thumb: long R/CT → factors (FFP/PCC); low MA/MCF → check FIBTEM (or TEG functional fibrinogen): low → fibrinogen, normal → platelets; high lysis → TXA.
V1-037.src: Rossaint R et al., European guideline on management of major bleeding after trauma, 6th ed., Crit Care 2023;27:80 (viscoelastic-guided therapy)

V1-038.topic: The CRASH trials and why TXA must be within 3 hours
V1-038.q: TXA in trauma: what did CRASH-1, CRASH-2 and CRASH-3 show, and why must TXA be given within 3 hours?
a: **CRASH-1**: high-dose steroids in TBI **increased mortality**. Steroids are not given in TBI.

**CRASH-2** (20,211 bleeding trauma patients, within 8 h): TXA **1 g over 10 min, then 1 g over 8 h**: all-cause deaths **14.5% vs 16.0%** (RR 0.91); bleeding deaths 4.9% vs 5.7%. Benefit only **within 3 h**; **after 3 h** it **increased** bleeding deaths.
**CRASH-3** (TBI, 12,737 patients): primary outcome not significant (RR 0.94); benefit in **mild to moderate TBI (GCS 9–15)** given within 3 h (RR 0.78); **none in severe TBI (GCS 3–8)**.

**Why 3 hours**: early after injury the problem is **hyperfibrinolysis**, which TXA blocks. Later many move to **fibrinolysis shutdown** (the leading hypothesis, not proven) and a **prothrombotic** phase, so TXA no longer helps and can harm.
Practice: give it **as early as possible**, ideally before hospital, to anyone bleeding or at risk.
V1-038.src: CRASH Trial Collaborators, Lancet 2004 (CRASH-1); CRASH-2 Collaborators, Lancet 2010 and Lancet 2011 (timing analysis); CRASH-3 Collaborators, Lancet 2019

V1-039.topic: REBOA zones and the UK-REBOA trial
V1-039.q: What is REBOA, which zone do you use for which bleed, and what did the UK-REBOA trial show?
a: **REBOA**: resuscitative endovascular balloon occlusion of the aorta; a balloon in the aorta stops flow below it.
**Zone I** (descending thoracic aorta): abdominal bleeding. **Zone II**: the visceral segment; **no-occlusion zone**. **Zone III** (infrarenal to bifurcation): **pelvic** bleeding.
**UK-REBOA** (JAMA 2023): **90 patients**, **16 UK major trauma centres**, **stopped early** for a harm signal: the only RCT of REBOA in trauma suggests harm.
90-day mortality **54% vs 42%** with standard care (**OR 1.58**); **86.9% probability of harm**; deaths from bleeding came **earlier**.
Role: a **bridge to haemostasis only**. It must not delay surgery or interventional radiology.
V1-039.src: Jansen JO et al., UK-REBOA trial, JAMA 2023

V1-040.topic: ATLS 11th edition: xABCDE and spinal motion restriction
V1-040.q: ATLS 11th edition: what changed? Explain xABCDE and why spinal motion restriction has replaced immobilisation.
a: **xABCDE**: **X = exsanguinating external haemorrhage first**: tourniquet, packing, **pelvic binder**, then A, B, C, D, E.

**Spinal motion restriction**: **selective, criteria-based**, fewer **rigid collars and long boards**. **Why**: no proven benefit; harms airway, ICP, breathing, skin (sores), aspiration, adds imaging; in **penetrating** trauma it delays care and is linked to higher mortality.
**Damage control resuscitation**: permissive hypotension; **crystalloid only as a bridge**; **early MTP**; **1:1:1 or low-titre group O whole blood**.
**TXA**: within **3 h**, 1 g plus 1 g; a **2 g bolus** is supported in TBI.
**Airway**: **video laryngoscopy preferred**; **resuscitate before induction**.
**TBI**: **SBP 100–110 or more by age**; **tiered ICP** management.
Also new: team leadership, trauma-informed care, and disaster care.
V1-040.src: American College of Surgeons, ATLS Advanced Trauma Life Support, 11th ed., 2025

V1-041.topic: eFAST: what it shows, what it misses, next step
V1-041.q: Spotter: eFAST. What does it look for, what does it miss, and what is your next step for a retroperitoneal bleed with a pelvic fracture?
a: **eFAST** (extended FAST): bedside ultrasound in the primary survey, an adjunct to C.

**Looks for**: free fluid in **RUQ (Morison's pouch), LUQ (splenorenal), pelvis** and **subxiphoid pericardium**; plus **both anterior chest windows** for pneumothorax (lung sliding) and **haemothorax**.

**Misses**: the **retroperitoneum**, **hollow-viscus and diaphragm** injury, the **grade** of solid-organ injury, **small volumes (needs about 200 mL or more)**, and **pelvic fracture bleeding**; it depends on the operator.
**Negative eFAST does not exclude bleeding**: repeat it, and use CT or CT angiography when the patient is stable enough.

**Retroperitoneal bleed with pelvic fracture**: **pelvic binder**; if stable or responding → **CT angiography**, blush → **angio-embolisation**; if unstable despite binder and blood → **preperitoneal packing** with external fixation, or direct angio-embolisation; REBOA zone III as a bridge.
V1-041.src: American College of Surgeons, ATLS 11th ed., 2025; Rossaint R et al., European trauma bleeding guideline, 6th ed., Crit Care 2023;27:80

V1-042.topic: Pelvic fracture with shock: binder, angio or packing, REBOA
V1-042.q: Pelvic fracture with haemorrhagic shock: how do you choose between angio-embolisation and preperitoneal packing?
a: **Bind first**: pelvic binder centred on the **greater trochanters**.
**Resuscitate**: damage control resuscitation, massive transfusion 1:1:1, TXA within 3 h; SBP 80–90 if no TBI.
**Transient responder** with a **contrast blush** (arterial bleeding) on CT → **angio-embolisation**.
**Non-responder** (unstable despite binder and blood) → **preperitoneal packing** in theatre.

**Why the split**: 80–90% of pelvic bleeding is **venous** (presacral plexus, fracture surfaces) → packing plus **mechanical stabilisation (external fixator or C-clamp)**; about 10–20% is **arterial** → angio-embolisation.
**Positive FAST and unstable** → laparotomy plus preperitoneal packing.
**REBOA zone III** (infrarenal) can be a **bridge** to haemostasis; it does not replace it.
V1-042.src: Rossaint R et al., European guideline on management of major bleeding after trauma, 6th ed., Crit Care 2023;27:80; Jansen JO et al., UK-REBOA, JAMA 2023

V1-043.topic: Compartment syndrome: limb delta pressure and abdominal definition
V1-043.q: Compartment syndrome: how do you diagnose it in a limb and in the abdomen, and at what pressure do you act?
a: **Limb signs**: **pain out of proportion** to the injury and **pain on passive stretch** of the muscles in that compartment.
**Delta pressure** = diastolic BP − compartment pressure. **Under 30 mmHg** → **fasciotomy**.
**Abdominal compartment syndrome**: sustained **IAP over 20 mmHg** with **new organ dysfunction**.
**Causes in ICU**: massive fluid resuscitation (burns, trauma), electrical injury; deep muscle damage can be hidden under intact skin.

**Act**: limb → fasciotomy. Abdomen → medical measures first (sedation, NG and rectal decompression, drain ascites, avoid excess fluid); **decompressive laparotomy for overt ACS** not responding to them.
V1-043.src: Kirkpatrick AW et al., WSACS consensus definitions and guidelines, Intensive Care Med 2013; ABA ABLS Provider Manual 2018

V1-044.topic: Venous air and fat embolism: detection and treatment
V1-044.q: Air vs fat embolism: how do you recognise each, and how do you treat venous air embolism?
a: **Air embolism**: sudden collapse during a procedure (lines, neurosurgery, open veins); **mill-wheel murmur**; **sudden fall in ETCO2** (dead space).
**Treat air**: **stop entry**; **flood the field**; **left lateral, head-down** position; **aspirate** air through a central line; **100% oxygen**.
**Fat embolism**: **24–72 h after a long-bone fracture**; **hypoxia + petechiae + confusion** (Gurd criteria).
**Amniotic fluid embolism**: sudden collapse in labour, then **DIC**.
Tell them apart by **timing**: air is instant and procedural; fat is delayed by a day or more; AFE is in labour or just after.
V1-044.src: Gurd AR, Wilson RI, J Bone Joint Surg Br 1974 (fat embolism criteria); Mirski MA et al., Anesthesiology 2007 (venous air embolism)

questions.text: How do you assess perfusion at the bedside?

steps.bridge: Every shock ends in dysoxia, and the clinical signs come first. Next: why the skin shows it so early →

lesson.text:
Every kind of shock, whatever started it, ends in the same place. Bleeding, sepsis, a failing heart, a blocked pulmonary artery. The causes are different, but the final common pathway is one.

[[That pathway is tissue dysoxia: the cells' demand for oxygen is not met by the oxygen delivered and used.]]

Notice the last two words. Delivered and used. Most of the time the problem is delivery. Too little flow, too little haemoglobin, too little oxygen on the haemoglobin. But sometimes the oxygen arrives and the cell can't use it. Keep that second door in mind. It will matter a great deal when we reach ScvO2 in sepsis.

Now, how does the body behave when delivery starts to fail? It defends the organs it can't live without, the brain and the heart. And it does that with the sympathetic system. The heart speeds up. The vessels to the skin, the gut and the kidney clamp down. The pressure is held up by squeezing the periphery.

That's why the clinical signs come first, and why they come in this shape. Thirst. Fast breathing. A fast heart. Cold hands and feet, with weak peripheral pulses. Mottled skin and a slow capillary refill. Confusion. And a falling urine output.

As an anaesthetist, you have seen exactly this. The bleeding patient who keeps a respectable pressure with a racing heart and cold, grey hands, long before the pressure finally falls. The pressure is the last thing to go, because the body spends everything else to protect it.

Now the panel's favourite part. Four findings that signal inadequate oxygen delivery, but are easily missed. A rising lactate. A falling ScvO2. Oliguria. And an altered sensorium.

[[Four signs that are easily missed: a rising lactate, a falling ScvO2, oliguria, and an altered sensorium.]]

Why are they missed? Because none of them sets off an alarm. The monitor beeps for a low pressure. It doesn't beep for a quiet, slightly confused patient with an empty urine bag. You have to go looking.

So the clinical examination gives you three windows. The brain, through the mental state. The kidney, through the urine. And the skin. Of the three, the skin is the one you can look at in seconds, and the one that changes first.

So why does the skin fail so early?

steps.bridge: Skin has no autoregulation, so it fails first. Next: how to grade mottling at the knee →

lesson.text:
To understand the skin, start with the organs that are not like it.

The brain, the heart and the kidney have autoregulation. Across a wide range of pressure, they adjust the tone of their own small arteries to keep their blood flow steady. When the pressure falls, they open up. They look after themselves.

The skin has none of that.

[[The cutaneous circulation has no autoregulation. So when the sympathetic system clamps down to defend the pressure, the skin is the first to lose its flow.]]

The skin's vessels are run by the sympathetic system, mainly to control body temperature. So when the body is short of flow and the sympathetic drive rises, the skin is simply switched off. That isn't a failure of the skin. It's the body choosing to sacrifice it.

And that makes the skin a superb early warning. It's like the canary the miners carried. The canary is more sensitive than the miners, so it shows the danger first, while the miners still feel fine. The skin shows the shortfall while the pressure, the thing you're watching, still looks fine.

So what can you measure at the skin? Three things.

The first is a temperature gradient. Take the central temperature, at the tympanic membrane, and compare it with the peripheral temperature, at the great toe. When perfusion is inadequate, the toe cools and the gap widens. [[Skin temperature tracks cardiac output. A widening core-to-toe gradient means the periphery is being shut down.]] With an infrared thermometer, you can even follow it continuously.

The second is capillary refill time. And the third is the mottling score. We'll take each of those in turn.

One honest caution. The skin tells you about sympathetic tone, and other things change that tone too. A cold room cools the toe. A vasopressor narrows the skin's vessels. So read the skin in context, and above all, read its trend.

Let's start with the one you can see from the end of the bed. Mottling.

steps.bridge: A higher mottling score predicts death in shock. Next: how to do capillary refill properly →

lesson.text:
Mottling is the patchy, purple, lace-like discolouration of the skin. It's what failing skin flow looks like. And it usually begins around the knee.

The mottling score turns that picture into a number, from zero to five, by how far up the leg the mottling has spread. It was described by Hafid Ait-Oufella and colleagues in Paris, in two thousand and eleven.

{{pic}}

Zero is no mottling. One is a small area at the centre of the knee. Two, it doesn't go beyond the upper border of the kneecap. Three, not beyond the mid-thigh. Four, not beyond the fold of the groin. And five, beyond the groin fold.

You don't need to memorise it as a table. Just follow the leg upwards. Centre of the knee, top of the kneecap, mid-thigh, groin, and beyond.

[[A higher mottling score predicts death in shock. The further up the leg it climbs, the worse the outlook.]]

And it has one great strength. You can score it from the end of the bed, in seconds, with no equipment at all.

Where is it of limited use? In dark skin, where the colour change is hard to see. In burns. And in amputations, where the leg it's scored on isn't there.

Now the test you can do with one finger. Capillary refill.
lesson.cap: Mottling score 0–5: knee centre, top of kneecap, mid-thigh, groin fold, beyond the groin.

steps.bridge: CRT is upper limb, firm pressure, abnormal above 3 s. Next: what lactate adds and how often to measure it →

lesson.text:
Capillary refill is as old as clinical medicine. Press the skin until it blanches, let go, and time how long the colour takes to come back. The pressure empties the capillaries. The time to refill tells you how briskly blood is reaching them.

But the technique matters, and this is where marks are won and lost.

Use the distal phalanx of the index finger. Press firmly, until it blanches, and hold the pressure for about ten seconds. Then release, and time the return of colour. And the hand should be held at or above the level of the heart.

Why the upper limb? Here's a trap the panel loves.

[[Don't test the lower limb. In a dependent limb, passive venous filling gives a falsely normal refill.]]

Think about it. In a leg hanging down, the capillaries can refill backwards, from the veins, simply by gravity. So the colour comes back quickly even when the arterial flow is poor. The test looks reassuring exactly when it shouldn't.

The thresholds. At the finger, above three seconds is abnormal. At the knee, above five seconds.

[[Capillary refill is abnormal above three seconds at the finger, and above five seconds at the knee.]]

Why has this simple test become so important? Because it's fast in two senses. You can do it in seconds. And it responds within minutes when the flow improves. Lactate, as we'll see, takes hours to come down.

That idea was put to the test in a trial called ANDROMEDA-SHOCK. Four hundred and twenty-four patients with septic shock. One group was resuscitated to normalise the capillary refill. The other, to bring the lactate down by twenty percent every two hours. Twenty-eight-day mortality was thirty-four point nine percent with capillary refill, against forty-three point four with lactate. A hazard ratio of zero point seven five. But the p value was zero point zero six.

So the sentence, capillary refill guided resuscitation reduced mortality, is false. It favoured capillary refill, but it did not reach significance. We'll take that trial apart properly in its own lesson, along with the second trial that followed it.

One honest caution. Capillary refill depends on the person doing it. Different hands give different answers. So standardise the pressure, the time and the site, and repeat it.

Now, the marker every resident reaches for first. Lactate.

steps.bridge: The lactate trend matters more than one value. Next: which marker tracks flow faster than lactate →

lesson.text:
Most residents learn lactate as a simple story. No oxygen, so the cell switches to anaerobic glycolysis, and lactate spills out. That story is true. But in sepsis, it's only a small part of the truth.

Start with the basics. The body makes about fourteen to fifteen hundred millimoles of lactate every day, and it isn't waste. The liver and the kidneys clear most of it, partly by burning it as fuel and partly by turning it back into glucose. So the level in the blood is a balance. What's being made, against what's being cleared.

That balance gives you two ways to raise it. Make more, or clear less.

Now, in septic shock, why does it rise? Mostly not because of hypoxia.

[[In septic shock, lactate rises mostly from beta-two driven aerobic glycolysis, plus reduced clearance by the liver. Tissue hypoxia is only one contributor.]]

Here's how that works. Adrenaline, the body's own and the one in your infusion, stimulates beta-two receptors on muscle. That speeds up the sodium-potassium pump. The pump burns energy fast, and the cell feeds it by running glycolysis faster than the mitochondria can take up the pyruvate. The surplus pyruvate becomes lactate. And all of this happens with plenty of oxygen around.

Add to that a liver that is itself poorly perfused and inflamed, clearing less. Two pushes in the same direction.

Hypoxia does contribute, and more so in low-flow shock, the bleeding patient or the failing heart. But in sepsis, a high lactate is as much a marker of stress as of hypoxia.

You have seen the drug version of this in theatre and recovery. The asthmatic on salbutamol nebulisers whose lactate climbs to four, while she's pink and warm. That's beta-two stimulation, not hypoperfusion.

[[Beta-two stimulation, from adrenaline or salbutamol, raises lactate without any shortage of oxygen.]]

The cut-off is two millimoles per litre. It's part of the definition of septic shock.

But the real value of lactate is not one number. It's the trend.

[[A falling lactate means reperfusion, and is linked to lower mortality whatever the starting value. A persistent rise means a poor outcome.]]

And because the level reflects production and clearance together, it changes slowly. So measure it every one to two hours. Any more often, and there's little new to see.

So lactate is slow. Is there a marker that tracks flow faster?

steps.bridge: A CO2 gap above 6 means low flow, even with normal lactate. Next: how strong the evidence is for each marker →

lesson.text:
There is, and it comes from the same blood you already sample. The veno-arterial CO2 gap. The central venous PCO2 minus the arterial PCO2.

Normal is two to six millimetres of mercury. Above six means tissue hypoperfusion.

Now the question that the professor will ask. Does it mark flow, or hypoxia?

[[The CO2 gap marks flow, not hypoxia. It is inversely related to cardiac output.]]

Here's why. The tissues make carbon dioxide all the time. The blood flowing through them carries it away. By the Fick principle, the CO2 the body produces equals the cardiac output multiplied by the difference in CO2 content between venous and arterial blood. Rearrange it, and the gap is the CO2 production divided by the cardiac output.

{{**Fick for CO2:** VCO₂ = CO × (CvCO₂ − CaCO₂)
so the gap ≈ VCO₂ ÷ CO
In the usual range, PCO₂ tracks CO₂ content roughly linearly, so we use the pressures.}}

Picture a factory pouring a steady amount of dye into a river every minute. When the river runs fast, the dye is carried away and the water downstream is pale. When the river slows, the same dye piles up, and the water downstream turns dark. The dye is the CO2. The river is the cardiac output. The darkness downstream is the gap.

{{pic}}

Look at the curve. As the output falls, the gap rises, slowly at first and then steeply. And the dashed curve shows the other half of the analogy. Pour in more dye, with fever or shivering, and the gap is wider at any flow.

Why is it so useful? Two reasons. It changes faster than lactate, so it helps early in shock. And a gap above six reveals hypoperfusion even when the lactate is normal.

And the most testable combination of all. An ScvO2 above seventy percent, which looks reassuring, with a gap above six.

[[A normal ScvO2 with a gap above six means flow is still inadequate. The answer is to raise the cardiac output.]]

It's prognostic too. A high gap early in septic shock is linked to organ dysfunction and death.

One honest caution. The gap is a global number. A normal gap does not exclude hypoperfusion in one region, such as the gut.

Now we have a handful of markers. How strong is the evidence for each?
lesson.cap: The CO2 gap rises as cardiac output falls. Above 6 mmHg means low flow; more CO2 production lifts the curve.

lesson.text:
Here's the evidence, marker by marker, and the main weakness of each. This is a table to see once, and then to hear as a pattern.

{{Marker | Evidence | Main drawback
Lactate | Meta-analysis | Lab time; raised outside shock
ScvO2 | RCT | Central line; weak under anaesthesia
O2 challenge | RCT | Special monitor; intubated only
CO2 gap | Cohort | Central line and blood samples
Mottling | Cohort | Burns, amputations, dark skin
CRT | RCT ×2 | Inter-rater variability
Sublingual video | Cohort | Special device; educational}}

Lactate is the one backed by meta-analysis. Its weakness is that it needs a blood sample and lab time, and it rises outside shock.

ScvO2 has trial support, but needs a central line, and it's less useful under anaesthesia, when oxygen consumption falls. The oxygen challenge test has trial support too, but it needs a special monitor and works only in intubated patients.

Capillary refill now rests on two randomised trials, ANDROMEDA-SHOCK in twenty nineteen, and ANDROMEDA-SHOCK two in twenty twenty-five. Older notes call it cohort-level. That's out of date.

[[Capillary refill now rests on two randomised trials. Older notes that grade it as cohort evidence are out of date.]]

The CO2 gap, mottling and sublingual microscopy have only cohort evidence.

So which marker do you trust most? Here's the answer the panel wants.

[[No single marker. I trust a falling lactate together with a normalising capillary refill, repeated over time.]]

spine: What it is: perfusion is whether oxygen delivery meets tissue demand. A normal MAP alone does not prove it.
Clinical first: mental state, urine output, and the skin: capillary refill time, mottling score and the toe-to-core temperature gradient.
Global markers: lactate trend, ScvO2 and the veno-arterial CO2 gap. A gap above **6 mmHg** means low flow even when ScvO2 looks normal.
Why lactate is not pure hypoxia: in sepsis it is largely β2-driven aerobic glycolysis plus poor liver clearance, so I read it as a trend.
Evidence: CRT tested in two RCTs. **ANDROMEDA-SHOCK** missed on mortality (**34.9 vs 43.4%**, p = 0.06); ANDROMEDA-SHOCK-2 won on a composite, through less organ support.
Which I trust most: no single marker. I trust a falling lactate together with a normalising CRT, repeated over time.

open.text:
Let me start with a patient.

Patient A is sixty, two days after a bowel resection. The monitor shows a MAP of seventy. The nurse is happy, and on paper, so is the chart. But look at him. His knees are blotchy and purple. When you press his fingertip, the colour takes five seconds to come back. He's a little muddled about where he is. And the urine bag hasn't moved in two hours.

Is he perfused?

This is the first question of a new package, haemodynamics. And it begins with the most basic question in the whole of critical care. Not, what is the pressure? But, is the oxygen reaching the cells?

We measure pressure because it's easy. But pressure is only the push. What the tissues need is the flow that the push produces, carrying enough oxygen for what they are using.

[[A normal MAP alone does not prove perfusion. Pressure is the push. Perfusion is whether oxygen delivery meets what the tissues need.]]

What is the professor really checking here? First, that you look at the patient before the numbers: the brain, the kidney and the skin. Second, that you know the global markers in the blood, and what each one really measures. And third, the honest part. How good is the evidence for each marker, and which ones do you trust?

The trap is the single number. The resident who says, I check the lactate, and stops there, has missed most of the answer.

So here's the plan. First, what every kind of shock has in common. Then the skin, and why it fails first. Then the two skin tests, mottling and capillary refill. Then lactate. Then the CO2 gap. And finally, the evidence behind each one.

close.text:
So let's bring it together.

Perfusion is whether oxygen delivery meets what the tissues need. And a normal MAP alone does not prove it.

I start with the patient. The mental state, the urine output, and the skin: the capillary refill time, the mottling score, and the gradient from core to toe. The skin goes first, because it has no autoregulation.

Then the global markers. The lactate trend, the ScvO2, and the CO2 gap. [[A gap above six means low flow, even when the ScvO2 looks normal.]]

Lactate is not pure hypoxia. In sepsis it's largely beta-two driven aerobic glycolysis, plus poor clearance by the liver. So I read it as a trend.

The evidence. Capillary refill has been tested in two trials. ANDROMEDA-SHOCK missed on mortality, thirty-four point nine against forty-three point four percent, with a p value of zero point zero six. ANDROMEDA-SHOCK two won on a composite, through less organ support.

And which do I trust most? No single marker. A falling lactate with a normalising capillary refill, repeated over time.

That's your answer. What perfusion is, the clinical signs first, the global markers, why lactate misleads, the evidence, and what you trust.

But here's something to carry forward. Today, lactate kept turning out to be less simple than it looks. It rises with adrenaline. It rises with salbutamol. It's slow. And yet it sits right inside the definition of septic shock.

So what exactly is the role of lactate in sepsis? And is a high lactate always hypoperfusion? That's next.

questions.text: What is the role of lactate in sepsis?

steps.bridge: Lactate above 2 is part of the septic shock definition. Next: where lactate comes from and why it rises →

lesson.text:
Start with the definitions, Sepsis three, from twenty sixteen.

Sepsis is life-threatening organ dysfunction caused by a dysregulated host response to infection. Organ dysfunction is a rise in the SOFA score of two or more.

And septic shock is sepsis that needs a vasopressor to keep the MAP at sixty-five or above, and a lactate above two millimoles per litre, despite adequate fluid resuscitation.

[[Septic shock needs both: a vasopressor for a MAP of sixty-five, and a lactate above two, despite adequate fluid.]]

Notice that word, both. A vasopressor alone is not enough. A high lactate alone is not enough. That's the commonest slip in the viva.

And notice what lactate is doing in that definition. It's the one blood test in it. It's there because it marks a group of patients whose risk of death is much higher. So it's a marker of how sick the patient is, not a pure measure of hypoxia.

And severe sepsis? That term was eliminated.

So if lactate defines the sickest patients, why does it rise?

steps.bridge: Its trend predicts outcome; β2 stimulation also raises it. Next: which causes are hypoxic and which are not →

lesson.text:
You met the mechanism in the last lesson. In septic shock, lactate rises mostly from beta-two driven aerobic glycolysis, from the body's own catecholamines and the ones you infuse, plus reduced clearance by the liver. Hypoxia is only one part. And because the level is a balance of production and clearance, it changes slowly, so it's the trend, every one to two hours, that counts.

Now hold Patient C in mind. He's on adrenaline. That alone can push his lactate up, with his tissues well perfused.

steps.bridge: Type A is hypoxic; type B is drugs, liver and disease. Next: how the 2026 guideline wants lactate used →

lesson.text:
So let's sort the causes properly. Lactic acidosis comes in two main types, and the dividing line is one question. Is oxygen failing to reach the tissues, or not?

Type A is hypoxic. Oxygen delivery fails. Think of every part of the delivery chain. The flow can fail: shock, cardiac arrest, hypovolaemia, left ventricular failure, mesenteric ischaemia, and sepsis. The carrier can fail: severe anaemia, carbon monoxide, methaemoglobinaemia. Or the oxygen itself is short: hypoxaemia. And one more group, where demand simply outruns delivery: heavy exercise and seizures.

[[Type A is hypoxic: oxygen delivery fails. Exercise and seizures are type A too, because demand outruns delivery.]]

Type B is everything where oxygen is getting there. It has three subtypes.

B one is underlying disease. Liver failure and renal failure, which can't clear it. Diabetes and DKA. Malignancy, the Warburg effect, where tumour cells run glycolysis even with oxygen. Thiamine deficiency, because thiamine is the cofactor for pyruvate dehydrogenase, the enzyme that feeds pyruvate into the Krebs cycle. And hypoglycaemia.

B two is drugs and toxins. Metformin. Salicylates. Ethylene glycol. Beta-agonists. Cyanide. Cocaine. HIV drugs. Alcohol. And one you know well as an anaesthetist, propofol, in the propofol infusion syndrome.

B three is hereditary. Mitochondrial myopathies, and defects of gluconeogenesis.

{{Type | Mechanism | Examples
A | Hypoxic: delivery fails | Shock, arrest, anaemia, CO, hypoxaemia; exercise, seizures
B1 | Underlying disease | Liver or renal failure, DKA, malignancy, thiamine deficiency
B2 | Drugs and toxins | Metformin, salicylates, β-agonists, cyanide, propofol, alcohol
B3 | Hereditary | Mitochondrial myopathies, gluconeogenesis defects}}

One small trap. Some notes put alcohol under B one. The standard classification puts it in B two, as a toxin. Either may be keyed, so say which you mean.

[[Type B is not hypoxic: disease, drugs and toxins, or inherited defects.]]

Now notice where sepsis sits. It's listed under type A. But by the mechanism we just learned, much of its lactate behaves like type B. Sepsis lives in both worlds. That's why a high lactate in sepsis can't be read on its own.

So how does the twenty twenty-six guideline want you to use it?

steps.bridge: Use serial values; do not chase normal with fluid. Next: where lactate sits among the other resuscitation tools →

lesson.text:
The twenty twenty-six Surviving Sepsis Campaign has a short set of statements on cultures, lactate and early antibiotics.

Blood cultures. As soon as possible, and ideally before antimicrobials. Remember they're positive in only about thirty percent of sepsis.

Now lactate, the heart of this lesson.

[[Use serial lactate measurements to guide resuscitation. Do not chase normalisation with fluid alone.]]

And when is lactate clearance misleading? In liver disease, with metformin, and with linezolid. In all three, the lactate clears slowly for reasons that have nothing to do with flow. A failing liver can't clear it. Metformin and linezolid interfere with the mitochondria. In those patients, lean on capillary refill time instead.

And one new statement. Antibiotics in the ambulance are suggested for definite or probable sepsis with hypotension, when the transfer will take more than sixty minutes.

So lactate is one of several tools. Where does the guideline put it among the others?

steps.bridge: Lactate is suggested serially, CRT as an adjunct. Next: the full answer on type B and the 2-hourly target →

lesson.text:
The twenty twenty-six guideline takes a position on four tools that guide resuscitation. All four are conditional.

Dynamic measures are suggested over clinical examination or static measures. That means a passive leg raise, or a fluid bolus, judged by the change in stroke volume, or by stroke volume variation or pulse pressure variation. The certainty was upgraded from very low to low.

Capillary refill time is suggested as an adjunct to other measures of perfusion.

Lactate is suggested as serial measurements.

And cardiac output monitors? Insufficient evidence.

[[Dynamic measures are preferred over static ones, capillary refill is an adjunct, and lactate is measured serially.]]

And notice what is missing. CVP is a static measure, and it is not recommended as a guide. We'll come back to dynamic measures properly when we reach fluid responsiveness.

Now let's put the whole answer together.

So here's the answer, built in the order the panel likes.

First, the definition. Septic shock needs a vasopressor for a MAP of sixty-five and a lactate above two, despite adequate fluid.

Second, the mechanism. Lactate rises largely from beta-two driven aerobic glycolysis, from the body's own catecholamines and the ones we infuse, plus reduced clearance by the liver. Anaerobic glycolysis is only one part.

Third, the types. Type A is hypoxic. Type B is not: adrenaline, a failing liver, metformin.

[[So a high lactate is not always hypoperfusion. Read it alongside capillary refill, mottling, urine output and the CO2 gap.]]

Fourth, how to use it. Measure it serially, about every two hours. And aim for a fall of at least ten percent every two hours, not for a normal value.

{{**SSC 2026 lactate:** serial, about every 2 h · aim ≥10% fall per 2 h · do not give fluid just to normalise it}}

[[Do not give fluid just to normalise lactate. If clearance is slow, from liver disease, metformin or linezolid, lean on capillary refill.]]

Now go back to Patient C. His lactate is rising, but every other window says perfused. Warm hands, a refill of two seconds, a good urine output. And he's on adrenaline. That rise is most likely the drug, through beta-two stimulation, not a hidden fluid deficit. Two more litres would not fix it. And it could do him harm, in lungs that are already infected.

What you do is look at the other markers, and keep trending.

spine: What it is: lactate is a marker of stress and perfusion. Above **2 mmol/L** with a vasopressor for MAP ≥65, despite adequate fluid, defines septic shock.
Why it rises: in sepsis it is mostly β2-driven aerobic glycolysis plus poor liver clearance. Tissue hypoxia is only one part.
Not always hypoperfusion: adrenaline, salbutamol, metformin and liver failure all raise it without hypoxia.
What I do: measure about every 2 hours and aim for a fall of at least 10% per 2 hours, alongside capillary refill time.
