Caution: SSC 2026 says do not give fluid just to normalise lactate. If clearance is slow, I lean on capillary refill.

open.text:
Let me start with a call from the ward.

Patient C has septic shock from a chest infection. He's been well filled, and he's on an adrenaline infusion. His MAP is seventy-five. His hands are warm, his capillary refill is two seconds, and his urine is flowing. But his lactate has climbed, from three to five. The junior on call wants to give him another two litres of fluid.

Should he?

In the last lesson, we said that lactate is a marker of stress as much as of hypoxia. Today, we put that idea to work at the bedside.

This question looks simple. Lactate above two is septic shock, measure it, bring it down. But what the professor is really checking is whether you understand what lactate actually measures. Do you know why it rises? Do you know the causes that have nothing to do with oxygen? And do you know how the twenty twenty-six guideline wants you to use it?

The trap is treating every high lactate as a fluid deficit. Chasing the number with fluid is exactly what the guideline warns against.

So here's the plan. First, where lactate sits in the definition of septic shock. Then, briefly, why it rises. Then the types of lactic acidosis, hypoxic and not. Then how the guideline wants it measured, and where it sits among the other tools. And finally, the answer, and what to do for Patient C.

close.text:
So let's bring it together.

[[Lactate is a marker of stress and of perfusion. Above two, with a vasopressor for a MAP of sixty-five despite adequate fluid, it defines septic shock.]]

Why does it rise? In sepsis, mostly from beta-two driven aerobic glycolysis, plus poor clearance by the liver. Tissue hypoxia is only one part.

So it's not always hypoperfusion. Adrenaline, salbutamol, metformin and liver failure all raise it without any shortage of oxygen.

What I do. Measure it about every two hours, and aim for a fall of at least ten percent every two hours, alongside the capillary refill time.

And the caution. The twenty twenty-six guideline says, do not give fluid just to normalise lactate. If clearance is slow, I lean on capillary refill.

That's your answer. What it is, why it rises, when it isn't hypoperfusion, what you do, and the caution.

But here's something to carry forward. Twice today, when lactate let us down, the answer was the same. Lean on capillary refill. A press of the fingertip, standing in for a blood test.

Can a finger really guide resuscitation better than a lab value? Two large trials set out to answer exactly that. That's next.

questions.text: What did the recent capillary refill time study show?

steps.bridge: CRT is a finger test with clear thresholds. Next: what the first trial compared and found →

lesson.text:
You learned the test in the first lesson. Index finger, the hand at or above the level of the heart, firm pressure until it blanches, then time the return of colour. Abnormal above three seconds at the finger, and above five at the knee. Never a dependent leg, because passive venous filling gives a falsely normal result.

It works because the skin has no autoregulation, so it shows low flow early. And it improves within minutes when flow returns. That speed is the whole idea behind both trials.

steps.bridge: CRT beat lactate on organ dysfunction but missed on mortality, p = 0.06. Next: what the 2025 follow-up trial showed →

lesson.text:
ANDROMEDA-SHOCK, published in twenty nineteen.

Four hundred and twenty-four patients with septic shock. Two strategies. In one, resuscitation aimed to normalise the capillary refill, to three seconds or less. In the other, it aimed to bring the lactate down by twenty percent every two hours.

The result. Twenty-eight-day mortality was thirty-four point nine percent in the capillary refill group, against forty-three point four percent in the lactate group. And there was less organ dysfunction with capillary refill.

[[ANDROMEDA-SHOCK: mortality thirty-four point nine against forty-three point four percent, with a p value of zero point zero six. Not significant, but less organ dysfunction.]]

Now, why does zero point zero six matter so much, when the difference looks so large? Because the trial was not big enough to rule out chance for a difference of that size. By the usual threshold of zero point zero five, it missed. So you can say capillary refill was at least as good as lactate, and probably better for organ dysfunction. You cannot say it saved lives.

{{**ANDROMEDA-SHOCK (2019):** n = 424 · CRT ≤3 s vs lactate fall 20% per 2 h
28-day mortality 34.9% vs 43.4% · HR 0.75 · P = 0.06}}

And its effect on the guideline? Capillary refill entered it, as an adjunct.

So the question was left hanging. A big difference, but not a proven one. And that's exactly what the second trial set out to settle.

steps.bridge: ANDROMEDA-SHOCK-2 won on organ support, not on mortality. Next: what the 2026 guideline does with CRT →

lesson.text:
ANDROMEDA-SHOCK two, published in twenty twenty-five.

This time, one thousand four hundred and sixty-seven patients, in eighty-six ICUs across nineteen countries. And the question was different. Not capillary refill against lactate. Instead, six hours of capillary refill targeted resuscitation, built into a structured, phenotype-based package, against usual care.

The outcome was hierarchical, and it was analysed as a win ratio. So let's understand that first, because the panel will ask.

Imagine a tournament. Every patient in one arm plays a match against every patient in the other. The first rule decides the match: who survived. If that's a tie, the match goes to the second rule: who needed organ support for less time. If that's tied too, the third rule: who had the shorter stay. Then you count up. The win ratio is the number of wins divided by the number of losses. Above one, the strategy wins.

[[ANDROMEDA-SHOCK two won on a win ratio of one point one six, on a hierarchy of mortality, duration of organ support and length of stay.]]

The confidence interval ran from one point zero two to one point three three, with a p value of zero point zero four. So it was a real win.

But where did the win come from? Look at mortality on its own. Twenty-six point five percent, against twenty-six point six. No difference at all.

[[Mortality was twenty-six point five against twenty-six point six percent. The win came from less organ support, not from fewer deaths.]]

{{**ANDROMEDA-SHOCK-2 (JAMA 2025):** n = 1467 · 86 ICUs · 19 countries · 6 h of CRT-targeted care vs usual care
Win ratio **1.16** (95% CI 1.02–1.33, P = 0.04) · 28-day mortality 26.5% vs 26.6%}}

So here's the honest summary. Capillary refill targeted resuscitation now has randomised support. It's positive on a composite outcome, and not on mortality.

And one practical point, because both trials depend on it. The technique. You heard it at the start, so just add the timing. Hold the firm pressure for ten seconds, then time the colour. Normal is three seconds or less.

The weakness is inter-rater variability. Two people can press differently and count differently. So standardise the pressure, the time and the site, and repeat it.

So what did the guideline do with both trials?

You met the twenty twenty-six guideline's tools in the lactate lesson. Dynamic measures are preferred over static ones. Lactate is measured serially. And capillary refill time is suggested as an adjunct to other measures of perfusion. Every one of these statements is conditional.

So the guideline position matches the evidence. Capillary refill earns its place next to lactate, not in place of it.

spine: What it is: capillary refill time is a fast bedside test of skin perfusion. Firm pressure on the index finger for 10 seconds; normal is 3 seconds or less.
Why it works: skin has no autoregulation, so it shows low flow early, and CRT responds within minutes, faster than lactate.
Evidence: **ANDROMEDA-SHOCK** 2019, CRT vs lactate targets: mortality **34.9 vs 43.4%**, p = 0.06, with less organ dysfunction.
Evidence: **ANDROMEDA-SHOCK-2** 2025, **1467** patients: CRT-targeted care won (win ratio **1.16**) through less organ support. Mortality was **26.5 vs 26.6%**.
What I do: SSC 2026 suggests CRT as an adjunct target. I use it with lactate, not in place of it.
Caution: measure on the upper limb, not a dependent leg, and standardise the technique; inter-rater variability is the main weakness.

open.text:
Here's a strange contest.

In one corner, a blood test, run on a gas machine, with a number to two decimal places. In the other, the oldest test in medicine. You press a fingertip, let go, and count.

Which of the two should steer the resuscitation of a patient in septic shock?

A team led by Glenn Hernández, in Chile, thought the finger deserved a fair fight. Their reasoning was simple. Lactate falls slowly, over hours, and it rises for reasons that have nothing to do with flow. So a team chasing lactate may keep pushing fluid and drugs into a patient whose tissues are already reperfused. Capillary refill, on the other hand, responds within minutes.

So they ran a trial. And then, years later, a second, much bigger one.

What is the professor really checking with this question? First, that you know what each trial compared. Second, that you quote the result honestly, including the p value of the first one. Third, that you can explain what a win ratio is, because the second trial was won on one. And fourth, what the twenty twenty-six guideline did with all of this.

The trap is the confident sentence. Capillary refill reduced mortality. It's the sentence the panel is waiting for, and it's wrong, for both trials.

So here's the plan. First, a quick reminder of how to do the test. Then the first trial. Then the second. And then the guideline.

close.text:
So let's bring it together.

Capillary refill time is a fast bedside test of skin perfusion. Firm pressure on the index finger for ten seconds. Normal is three seconds or less.

It works because the skin has no autoregulation, so it shows low flow early. And it responds within minutes, faster than lactate.

The first trial. ANDROMEDA-SHOCK, twenty nineteen. Capillary refill against lactate targets. Mortality thirty-four point nine against forty-three point four percent, a p value of zero point zero six, with less organ dysfunction.

The second. ANDROMEDA-SHOCK two, twenty twenty-five, one thousand four hundred and sixty-seven patients. Capillary refill targeted care won, with a win ratio of one point one six, through less organ support. Mortality was twenty-six point five against twenty-six point six.

[[The twenty twenty-six guideline suggests capillary refill as an adjunct target. I use it with lactate, not in place of it.]]

And the caution. Measure it on the upper limb, not a dependent leg, and standardise the technique. Inter-rater variability is its main weakness.

That's your answer. What it is, why it works, both trials with their numbers, what I do, and the caution.

But here's something to carry forward. When you press that fingertip, you're watching the smallest vessels in the body: the arterioles, capillaries and venules. Capillary refill is an indirect window onto them.

What if you could look at those vessels directly? And what would you see in a patient whose pressure is perfect, but whose tissues are still starving? That's the microcirculation, and it's next.

questions.text: What are the microcirculatory parameters in shock?

steps.bridge: Macro can be fixed while micro still fails; MFI, PPV and TVD measure it. Next: which blood test shows micro flow is still low →

lesson.text:
Start with what should happen.

When you restore the MAP and the cardiac output, flow through the small vessels should recover too. The big circulation and the small one move together. That's called haemodynamic coherence, a term Can Ince used in twenty fifteen.

And in sepsis, that coherence is often lost.

[[Loss of coherence means the macrocirculation is fixed while the microcirculation is still failing. A normal MAP does not mean the tissues are perfused.]]

Why would that happen? Because in sepsis, the problem isn't only the pump or the pressure. The endothelium is injured. Small vessels are plugged by white cells and micro-clots. Some capillaries stop, while their neighbours flow fast. Blood takes the open routes and bypasses the closed ones.

Think of a town whose water mains are at full pressure, while some houses have dry taps, because the small pipes to those houses are blocked. Measuring the mains pressure tells you nothing about those houses. And raising the mains pressure further won't open a blocked pipe. That is exactly why pushing the MAP higher often fails to rescue the microcirculation.

So how do you look at the small vessels directly?

You put a small handheld microscope under the tongue. Sublingual videomicroscopy. The modern devices use sidestream dark-field imaging, or incident dark-field imaging. The light is absorbed by haemoglobin, so the red cells appear as dark dots moving through the vessels, and you can see which vessels flow and which don't.

From those videos, a twenty eighteen consensus set out the parameters. Here they are.

{{**Sublingual microcirculation (2018 consensus)**
TVD · total vessel density
PVD · perfused vessel density
PPV · proportion of perfused vessels (not pulse pressure variation)
MFI · microvascular flow index
Heterogeneity index}}

Total vessel density is how many small vessels there are. Perfused vessel density is how many of them are flowing. The proportion of perfused vessels is the second divided by the first. And note the trap. In this context, PPV means the proportion of perfused vessels, not pulse pressure variation.

[[The core parameters are total vessel density, perfused vessel density, the proportion of perfused vessels, and the microvascular flow index.]]

The microvascular flow index grades the flow itself, from no flow, through intermittent and sluggish, to continuous. And the heterogeneity index captures the patchiness, some vessels flowing and others stopped.

That patchiness matters beyond this lesson. When blood shunts past closed capillaries, it returns to the veins still full of oxygen. Hold on to that. It's why ScvO2 can look normal in septic shock.

One honest caution. Videomicroscopy needs a special device, and the evidence for it is only cohort-level. It's still mainly a research and teaching tool, and not yet a treatment target.

So at the bedside, you use surrogates. The first is a blood test.

steps.bridge: A CO2 gap above 6 means flow is still inadequate. Next: how mottling shows micro failure at the bedside →

lesson.text:
You met the CO2 gap in the first lesson. Central venous minus arterial PCO2, normally two to six, and above six it means hypoperfusion. It marks flow, not hypoxia, because by the Fick principle it rises as the cardiac output falls.

For Patient D, the key point is this. A gap above six tells you flow is still inadequate, even when the ScvO2 and the lactate look reassuring. But it's a global number, so a normal gap doesn't exclude regional failure.

steps.bridge: Mottling spreads from the knee as micro flow fails. Next: the fastest bedside micro test →

lesson.text:
The second surrogate is the mottling score, which you met in the first lesson. It grades how far the mottling has climbed the leg, from the centre of the knee, to the top of the kneecap, the mid-thigh, the groin, and beyond. A higher score predicts death in shock.

Mottling is the microcirculation made visible. It's the skin's small vessels failing, patch by patch, the same patchiness the microscope shows under the tongue. It's harder to read in dark skin, burns and amputations.

And the third surrogate is the fastest of all, capillary refill. Index finger, upper limb, firm pressure, and abnormal above three seconds. You've now met it twice, with both ANDROMEDA trials behind it.

For the microcirculation, its value is speed. It responds within minutes when small-vessel flow improves, so it tells you quickly whether what you've just done has reached the tissues.

spine: What it is: the microcirculation is where oxygen actually reaches cells. In shock it can fail even after MAP and cardiac output are corrected.
Why: haemodynamic coherence is lost in sepsis. Macro is fixed, micro is not, so normal pressures can hide ongoing tissue hypoperfusion.
Measures: sublingual SDF or IDF videomicroscopy gives microvascular flow index, proportion of perfused vessels and total vessel density.
What I do: at the bedside I use surrogates. Capillary refill, mottling score, a CO2 gap above **6 mmHg**, and the lactate trend.
Caution: videomicroscopy needs a special device and has only cohort evidence. It is not yet a treatment target.

open.text:
Let me start with a paradox.

Patient D has septic shock. You've done everything right. He's had his fluid, he's on noradrenaline, his MAP is seventy-five, and the monitor says his cardiac output is normal. By every number on the screen, he's resuscitated.

But his knees are mottled. His capillary refill is four seconds. And his lactate won't come down.

How can the big numbers be right while the tissues are still failing?

The answer lies in the part of the circulation the monitor never shows you. The microcirculation. The arterioles, capillaries and venules, the vessels where oxygen actually leaves the blood and enters the cells.

In two thousand and two, Daniel De Backer and colleagues in Brussels looked directly at these vessels under the tongues of patients with septic shock. They saw far fewer perfused small vessels than in healthy volunteers. The big circulation could look fine, while the small one was failing.

What is the professor checking with this question? First, the idea of haemodynamic coherence, and its loss. Second, how the microcirculation is measured, and the names of the parameters. Third, what you actually use at the bedside. And fourth, the honest limit: none of this is yet a treatment target.

So here's the plan. First, coherence, and the direct measures. Then the three bedside surrogates you already know: the CO2 gap, mottling, and capillary refill.

close.text:
So let's bring it together.

The microcirculation is where oxygen actually reaches the cells. And in shock, it can fail even after the MAP and the cardiac output are corrected.

Why? Because haemodynamic coherence is lost in sepsis. [[The macrocirculation is fixed, the microcirculation is not, so normal pressures can hide ongoing tissue hypoperfusion.]]

How is it measured? Sublingual videomicroscopy, with sidestream or incident dark-field imaging. It gives the microvascular flow index, the proportion of perfused vessels, and the total vessel density.

What do I do at the bedside? I use surrogates. Capillary refill, the mottling score, a CO2 gap above six, and the lactate trend.

And the caution. Videomicroscopy needs a special device and has only cohort evidence. It is not yet a treatment target.

That's your answer. What it is, why it fails, how it's measured, what I use at the bedside, and the caution.

But here's something to carry forward. In three lessons now, one blood test has kept appearing. The CO2 gap. It sees low flow when lactate is normal. It sees low flow when ScvO2 looks fine.

So how exactly do you interpret it? And what do you do when it's high? That's next.

questions.text: What is the Pcv-aCO2 gap and how do you interpret it?

steps.bridge: The gap marks flow, not hypoxia, and is abnormal above 6. Next: what to do with a high gap in each setting →

lesson.cap: The gap rises as cardiac output falls. Above 6 mmHg means low flow.

steps.bridge: A high gap with good ScvO2 means raise flow. Next: what access the gap needs compared with other markers →

lesson.text:
So the gap is above six. What do you do? That depends on two more questions. Is the rest of perfusion normal? And what is the ScvO2?

Take the first situation. The gap is high, but tissue perfusion is otherwise normal. And normal here means something specific. A lactate below two, a normal urine output, no mottling, and warm extremities.

[[A high gap with otherwise normal perfusion: observe, don't act, and exclude the other causes of a high gap.]]

What are those other causes? Three of them. Acute hyperventilation. Venous hyperoxia. And a high CO2 production. Look again at the dashed curve in the last picture. Fever, shivering or agitation make more CO2, so the gap widens at the same flow. And venous hyperoxia works through the Haldane effect. When venous haemoglobin carries more oxygen, it holds less CO2, so the venous PCO2 rises without any change in flow.

Now the second situation. The gap is high, perfusion is poor, and the ScvO2 is below seventy percent. Both markers agree. Oxygen delivery is short. So you raise delivery. Raise the cardiac output first. Then the arterial saturation, with FiO2 and PEEP, to an SaO2 above ninety-five percent. And transfuse if the haemoglobin is low.

And the third situation, the most testable one. The gap is high, perfusion is poor, but the ScvO2 is above seventy percent. The saturation looks fine, but the flow is still inadequate.

[[A high gap with a normal ScvO2 means raise the flow: fluid if the patient is fluid-responsive, and if not, an inotrope, or lower the oxygen consumption.]]

{{High gap above 6 mmHg, and… | What I do
Perfusion otherwise normal | Observe; exclude hyperventilation, venous hyperoxia, high VCO₂
Poor perfusion, ScvO₂ <70% | Raise DO₂: CO first, then SaO₂ >95% (FiO₂, PEEP), transfuse if Hb low
Poor perfusion, ScvO₂ >70% | Raise flow: fluid if responsive, else inotrope; lower VO₂}}

That's Patient E. Her ScvO2 of seventy-four is falsely reassuring. Her gap of nine says her flow is still too low. So first, is she fluid-responsive? If yes, fluid. If not, an inotrope.

Now one step further, because a sharp panel may take you there. The gap alone tells you about flow. But you can ask a second question. Is the cell actually short of oxygen?

Divide the CO2 gap by the arterio-venous oxygen content difference. Normally, the CO2 the tissues make roughly matches the oxygen they use. When the CO2 side rises out of proportion to the oxygen side, CO2 is being made beyond what oxygen consumption explains, as when bicarbonate buffers the acid of anaerobic metabolism.

[[A ratio of the CO2 gap to the arterio-venous oxygen content difference above about one point four suggests anaerobic metabolism.]]

One honest caution, in the other direction. A normal gap does not exclude hypoperfusion when the cardiac output is high. A fast river washes the dye away, even if some side streams are blocked.

So what does the gap need from you, compared with the other markers?

Here are the four global markers, side by side. The cut-off for each, and what access each one needs.

{{Marker | Cut-off | Needs
SvO₂ | 70% | Pulmonary artery catheter
ScvO₂ | 70% | Central venous catheter
Lactate | 2 mmol/L | Blood sample
CO₂ gap | 6 mmHg | Arterial AND central venous catheters}}

The mixed venous saturation, SvO2, cut-off seventy percent, needs a pulmonary artery catheter. The ScvO2, also seventy, needs only a central line, and it's used in place of SvO2 for clinical purposes. Lactate, two millimoles per litre, needs just a blood sample.

And the CO2 gap, six millimetres of mercury, needs both an arterial line and a central venous line.

[[The CO2 gap needs both an arterial and a central venous catheter. But many patients in septic shock already have both, and then it costs you only two samples.]]

One caution from this card. A high ScvO2 can come from shunting, or luxury perfusion, not from good health. ScvO2 stands in for SvO2 as a trend, but in shock their absolute values drift apart. That's our next lesson.

spine: What it is: the difference between central venous and arterial PCO2. Normal **2–6 mmHg**; above **6 mmHg** means tissue hypoperfusion.
Why: by the Fick principle the CO2 gap is inversely related to cardiac output. Low flow lets CO2 build up in venous blood. It marks flow, not hypoxia.
Normal ScvO2 with a high gap: oxygen saturation looks fine but flow is still inadequate. I raise cardiac output: fluid if responsive, otherwise an inotrope.
Low ScvO2 with a high gap: oxygen delivery is short. I raise cardiac output first, then SaO2 with FiO2 and PEEP, and transfuse if haemoglobin is low.
Beyond flow: gap ÷ arterio-venous O2 content difference above about **1.4** suggests anaerobic metabolism. A normal gap does not exclude hypoperfusion when cardiac output is high.
Caution: hyperventilation, venous hyperoxia and high CO2 production also widen it. It needs both arterial and central venous lines.

open.text:
Let me give you three numbers from one patient.

Patient E has septic shock, six hours into resuscitation. Her ScvO2 is seventy-four percent. Her lactate is two point five, and falling slowly. And her venous-to-arterial CO2 gap is nine.

The ScvO2 says she's fine. The lactate says she's nearly fine. The gap says her flow is still too low. Which do you believe, and what do you do next?

This is the question where the CO2 gap stops being a number on a card and becomes a decision. You already know what it is. Today we use it.

What is the professor really checking? First, the definition and the normal range. Second, the Fick logic, why it marks flow and not hypoxia. Third, and this is the heart of it, what you do with a high gap, in each setting, with the ScvO2 beside it. And fourth, the things that widen the gap without any change in flow. A resident who sees a high gap and reaches straight for an inotrope, without checking for those, has fallen into the trap.

So here's the plan. First, a short reminder of the physiology. Then what to do with a high gap, in three situations. And then where the gap sits among the other global markers, and what it needs from you.

close.text:
So let's bring it together.

The CO2 gap is the difference between central venous and arterial PCO2. Normal is two to six, and above six means tissue hypoperfusion.

Why? By the Fick principle, the gap is inversely related to the cardiac output. Low flow lets CO2 build up in the venous blood. [[It marks flow, not hypoxia.]]

A normal ScvO2 with a high gap: the saturation looks fine, but the flow is still inadequate. I raise the cardiac output, with fluid if responsive, otherwise an inotrope.

A low ScvO2 with a high gap: oxygen delivery is short. I raise the cardiac output first, then the SaO2 with FiO2 and PEEP, and transfuse if the haemoglobin is low.

Beyond flow: the gap divided by the arterio-venous oxygen content difference, above about one point four, suggests anaerobic metabolism. And a normal gap does not exclude hypoperfusion when the cardiac output is high.

And the caution. Hyperventilation, venous hyperoxia and a high CO2 production also widen it. And it needs both arterial and central venous lines.

That's your answer. What it is, why, the two ScvO2 situations, beyond flow, and the caution.

But here's something to carry forward. All through this lesson, the gap leaned on its partner, the ScvO2. A low ScvO2 meant one thing, a normal one meant another. And Patient E's ScvO2 of seventy-four turned out to be lying.

So how should you read ScvO2 itself? Why does it fall, why does it sometimes rise, and when can you trust it? That's next.

questions.text: How do you interpret ScvO2 in shock?

steps.bridge: A low value means supply fails demand; normal does not exclude hypoxia. Next: how ScvO2 differs from true SvO2 →

lesson.text:
Start with the true mixed venous saturation, the SvO2. It's sampled from the pulmonary artery, through a PA catheter, where the venous blood from the whole body has finally mixed. Normal is sixty-five to seventy-five percent.

Why is it so useful? Because it's the oxygen left over, after the whole body has taken what it needs.

Here's the Fick principle for oxygen. The oxygen the body consumes equals the cardiac output, multiplied by the difference in oxygen content between arterial and venous blood. Rearrange it for the venous saturation, and you get this.

{{**Fick, rearranged:** SvO₂ ≈ SaO₂ − VO₂ ÷ (CO × Hb × 1.34 × 10)
(CO in L/min, Hb in g/dL; dissolved O₂ ignored)
Down: low SaO₂, low Hb, low CO, high VO₂}}

Read it slowly. The venous saturation starts at the arterial saturation, and falls by however much the tissues took, divided by how much oxygen was delivered.

Think of a delivery van. It leaves the depot full, that's the SaO2. It drops parcels at every house on the round, that's the consumption. It comes back with whatever is left, that's the SvO2. The houses still need the same number of parcels. So it comes back emptier if the van was small, which is anaemia. If it made fewer trips, which is a low cardiac output. If it left half-loaded, which is hypoxaemia. Or if the houses took more than usual.

So the causes of a low value fall into two groups.

[[A low SvO2 means supply is failing demand: delivery is down, or consumption is up.]]

Delivery down: a low cardiac output, hypovolaemia, hypoxia, anaemia. Consumption up: fever, pain, shivering, agitation, thyrotoxicosis.

Now the high values. Back to the van. It also comes back full if some houses refuse their parcels, or if it skips whole streets. Those are the two great traps of sepsis.

Skipping streets is shunting. Blood bypasses closed capillaries, the patchy microcirculation of the last lesson, and returns to the veins still full of oxygen. Refusing parcels is cytotoxic hypoxia. The oxygen arrives, but the cells' mitochondria can't use it. Either way, the venous saturation is high, while the tissues starve.

It also rises for innocent reasons. Consumption falls under sedation, anaesthesia and analgesia. And delivery rises with fluid, transfusion, inotropes and oxygen. You've seen this in theatre. Under anaesthesia, consumption falls, so the venous saturation rises.

[[So does a normal value guarantee adequate oxygenation? No. A low value means mismatch. A normal or high one does not exclude tissue hypoxia.]]

So that's the true mixed venous saturation. But you rarely have a PA catheter. So what does the central line give you instead?

steps.bridge: In shock ScvO2 reads higher than SvO2; both cut at 70%. Next: where ScvO2 sits among the global markers →

lesson.text:
The ScvO2 is taken from a central venous catheter, with its tip in the superior vena cava. So it samples the upper body. The SvO2, from the pulmonary artery, samples the whole body.

And that difference in what they sample produces a pattern the panel loves, because it reverses.

In health, the ScvO2 is lower than the SvO2, by about two to three percent. Why? Because the upper body includes the brain, and the brain extracts more oxygen than the rest of the body. The lower body includes the kidneys, which receive a large flow and take relatively little from it, so the blood in the inferior vena cava is better saturated.

Now in shock, the relationship flips.

[[In shock, ScvO2 becomes higher than SvO2. Brain flow is preserved, while gut and kidney flow fall, so the lower-body blood is more desaturated.]]

Think back to the first lesson. The body defends the brain and steals from the gut and the kidney. So the upper body blood stays relatively well saturated, while the lower body blood, from the starved gut and kidney, comes back much emptier. The SVC sample misses that.

The cut-off is seventy percent for both. But the two correlate poorly in shock.

[[A reassuring ScvO2 can hide a much lower true mixed venous saturation.]]

So ScvO2 is good as a trend, and less trustworthy as an absolute number in a shocked patient. How does it compare with the other global markers?

steps.bridge: ScvO2 needs only a central line, cut-off 70%. Next: test the traps on ScvO2 and its partners →

lesson.text:
You met this table in the last lesson. ScvO2 and SvO2 both cut at seventy percent, but ScvO2 needs only a central line, which is why it's used in place of SvO2. Lactate cuts at two, and needs only a blood sample. The CO2 gap cuts at six, and needs both arterial and central venous lines.

The point for ScvO2 is the caution on that card. A high ScvO2 can mean shunting or luxury perfusion, not good health. So pair it with the gap and the lactate.

Now let me test you. I'll give you a statement. Decide, true or false, before I give the answer.

In shock, ScvO2 is lower than SvO2. False. It's higher in shock. The normal relationship reverses.

A CO2 gap above six indicates tissue hypoxia. False. It marks low flow, not hypoxia.

A normal SvO2 rules out tissue hypoxia. False. Sepsis and cytotoxic hypoxia give normal or high values.

Metformin causes type B two lactic acidosis. True. B two is drugs and toxins.

ANDROMEDA-SHOCK showed a significant mortality benefit for capillary refill guided resuscitation. False. The p value was zero point zero six.

Capillary refill should be measured in the lower limb. False. Use the upper limb, above heart level. The leg gives a false normal.

And near-infrared spectroscopy, NIRS, mainly reflects venous oxygen saturation. True. About seventy-five percent of cerebral blood volume is venous.

[[Every one of the false statements is a trap the panel uses. The reversal of ScvO2 in shock, and flow not hypoxia for the gap, are the two they reach for most.]]

spine: What it is: oxygen saturation of SVC blood from a central line, normally **70%** or more. By Fick, it falls when delivery (CO, Hb, SaO2) fails to meet consumption.
Low ScvO2: delivery is short (low cardiac output, anaemia, hypoxaemia) or demand is high (fever, pain, shivering). I raise delivery.
High ScvO2 in septic shock: shunting past capillaries and cells that cannot use oxygen. A normal or high value does not exclude tissue hypoxia.
What I do: pair ScvO2 with the CO2 gap and lactate. Normal ScvO2 with a gap above 6 still means flow is inadequate.
Caution: in shock ScvO2 runs higher than mixed venous SvO2, because brain flow is preserved. Targeting ScvO2 as in Rivers EGDT was not supported by **ProCESS, ARISE and ProMISe**.

open.text:
Let me start with a number that was once at the very centre of sepsis care.

In two thousand and one, Emanuel Rivers published a trial of early goal-directed therapy in septic shock. One of its targets was an ScvO2 of seventy percent or more, chased with fluid, blood and inotropes. The results were striking, and for over a decade, that target sat in sepsis protocols across the world.

Then three large trials tested the approach again. ProCESS, ARISE and ProMISe. And none of them found a benefit.

So here's the puzzle. The physiology behind ScvO2 is sound. It comes straight from the Fick principle. Why would a sound number fail as a target?

Part of the answer is that ScvO2 is honest when it's low, and much less honest when it's normal or high. And that is exactly what this question is testing.

What is the professor checking? First, what ScvO2 is, and its normal value. Second, the Fick logic, and the causes of a low value. Third, why a normal or high value does not exclude tissue hypoxia. Fourth, how ScvO2 differs from true mixed venous saturation, especially in shock. And finally, the trials.

So here's the plan. First, mixed venous saturation and what moves it. Then ScvO2 against SvO2. Then where ScvO2 sits among the other markers. And then I'll test you on the traps.

close.text:
So let's bring it together.

ScvO2 is the oxygen saturation of SVC blood from a central line, normally seventy percent or more. By the Fick principle, it falls when delivery, through cardiac output, haemoglobin and SaO2, fails to meet consumption.

A low ScvO2 means delivery is short, from a low cardiac output, anaemia or hypoxaemia, or demand is high, from fever, pain or shivering. So I raise delivery.

A high ScvO2 in septic shock can mean shunting past closed capillaries, or cells that can't use oxygen. [[A normal or high ScvO2 does not exclude tissue hypoxia.]]

What I do. I pair it with the CO2 gap and the lactate. A normal ScvO2 with a gap above six still means flow is inadequate.

And the caution. In shock, ScvO2 runs higher than mixed venous SvO2, because brain flow is preserved. And targeting ScvO2, as in Rivers' early goal-directed therapy, was not supported by ProCESS, ARISE and ProMISe.

That's your answer. What it is, low values, high values, what I do, and the caution.

But here's something to carry forward. ScvO2 and SvO2 run apart because of one organ: the brain, which extracts more oxygen than the rest of the body.

So what if you sampled the blood leaving the brain alone? What could the brain's own venous saturation tell you, in a patient with a head injury? That's next. Jugular venous oxygen saturation.

questions.text: What is jugular venous oxygen saturation?

lesson.text:
Start with the anatomy. Blood leaves the brain through the internal jugular veins. Just below the skull base, each one widens into a small dilatation, the jugular bulb.

So the catheter is placed retrograde. You go into the internal jugular vein and thread the catheter upwards, against the flow, towards the head, until the tip sits in the jugular bulb. Usually on the dominant side. And you confirm it on an X-ray, with the tip above the lower border of the first cervical vertebra.

Why so high? Because the bulb drains about seventy percent of its blood from the hemisphere on the same side, with less than three percent from outside the brain. Lower down, veins from the face and neck join, and the sample is no longer pure brain blood.

[[SjvO2 is the saturation of blood leaving the brain, sampled from a retrograde catheter in the jugular bulb.]]

Now the normal range. Fifty-five to seventy-five percent. That's lower than the mixed venous saturation, and you know why. The brain extracts more oxygen than the rest of the body. It's the same reason ScvO2 is lower than SvO2 in health.

[[Normal SjvO2 is fifty-five to seventy-five percent. Below fifty percent means cerebral ischaemia.]]

Now the causes of a low value. Sort them exactly as you sorted the SvO2. Supply down, or demand up.

{{**Low SjvO₂** (<50% = ischaemia)
Supply down | Demand up
Anaemia | Agitation
Hypotension | Pain
Raised ICP | Fever
Hypocapnia (vasoconstriction) | Seizures
Hypoxaemia (SaO₂ <90%) |}}

Supply down. Anaemia. Hypotension. Raised ICP, which squeezes the cerebral perfusion. Hypoxaemia, with an SaO2 below ninety percent. And hypocapnia.

That last one is Patient F. CO2 is the strongest controller of cerebral vessel tone. Lower it, and the vessels constrict. That's why hyperventilation lowers the ICP, because less blood in the skull means less pressure. But constrict too far, and the brain's supply falls below its need. The SjvO2 is how you'd see that happening. If it falls below fifty as you hyperventilate, you've gone too far.

Demand up. Agitation, pain, fever and seizures. A seizing brain burns oxygen fast.

Now the high value, above seventy-five percent. It has two very different meanings.

The first is hyperaemia. More blood is reaching the brain than it needs, so less is extracted.

The second is the grim one. Brain tissue that can no longer extract oxygen. If the cells are dead, they take nothing, and the venous blood comes back almost as full as it went in.

[[A high SjvO2, above seventy-five percent, means hyperaemia, or brain tissue that is no longer extracting oxygen, which can mean infarcted or dead brain.]]

Notice the parallel with sepsis. There, a high ScvO2 could mean cells that can't use oxygen. Here, a high SjvO2 can mean cells that are no longer alive to use it. A high venous saturation is never automatically good news.

And the limitation the panel will reach for. The brain receives fifteen to twenty percent of the cardiac output, and SjvO2 is a global measure for that hemisphere. So it can miss a regional ischaemic area. A normal value doesn't mean every part of the brain is safe.

spine: What it is: SjvO2 is the saturation of blood leaving the brain, via a retrograde IJ catheter to the jugular bulb, usually dominant side; X-ray tip above lower border of C1.
Normal: **55–75%**, lower than SvO2 because the brain extracts more oxygen. Below **50%** means cerebral ischaemia.
Low value: supply down (anaemia, hypotension, raised ICP, hypocapnia, hypoxaemia) or demand up (fever, seizures, pain, agitation).
High value, above **75%**: hyperaemia, or brain tissue that is no longer extracting oxygen, which can mean infarcted or dead brain.
Caution: it is a global measure from one side. A normal value can miss regional ischaemia.

open.text:
Let me start in the neuro ICU.

Patient F has a severe head injury. His intracranial pressure is high, and the team is hyperventilating him to bring it down. His PaCO2 is lower than usual. The ICP falls. Good.

But here's the question nobody at the bedside can answer by looking. In lowering his CO2, have you narrowed his cerebral vessels so much that you're now starving his brain of oxygen?

The ScvO2 can't tell you. The lactate can't tell you. You need a window onto the brain itself.

That window is jugular venous oximetry. The SjvO2. The saturation of the blood leaving the brain.

It's the same idea you've just learned, the Fick principle, but for one organ. The oxygen left in the venous blood tells you whether supply is keeping up with demand. Only now, the organ is the brain.

What is the professor checking? First, where the catheter goes, and how you confirm it. Second, the normal range and the ischaemic threshold. Third, the causes of a low value, sorted by mechanism. Fourth, what a high value means, including the grim meaning. And finally, its limitation.

This question has only one card, so we'll take it slowly, from the catheter to the caution.

close.text:
So let's bring it together.

SjvO2 is the saturation of the blood leaving the brain. It's sampled through a retrograde internal jugular catheter to the jugular bulb, usually on the dominant side, with the tip on X-ray above the lower border of the first cervical vertebra.

[[Normal is fifty-five to seventy-five percent, lower than SvO2 because the brain extracts more oxygen. Below fifty percent means cerebral ischaemia.]]

A low value means supply is down, from anaemia, hypotension, raised ICP, hypocapnia or hypoxaemia. Or demand is up, from fever, seizures, pain or agitation.

A high value, above seventy-five, means hyperaemia, or brain tissue that is no longer extracting oxygen, which can mean infarcted or dead brain.

And the caution. It's a global measure from one side. A normal value can miss regional ischaemia.

That's your answer. What it is, the normal range, low values, high values, and the caution.

But here's something to carry forward. We've just gone deep. A catheter threaded up into the skull base, to read one organ's oxygen.

Now let's go the other way, to the simplest number in all of shock. Two vital signs that every patient already has, divided one by the other. It flags hidden bleeding while the blood pressure still looks safe. That's the shock index, and it's next.

questions.text: What is shock index and modified shock index?

steps.bridge: Shock index over 1 is one of the occult-shock flags in trauma. Next: how the modified index differs and how to calculate both →

lesson.text:
For decades, trauma teaching ran in alphabetical order. Airway, then breathing, then circulation. And for most patients, that's right. But in the patient who is bleeding to death, the order is now often changed. It's called resequenced resuscitation, circulation before airway.

Here's the sequence.

First, control massive external bleeding. Nothing else matters if it's still pouring out.

Second, basic airway manoeuvres. Intubate straight away only for dangerous hypoxia, or a dynamic airway injury that's about to close.

Third, look actively for occult shock. Shock that the blood pressure isn't showing yet. And here is where our index appears.

[[Flags of occult shock: a systolic below one hundred and ten, a shock index over one, a flat IVC with bleeding, a lactate over four or a base deficit over six, loss of central pulses, and cold limbs.]]

Notice that the systolic flag is one hundred and ten, not ninety. In trauma, a systolic that would look acceptable in the ward is already a warning.

Fourth, treat the shock. Blood products and tranexamic acid. Bind the pelvis. Decompress the chest. Treat tamponade. And vasopressors if the shock is neurogenic.

Fifth, and only then, intubate. Use twenty-five to fifty percent of the usual induction dose, with a full paralytic dose, and be ready for collapse.

Why does that order matter so much? This is where you speak as an anaesthetist.

[[Intubating a bleeding patient before filling the tank can cause arrest. Positive pressure and induction drugs remove the remaining preload and tone.]]

Think about what keeps that young man alive. His sympathetic system has clamped his veins, pushing every last drop of blood back to his heart, and tightened his arteries to hold the pressure up. Now you give an induction agent. It removes that sympathetic tone. And then you start positive pressure ventilation, which raises the pressure in the chest and cuts the venous return still further. Preload and tone, taken away in a single minute, from a patient running on both. That's why the dose is reduced and the paralytic dose is not. The paralytic itself does little to his pressure, and a full dose gives you good intubating conditions quickly, even with a slow circulation.

So the shock index is one of the flags that decides whether you're in this pathway at all. Let's look at it properly.

The shock index is the heart rate divided by the systolic blood pressure. Normal is zero point five to zero point seven.

[[The shock index is heart rate divided by systolic pressure. Normal is zero point five to zero point seven. Over one flags occult shock in trauma.]]

Why does a ratio work, when each number alone misleads? Because of the order in which compensation happens. As blood is lost, the heart rate rises first. The systolic pressure is held up, by vasoconstriction, until late. So the heart rate is climbing while the pressure is still flat. Put one on top of the other, and the ratio climbs early, during compensated haemorrhage, while the blood pressure still looks acceptable.

Now the modified shock index. It's the heart rate divided by the mean arterial pressure, instead of the systolic.

Why would that help? Because the MAP includes the diastolic pressure. And the diastolic pressure reflects vascular tone. So the modified index brings tone into the ratio, which the systolic alone leaves out.

Normal modified shock index is zero point seven to one point three. And a value above one point three has been linked to higher mortality, in work by Liu and colleagues in twenty twelve.

[[The modified shock index is heart rate divided by MAP. Normal is zero point seven to one point three, and above one point three is linked to higher mortality.]]

Now the worked example. Take Patient G. A heart rate of one hundred and twenty, and a systolic of one hundred.

{{**Shock index** = HR ÷ SBP = 120 ÷ 100 = **1.2**   (normal 0.5–0.7)
**Modified shock index** = HR ÷ MAP = 120 ÷ 75 = **1.6**   (normal 0.7–1.3)}}

One hundred and twenty divided by one hundred gives a shock index of one point two. Over one. And if his MAP is seventy-five, the modified index is one hundred and twenty divided by seventy-five, which is one point six. Both are abnormal, in a man whose pressure someone called fine.

So what do you do? You treat it as bleeding until proven otherwise. Activate the haemorrhage pathway, and find the source.

One honest caution. Anything that changes the heart rate or the pressure on its own will distort the ratio. Beta-blockers stop the heart rate rising, so the index stays falsely low. A pacemaker fixes the rate. Pain raises it. And pregnancy changes both heart rate and pressure. So don't trust a single value. Trend it, and pair it with the lactate or the base deficit.

spine: What it is: shock index is heart rate divided by systolic BP, normal 0.5–0.7. Modified shock index is heart rate divided by mean arterial pressure.
Why: heart rate rises before blood pressure falls, so the ratio rises early in compensated bleeding, while BP still looks safe.
What I do: in trauma a shock index over **1** flags occult shock and predicts need for transfusion. I treat it as bleeding until proven otherwise: activate the haemorrhage pathway, find the source.
Worked example: heart rate 120 and systolic 100 gives a shock index of 1.2.
Caution: beta-blockers, pacing and pregnancy change heart rate and BP. I trend it and pair it with lactate or base deficit.

open.text:
Let me start in the emergency department.

Patient G came off a motorbike. He's talking, a little pale. His heart rate is one hundred and twenty. His systolic pressure is one hundred. Someone says, his pressure's fine, let's get him to the scanner.

Is it fine?

A systolic of one hundred looks safe. But that young man may already have lost a large share of his blood volume, and he's holding his pressure up the only way he can, with his heart rate and his vessels. When that compensation fails, it fails fast.

In nineteen sixty-seven, two surgeons, Allgöwer and Burri, proposed a simple way to see through that compensation. Don't look at the heart rate or the pressure alone. Divide one by the other. They called it the shock index.

What is the professor checking? First, the two definitions, the shock index and the modified one, and their normal values. Second, why the ratio works, when each number alone misleads. Third, what you do with a high value in trauma. And fourth, the situations where it lies.

The trap is reassurance from a normal systolic pressure. The blood pressure is the last thing to fall.

So here's the plan. First, where the shock index sits in the modern trauma primary survey, and why it changes what you do first. Then the two indices themselves, with a worked example.
