So let's bring it together.

The shock index is heart rate divided by systolic blood pressure, normally zero point five to zero point seven. The modified shock index is heart rate divided by mean arterial pressure.

Why does it work? Because the heart rate rises before the blood pressure falls. So the ratio rises early, in compensated bleeding, while the pressure still looks safe.

[[In trauma, a shock index over one flags occult shock and predicts the need for transfusion. I treat it as bleeding until proven otherwise.]]

So I activate the haemorrhage pathway, and find the source.

The worked example. A heart rate of one hundred and twenty and a systolic of one hundred gives a shock index of one point two.

And the caution. Beta-blockers, pacing and pregnancy change the heart rate and the pressure. So I trend it, and pair it with the lactate or the base deficit.

That's your answer. What it is, why it works, what I do, the example, and the caution.

But here's something to carry forward. The shock index tells you that shock is there. It doesn't tell you what kind. Is it bleeding, a failing heart, a tamponade, a clot in the lung, or sepsis? Each one needs a different first move, and the wrong one can kill.

So how do you name the shock, at the bedside, in minutes? You pick up the ultrasound probe. That's next.

questions.text: How do you approach undifferentiated shock with POCUS?

steps.bridge: Pump, tank, pipes sorts shock in minutes and each finding has a first move. Next: the four goals of a focused echo →

lesson.text:
The framework most people use is called RUSH, the Rapid Ultrasound in Shock exam, described by Perera and colleagues in twenty ten. And it organises everything around one idea. Think of the circulation as plumbing. A pump, a tank, and pipes. Scan them in that order.

[[Pump, tank, pipes: scan the heart, then the volume, then the vessels. Each finding has a first move.]]

The pump is the heart. Three questions. Is there a pericardial effusion, and is it compressing the heart? Look for collapse of the right atrium in systole, or of the right ventricle in diastole. That's tamponade. Then the left ventricle. Is it hyperdynamic, normal, or poor? And the right ventricle. Is it as big as the left, or bigger? With McConnell's sign, that's acute pressure overload of the right ventricle, most likely a PE.

The tank is the volume. How big is the IVC, and how much does it collapse? Then the lungs, for lung sliding, B-lines and pleural fluid. And the abdomen, for free fluid.

The pipes are the vessels. The abdominal aorta for an aneurysm, and the aortic root for dissection. And the femoral and popliteal veins for a DVT.

Now the part that wins the viva. Each finding comes with a first move.

{{Finding | First move
Tamponade | Drain; fluid as a bridge
Dilated RV, suspected PE, and shock | Systemic thrombolysis (ESC high-risk PE)
Poor LV | Noradrenaline for MAP, then inotrope; no more fluid if congested
Small collapsing IVC, hyperdynamic LV | Fluid
Hyperdynamic LV, full tank | Vasopressor (distributive)
No sliding with lung point, in shock | Decompress
Aneurysm or dissection | Surgery}}

Tamponade: drain it, with fluid as a bridge while you prepare. A dilated right ventricle with suspected PE, and shock: that's high-risk PE by the European guideline, and it needs systemic thrombolysis. A poorly contracting left ventricle: noradrenaline for the MAP, then an inotrope, and no more fluid if the patient is congested.

A small, collapsing IVC with a hyperdynamic left ventricle: the tank is empty, so give fluid. A hyperdynamic left ventricle with a full tank: the pump is fine and the tank is full, so the pipes have lost their tone. That's distributive shock, and it needs a vasopressor.

Absent lung sliding with a lung point, in a shocked patient, is a tension pneumothorax until proven otherwise. Decompress it. And if there's no sliding, no B-lines and no lung pulse, think the same. An aneurysm or a dissection goes to surgery.

Notice how this connects to everything before it. The shock index told you that shock was there. The lactate and the skin told you that perfusion was failing. Now the probe tells you why.

One honest caution, and we'll come back to it at the end. The IVC only suggests fluid responsiveness. Confirm it with a dynamic test once the patient is stable.

So let's look at the pump more carefully. How do you structure a focused look at the heart?

steps.bridge: FATE excludes obvious causes, then judges size and squeeze. Next: how to call tamponade on echo →

lesson.text:
A structured, focused heart scan is FATE, focus-assessed transthoracic echocardiography, described by Jensen and colleagues in two thousand and four. It has four goals, and they run from the dangerous to the detailed.

Goal one. Exclude obvious pathology. Pleural and pericardial effusions, valvular disease, aortic dissection and pulmonary embolism. These are the things that change your hand immediately.

Goal two. Assess wall thickness and chamber dimensions. Hypertrophy, the relative size of the left and right ventricles, and chamber enlargement.

Goal three. Assess contractility. In FATE this is qualitative, an eyeball across all the views, in five grades. Hyperdynamic, normal, and mild, moderate or severe dysfunction.

Goal four. Image the pleura on both sides. A transudate is anechoic, black and clean. A plankton sign, specks swirling in the fluid, points to infection or a haemothorax.

[[FATE has four goals: exclude obvious pathology, assess walls and chambers, assess contractility, and image both pleurae.]]

Now, the first thing on that list that can kill in minutes is fluid around the heart. How do you call tamponade?

steps.bridge: RV diastolic collapse is the more specific sign. Next: how to spot RV overload →

lesson.text:
Start with the physics. The pericardium is a tough, fixed sac. When fluid fills it, the pressure inside the sac rises. And that pressure squeezes whichever chamber has the lowest pressure at that moment. That's the right side of the heart, because it's the low-pressure side.

So tamponade shows up as collapse of the right-sided chambers, each at the moment its own pressure is lowest.

The right atrium collapses in late diastole and early systole. That's when the atrium has just emptied, and its pressure is at its lowest. The longer the collapse lasts, the more it means. The usual criterion is collapse for more than a third of the cardiac cycle. Its accuracy varies between studies, so don't lean on a single figure.

The right ventricle collapses in early diastole, before it has filled. And it's most evident in expiration. Why? Because in a spontaneously breathing patient, inspiration draws more blood into the right heart, which props the ventricle open. In expiration, that support is gone, and the collapse shows.

[[Right ventricular diastolic collapse is the more specific sign of tamponade, with a specificity above ninety percent.]]

And it's more than a picture. When the right ventricle collapses in diastole, it can't fill, and the cardiac output falls significantly. That's why this is the sign that matches the haemodynamic crisis.

Now the IVC. In tamponade, the right atrial pressure is high, so the IVC is full and barely moves with breathing. That's IVC plethora.

[[IVC plethora is very sensitive for tamponade, about ninety-seven percent, but non-specific. Any raised venous pressure does the same.]]

So a normal-sized, collapsing IVC makes tamponade unlikely. But a plethoric IVC on its own proves nothing. Heart failure, a PE, or a big fluid load will all give you one.

One honest caution. It's the speed of collection, more than the volume, that decides whether fluid tamponades the heart. A small effusion that gathers fast can tamponade, while a large one that gathered slowly may not.

Now the other right-sided emergency. How do you spot a right ventricle in trouble?

steps.bridge: RV as big as LV, TAPSE under 17 and a full IVC mean overload. Next: the sign that points to PE →

lesson.text:
There are seven echo signs of right ventricular overload. Learn them in three groups: size, function and pressure.

Size. The right ventricular cavity is as big as the left ventricle, or bigger. Normally, the right ventricle is clearly the smaller one.

Function. TAPSE below seventeen millimetres. A fractional area change below thirty-five percent. And longitudinal strain of the free wall below twenty percent.

Pressure. A tricuspid regurgitant velocity above two point eight metres a second. And a distended IVC that collapses less than fifty percent.

{{**RV overload:** RV ≥ LV · TAPSE <17 mm · FAC <35% · free-wall strain <20% · TR V >2.8 m/s · IVC distended, <50% collapse · RV wall thickened = chronic}}

And the seventh sign is the one that tells you the timing. An increased right ventricular wall thickness.

[[A thickened right ventricular wall means chronic overload. An acutely loaded right ventricle dilates; it doesn't have time to hypertrophy.]]

Why does that matter in shock? Because a dilated, thin-walled right ventricle in a shocked patient is an acute event, and PE is the first thing to think of. A thick-walled one has been under pressure for months or years, usually from chronic pulmonary hypertension, and that changes how you read everything else.

But dilatation alone doesn't tell you the cause. Is there a sign that points specifically to PE?

steps.bridge: Free wall down, apex spared points to acute PE (RV infarct can mimic it). Next: what the IVC tells you about the tank →

lesson.text:
There is. McConnell's sign.

[[McConnell's sign is hypokinesia of the right ventricular free wall with sparing of the apex. It points to acute pulmonary embolism.]]

So the free wall, the lateral wall, moves poorly, while the apex keeps contracting. It's a regionally abnormal right ventricle with a normal tip.

Two traps. First, a globally hypokinetic right ventricle, with the apex moving poorly too, is not McConnell's sign, and does not point at PE. Second, a right ventricular infarct can mimic it. So read it with the story and the ECG.

Now the last part of the scan, and the part most often over-read. The tank.

The IVC is the first thing most residents look at in shock, and the thing they trust most. It deserves less trust than it gets.

You check two things. The absolute diameter, and how much it collapses with inspiration.

{{IVC | Diameter | Collapsibility
Less likely fluid-responsive | >2 cm | <50%
More likely fluid-responsive | <1 cm | >50%
In between | 1–2 cm | grey zone}}

An IVC larger than two centimetres, collapsing less than fifty percent, makes the patient less likely to be fluid-responsive. An IVC smaller than one centimetre, collapsing more than fifty percent, makes him more likely to respond.

And between one and two centimetres? That's an unclassified middle. Many of your patients will sit there.

[[A small, collapsing IVC only suggests fluid responsiveness. It predicts modestly, and worse in spontaneous breathing.]]

Why is it so weak? Because the IVC isn't only a measure of volume. Its size also reflects the right atrial pressure, the pressure in the abdomen, and the effort of breathing. A patient breathing hard, with big swings in chest pressure, can collapse even a well-filled IVC. And a tense abdomen can squash it. So the IVC tells you about the tank, but it can't tell you whether the heart will use more fluid.

[[So confirm it with a dynamic test: a passive leg raise, or the change in VTI.]]

One small trap. These cut-offs are not the same as the ones you use to estimate right atrial pressure, which use two point one centimetres. Same vessel. Two different questions, and two different sets of thresholds.

spine: What it is: a rapid, structured scan to name the shock type. I use pump, tank and pipes.
Pump: effusion with RV diastolic collapse is tamponade; a dilated RV with McConnell's sign is PE; a poorly contracting LV is cardiogenic shock.
Tank and pipes: IVC, lung sliding and B-lines, free fluid; then the aorta for aneurysm or dissection and the leg veins for DVT.
What I do: tamponade, drain; PE with RV failure and shock, thrombolyse; poor LV, noradrenaline then an inotrope; empty tank, fluid; hyperdynamic heart with a full tank, vasopressor.
Caution: a small collapsing IVC only suggests fluid responsiveness. I confirm with a passive leg raise or VTI change.

open.text:
Let me give you a patient with no label.

Patient H is on the ward, and has suddenly become shocked. A MAP of fifty-five. Cold, clammy and breathless. The history is thin. It could be sepsis. It could be a bleed. It could be his heart. It could be a pulmonary embolus, or blood around the heart.

And here's the problem. Each of those has a different first move. Fluid would help the bleed and the sepsis. It could drown the failing heart. A tamponade needs a needle. A massive PE with shock needs a thrombolytic. A vasopressor alone will help some of them and not others.

So you can't treat shock until you've named it. And you have to name it in minutes, at the bedside, before you have a CT, a formal echo or a cardiac output monitor.

That's what point-of-care ultrasound gives you. Not a full echocardiogram, but a set of focused yes-or-no questions, each one with a first move attached.

What is the professor checking? First, that you have a framework, and don't just wave the probe around. Second, the signs that name each kind of shock: tamponade, PE, a failing left ventricle, an empty tank. Third, what you do for each one. And fourth, the honest limit of the IVC.

So here's the plan. First, the framework. Then a structured look at the heart. Then tamponade. Then the right ventricle, and the sign that points to PE. And finally, the IVC.

close.text:
So let's bring it together.

POCUS in undifferentiated shock is a rapid, structured scan to name the shock type. I use pump, tank and pipes.

The pump. An effusion with right ventricular diastolic collapse is tamponade. A dilated right ventricle with McConnell's sign is PE. A poorly contracting left ventricle is cardiogenic shock.

The tank and the pipes. The IVC, lung sliding and B-lines, and free fluid. Then the aorta for an aneurysm or dissection, and the leg veins for a DVT.

[[Tamponade, drain. PE with right ventricular failure and shock, thrombolyse. Poor left ventricle, noradrenaline then an inotrope. Empty tank, fluid. Hyperdynamic heart with a full tank, vasopressor.]]

And the caution. A small, collapsing IVC only suggests fluid responsiveness. I confirm it with a passive leg raise, or a change in VTI.

That's your answer. What it is, the pump, the tank and pipes, what I do, and the caution.

But here's something to carry forward. Today, the scan ended on a question it couldn't answer. The IVC tells you how full the tank looks. It doesn't tell you whether one more bolus of fluid will actually raise the cardiac output.

And that's the question behind half of all the decisions in this package. Will this patient respond to fluid? How do you know, before you give it? And why do the static numbers, like the CVP, fail so badly?

That's fluid responsiveness, and it's next.

questions.text: How do you assess fluid responsiveness?

steps.bridge: A responder raises stroke volume by over 10–15%; only half do. Next: which families of tests predict it, and how well →

lesson.text:
Start with the heart's own law. More than a century ago, Otto Frank and Ernest Starling showed that the more a ventricle is filled, the harder it contracts, until it reaches a plateau. Stretch the muscle fibres, and the next beat is stronger. Plot stroke volume against preload, the filling volume at the end of diastole, and you get a curve. Look at it on your screen.

{{pic}}

At the left, the curve is steep. Here, a little more filling buys a lot more stroke volume. To the right, it flattens. Here, more filling buys almost nothing.

Now give the same bolus to two patients. Patient A sits on the steep part. His stroke volume jumps. Patient B sits on the flat part. The same fluid moves him along the curve, but his stroke volume hardly changes.

[[A responder is a patient on the steep part of his curve. That's why the definition is about stroke volume, not pressure.]]

So the definition. A patient is fluid responsive if his stroke volume, or cardiac index, rises by more than ten to fifteen percent after a fluid challenge. And the striking fact. Only about half of patients do.

Why does that matter so much? Because fluid in Patient B isn't harmless. If it doesn't raise his output, it can't raise his perfusion. It only raises his venous pressures. The water leaves the vessels, into the lung, where it impairs gas exchange, and into the other organs as oedema.

[[Fluid that doesn't raise the stroke volume doesn't help the tissues. It only floods them.]]

And here's the subtle part the panel likes. Even a true responder may not get better clinically. Why? Several reasons, especially in sepsis. Right atrial pressure doesn't rise in a straight line with volume. The vessels are leaky, so the bolus doesn't stay in the circulation. Septic patients hold more of their blood in the unstressed volume, blood that fills the veins without pushing it back to the heart. The fluid dilutes the blood, lowers its viscosity and lowers the afterload, so the pressure can fall even as the flow rises. And sepsis itself depresses contractility.

One more thing. Patient A and Patient B can't be told apart by looking at them. The curve is different in every heart, and it moves through the day. So you can't guess where a patient sits. You have to test it.

And that brings us to the tests themselves.
lesson.cap: Same fluid, two hearts. On the steep part stroke volume jumps; on the flat part it barely moves.

steps.bridge: Static tests are near coin-toss; challenges are best. Next: why CVP in particular fails →

lesson.text:
There are three families of tests, and each asks the heart a different question.

The first family is static. A single pressure or a single size, taken at one moment. CVP, the wedge pressure, the diameter of the IVC or the superior vena cava, the corrected flow time, and the end-diastolic volumes of the ventricles. Their ROC area is about zero point five to zero point six.

Pause on that number. An ROC area of zero point five is a coin toss. So the static measures are barely better than flipping a coin.

Why so poor? Look back at the curve. A single point tells you where the patient sits only if you know the shape of his curve. And you don't. The same filling can be on the steep part in one heart, and on the flat part in another.

[[A static number tells you where he is. It doesn't tell you the slope he's on.]]

The second family is dynamic. These use the heart-lung interaction. The ventilator breath itself acts as a small, repeated preload challenge, and you watch how much the stroke volume swings. Pulse pressure variation, stroke volume variation, the pleth variability index, the variation in aortic blood flow, and the respiratory variation of the IVC or superior vena cava. Their ROC area is about zero point seven to zero point eight.

The third family is the challenge. You actually move the patient along his curve and measure the result. A real one, a rapid fluid challenge of one hundred to two hundred and fifty millilitres. Or a virtual one, the passive leg raise, where you borrow his own blood. Their ROC area is about zero point nine.

[[Static tests are near a coin toss. Dynamic indices are good. A challenge, real or virtual, is best.]]

And there's a logic in that order. The more directly a test probes the slope, the better it performs.

{{**Family** | **Examples** | **ROC**
Static | CVP, PAOP, IVC/SVC diameter, EDV | 0.5–0.6
Dynamic | PPV, SVV, PVI, IVC/SVC variation | 0.7–0.8
Challenge | PLR; fluid challenge 100–250 mL | ~0.9}}

One small trap. Some notes put IVC variation in the static group. It behaves as a dynamic index, because it's a change with breathing, not a single diameter.

The worst of the static group, and the most famous, is the CVP. Let's see exactly how badly it does.

steps.bridge: CVP has a ROC of 0.56 and should not guide fluid. Next: when PPV and SVV stop being valid →

lesson.text:
For decades, CVP was the number we resuscitated to. Then the studies were pooled, in the meta-analyses led by Marik.

The ROC area of CVP for predicting fluid responsiveness was zero point five six. The correlation between the baseline CVP and the change in stroke index after fluid was zero point one eight, close to none. And in a separate study of ventilated patients, by Osman and Teboul, a CVP below eight, the classic sign of an empty patient, had a positive predictive value of only forty-seven percent. No better than a coin.

The wedge pressure did no better. It correlates poorly with the end-diastolic volume of the left ventricle, and fails to reflect preload even in healthy volunteers.

[[The conclusion was blunt. No data support using CVP to guide fluid therapy, and the practice should be abandoned.]]

One honest nuance. The extremes still carry a little information. Most patients with a very low CVP will respond, and most with a very high one won't. It's the wide middle where CVP predicts nothing, and that's where most of your patients sit. We'll come back to what CVP is still good for, because it isn't useless. It's just not a responsiveness test.

So if static pressures fail, the dynamic indices should save us. But they come with conditions.

steps.bridge: PPV needs a passive patient, sinus rhythm, tidal volume 8 and a closed chest. Next: the test that works when PPV fails →

lesson.text:
To see why pulse pressure variation has conditions, you first have to see why it works.

Picture a passive patient on a ventilator. With each machine breath, the pressure in the chest rises. That squeezes the great veins and lowers the return of blood to the right heart. At the same time, the inflated lung raises the afterload on the right ventricle. So during inspiration, the right ventricle puts out less.

That smaller right-sided output takes a few beats to cross the lungs. So it reaches the left ventricle during expiration. Meanwhile, as the lung inflates, it squeezes blood out of the pulmonary veins into the left heart. So the left ventricle's stroke volume is highest during inspiration, and lowest during expiration.

[[Each machine breath is a small, repeated preload challenge. If the heart is on the steep part of its curve, the stroke volume swings with every breath.]]

On the flat part, the same change in preload hardly moves the stroke volume. So a big swing means a responder. On the arterial line, you see it as the pulse pressure rising and falling with the breaths. Above thirteen percent suggests response. Cannesson showed that nine to thirteen percent is a grey zone, where the test can't decide.

Now the conditions follow almost by themselves. The test needs a regular, known stimulus, and a regular heart to read it.

First, spontaneous breathing efforts. His own breaths vary in size and pull the chest pressure the other way. The stimulus is no longer standard.

Second, arrhythmias. In atrial fibrillation, the stroke volume varies from beat to beat because of the rhythm, not the breath.

Third, the ventilation itself. A tidal volume below eight millilitres per kilo is too small a push to swing the preload, so you get a false negative. Poor lung compliance does the same, because a stiff lung passes less of the airway pressure on to the heart and vessels. And if the heart rate is low compared with the breathing rate, a ratio below about three point six, there are too few beats in each breath to catch the swing.

Fourth, the chest and abdomen. With an open chest, the breath no longer squeezes the heart. And a raised abdominal pressure distorts the swing.

Fifth, right heart failure. Here the swing can come from the breath loading a struggling right ventricle, not from preload, so a big variation can mislead you.

[[Pulse pressure variation needs a passive patient, in sinus rhythm, on eight millilitres per kilo, with a closed chest.]]

And the trap in the options. Sinus tachycardia on its own, a low SVR, and controlled ventilation are not confounders. Controlled ventilation is exactly what the test requires.

{{**PPV not valid:** spontaneous efforts · arrhythmia · Vt < 8 mL/kg · low compliance · HR/RR < 3.6 · open chest · raised IAP · RV failure
**PPV > 13%** suggests response; **9–13%** grey zone (Cannesson 2011)}}

So what do you do in the many patients who fail these conditions? You let the patient give himself the fluid.

steps.bridge: Leg raising gives about 300 mL and must be read on cardiac output. Next: a ventilator-only test that tolerates arrhythmia →

lesson.text:
The passive leg raise is a fluid challenge with no fluid. You borrow the patient's own blood, measure what it does, and then give it back.

Here's how. Start with the patient semi-recumbent, trunk at forty-five degrees. Then use the bed to tilt him, so the trunk goes flat and the legs come up. Don't lift the legs by hand. Don't touch the patient at all. Pain, a cough or arousal raises the output by itself, and the test is ruined.

Why start semi-recumbent, and not flat? Because tipping the trunk down also recruits blood from the splanchnic circulation, the large reservoir in the abdomen, and not just the blood in the legs. Together, that's about three hundred millilitres of the patient's own blood.

The effect comes within about sixty to ninety seconds. And when you bring him back to the starting position, it fully reverses. That's the beauty of it. [[It's a fluid challenge you can take back.]]

Now the crucial part. What do you measure? Not the blood pressure. You need the cardiac output or the stroke volume, measured in real time. Pulse contour analysis, the velocity time integral on echo, or oesophageal Doppler. The effect is brief, so you need a monitor that can catch it as it happens.

[[A rise in cardiac output or stroke volume of ten percent or more is a positive leg raise.]]

If you're using end-tidal carbon dioxide instead, a rise of five percent or more is positive. And after the test, return to baseline and measure again.

Why not blood pressure? Because changes in pulse pressure are much less accurate than changes in output. A real rise in stroke volume may hardly move the pressure, so you'd miss true responders.

And here's why this test matters so much. It doesn't depend on the ventilator, or on the rhythm. It stays valid with spontaneous breathing, with arrhythmias, and at low tidal volume. Exactly the patients where pulse pressure variation fails.

One small trap. If you use the LVOT VTI, a responder is a rise of ten to fifteen percent. A fall, or a change of two to five percent, is not a response.

But what if your patient is ventilated, and moving him isn't possible? There's a test that uses only the ventilator.

steps.bridge: A 15 s end-expiratory hold that raises output by 5% means a responder. Next: does a positive test mean I give fluid →

lesson.text:
The end-expiratory occlusion test. You pause the ventilator at the end of expiration, for fifteen seconds.

Why does that work? Every machine breath raises the pressure in the chest and impedes venous return. Stop the breaths, and you remove that impediment. For fifteen seconds, more blood flows back to the heart. It's a brief self-fluid-challenge, delivered by the ventilator.

[[If the pulse pressure or the cardiac output rises by more than five percent during the hold, he's a responder.]] The reported sensitivity is eighty-seven percent, and the specificity one hundred.

And notice why it survives where pulse pressure variation fails. The hold lasts fifteen seconds, so its effect spans several cardiac cycles. An irregular rhythm averages out, and so does some spontaneous breathing activity. It stays valid in arrhythmias.

The limits are practical. He must be ventilated, and able to tolerate a fifteen-second hold. And you need continuous, real-time monitoring, because a five percent change is small.

So now you have a test for each situation. But a positive test raises the most important question of all.

Choosing the test is simpler than it seems, once you ask the right questions in order.

First, does this patient need a test at all? Sometimes not. In acute circulatory failure with obvious hypovolaemia, and in the initial phase of septic shock, you give fluid without testing. Testing there only delays the obvious.

Second, can I use pulse pressure variation? Three conditions rule it out. Spontaneous breathing. Cardiac arrhythmia. And ARDS with a low tidal volume or low lung compliance. In a modern ICU, that's a great many patients.

Third, if those are present, what still works? The passive leg raise, the end-expiratory occlusion test, and the mini fluid challenge, a hundred millilitres over one minute, positive if the VTI rises by more than ten percent. IVC variation can still be used in arrhythmias. And the occlusion test needs a ventilated patient who tolerates the fifteen-second hold.

And now the question the panel is waiting for. The test is positive. Do you give the fluid?

[[Not automatically. Preload responsiveness is not, by itself, an indication for fluid.]]

Think about it. Most healthy people are fluid responsive. You probably are, right now. Your heart sits on the steep part of its curve. That doesn't mean you need a litre of saline. A positive test only tells you that fluid would raise the output. It doesn't tell you the output needs raising, or that the patient can handle the extra water.

[[A positive test says he can respond. Whether he needs it, and whether he can tolerate it, still decide.]]

What decides, in the end, is the risk of fluid overload. That's the idea of fluid tolerance, and it gets a full lesson of its own.

spine: What it is: a patient is fluid responsive if stroke volume or cardiac output rises by **10–15%** or more after fluid. Only about half are.
Why not CVP: static pressures do not track volume on a curved compliance curve. CVP has a ROC area of **0.56**, near coin-toss.
What I do: passive, ventilated, sinus rhythm, Vt 8 mL/kg, closed chest: I use PPV. Above **13%** suggests response; **9–13%** is a grey zone (Cannesson 2011).
Otherwise: passive leg raise with real-time cardiac output (a rise of 10% or more), end-expiratory occlusion (above 5%), or a 100 mL mini fluid challenge.
Caution: IVC variation is limited and observer-dependent. A positive test only says he can respond; fluid tolerance and need still decide.

open.text:
Let me start with a patient. Patient A, sixty years old, septic, on a ventilator. His pressure is soft, his lactate is up, and the nurse has a bag of crystalloid in her hand. She asks you one question. Shall I run it in?

For a long time, we answered that question by giving the fluid and watching. And here's the uncomfortable fact this whole question rests on. Only about half of patients like him will actually raise their cardiac output with that bag. In the other half, the fluid does nothing for the heart, and goes on to the lungs, the gut and the kidneys as oedema.

So the real question is not, is he dry? It's this. If I give him fluid, will his heart pump more?

That is what fluid responsiveness means, and it's what the professor wants you to define first. Then he's checking three things. Do you know why the old static numbers, like CVP, fail? Do you know the conditions each dynamic test needs, so you don't use pulse pressure variation where it's invalid? And do you know that a positive test is not a prescription?

That last one is the trap. The resident who says, he's a responder, so I'll give fluid, has missed half the answer.

So here's the plan. First, the definition, and the curve that explains it. Then the three families of tests, and how well each performs. Then why CVP fails. Then the conditions for pulse pressure variation. Then the tests that work when it fails, the leg raise and the end-expiratory hold. And finally, how to choose, and what still decides whether the bag goes in.

close.text:
So let's bring it together.

[[A patient is fluid responsive if his stroke volume or cardiac output rises by ten to fifteen percent or more after fluid. Only about half are.]]

Why not CVP? Because a static pressure can't tell you the slope of a curved line. Its ROC area is zero point five six, close to a coin toss.

What do you do? In a passive, ventilated patient in sinus rhythm, on eight millilitres per kilo, with a closed chest, you use pulse pressure variation. Above thirteen percent suggests response, and nine to thirteen is a grey zone.

Otherwise, a passive leg raise with real-time cardiac output, positive at a rise of ten percent or more. Or an end-expiratory occlusion, positive above five percent. Or a mini fluid challenge of a hundred millilitres.

And the caution. IVC variation is limited, and depends on the observer. And a positive test only says he can respond. Need and tolerance still decide.

That's your answer to the panel. The definition, why the static numbers fail, the test you choose, the alternatives, and the caution.

But here's something to carry forward. Of all these tests, one is the workhorse, the one that works whatever the rhythm and whatever the ventilator. And it's also the one most often done wrong. In the next lesson, we take the passive leg raise apart, step by step.

questions.text: Explain passive leg raising.

steps.bridge: Start semi-recumbent and read cardiac output, not BP; a 10% rise is positive. Next: where the test fails →

lesson.text: You met this test in the last lesson. Start semi-recumbent, trunk at forty-five degrees, and tilt with the bed, without touching the patient. About three hundred millilitres of his own blood comes from the legs and the splanchnic bed, within sixty to ninety seconds, and it fully reverses. [[Measure cardiac output or stroke volume in real time, and call it positive at a rise of ten percent or more.]] For Patient C, that's the whole point. It works whatever his rhythm and his breathing. So where does it fail?

steps.bridge: Raised abdominal pressure gives a false negative. Next: test yourself on the traps of PLR and its partners →

lesson.text:
The limitations come in two groups. The ones where the reading is wrong, and the ones where the test can't be done.

First, the reading. You can't judge the test from arterial pressure. Changes in pulse pressure are less accurate than changes in cardiac output or stroke volume. If all you have is a blood pressure, you don't really have a leg raise.

Second, and this is the one the panel likes. Raised intra-abdominal pressure gives a false negative. Why? The blood you've mobilised from the legs and the abdomen has to travel up the IVC to reach the heart. A tense abdomen compresses that path, so the borrowed blood never arrives. [[In intra-abdominal hypertension, a negative leg raise doesn't mean he won't respond.]]

Then the practical limits. It can't be done where moving the patient isn't possible or allowed, or after a leg amputation. And it's a problem in intracranial hypertension, where tilting the head and trunk flat is unwelcome.

Now let's test all of it.

Seven statements. Answer each one in your head before I give it to you.

First. A CVP of four reliably predicts fluid responsiveness. False. The ROC area is zero point five six, and a CVP below eight has a positive predictive value of only forty-seven percent.

Second. Pulse pressure variation remains valid in a patient triggering the ventilator. False. Spontaneous efforts invalidate both pulse pressure and stroke volume variation.

Third. Raised intra-abdominal pressure can make a passive leg raise falsely negative. True. It's a listed limitation of the test.

Fourth. During a positive-pressure breath, left ventricular stroke volume is lowest in inspiration. False, and this one catches people. It's highest in inspiration, and lowest in expiration, because the fall in right-sided output takes a few beats to cross the lungs.

[[Under positive pressure, the left ventricle's stroke volume is highest in inspiration and lowest in expiration.]]

Fifth. The mini fluid challenge uses a hundred millilitres over one minute. True. And it's positive if the VTI rises by more than ten percent.

Sixth. A passive leg raise can be judged by the change in mean arterial pressure. False. It needs real-time cardiac output or stroke volume. Pressure changes are too inaccurate.

Seventh. The end-expiratory occlusion test is valid in atrial fibrillation. True. Its effect spans several cardiac cycles.

Now let's bring it together.

spine: What it is: a reversible self-fluid-challenge. Tilting from semi-recumbent to legs up shifts about **300 mL** of blood from the legs and splanchnic bed.
How: start at trunk 45°, tilt with the bed, do not touch the patient. Effect comes within 60–90 seconds and reverses on return.
What I measure: cardiac output or stroke volume in real time, by pulse contour, echo VTI or oesophageal Doppler. A rise of **10%** or more is positive.
Why not BP: pulse pressure changes are much less accurate than changes in cardiac output, so BP misses true responders.
Caution: unreliable with raised intra-abdominal pressure (false negative), pain or arousal, leg amputation, and where moving the patient is not allowed.

open.text:
Let me start with a patient. Patient C, breathing on his own, in atrial fibrillation, with a soft pressure. Pulse pressure variation is useless in him, for two reasons at once. And you don't want to give a bolus blindly.

So you reach for the one test that doesn't care about his rhythm or his breathing. You tilt the bed. That's the passive leg raise. It sounds almost too simple to be a viva question.

But what the professor is really checking is whether you know how to do it properly. Where do you start? What do you measure? Why not the blood pressure? And when does it lie?

The trap is the resident who lifts the legs from flat, watches the blood pressure, and calls it negative. Every step of that is wrong.

So here's the plan. First, the method and the measurement, briefly, since you've met them. Then the limitations, especially the one that gives a false negative. And then we test you, with seven true-or-false traps from this whole topic.

close.text:
So, the passive leg raise.

[[It's a reversible self-fluid-challenge. Tilting from semi-recumbent to legs up shifts about three hundred millilitres of blood from the legs and the splanchnic bed.]]

How do you do it? Start with the trunk at forty-five degrees, tilt with the bed, and don't touch the patient. The effect comes within sixty to ninety seconds, and reverses when you return.

What do you measure? Cardiac output or stroke volume in real time, by pulse contour, echo VTI or oesophageal Doppler. A rise of ten percent or more is positive.

Why not blood pressure? Because pulse pressure changes are much less accurate than changes in output, so blood pressure misses true responders.

And the caution. It's unreliable with raised intra-abdominal pressure, which gives a false negative, with pain or arousal, after a leg amputation, and where moving the patient isn't allowed.

That's your answer.

But here's something to carry forward. Think of the patient you ventilate most carefully of all. The one with ARDS, on six millilitres per kilo. Pulse pressure variation fails in him by design, because you made the breath small. So how do you test him? That's next.

questions.text: How do you assess fluid responsiveness in a patient on low tidal volume ventilation?

steps.bridge: PPV and SVV fail below 8 mL/kg and with poor compliance. Next: how to rescue PPV at low tidal volume →

lesson.text: You met these conditions at the start of this block. Pulse pressure variation needs a passive patient, sinus rhythm, a closed chest, and a tidal volume of at least eight millilitres per kilo. Patient D fails the last one on purpose. A small breath is too small a preload challenge to swing the stroke volume, and a stiff lung passes even less of the pressure on to the heart. [[So at low tidal volume, a low pulse pressure variation can be a false negative, not reassurance.]] Can we rescue it?

steps.bridge: Raise tidal volume from 6 to 8 and look for a PPV rise above 3.5%. Next: a ventilator test that needs no tidal volume change →

lesson.text:
Yes. With the tidal volume challenge. If the breath is too small to test the heart, make it bigger, briefly.

Raise the tidal volume from six to eight millilitres per kilo, for one minute. Read the pulse pressure variation before and after. [[If the absolute pulse pressure variation rises by more than three point five percent, he's a responder.]]

Why does it work? A bigger breath is a bigger preload challenge. If the heart sits on the steep part of its curve, the bigger push shows up as a bigger swing. On the flat part, even the bigger push changes little. Notice that you're reading the change, not the starting value. And then return him to six millilitres per kilo. A minute at eight is a small price. Leaving him there is not.

Pulse pressure variation has a cousin, the pleth variability index, from the pulse oximeter. It measures how much the pleth amplitude swings with breathing. Above fourteen percent suggests response. But it has every limitation of pulse pressure variation, plus one more. The pleth signal depends on finger perfusion, which is sensitive to sympathetic tone. In a cold, vasoconstricted, shocked patient, that's exactly what you can't rely on. Its agreement with pulse pressure variation is poor.

{{**Tidal volume challenge:** Vt 6 → 8 mL/kg for 1 min; absolute ΔPPV > 3.5% = responder
**PVI** (device) = (PImax − PImin) ÷ PImax × 100; > 14% suggests response}}

But what if you don't want to touch the tidal volume at all?

steps.bridge: A 15 s end-expiratory hold that raises output over 5% is positive. Next: the bedside test that needs no ventilator change →

lesson.text: Then use the hold. You met the end-expiratory occlusion test at the start of this block. Pause the ventilator at end-expiration for fifteen seconds. A rise in output of more than five percent means a responder, and it needs no change in tidal volume. One refinement at low tidal volume. If you're measuring with echo VTI, a five percent change is hard to see. So add an end-inspiratory hold as well, and add the two changes together. A combined change of about thirteen percent or more suggests response. That comes from Jozwiak and colleagues, in twenty seventeen.

steps.bridge: Leg raising works whatever the tidal volume, if output is measured live. Next: how to choose between these tests →

lesson.text: And the leg raise. It doesn't use the ventilator at all, so the tidal volume doesn't matter. Tilt from semi-recumbent, borrow about three hundred millilitres, and measure the output in real time. A rise of ten percent or more is positive. In ARDS, it has one more attraction. [[If he's a non-responder, you've learned it without giving his lung a single drop.]] So with three tools in hand, how do you choose?

You know the order. First, does he need a test at all? Then, can I use pulse pressure variation? In Patient D, ARDS with a low tidal volume is one of the three conditions that rules it out. So you choose the tidal volume challenge, the occlusion test, or the leg raise. [[And if the test is positive, the risk of fluid overload still decides.]] Responsiveness is never, by itself, a reason to give fluid. In a wet ARDS lung, that matters more than anywhere.

spine: What it is: at a lung-protective tidal volume of 6 mL/kg, the breath is too small to swing preload, so PPV and SVV give false negatives below **8 mL/kg**.
Tidal volume challenge: raise tidal volume from 6 to 8 mL/kg for 1 minute. A rise in PPV of **3.5%** or more predicts response.
End-expiratory occlusion: 15 s hold, output up **5%** or more is positive. With echo VTI at low Vt, I add an end-inspiratory hold; combined change ≥ about **13%** (Jozwiak 2017).
Passive leg raise: works at any tidal volume, but needs real-time cardiac output; a rise of 10% or more is positive.
Caution: return to 6 mL/kg after the challenge. A positive test still needs a reason to give fluid and evidence he can tolerate it.

open.text:
Here's a paradox. Patient D has ARDS. You've done everything right. Six millilitres per kilo, a plateau under thirty, a low driving pressure. But his noradrenaline keeps creeping up, and you wonder whether he needs fluid.

His pulse pressure variation reads six percent. Not a responder, it seems. But that number may be a false comfort you created yourself. By protecting his lung with a small breath, you've taken away the push that pulse pressure variation depends on.

And this patient matters, because in ARDS, unnecessary fluid is especially costly. Extra water can end up in the very lung you're trying to protect.

What the professor is checking is whether you know that pulse pressure variation fails here, and why. And then whether you can rescue it, or replace it.

So here's the plan. First, why it fails. Then the tidal volume challenge, which rescues it. Then the end-expiratory hold. Then the leg raise. And finally, how to choose.

close.text:
So let's bring it together.

[[At a lung-protective tidal volume of six millilitres per kilo, the breath is too small to swing preload. So pulse pressure and stroke volume variation give false negatives below eight millilitres per kilo.]]

The tidal volume challenge. Raise the tidal volume from six to eight for one minute. A rise in pulse pressure variation of more than three point five percent predicts response.

The end-expiratory occlusion. A fifteen-second hold, positive at more than five percent. With echo VTI at low tidal volume, add an end-inspiratory hold, and a combined change of about thirteen percent is positive.

The passive leg raise works at any tidal volume, as long as the output is measured live. A rise of ten percent or more is positive.

And the caution. Return to six millilitres per kilo after the challenge. And a positive test still needs a reason to give fluid, and evidence that he can tolerate it.

That's your answer.

But here's something to carry forward. In all of these, we've measured the heart. There's one test that looks at a vein instead, and every resident with a probe reaches for it first. A big vessel running through the liver, collapsing or not. How much can the IVC really tell you? That's next.

questions.text: How does IVC ultrasound help and what are its limitations?

steps.bridge: Subcostal long axis, M-mode about 1 cm below the hepatic vein. Next: what size and collapse say about RA pressure →

lesson.text:
The view first, because a wrong measurement makes everything after it wrong.

Use the subcostal approach, in the longitudinal view, with the probe in a north-south orientation. The IVC lies slightly to the right of the midline. So place the transducer just below the xiphisternum, one to two centimetres to the right.

Then put the M-mode line across the IVC, one centimetre caudal to where the hepatic vein joins it. [[Measure one centimetre below the hepatic vein junction. Not at the junction, and not at the diaphragm.]] Measure elsewhere, and the diameter changes, and so does your estimate of right atrial pressure. From the M-mode trace, you then read the maximum and the minimum diameter.

steps.bridge: Small and collapsing means low RA pressure; big and fixed means high. Next: how it performs as a fluid test →

lesson.text:
Now, what do size and collapse tell you? They estimate the right atrial pressure.

The IVC is a soft, compliant vein, sitting just below the right atrium. When the atrial pressure is low, the IVC is small. And when the patient sniffs, the pressure in his chest falls, and the IVC collapses easily. When the atrial pressure is high, the IVC is distended by that pressure. It's large, and a sniff barely moves it.

So there are three bands. An IVC of two point one centimetres or less that collapses by more than half on sniffing means a normal right atrial pressure, zero to five, which you take as three. An IVC above two point one that collapses by less than half means a high pressure, ten to twenty, which you take as fifteen.

[[Small and collapsing means low right atrial pressure. Big and fixed means high.]]

And the middle band, five to ten, taken as eight, is the trap. It has two opposite looks that give the same answer. A small IVC that barely collapses, or a large one that collapses well. Only the two extremes are internally consistent.

{{**RAP (mmHg)** | **IVC** | **Sniff collapse**
0–5 (3) | ≤ 2.1 cm | > 50%
5–10 (8) | ≤ 2.1 cm | < 50%
5–10 (8) | > 2.1 cm | > 50%
10–20 (15) | > 2.1 cm | < 50%}}

In the high band, look for the secondary signs of a raised right atrial pressure. A large right atrium. A hypertrophied right ventricle. Hepatic vein flow with the systolic wave smaller than the diastolic. And a tricuspid E over e prime above six. Hold on to that hepatic vein sign. It will become a whole lesson of its own.

But notice what all this gives you. A pressure. So how does the IVC do as a fluid test?

steps.bridge: Distensibility above 18% in ventilated patients; accuracy is moderate. Next: what the size-and-collapse rule claims →

lesson.text:
In a passive, ventilated patient, the IVC moves the other way. Each machine breath raises the pressure in the chest and holds back the blood returning to the heart, so the vein widens during inspiration. How much it widens is the distensibility index. The maximum minus the minimum, divided by the minimum.

[[A distensibility index above eighteen percent suggests a responder, in a ventilated patient.]]

The logic is the same as pulse pressure variation. A vein that isn't yet full swings a lot with each breath. A full, tense vein barely moves.

But how well does it perform? Moderately. In the meta-analysis, the sensitivity was about zero point seven, the specificity zero point eight, and the ROC area zero point eight two. And agreement between observers is poor. Two people scanning the same patient can get different answers.

And one trap in breathing patients. In someone making strong inspiratory efforts, in severe asthma or a COPD exacerbation, the IVC collapses because of the large negative swing in his chest. That's a false positive. It doesn't prove he's hypovolaemic.

{{**dIVC** = (Dmax − Dmin) ÷ Dmin × 100; > 18% = fluid responsive (ventilated)
Meta-analysis: sensitivity 0.69, specificity 0.80, AUROC 0.82; poor inter-observer reliability}}

So what about the simple rule of thumb that many residents quote?

steps.bridge: That rule overstates it; a small IVC only suggests response. Next: the indices by breathing mode and the traps →

lesson.text: You met this rule with the shock scan. An IVC above two centimetres that collapses by less than half makes a patient less likely to respond. An IVC below one centimetre that collapses by more than half makes him more likely to. Between one and two, the rule says nothing. And notice that these cut-offs aren't the ones for right atrial pressure. Same vein, two questions. [[A small, collapsing IVC only suggests fluid responsiveness. Confirm it with a leg raise or a VTI change.]] So let's put the two indices side by side.

Here's the key to the whole IVC story. The vein is passive. It follows the pressure around it. And the pressure in the chest moves in opposite directions in the two kinds of breath.

A spontaneous breath in lowers the pressure in the chest, and the IVC narrows. So in a breathing patient, you measure how much it collapses. That's the collapsibility index. The maximum minus the minimum, divided by the maximum.

A positive-pressure breath raises the pressure in the chest, and the IVC widens. So in a passive, ventilated patient, you measure how much it distends. That's the distensibility index. The same difference, divided by the minimum.

[[A spontaneous breath collapses the IVC. A machine breath distends it. So you use collapsibility in one, and distensibility in the other.]]

{{**Collapsibility** (spontaneous) = (Dmax − Dmin) ÷ Dmax
**Distensibility** (passive, ventilated, Vt ≥ 8 mL/kg) = (Dmax − Dmin) ÷ Dmin; > 18% suggests response}}

In the ventilated patient, the distensibility rule needs the same conditions as pulse pressure variation. Passive, and a tidal volume of at least eight millilitres per kilo.

In the breathing patient, an IVC of two point one centimetres or less, with more than half collapsing on sniff, means a low right atrial pressure. But it only suggests responsiveness. Why so weak? Because the stimulus is his own effort, and that varies from breath to breath. A gentle breath barely moves the IVC. A big gasp can collapse it even in a full patient.

Then the false readings. Group them by what they do to the vein.

One squeezes it from outside. Raised intra-abdominal pressure compresses the IVC.

Some keep it full from above. Right ventricular failure, severe tricuspid regurgitation and high PEEP all raise the pressure the IVC drains into, in the right atrium and the chest, so the IVC looks big and fixed, whatever the patient's response.

And one narrows it with effort. Active expiration, pushing out with the abdominal muscles.

[[The IVC follows the pressure around it, not just the volume inside it. Anything that changes that pressure misleads it.]]

So in the viva, say it like this. A small, collapsing IVC suggests fluid responsiveness. Its pooled performance is moderate, and observers disagree. So I confirm it with a passive leg raise or a change in VTI.

spine: What it is: IVC size and its change with breathing estimate RA pressure. Up to 2.1 cm with over 50% collapse on sniff means low RA pressure.
Why two indices: spontaneous breaths collapse the IVC, so I use collapsibility. Positive-pressure breaths distend it, so I use distensibility; above **18%** suggests response.
Evidence: as a fluid test, pooled performance is moderate (sensitivity about 0.6–0.7, specificity about 0.7–0.8), with poor agreement between observers.
What I do: a small collapsing IVC only suggests fluid responsiveness. I confirm with a passive leg raise or a VTI change.
Caution: raised abdominal pressure, RV failure, severe TR, high PEEP and active expiration all mislead.

Let me start with a picture every resident knows. You put the probe under the xiphisternum, and there's the IVC, a dark band running up into the right atrium. In one patient, it's thin and flapping with each breath. In another, it's fat and still.

It's tempting to read that as empty or full, and to give fluid to the first one. Sometimes you'd be right. But the IVC is answering a different question from the one you're asking. It tells you mostly about the pressure in the right atrium. Fluid responsiveness is about the slope of the heart's curve. Those aren't the same thing.

What the professor is checking here is four things. Can you take a correct measurement? Do you know the two indices, one for a breathing patient and one for a ventilated one, and why they're opposite? Do you know how modestly the IVC performs as a fluid test? And do you know what fools it?

So here's the plan. First, the view. Then what size and collapse say about right atrial pressure. Then the IVC as a fluid test. Then the rule of thumb, and why it overstates things. And finally, the two indices and the traps.

So let's bring it together.

[[IVC size and its change with breathing estimate the right atrial pressure. Up to two point one centimetres, with more than half collapsing on sniff, means a low pressure.]]

Why two indices? A spontaneous breath collapses the IVC, so you use collapsibility. A positive-pressure breath distends it, so you use distensibility, and above eighteen percent suggests response.

As a fluid test, its pooled performance is moderate. Sensitivity about zero point six to zero point seven, specificity about zero point seven to zero point eight, with poor agreement between observers.

So what do you do? A small, collapsing IVC only suggests fluid responsiveness. You confirm it with a passive leg raise or a VTI change.

And the caution. Raised abdominal pressure, right ventricular failure, severe TR, high PEEP and active expiration all mislead.

That's your answer.

But here's something to carry forward. Look at the other end of the IVC story. A big, fixed IVC, in a patient whose heart may still be responsive. His heart could take more. But can his body? That's a different question altogether, and it has its own name. Fluid tolerance. That's next.

questions.text: What is fluid tolerance?

steps.bridge: Only half respond, and fluid in a non-responder causes oedema. Next: does a positive test mean I give fluid →

lesson.text: You met this at the start of the block. A responder raises his stroke volume by more than ten to fifteen percent, and only about half of patients do. Fluid that doesn't raise the output doesn't help the tissues. [[It goes on to the lungs and other organs as oedema.]] And remember the leaky vessels of sepsis. Even in a responder, part of the bolus leaves the circulation. That leak is exactly why tolerance becomes a question of its own.

steps.bridge: No; the risk of overload still decides. Next: what fluid tolerance is and how to judge it →

lesson.text: And you met this one too. A positive test is not, by itself, an indication for fluid. You're probably fluid responsive yourself, right now, and you don't need a drip. [[What still decides is the risk of fluid overload.]] For Patient E, that risk is no longer theoretical. He's showing it. So let's name it properly.

steps.bridge: Tolerance is a separate question, judged by congestion markers. Next: how PiCCO measures lung water →

lesson.text:
Fluid tolerance is the ability to take more fluid without harm from congestion.

Now put it beside the other two questions, because the panel wants to see you keep them apart. Need asks, is he hypoperfused? Responsiveness asks, will his stroke volume rise? Tolerance asks, can his body take the extra water?

[[Need, responsiveness and tolerance are three separate questions. Being responsive is not being in need, and it's not being tolerant.]]

Why can a patient be responsive and still intolerant? Go back to the curve. Responsiveness is about the heart. It says the ventricle is on the steep part. But the fluid doesn't stay in the heart. In capillary leak, as in sepsis, each bolus partly leaks into the lung and the tissues, even while the stroke volume rises. And in a failing right ventricle, the extra volume backs up into the veins, raising the pressure behind the heart, in the liver, the gut and the kidney.

[[In capillary leak or right ventricular failure, a responder still gains oedema with each bolus.]]

So how do you see intolerance at the bedside? Think from the lung outwards, and from the veins backwards.

In the lung. New B-lines on lung ultrasound. Worsening oxygenation. And if he has a PiCCO, a raised extravascular lung water.

In the veins. A rising CVP. And a rising VExUS grade, the ultrasound picture of venous congestion. We'll build VExUS properly in the next lesson.

Now the decision. Patient E is responsive but intolerant. What do you do?

[[You don't give the fluid. You support the circulation another way.]]

If the problem is lost tone, as in sepsis, use a vasopressor. If the problem is a weak pump, use an inotrope. Either way, you raise the perfusion without adding water.

And once perfusion is restored and he's stable, you go further. You take the fluid back off. That's de-resuscitation. Diuretics first, and ultrafiltration if needed.

One honest caution. There's no single number for tolerance. It's a judgement built from several markers, and you repeat it, because it changes as the patient changes.

steps.bridge: EVLW above 10 mL/kg means pulmonary oedema. Next: what a rising CVP means in a failing RV →

lesson.text:
If he has a PiCCO, you can put numbers on preload and lung water. Here are the variables, and what each tells you.

The global end-diastolic volume, indexed, is six hundred and eighty to eight hundred millilitres per square metre. It's preload as a volume, not a pressure.

The extravascular lung water is the water outside the vessels of the lung. Normal is about three to seven millilitres per kilo. [[Above ten millilitres per kilo means pulmonary oedema.]] It rises in both hydrostatic oedema and ARDS.

So lung water alone doesn't tell you why. That's the job of the pulmonary vascular permeability index. Normal is below three. High lung water with a normal index means hydrostatic oedema. High lung water with a raised index means leaky lungs, as in ARDS.

[[Lung water tells you there is water. The permeability index tells you why.]]

Two more are about the pump. The cardiac function index, four and a half to six and a half per minute. And the global ejection fraction, twenty-five to thirty-five percent.

{{**GEDVI** 680–800 mL/m² · **EVLW** ~3–7 mL/kg normal, > 10 = oedema · **PVPI** < 3 (raised = leak) · **CFI** 4.5–6.5 /min · **GEF** 25–35%}}

That's the lung side of tolerance. Now the venous side.

steps.bridge: A rising CVP in RV dysfunction is ominous; the trend tells you. Next: how to take fluid off once stable →

lesson.text:
A rising CVP in a patient with right ventricular dysfunction is an ominous sign.

Why ominous? Because a failing right ventricle can't take the volume. It's on the flat part of its curve. So each extra bolus raises the pressure behind it, in the veins of the liver, the gut and the kidney, instead of raising its output.

[[In right ventricular dysfunction, it's the trend of the CVP with fluid and inotropes that informs you, not one number.]]

The bedside signs belong here too. A raised JVP reflects a raised atrial pressure. Kussmaul's sign, a JVP that rises on inspiration, can point to the cause of the right heart failure.

And the waveform tells you more. In severe tricuspid regurgitation, there's a dominant V wave during ventricular systole, from blood regurgitating back into the atrium, followed by a sharp Y descent as that large atrial volume empties. In pulmonary hypertension, there's a dominant A wave, because the atrium contracts against an increased resistance.

[[V wave is tricuspid regurgitation, in systole. A wave is pulmonary hypertension, at atrial contraction.]]

So for Patient E, a CVP that climbs with each bolus is a signal to stop. And once he's stable, the next step is to take the fluid back off.

Active fluid removal is new in the Surviving Sepsis guidelines of twenty twenty-six. It's a conditional suggestion, and it's also called de-resuscitation.

When? After the acute resuscitation phase. In whom? A patient who is haemodynamically stable, with no evidence of tissue hypoperfusion. How? Diuretics first, and ultrafiltration if they're not enough, or if the overload is gross.

And why? Because a positive fluid balance causes tissue and pulmonary oedema, and effusions.

[[Once he's perfused and stable, take the fluid back off. Diuretics first.]]

spine: What it is: fluid tolerance is the ability to take more fluid without harm from congestion. It is separate from need and from responsiveness.
Why: in capillary leak or a failing RV, a patient can raise stroke volume with fluid and still gain lung and organ oedema.
How I judge it: VExUS grade, B-lines on lung ultrasound, a rising CVP, lung water on PiCCO above **10 mL/kg**, and oxygenation.
Responsive but intolerant: I stop fluid and use a vasopressor for tone or an inotrope for the pump.
Caution: once perfused and stable, I de-resuscitate with diuretics first, as SSC 2026 now suggests.

open.text:
Let me start with a patient who looks like a success. Patient E, septic shock, day two. You do a passive leg raise, and his cardiac output rises by fifteen percent. A clear responder.

But listen to his chest. Crackles at both bases. His oxygen requirement has doubled overnight. His IVC is big and fixed. He has had litre after litre since admission.

So he's responsive. Should you give more?

This question exists because for years we merged three separate questions into one. Does he need fluid? Will he respond to it? And can he tolerate it? The last lessons answered the second. Today is about the third.

What the professor is checking is whether you can define tolerance cleanly, keep it apart from need and from responsiveness, name the bedside markers of intolerance, and say what you do in the patient who is responsive but intolerant. That's the trap. The resident who says, he's a responder, so more fluid, has just put Patient E's lungs under water.

So here's the plan. First, a reminder of why fluid in the wrong patient harms. Then why a positive test isn't a prescription. Then tolerance itself. Then two of its markers in detail, lung water, and a rising CVP in a failing right ventricle. And finally, how to take the fluid back off.

close.text:
So let's bring it together.

[[Fluid tolerance is the ability to take more fluid without harm from congestion. It's separate from need, and separate from responsiveness.]]

Why does it matter? Because in capillary leak, or with a failing right ventricle, a patient can raise his stroke volume with fluid and still gain lung and organ oedema.

How do you judge it? The VExUS grade, B-lines on lung ultrasound, a rising CVP, lung water on PiCCO above ten millilitres per kilo, and oxygenation.

If he's responsive but intolerant, stop the fluid. Use a vasopressor for tone, or an inotrope for the pump.

And the caution. Once he's perfused and stable, de-resuscitate, diuretics first, as the twenty twenty-six sepsis guidelines now suggest.

That's your answer.

But here's something to carry forward. Of all the tolerance markers, one lets you see venous congestion with your own probe, in the liver and the kidney, at the bedside. It's the one the panel asks about more and more. VExUS. That's next.

questions.text: What is VExUS?

steps.bridge: VExUS starts at the IVC and grades three Doppler sites. Next: how the IVC and hepatic vein reflect RA pressure →

lesson.text:
VExUS grades systemic venous congestion at the bedside, in steps, starting at the IVC.

Step one, the IVC. If it's two centimetres or less, that's grade zero. No significant congestion, and you stop. Why start there? Because without a raised right atrial pressure, there's nothing to back up into the organs.

Step two. If the IVC is above two centimetres, you put pulsed Doppler on three veins, each further from the heart. The hepatic vein, the portal vein and the intrarenal veins. Look at the picture on your screen. Normal on the left, mild in the middle, severe on the right.

{{pic}}

The idea behind all three is the same. The hepatic veins drain straight into the IVC, so they always carry some of the heart's pulsation. But the portal vein is separated from the heart by the sinusoids of the liver, which buffer the pulsation, and the veins inside the kidney are normally buffered too. So both normally flow steadily. As the right atrial pressure rises, the pulsation is pushed further and further back, and the steady flow becomes pulsatile, then broken.

The hepatic vein first. Normally the systolic wave is bigger than the diastolic, S bigger than D. If S becomes smaller than D, that's mild. If S reverses, that's severe.

The portal vein next. Normally it flows almost steadily. A pulsatility of thirty percent or more is mild. Fifty percent or more is severe.

And the intrarenal veins. Normally the flow is continuous. Pulsatile flow, with separate S and D waves, is mild. Flow only in diastole, a single D wave, is severe.

[[The further from the heart you find pulsatile flow, the deeper the congestion.]]

Then you add it up. Grade one is a big IVC with normal or only mild patterns. Grade two is one severe pattern. Grade three is two or more severe patterns.

{{**Grade 0** IVC ≤ 2 cm · **1** IVC > 2 cm, normal or mild only · **2** one severe · **3** two or more severe
Severe: hepatic S reversal · portal pulsatility ≥ 50% · intrarenal D-only}}

Now the why. Renal perfusion pressure is the MAP minus the CVP. Patient F has a MAP of seventy. With a CVP of five, the kidney sees sixty-five. With a CVP of twenty, it sees only fifty. Same MAP, a much worse kidney.

[[Venous congestion lowers the renal perfusion pressure, so acute kidney injury follows even with a good MAP.]]

The score was derived by Beaubien-Souligny and colleagues in cardiac surgery patients, where grade three predicted acute kidney injury. Validation in the general ICU is still limited. That's the honest caution.

So, the IVC is the gate. Let's remind ourselves what it, and the hepatic vein, say about the right atrium.
lesson.cap: Hepatic, portal and intrarenal Doppler: normal, mild and severe. Schematic, flow toward the heart drawn up.

steps.bridge: A big fixed IVC and hepatic S/D below 1 mean high RA pressure. Next: how RV overload spills into systemic congestion →

lesson.text: You met this table with the IVC. Small and collapsing means a low right atrial pressure. Big and fixed, above two point one centimetres with less than half collapsing on sniff, means a high one, ten to twenty. [[In that high band, a hepatic vein S smaller than D is one of the secondary signs.]] That's exactly where VExUS picks up the trail. The IVC is the gate, and the hepatic vein is the first room beyond it. And the commonest engine behind a full IVC and a congested liver? A right ventricle that can't cope.

steps.bridge: RV failure raises RA pressure and congests the organs. Next: how that congestion hits the kidney and liver →

lesson.text:
Trace the spiral of right ventricular pressure overload. It's a loop, and once you see where it closes, you see why it kills.

It starts with a rise in the load the right ventricle pumps against. Two things happen at once. The wall tension rises, and the ventricle dilates.

Higher wall tension raises the oxygen demand of the muscle. Meanwhile, coronary perfusion falls. So you get arrhythmias, right ventricular ischaemia, injury and inflammation, and they all feed back into weaker contraction.

The weak ventricle does two things. Its output falls. And it alters the interdependence of the two ventricles, in systole or diastole. The dilated right ventricle pushes the septum towards the left.

Both lead to the same place. Less preload for the left ventricle. So the cardiac output falls, the pressure falls, and you have shock. And shock lowers the coronary perfusion even further.

[[The loop closes through coronary perfusion. Shock starves the right ventricle, which weakens it, which deepens the shock.]]

That's why restoring the coronary perfusion gradient, with noradrenaline, is an early step in managing right ventricular failure, not a late one.

And there's a second limb, the one that matters for today. Tricuspid or pulmonary regurgitation adds volume overload. The right atrial pressure rises, the CVP rises, and the back-pressure spreads into the systemic veins. That's systemic congestion, the thing VExUS sees.

[[Both limbs end in the same place, organ dysfunction or failure.]]

And now you see why fluid is so dangerous here. In a ventricle already on this spiral, more volume dilates it further, shifts the septum further, and raises the back-pressure further.

So what happens when the load isn't sudden, but slow?

Chronic right ventricular failure usually comes from a gradual rise in afterload, from pulmonary hypertension. And the commonest origin of that is left heart failure. Less often, it comes from chronic volume overload, from right-sided lesions such as tricuspid regurgitation.

At first, the ventricle compensates, as the left one does, with myocyte hypertrophy and fibrosis. If the load persists, it decompensates. Myocytes are lost and replaced by fibrosis.

Now the subtle point the panel enjoys. When the left heart fills poorly in chronic right failure, it isn't mainly because the right ventricle pushes too little forward. [[Left heart filling falls mainly because the dilated right ventricle squeezes the left, through ventricular interdependence. It's mechanical.]] That's why pushing the right ventricle's output alone doesn't fix the low cardiac output.

And the venous side follows. Peripheral oedema and abdominal congestion. When that congestion reaches the kidney and the liver, you get the cardiorenal and cardiohepatic syndromes. That's the kidney of Patient F, and it's why a VExUS grade belongs in his assessment.

spine: What it is: VExUS is a bedside ultrasound grade of venous congestion, from grade 0 to grade 3.
How: if the IVC is over 2 cm, I Doppler the hepatic vein, the portal vein and the intrarenal veins. The more sites severely abnormal, the higher the grade.
Cut-offs: hepatic S reversal is severe; portal pulsatility **30%** mild, **50%** severe; intrarenal flow pulsatile with separate S and D is mild, D-only is severe.
Why the kidney suffers: renal perfusion pressure is MAP minus CVP. Congestion raises the back-pressure, so the kidney is under-perfused even with a good MAP.
What I do: a rising grade means stop fluid and start decongestion. It is a tolerance marker, not a responsiveness test.

open.text:
Here's a puzzle. Patient F, after cardiac surgery. His MAP is a comfortable seventy. His cardiac output is fine. And yet his urine output is falling, and his creatinine is rising.

The kidney has a good pressure going in. So why is it failing?

Because perfusion isn't about the pressure going in. It's about the difference between the pressure going in and the pressure coming out. If the veins are congested, the back-pressure rises, and the gradient across the kidney falls, even with a perfect MAP.

You can't see that back-pressure on the monitor. But you can see it with a probe. That's VExUS, the venous excess ultrasound score.

What the professor is checking is whether you know the steps in order, starting at the IVC. The three Doppler sites, with their mild and severe patterns. How they add up to a grade. And why the kidney suffers. And the trap? Treating VExUS as a test of fluid responsiveness. It isn't. It's a marker of tolerance.

So here's the plan. First, the protocol and the grades. Then the IVC and the hepatic vein as mirrors of the right atrium. Then how a failing right ventricle drives this congestion. And finally, how that congestion reaches the kidney and the liver.

How do you do it? If the IVC is over two centimetres, Doppler the hepatic vein, the portal vein and the intrarenal veins. The more sites severely abnormal, the higher the grade.

The cut-offs. Hepatic S reversal is severe. Portal pulsatility of thirty percent is mild, and fifty percent is severe. Intrarenal flow that's pulsatile with separate S and D is mild, and D only is severe.

Why does the kidney suffer? Because renal perfusion pressure is MAP minus CVP. Congestion raises the back-pressure, so the kidney is under-perfused even with a good MAP.

What do you do? A rising grade means stop the fluid and start decongestion. It's a tolerance marker, not a responsiveness test.

That's your answer.

But here's something to carry forward. Of the three Doppler sites, the hepatic vein is the one the panel is most likely to put on a screen and ask you to read. What do its waves mean, and when do they fool you? That's next.

questions.text: Liver POCUS — what can hepatic vein Doppler tell you?

steps.bridge: Hepatic S/D below 1 is a secondary sign of high RA pressure. Next: the full set of hepatic patterns and their place in VExUS →

lesson.text: Remember the secondary signs of a high right atrial pressure, from the IVC lesson. Alongside a large right atrium and a hypertrophied right ventricle, there was hepatic vein flow with the systolic wave smaller than the diastolic. [[An S smaller than D in the hepatic vein is a secondary sign of a raised right atrial pressure.]] Today, we take that one sign and open it out into the full set of patterns.

Where do you get it? Pulsed-wave Doppler in a hepatic vein close to the IVC, from a subcostal or a right intercostal window. And put the ECG on, because you need to know which wave belongs to which part of the cardiac cycle.

Now the normal pattern. Look at the top row on your screen.

{{pic}}

There's first a small wave going away from the heart. That's the a wave. When the right atrium contracts, it pushes a little blood back up the veins. Then come two waves towards the heart. The S wave, in ventricular systole, as the atrium relaxes and the tricuspid ring moves down, drawing blood in. And the D wave, in diastole, when the tricuspid valve opens and blood runs on into the right ventricle.

Normally, S is bigger than D.

Now raise the right atrial pressure. A full, tense atrium can't draw blood in so well in systole. So the S wave shrinks.

[[S smaller than D is mild congestion. A raised right atrial pressure blunts systolic filling.]]

Go further, as with severe tricuspid regurgitation, and blood is pushed back up the veins during systole. Now the S wave points away from the heart.

[[S reversal, flow away from the heart in systole, is severe congestion.]]

Then place it in VExUS. The hepatic vein is one of three Doppler sites, with the portal vein and the intrarenal veins. It's scored only once the IVC is above two centimetres.

And on the same scan, look for two more things. Ascites. And the portal flow, where pulsatility of thirty percent or more is mild, and fifty or more is severe.

Now the trap. Atrial fibrillation. In AF, there's no atrial contraction, so the a wave is lost. And the S wave is blunted. So S smaller than D can occur without any congestion at all.

So read the hepatic vein with the rhythm, and with the clinical picture. Never alone.
lesson.cap: Top row: hepatic vein. Normal S bigger than D; mild S smaller than D; severe S reversed.

spine: What it is: Doppler of a hepatic vein shows how right atrial pressure is transmitted back into the liver.
Normal: the systolic wave is bigger than the diastolic wave, S greater than D.
Why it changes: raised RA pressure blunts systolic filling, so S becomes smaller than D (mild). In severe congestion S reverses.
VExUS: the hepatic vein is one of three Doppler sites, with portal and intrarenal veins, scored once the IVC is over 2 cm.
Caution: on the same scan I check portal pulsatility and ascites. I read it with the clinical picture, not alone.

open.text:
The examiner turns the ultrasound screen towards you. A Doppler trace from a vein in the liver, a row of waves above and below the line. He asks just one thing. What does this tell you?

This is a spotter. You have a few seconds to name it, and a minute to interpret it. And the hepatic vein is a lovely thing to interpret, because it drains straight into the IVC, just below the right atrium. Whatever the right atrium does, the hepatic vein shows.

What the professor is checking is whether you know the normal pattern and why it looks that way, the two abnormal patterns and what each means, where it fits in VExUS, and the one rhythm that fools it.

So here's the plan. First, the link to the right atrial pressure. Then the waves themselves, normal, mild and severe.
