So let's bring it together.

[[Doppler of a hepatic vein shows how the right atrial pressure is transmitted back into the liver.]]

Normal is a systolic wave bigger than the diastolic. S bigger than D.

Why does it change? A raised right atrial pressure blunts systolic filling, so S becomes smaller than D, which is mild. In severe congestion, S reverses.

In VExUS, the hepatic vein is one of three Doppler sites, with the portal and intrarenal veins, scored once the IVC is over two centimetres.

And the caution. On the same scan, check portal pulsatility and ascites. Remember that AF can make S smaller than D by itself. And read it with the clinical picture, not alone.

That's your spotter answer.

But here's something to carry forward. Every one of these ultrasound signs is, at heart, a picture of one pressure, the pressure in the right atrium. And there's a number on your monitor that has measured that pressure for decades. We've spent this block telling you not to trust it for fluid decisions. So is it useless? That's next. The CVP.

questions.text: What is the advantage of CVP in fluid management?

steps.bridge: CVP is RV filling pressure and the downstream pressure for organs. Next: why it cannot stand in for preload →

lesson.text:
CVP is the pressure in the thoracic veins near the right atrium. It's the filling pressure of the right ventricle. And, just as important, it's the downstream pressure for organ perfusion, the pressure the organs have to drain against.

It reflects the interplay of three things. The circulating blood volume, the venous tone, and the function of the right ventricle. [[CVP is three things mixed together: volume, venous tone and right heart function.]] That's its weakness as a volume marker, because a high CVP can mean too much blood, tight veins, or a failing right ventricle. And it's also, as we'll see, its strength.

Normal is about one to seven millimetres of mercury, in an awake, spontaneously breathing patient.

And its standing today? It has been de-emphasised as a marker of fluid responsiveness. The Surviving Sepsis guidelines of twenty sixteen dropped the CVP target.

But why does a filling pressure fail to tell us about filling?

steps.bridge: Pressure is not volume on a curved compliance line. Next: how badly CVP predicts fluid response →

lesson.text:
Strictly, preload isn't a pressure. It's a volume, the end-diastolic volume. CVP is a pressure standing in for that volume.

For that stand-in to work, three assumptions must hold. First, that ventricular volume and pressure are linearly related. Second, that the relationship is constant. And third, that the left ventricle's end-diastolic pressure tracks the atrial pressure, the CVP.

Now look at what really happens. The diastolic pressure-volume curve of the ventricle isn't a straight line. It's curved. At low volumes, it's flat, and a lot of volume raises the pressure only a little. At high volumes, it's steep, and a little volume raises the pressure a lot.

[[On a curved line, the same pressure means different volumes, depending on where the heart sits on it.]]

And the curve isn't constant either. In diastolic dysfunction, the stiff ventricle, the pressure rises abnormally for a given volume. So the same CVP can mean a full, compliant heart, or a much emptier, stiff one.

Think of two balloons, one thin-walled and one thick-walled. Blow both to the same pressure. The thin one holds far more air. The pressure tells you nothing about the volume unless you know the wall.

[[Filling pressure can't be equated with filling volume when the stiffness is abnormal, or changing fast.]] In the ICU, it's often both.

So how badly does CVP do in practice?

steps.bridge: ROC 0.56: do not use CVP to decide on fluid. Next: so what is CVP still good for →

lesson.text: You met the numbers at the start of this block. An ROC area of zero point five six. A correlation with the change in stroke index of zero point one eight. And a CVP below eight with a positive predictive value of only forty-seven percent. [[Don't use a CVP value to decide on fluid.]] Only the extremes carry a little information. So if it can't predict response, what is it still good for?

steps.bridge: CVP is a safety limit, a back-pressure and a trend. Next: what CVP and its waveform mean in RV failure →

lesson.text:
Here's where you win the question. CVP fails as a predictor. But it has four real uses, and none of them is about predicting response.

First, a tolerance and safety limit. If you give fluid and the CVP rises while the cardiac output doesn't, the heart is telling you it's on the flat part of its curve.

[[A CVP that rises with fluid while the output doesn't is a stop signal.]]

Second, back-pressure. Remember Patient F's kidney. Organ perfusion pressure is the MAP minus the CVP. A high CVP lowers the renal perfusion pressure even with a good MAP. So a high CVP isn't just a number. It's a kidney being squeezed from behind.

Third, the trend. The change with fluid or inotropes means more than any single value. And a rising CVP in right ventricular dysfunction is ominous.

Fourth, the waveform and the comparison. A large V wave points to tricuspid regurgitation. And a CVP higher than the wedge pressure suggests acute right ventricular failure.

And there's a bonus. The line itself. Through it, you sample the central venous oxygen saturation, and the venous half of the carbon dioxide gap.

[[CVP is a poor predictor of response, but a good safety limit, back-pressure and trend.]]

So in the viva, never say CVP is useless. Say this. A single CVP shouldn't decide a bolus. But I use its trend as a tolerance limit, and I remember it's the back-pressure on every organ.

steps.bridge: A rising CVP in a failing RV is ominous; read the trend. Next: what other markers the central line gives →

lesson.text: You met this with fluid tolerance. In right ventricular dysfunction, a rising CVP is ominous, and it's the trend with fluid and inotropes that informs you. And the waveform tells you why. A dominant V wave with a sharp Y descent means severe tricuspid regurgitation. [[A dominant A wave means the atrium is pushing against pulmonary hypertension.]] So the CVP isn't just a number. It's a pressure trace you can read. And the line gives you more than pressure.

steps.bridge: The same line gives ScvO2 and the CO2 gap. Next: why CVP targets left the sepsis bundle →

lesson.text: You met these markers in the perfusion block. The same central line that gives you the CVP lets you sample the central venous oxygen saturation, with a cut-off of seventy percent, used in place of the mixed venous value. And together with an arterial line, it gives you the venous-to-arterial carbon dioxide gap, with a cut-off of six millimetres of mercury. [[One central line gives you a pressure, an oxygen saturation and half of the carbon dioxide gap.]] So why did the CVP leave the sepsis targets?

In two thousand and one, Emanuel Rivers published early goal-directed therapy. Within six hours, three targets. A CVP of eight to twelve. A MAP of sixty-five or more. And a central venous saturation of seventy percent or more, using red cells to a haematocrit of thirty, then dobutamine. Hospital mortality fell from forty-six and a half to thirty and a half percent.

Then three large trials tested it. ProCESS and ARISE in twenty fourteen, and ProMISe in twenty fifteen. None showed a mortality benefit over usual care.

[[What survived was early recognition, early antibiotics and early fluids. Not the CVP or saturation targets.]]

One detail the panel may test. ProCESS had three arms. Protocolised EGDT. Protocolised standard care, with no central line, inotropes or transfusion. And usual care.

spine: What it is: CVP is the pressure near the right atrium. It reflects blood volume, venous tone and RV function together.
Why it fails: pressure is not volume. CVP predicts fluid responsiveness poorly, with a ROC area of **0.56**.
Where it helps: as a tolerance limit and back-pressure. Organ perfusion pressure is MAP minus CVP, so a rising CVP warns of renal congestion.
What I do: I follow the trend with fluid, read the waveform for TR and RV failure, and use the line for ScvO2 and the CO2 gap.
Evidence: Rivers' CVP target of **8–12** was not supported by ProCESS, ARISE and ProMISe, so CVP is no longer a resuscitation target.

open.text:
Here's the paradox. You've learned that CVP has an ROC area of zero point five six for predicting fluid responsiveness. Near a coin toss. And yet almost every patient in septic shock in your ICU has a central line, and the CVP is on every monitor.

So the panel asks a deliberately provocative question. What is the advantage of CVP in fluid management?

The weak answer is, there is none. The strong answer separates two jobs. CVP is a poor tool for deciding whether fluid will help. It's a useful tool for deciding when fluid has started to hurt.

What the professor is really checking is whether you know what CVP actually is, why it can't stand in for preload, what it's still good for, and why it left the sepsis targets.

So here's the plan. First, what CVP is. Then why pressure isn't volume. Then a quick look at the numbers. Then what CVP is still good for. Then the waveform in right heart failure, and what else the line gives you. And finally, the trial history that took CVP out of the sepsis targets.

And the evidence. Rivers' CVP target of eight to twelve wasn't supported by ProCESS, ARISE and ProMISe. So CVP is no longer a resuscitation target.

That's your answer.

But here's something to carry forward. A central line gives you one pressure. What if you need the whole circulation measured, the output, the pulmonary pressures, the lung water? Then you choose between two bigger tools, a pulmonary artery catheter and PiCCO. Which would you use? That's next.

questions.text: Pulmonary artery catheter or transpulmonary thermodilution (PiCCO) - which would you use?

steps.bridge: PiCCO needs a CVC and a femoral or axillary line and gives volumes and lung water. Next: the normal values of those variables →

lesson.text:
PiCCO uses transpulmonary thermodilution, and it needs two catheters. A central venous catheter, to inject a cold bolus. And a thermistor-tipped arterial catheter, in the femoral or the axillary artery, to sense it.

The cold bolus travels through the right heart, the lungs and the left heart before it reaches that artery. From the curve of temperature against time, the machine works out not only the cardiac output, but the volumes the bolus has passed through.

So intermittently, by thermodilution, it gives the cardiac output, the global end-diastolic volume, the intrathoracic blood volume, the extravascular lung water, the permeability index, the cardiac function index and the global ejection fraction.

And continuously, by pulse contour analysis of the arterial wave, it gives the arterial pressure, the heart rate, the stroke volume, stroke volume variation, the SVR, and a continuous cardiac output.

[[PiCCO gives you volumes and lung water. That's what it's for.]]

And its typical candidate is a patient with, or at risk of, pulmonary oedema or ARDS. That's Patient G.

steps.bridge: GEDVI is preload; EVLW above 10 mL/kg is oedema; PVPI separates ARDS. Next: what only each device can measure →

lesson.text: You met these numbers with fluid tolerance. The indexed global end-diastolic volume, six hundred and eighty to eight hundred millilitres per square metre, is preload as a volume. [[Lung water above ten millilitres per kilo means pulmonary oedema.]] And a raised permeability index says the lungs are leaky, as in ARDS. For Patient G, those two numbers answer the question that matters most. Is the fluid now flooding his lung? Next, what only each device can do.

steps.bridge: PAC gives pulmonary pressures and SvO2; PiCCO gives lung water. Next: where PiCCO numbers mislead →

lesson.text:
Put the two devices side by side.

Only the pulmonary artery catheter gives you the pulmonary artery pressures and the wedge pressure. With a special catheter, it also gives the right ventricular end-diastolic volume. And from its tip you sample mixed venous blood, for the mixed venous saturation.

Only PiCCO gives you the intrathoracic volumes and the extravascular lung water.

Both give the right atrial pressure. Both give the cardiac output. PiCCO gives it continuously, always, through the pulse contour. The PA catheter does that only with special technology.

And one risk belongs only to the PA catheter. Pulmonary artery rupture.

[[The PA catheter sees the pulmonary circulation. PiCCO sees the volumes and the water in the lung.]]

{{ | **PAC** | **PiCCO**
PA pressures, PAOP | Yes | No
RVEDV | Yes (special catheter) | No
ITBV, EVLW | No | Yes
RA pressure | Yes | Yes
Continuous CO | special technology | always
PA rupture | risk | none}}

So Patient H, with suspected pulmonary hypertension and a failing right ventricle, needs to see the pulmonary circulation. That's a PA catheter. Patient G, with rising lung water, needs PiCCO.

But PiCCO's numbers have weak points of their own.

steps.bridge: PiCCO needs recalibration and fails in PE or large effusions. Next: when a PA catheter is still indicated →

lesson.text:
Each PiCCO variable has one main drawback. Learn them as a set, because the panel likes to test them.

The thermodilution cardiac output isn't continuous. But it's as reliable as thermodilution through a PA catheter.

The pulse contour output needs regular recalibration.

The global end-diastolic volume can't separate the right ventricle from the left. It's the volume of all four chambers together.

Stroke volume variation has the limits of pulse pressure variation. It's invalid with spontaneous breathing, arrhythmias and ARDS.

The cardiac function index and the global ejection fraction underestimate left ventricular function when the right ventricle is dilated. Why? Because the global ejection fraction is four times the stroke volume, divided by the global end-diastolic volume. A dilated right ventricle swells that denominator, so the fraction looks worse than the left ventricle really is.

[[In a dilated right ventricle, PiCCO makes the left ventricle look worse than it is.]] That matters for Patient H.

And the lung water and permeability index are unreliable in pulmonary embolism, after lung resection, and with large pleural effusions. In an embolism, for example, the cold bolus can't reach the lung beyond the clot, so the water there goes uncounted.

So when is the PA catheter still the right choice?

steps.bridge: PAC is kept for pulmonary hypertension, cardiogenic shock and RV failure. Next: what the trials showed →

lesson.text:
The PA catheter is a diagnostic tool, not a therapy. And today its indications are few, and specific.

The evaluation and diagnosis of pulmonary hypertension. Candidacy for heart, lung or liver transplant. Cardiogenic shock and right ventricular failure. Mixed shock, or shock where the volume status is unclear. And high-risk cardiac surgery.

[[Its strength is separating things. Shock types, cardiogenic from non-cardiogenic oedema, tamponade, a left-to-right shunt.]]

In a non-cardiac ICU, there are few, if any, absolute indications. So you choose it for a reason, as in Patient H. And what did the trials show?

steps.bridge: No PAC trial showed benefit. Next: why the catheter failed to help →

lesson.text:
Here's the evidence, and it's sobering.

It begins with Connors, in nineteen ninety-six, the SUPPORT data. Observational, five thousand seven hundred and thirty-five patients in five American hospitals. Patients with a catheter had higher thirty-day mortality, an odds ratio of one point two four, with higher cost and longer stay.

Then the randomised trials. Sandham, in nearly two thousand high-risk surgical patients, one thousand nine hundred and ninety-four to be exact. No difference, and more pulmonary emboli, eight against none.

Richard, six hundred and seventy-six patients with shock or ARDS, in thirty-six French ICUs. No difference.

PAC-Man, one thousand and forty-one patients in sixty-five UK ICUs. No difference, with forty-six non-fatal complications.

ESCAPE, four hundred and thirty-three patients with heart failure. No difference, and more adverse events.

And FACTT, one thousand patients with ARDS, the catheter against a central line. No difference, and more arrhythmias.

[[Not one randomised trial showed that the PA catheter improves outcome.]]

{{**Connors 1996** 5,735, observational: ↑ 30-day mortality (OR 1.24)
**Sandham** 1,994 high-risk surgical: no difference; more PE (8 v 0)
**Richard** 676 shock/ARDS: no difference
**PAC-Man** 1041, 65 UK ICUs: no difference
**ESCAPE** 433 HF · **FACTT** 1000 ARDS vs CVC: no difference}}

So why did it fail?

The fault was rarely the catheter itself. It was in the chain from number to decision.

The data may be inaccurate. Clinicians often misinterpret them, and act on them in different ways.

Even when they're read correctly, the wedge pressure correlates poorly with stroke volume, and it doesn't predict fluid responsiveness. It's a pressure standing in for a volume, the same flaw as the CVP.

And a number invites action. The catheter prompted extra interventions, and some of them may have harmed.

Finally, most of it was studied before echocardiography was widespread.

[[A monitor helps only if it changes treatment for the better. The PA catheter's numbers were often misread, or acted on wrongly.]]

The same picture in cardiac surgery. Schwann, in five thousand and sixty-five CABG patients, found higher mortality with the catheter. Chiang, in over two million patients, found no benefit. And a Cochrane review in twenty thirteen found no change in mortality, length of stay or cost.

So in the viva, say it with balance. No trial showed benefit, so I don't use it routinely. But in pulmonary hypertension, right ventricular failure and cardiogenic shock, it measures what nothing else can.

spine: What it is: both give thermodilution cardiac output. The PA catheter adds pulmonary pressures, wedge and SvO2; PiCCO adds preload volumes and lung water.
Lung water: PiCCO's EVLW above **10 mL/kg** means pulmonary oedema. A raised PVPI points to leaky lungs (ARDS), a normal one to hydrostatic oedema.
What I use: PiCCO for septic shock with ARDS or risk of oedema. A PA catheter for RV failure, pulmonary hypertension and cardiogenic shock.
Evidence: PAC trials showed no outcome benefit. **PAC-Man** (**1041** patients) and Richard (**676**) found no difference.
Caution: PiCCO's GEF and CFI underestimate LV function when the RV is dilated; lung water misleads in PE, lung resection and large effusions. A PA catheter risks PA rupture.

open.text:
Let me give you two patients. Patient G, septic shock with ARDS, on high-dose noradrenaline, his lungs getting wetter by the hour. Patient H, in cardiogenic shock with right ventricular failure, and a pulmonary pressure you suspect is high.

Both need more than a CVP and an arterial line. Both could have their cardiac output measured by thermodilution. But they need different tools.

This is a compare-and-choose question. The panel isn't asking which is better in general. They're asking whether you know what each one uniquely measures, where each one misleads you, and which patient gets which.

And there's a trap on the evidence. The resident who says the pulmonary artery catheter improves outcome has walked into it. Not one randomised trial showed benefit. But the resident who calls it obsolete has walked into the opposite trap.

So here's the plan. First, PiCCO and what it measures. Then its variables. Then what only each device can measure. Then PiCCO's weak points. Then when a PA catheter is still indicated. Then the trials. And finally, why the catheter failed to help.

close.text:
So let's bring it together.

[[Both give a thermodilution cardiac output. The PA catheter adds pulmonary pressures, the wedge and the mixed venous saturation. PiCCO adds preload volumes and lung water.]]

Lung water on PiCCO above ten millilitres per kilo means pulmonary oedema. A raised permeability index points to leaky lungs, as in ARDS, and a normal one to hydrostatic oedema.

What do you use? PiCCO for septic shock with ARDS, or a risk of oedema. A PA catheter for right ventricular failure, pulmonary hypertension and cardiogenic shock.

The evidence. The PA catheter trials showed no outcome benefit. PAC-Man, with one thousand and forty-one patients, and Richard, with six hundred and seventy-six, found no difference.

And the caution. PiCCO's global ejection fraction and function index underestimate the left ventricle when the right is dilated. Its lung water misleads in pulmonary embolism, lung resection and large effusions. And a PA catheter risks pulmonary artery rupture.

That's your answer.

But here's something to carry forward. PiCCO reads the arterial waveform every beat. And so do you, every day, in theatre. But do you really read it? Its upstroke, its notch, its damping, and the diseases written into its shape. That's next.

questions.text: Describe arterial waveform patterns.

steps.bridge: Upstroke, peak, notch and run-off each map to one event. Next: what changes each part of the wave →

lesson.text:
Look at the trace on your screen. A normal arterial wave, with its landmarks lettered A to F.

{{pic}}

Walk it from left to right, and tie each landmark to one event.

A, the systolic upstroke. The aortic valve opens and the left ventricle ejects. That steep rise is peak aortic flow.

B, the peak systolic pressure. The maximum central arterial pressure.

C, the systolic decline. Contraction is ending, and the outflow from the aorta now exceeds the inflow.

D, the dicrotic notch. The aortic valve closes, and there's a brief rise in pressure at the aortic root.

[[The dicrotic notch is aortic valve closure. It marks the end of systole.]]

E, the diastolic run-off. No blood is coming from the ventricle now. The pressure falls gradually, because the aorta, stretched in systole, acts as a reservoir and keeps pushing blood forward.

And F, the end-diastolic pressure. The pressure of the vascular tree, sitting back on the closed aortic valve.

Two more points the panel may ask. The area under the curve, averaged over the cardiac cycle, gives the mean arterial pressure. [[MAP is the area under the curve, not simply the halfway point between systolic and diastolic.]]

And the delay from the R wave on the ECG to the upstroke is about one hundred and sixty to one hundred and eighty milliseconds. That's the time for the signal to reach the transducer.

So now you have the shape. What changes each part of it?
lesson.cap: Normal arterial wave, landmarks A to F: upstroke, peak, decline, dicrotic notch, run-off, end-diastole.

steps.bridge: Contractility shapes the upstroke; vascular tone sets diastole. Next: how to check that the trace is real →

lesson.text:
Each part of the wave has its own master.

The systolic upstroke follows anything that affects aortic flow. Contractility above all, then flow through the aortic valve, and the peripheral resistance.

The peak systolic pressure depends on the left ventricular contraction, the compliance of the central arteries, and the reflected pressure wave coming back from the periphery.

A more rapid systolic decline points to obstruction of the left ventricular outflow tract.

And the end-diastolic pressure follows vascular tone. It's high when the vascular tree is constricted, and low in vasoplegia.

[[Contractility shapes the upstroke. Vascular tone sets the diastole.]]

Now a trap worth a mark. Some notes call the high-diastolic state non-compliant vessels. Don't read that as an old, stiff aorta. True arterial stiffness does something different. It raises the systolic, lowers the diastolic, and widens the pulse pressure. Diastolic pressure follows tone, the SVR. High when constricted, low in vasoplegia.

But before you read anything into the shape, you have to know the shape is real.

steps.bridge: One or two small oscillations after a flush means optimal damping. Next: what over- and under-damped traces look like →

lesson.text:
That's the fast flush test. It checks the dynamic response of the whole system, the catheter, the tubing and the transducer. It tells you two things, the damping and the natural frequency.

Why do you need it? Because the fluid-filled tubing behaves like a spring. Give it a sharp kick, and it oscillates at its own natural frequency, and the oscillations die away at a rate set by its damping. Too little damping, and the system rings and exaggerates the wave. Too much, and it smooths the wave away.

So you pull the flush and release it suddenly. That's the kick. Then watch.

[[An optimally damped system shows only one or two oscillations after the flush, each no more than a third of the one before, then a crisp wave with a clear dicrotic notch.]]

You can go further. The natural frequency is the paper speed divided by the length of one oscillation cycle, measured peak to peak. And the amplitude ratio, the height of the second oscillation divided by the first, tells you the damping. A higher ratio means less damping.

{{**Natural frequency** = paper speed ÷ length of one cycle (peak to peak)
**Amplitude ratio** = D2 ÷ D1; higher = less damping (0.9 → damping coefficient 0.03; 0.1 → 0.59)}}

You don't need those numbers by heart. You need the habit. Flush first, then read. So what do the failures look like?

steps.bridge: Over-damped is slurred with low systolic; under-damped rings and overshoots. Next: the classic disease patterns →

lesson.text:
Look at the three traces on your screen, each after a fast flush.

{{pic}}

Trace B is optimal. One or two oscillations, each a third or less of the one before, and a clear dicrotic notch. The pressures are accurate.

Trace A is under-damped. Many oscillations after the flush, which we call ringing. The wave looks spiky, with an overshooting peak. The systolic reads too high, and the diastolic too low. The causes are long tubing, tachycardia, a hyperdynamic state, hypertension and atherosclerosis.

Trace C is over-damped. One or no oscillation, and a slow return. The wave looks slurred and rounded, and the notch is lost. The systolic reads too low, and the diastolic too high. The causes are air bubbles, clots, kinks, compliant tubing and a loose connection.

Now the most useful fact on this card.

[[In both errors, the mean arterial pressure is preserved. On a badly damped line, trust the MAP.]]

And one trap from the notes. Low-compliance tubing doesn't over-damp. It's the reverse. Soft, compliant tubing over-damps, which is why stiff tubing is used.

{{**Under-damped:** ringing, SBP ↑ DBP ↓, MAP same
**Over-damped:** slurred, SBP ↓ DBP ↑, MAP same}}

Now that you can trust the trace, read the diseases in it.
lesson.cap: After a fast flush: A under-damped, B optimal, C over-damped.

steps.bridge: Alternans, paradoxus, bisferiens and spike-and-dome each point to one disease. Next: how valve disease changes the trace →

lesson.text:
Look at the four abnormal traces on your screen.

{{pic}}

Trace A is pulsus alternans. The beats alternate between a high and a low pulse pressure. It points to severe left ventricular dysfunction.

Trace B is pulsus paradoxus. The systolic pressure falls by more than ten millimetres of mercury on inspiration. Kussmaul called it paradoxical in eighteen seventy-three, because the pulse faded on inspiration while the heart went on beating. But a small inspiratory fall is normal. Paradoxus is only an exaggeration of it, which is why it has been renamed pulsus normalis exaggeratus. The standard causes are cardiac tamponade, and severe asthma or COPD.

[[Pulsus paradoxus is an inspiratory fall in systolic pressure of more than ten millimetres of mercury. Think of tamponade.]]

Trace C is bisferiens. Two systolic peaks. Classically aortic regurgitation, also mixed aortic stenosis and regurgitation, and it can occur in HOCM.

Trace D is spike and dome. An early spike, a dip, then a late dome. That's HOCM, with dynamic obstruction of the outflow tract.

And the trace of poor cardiac function in general? A slurred, gradual upstroke, a narrow pulse pressure, and an absent dicrotic notch.

{{**Alternans** – severe LV dysfunction · **Paradoxus** (SBP falls > 10 mmHg on inspiration) – tamponade, severe asthma/COPD · **Bisferiens** – AR (also AS + AR; HOCM) · **Spike and dome** – HOCM}}

Notice that a weak heart can look rather like an over-damped line. Which brings us to the valves, and the same trap.
lesson.cap: Abnormal traces: A alternans, B paradoxus, C bisferiens, D spike and dome.

steps.bridge: AS is slow and small; AR is wide with low diastolic. Next: how breathing swings the trace in a ventilated patient →

lesson.text:
Aortic stenosis gives pulsus parvus et tardus. Small and late. A small, slow-rising upstroke with an anacrotic notch, a late peak, and an indistinct dicrotic notch.

Why? The narrow valve limits the rate at which the ventricle can eject. So the pressure rises slowly, and peaks late.

Aortic regurgitation is the opposite. A wide pulse pressure with a low diastolic, a brisk upstroke, and a fast diastolic run-off. It may be bisferiens.

Why? In diastole, blood falls back through the leaking valve into the ventricle. So the aortic pressure drops fast, and low.

[[Aortic stenosis is slow and small. Aortic regurgitation is wide, with a low diastolic.]]

Now the trap that opened this lesson. A slow, rounded aortic stenosis trace looks just like an over-damped one. How do you tell them apart? Do a fast flush first. If the flush response is optimal, the shape is real, and it's the valve.

[[Always flush first. Then read the shape.]]

And to complete the set. Alternans in left ventricular failure. Paradoxus in tamponade. Spike and dome in HOCM. And a swing with each breath, which is pulse pressure variation.

Look at the last trace on your screen. The biggest and the smallest pulse pressure, within one mechanical breath.

{{pic}}

You know why the trace swings. Each machine breath is a small preload challenge, and if the heart is on the steep part of its curve, the stroke volume rises and falls with it. The pulse pressure, systolic minus diastolic, follows the stroke volume. So you measure the swing in pulse pressure.

Take the biggest pulse pressure in the breath and the smallest. The pulse pressure variation is their difference, divided by their mean, times a hundred.

[[Divide by the mean of the two pulse pressures, not by the maximum.]]

Let's calculate it. The biggest beat is one hundred and fifty over seventy, a pulse pressure of eighty. The smallest is one hundred and twenty over sixty, a pulse pressure of sixty. The difference is twenty. The mean of eighty and sixty is seventy. Twenty divided by seventy is about twenty-nine percent.

{{**PPV** = (PPmax − PPmin) ÷ [(PPmax + PPmin) ÷ 2] × 100
150/70 → PP 80 · 120/60 → PP 60 · 20 ÷ 70 = **29%**}}

Normal pulse pressure variation doesn't exceed thirteen percent. Above that suggests fluid responsiveness. So twenty-nine percent is a strong signal, as long as the conditions hold. A passive patient, in sinus rhythm, on eight millilitres per kilo, with a closed chest.
lesson.cap: PP max and PP min within one mechanical breath.

spine: What it is: a normal trace has a sharp upstroke, a peak, a dicrotic notch at aortic valve closure, and a diastolic run-off.
Damping check: a fast flush with one or two small oscillations is optimal. Over-damped is slurred with low systolic; under-damped rings with high systolic.
Disease patterns: aortic stenosis is slow-rising and small; aortic regurgitation has a wide pulse pressure and low diastolic; alternans means LV failure.
More patterns: paradoxus, a fall of over 10 mmHg on inspiration, suggests tamponade; spike and dome suggests HOCM; a swing with each breath is PPV.
Caution: an AS trace can look over-damped. I always flush first, then read the shape.

open.text:
You've looked at an arterial trace thousands of times. In theatre, it's the line you trust most. But when did you last really read it?

In the viva, the examiner may put a trace in front of you and simply say, describe it. And there's a lot hiding in that wave. The heart's contractility in its upstroke. The aortic valve in its notch. The vessels' tone in its fall. The breath in its swing. And whether any of it is real, in its damping.

What the professor is checking is three things. Do you know the landmarks, and what each represents? Do you check the damping before you interpret anything? And can you name the classic patterns, and tell a disease from a damping error?

The trap is the resident who looks at a slow, rounded trace, says aortic stenosis, and never flushed the line.

So here's the plan. First, the normal wave and what shapes each part. Then the flush test and damping. Then the disease patterns, and the valves. And finally, the swing with breathing, pulse pressure variation.

close.text:
So let's bring it together.

[[A normal trace has a sharp upstroke, a peak, a dicrotic notch at aortic valve closure, and a diastolic run-off.]]

The damping check. A fast flush with one or two small oscillations is optimal. Over-damped is slurred, with a low systolic. Under-damped rings, with a high systolic. In both, the MAP holds.

The disease patterns. Aortic stenosis is slow-rising and small. Aortic regurgitation has a wide pulse pressure and a low diastolic. Alternans means left ventricular failure.

More patterns. Paradoxus, a fall of more than ten millimetres of mercury on inspiration, suggests tamponade. Spike and dome suggests HOCM. And a swing with each breath is pulse pressure variation.

And the caution. An aortic stenosis trace can look over-damped. Always flush first, then read the shape.

That's your spotter answer. And with it, you've closed this block. Will fluid help, and can he take it?

But here's something to carry forward. Everything in this block has been about one decision, one bolus at a time. Now put it into the commonest shock you'll treat. A patient in septic shock, arriving tonight. How much fluid, how fast, which fluid, and when do you stop? That's the next question. Fluid management in septic shock.

questions.text: Fluid management in septic shock.

steps.bridge: The first 30 mL/kg is a suggestion, by actual weight (adjusted or ideal if BMI >30), titrated in poor hearts. Next: which fluid do I give →

lesson.text:
So, the first step. The Surviving Sepsis guideline of twenty twenty-six says this. For sepsis-induced hypoperfusion or septic shock, give at least thirty millilitres per kilo of intravenous crystalloid in the first three hours.

Why give fluid at all? Because sepsis takes volume away from the circulation in two ways. The veins dilate, so the same blood fills a bigger container, and less of it pushes back towards the heart. And the capillaries leak, so plasma leaves the vessels altogether. Either way, less blood returns to the right heart, and the output falls. The first bolus fills that gap quickly, before the organs are hurt.

Now the part most residents get wrong.

[[Thirty per kilo is a suggestion, a conditional recommendation with low certainty. It is not a strong recommendation.]]

Old bundles and many lecture slides still print it as strong. If the professor asks for the grade, this is where marks are lost.

Why is the certainty low? Because no trial has randomised patients to thirty per kilo against some other first dose. The number reflects roughly what patients in the big resuscitation trials had already received before they were enrolled. So it's a sensible starting point, not a proven dose.

Which weight? Actual body weight. But if the body mass index is above thirty, use adjusted or ideal body weight. Think about why. Fat carries little blood, so blood volume tracks lean mass far more closely than total mass. A patient of a hundred and forty kilos does not need twice the fluid of our man.

And who should not get it blindly? The patient with impaired cardiac function, and the patient whose breathing is getting worse. In them, give the fluid in smaller steps and reassess after each one.

So for our patient, seventy kilos. About two litres in the first three hours, and the litre already running counts towards it.

[[At least thirty per kilo in three hours, by actual weight, adjusted or ideal if obese, and titrated in a poor heart.]]

Now, what goes into the bag?

steps.bridge: Crystalloid first, balanced preferred, saline in TBI, no starch. Next: when do I add a vasopressor →

lesson.text:
There are three families of fluid. Crystalloids, which are salt water: normal saline, or a balanced solution such as Ringer's lactate or Plasma-Lyte. The natural colloid, albumin. And the synthetic colloids, the starches and the gelatins.

The guideline's answer starts simply.

[[Crystalloid is first line, and that is a strong recommendation.]]

Why not a colloid, which should stay in the vessel longer? That was the old hope. A big molecule holds water inside the vessel, so you'd need less of it. But in sepsis the capillary wall is damaged, and the big molecules leak out too. And when the trials came, colloids saved no lives.

Worse, the starches hurt the kidney. In the CHEST trial, starch needed more renal replacement therapy, and the Scandinavian starch trial agreed, with more deaths as well. So starch carries a strong recommendation against. Gelatin is only suggested against, a conditional statement, because its evidence is thinner.

[[Starch, strong against. Gelatin, conditional against. Panels love that pair.]]

Within the crystalloids, balanced is preferred over saline, conditionally. The one exception is traumatic brain injury, where saline is preferred. That exception has its own question, and we'll take it apart there.

And albumin? Here the guideline has moved. In twenty twenty-one it suggested adding albumin for patients who had needed large volumes of crystalloid. In twenty twenty-six it prefers crystalloid alone, and albumin is left to case-by-case use, after large volumes or in cirrhosis. Your lecture probably still teaches the twenty twenty-one line.

{{FLUID | POSITION | STRENGTH
Crystalloid | First line | **Strong**
Balanced vs saline | Balanced preferred | Conditional
Saline | Preferred in TBI | Conditional
Albumin | Crystalloid alone preferred | Conditional
Starch | Against | **Strong**
Gelatin | Against | Conditional}}

So our patient gets a balanced crystalloid. And after the first litre, his pressure is still eighty-five over forty. When does the noradrenaline come in?

steps.bridge: In extremis, fluid and noradrenaline go in together. Next: why not just keep pouring fluid →

lesson.text:
Two patients, two speeds.

Patient A has a pressure of ninety over fifty. Warm, talking, a little drowsy. In her, you give the fluid bolus first, and if the hypotension persists, you start noradrenaline.

Patient B has a pressure of sixty over thirty. Cold and obtunded. In him, you don't wait.

[[In extremis, fluid and noradrenaline go in together, without delay.]]

Why the difference? Because a pressure that low is already starving the brain, the heart and the kidneys. A bolus takes time to run in, and in a vasodilated patient much of it may not lift the pressure at all. Noradrenaline works within minutes. It tightens the arterioles, and, as you'll see in its own lesson, it squeezes blood out of the veins towards the heart.

And don't wait for a central line. Start it through a peripheral vein. That has its own question too.

Our man sits between the two. Eighty-five over forty, and mottled. So the fluid goes on, and the noradrenaline is drawn up beside it, ready.

But why not simply keep pouring fluid until the pressure comes up?

steps.bridge: Only half respond, and fluid that does not help harms. Next: what tells me whether to give more →

lesson.text:
You met this card in the lesson on fluid responsiveness. A responder is a patient whose stroke volume rises by more than ten to fifteen percent after a fluid challenge, and only about half of patients are responders.

Fluid that does not raise output does not simply do nothing. It ends up as oedema, in the lung and in the other organs.

That's why every bolus after the first is a decision, not a reflex. So how do you make that decision?

steps.bridge: Dynamic tests guide further fluid; CRT and lactate support them. Next: restrictive or liberal after the first bolus →

lesson.text:
You've met this card in the lesson on lactate and perfusion. The guideline suggests dynamic measures over examination or static numbers: a passive leg raise, or a fluid challenge, with the stroke volume, or the pulse pressure or stroke volume variation, measured. Capillary refill time is an adjunct, and lactate is followed serially. The central venous pressure is a static number, and it is not a guide.

So before our man's second litre, you lift his legs and watch the stroke volume. But even when the test says yes, how much further should you go?

steps.bridge: CLOVERS: about 2.1 L less fluid, same mortality. Next: what do I do once the shock settles →

lesson.text:
After the first thirty per kilo, if the patient is still hypoperfused, do you keep giving fluid, or do you lean early on the vasopressor? Liberal, or restrictive?

The CLOVERS trial asked exactly that. Patients with sepsis-induced hypotension, enrolled after their first one to three litres. One arm got more fluid. The other got less fluid, and earlier vasopressors. The restrictive arm received about two point one litres less fluid. And ninety-day mortality was no different.

[[CLOVERS: about two litres less fluid, and the same ninety-day mortality.]]

Read that carefully. It doesn't say less is better. It says less is not worse. So the guideline says either strategy is acceptable, a conditional statement.

And how is further fluid decided? Not by the label on the strategy. By fluid responsiveness on a dynamic test, with capillary refill time and lactate beside it.

The trap is to tell the panel that CLOVERS proved restriction saves lives. It didn't. It showed that you can use less fluid safely.

So once our man's shock settles, what happens to all the fluid he has been given?

steps.bridge: Once stable, remove fluid, diuretics first. Next: the grades, CLASSIC, and the rule for stopping →

lesson.text:
You met active fluid removal in its own lesson. It's new in twenty twenty-six. It comes after the acute resuscitation phase, in a patient who is stable with no sign of hypoperfusion. Diuretics first, and ultrafiltration if they aren't enough.

[[The fluid that saved him on day one can flood his lungs by day three.]]

So resuscitation has an end, and the end is taking the fluid back off. Now let's put the whole answer in order.

Here's the whole algorithm, with the grade on each step, because a sharp panel will ask for the grades.

The first bolus. At least thirty millilitres per kilo of crystalloid in the first three hours. Conditional, low certainty. A starting point, individualised and reassessed with a passive leg raise, not a fixed dose.

The fluid. Balanced over saline, conditional, moderate certainty. The exception is traumatic brain injury, where saline is used, because the balanced solutions are slightly hypotonic.

After the first bolus. CLOVERS, and the CLASSIC trial in ICU septic shock, both found restrictive equal to liberal for mortality. So either strategy is acceptable.

If the hypotension persists, start noradrenaline, through a peripheral vein if need be. Don't wait for a central line.

Further fluid is guided by dynamic measures, not by static values or the central venous pressure, with capillary refill and serial lactate as adjuncts.

And now the rule for stopping, the part most answers leave out.

[[Stop when the patient is no longer fluid-responsive, or no longer fluid-tolerant.]]

Those are two separate tests. Responsive asks, will the heart use this fluid? Tolerant asks, can the lungs and the organs take it? A patient can still be responsive, his stroke volume still rising with a leg raise, and yet not tolerate more. His B-lines are spreading on ultrasound, his oxygenation is worsening. Then you stop, responsive or not.

{{**Septic shock fluids, SSC 2026**
≥30 mL/kg crystalloid in 3 h: conditional, low
Balanced > saline: conditional, moderate (saline in TBI)
Restrictive = liberal: CLOVERS, CLASSIC
More fluid: dynamic tests; CRT, lactate as adjuncts
Stop: not responsive OR not tolerant
Then: active removal, diuretics first}}

And then, once the patient is stable without hypoperfusion, active fluid removal, diuretics first.

[[Give, guide, stop, remove. That's the arc of fluid in septic shock.]]

spine: What it is: septic shock needs early volume, but only about half of patients respond to a bolus, and excess fluid causes organ oedema.
What I do: at least **30 mL/kg** balanced crystalloid in 3 hours (conditional, low certainty), saline if TBI, and peripheral noradrenaline if hypotension persists.
How I guide it: after the first bolus I give more only if a dynamic test such as passive leg raising is positive, with capillary refill time and serial lactate as adjuncts.
Evidence: **CLOVERS** gave about **2.1 L less fluid** with no difference in 90-day mortality, and CLASSIC agreed. So restrictive or liberal is acceptable.
When I stop: when the patient is no longer fluid-responsive or no longer tolerates fluid. Once stable, I start active fluid removal with diuretics.

open.text:
Let me start with a patient.

A man of sixty-five comes up from the emergency department with pneumonia. His pressure is eighty-five over forty. His hands are cold, his knees are mottled, and his lactate is four. He weighs seventy kilos. The registrar has already hung a litre of crystalloid, and he asks you two things. How much more? And of what?

That's the whole question. And it's harder than it sounds, because fluid is the first drug every septic patient gets, and it is also the drug we most often overdose.

Here's the tension. Sepsis dilates the veins and makes the capillaries leak, so the circulation runs short of effective volume, and early fluid restores flow. But only about half of patients actually raise their output with a bolus. In the other half, the fluid goes nowhere useful. It leaks into the lungs, the gut, the kidneys and the skin.

[[Fluid is a drug. It has a dose, a benefit and a toxicity, and the skill is knowing when to stop.]]

What is the professor really checking? First, do you know the first step, and that its grade is weaker than most people think. Second, which fluid. Third, when the vasopressor comes in. Fourth, how you decide on the second bolus, and the third. And finally, do you know when to stop, and when to take the fluid back off.

The trap is to answer with a fixed recipe. Thirty per kilo, then chase the central venous pressure, then more fluid. That was the old bundle. It is not the answer now.

So here's the plan. The first bolus and its grade. The choice of fluid. When noradrenaline starts. Why more fluid can harm. How you guide it. Restrictive or liberal. And finally, getting the fluid back off.

close.text:
So let's bring it together.

Septic shock needs early volume. But only about half of patients respond to a bolus, and fluid that isn't used becomes oedema in the organs.

[[So I give at least thirty per kilo of balanced crystalloid in the first three hours, a conditional, low-certainty suggestion. Saline if there's a brain injury. And peripheral noradrenaline if the hypotension persists.]]

After the first bolus, I give more only if a dynamic test, such as a passive leg raise, is positive, with capillary refill time and serial lactate as adjuncts.

The evidence: CLOVERS gave about two litres less fluid, with no difference in ninety-day mortality, and CLASSIC agreed. So restrictive or liberal is acceptable.

And I stop when the patient is no longer fluid-responsive, or no longer tolerates fluid. Once he is stable, I start active fluid removal, with diuretics first.

That's your answer. What the problem is, what I do, how I guide it, the evidence, and when I stop.

But here's something to carry forward. Today you met CLOVERS in a single sentence. A good panel won't leave it there. What exactly did the restrictive trials compare? Why does nearly every big fluid trial come back neutral? And how do you think about fluid across the days, not just the first hour?

That's the next question. Restrictive against liberal, and the evidence behind it.

questions.text: Restrictive versus liberal fluid strategy in septic shock - what is the evidence?

steps.bridge: The big resuscitation trials keep showing no difference between strategies. Next: what exactly did CLOVERS test →

lesson.text:
Walk the line of trials in order, because the order tells a story.

It begins with Rivers. Early goal-directed therapy, a protocol of fluid, pressors, blood and dobutamine, driven hard against targets in the first six hours. Mortality fell from forty-six and a half percent to thirty and a half. That one trial built the sepsis bundles.

Then three large trials, ProCESS in the United States, ARISE mainly in Australia and New Zealand, and ProMISe in England, tested the protocol against usual care.

[[All three found no difference in mortality between early goal-directed therapy and usual care.]]

Not because early care doesn't matter. The usual interpretation is that usual care had caught up. By then, everyone was giving early antibiotics and early fluid anyway.

Then CLOVERS. Restrictive against liberal fluid. No difference.

Then the capillary refill trials. ANDROMEDA-SHOCK compared targeting capillary refill time with targeting lactate. The mortality difference didn't reach significance, a P value of zero point zero six. And the second ANDROMEDA-SHOCK trial, in twenty twenty-five, compared capillary-refill-targeted resuscitation with usual care. It won on a ranked, combined outcome, mainly through less organ support. But mortality was the same, about twenty-six and a half percent in both arms.

{{TRIAL | TESTED | VERDICT
Rivers | EGDT | Mortality 46.5 → 30.5%
ProCESS, ARISE, ProMISe | EGDT vs usual care | No difference
CLOVERS | Restrictive vs liberal | No difference
ANDROMEDA-SHOCK | CRT vs lactate | NS (P 0.06)
ANDROMEDA-SHOCK-2 (2025) | CRT-targeted vs usual | Win ratio 1.16; mortality 26.5 vs 26.6%}}

The last two rows of this card are the steroid trials. They have their own question.

So what's the message?

[[Once the basics are done early and well, the exact amount of fluid matters less than we thought.]]

Now let's look at CLOVERS, the trial that asked our question directly.

steps.bridge: CLOVERS: less fluid, same 90-day mortality, so either is acceptable. Next: what happens after resuscitation →

lesson.text:
You met CLOVERS with the fluid algorithm. After the first one to three litres, the restrictive arm got earlier vasopressors and about two point one litres less fluid, and ninety-day mortality was the same. So the guideline accepts either strategy, and further fluid is decided by a dynamic test, not by the strategy.

Hold the distinction, because it's the whole interpretation. Less was not worse. It was not shown to be better. And if less fluid is safe, what do you do with the fluid already given?

steps.bridge: Fluid removal is now a guideline step, diuretics first. Next: CLASSIC, the ROSE phases and the targets →

lesson.text:
You met active fluid removal in its own lesson. After the acute resuscitation phase, in a patient who is stable with no sign of hypoperfusion, the guideline now suggests taking fluid off. Diuretics first, ultrafiltration if they aren't enough. It's conditional, and new in twenty twenty-six, and it's often called de-resuscitation.

[[Resuscitation is not finished when the pressure comes up. It's finished when the excess fluid is back out.]]

Now let's put the trials, the phases and the targets together.

Now the details, the ones that separate a good answer from a list.

CLOVERS first. Patients with sepsis-induced hypotension, enrolled after their first one to three litres. Restrictive, with earlier vasopressors, against liberal. About two point one litres less fluid in the first twenty-four hours. Ninety-day mortality fourteen percent against fourteen point nine. No difference.

CLASSIC second. A different setting: ICU patients with septic shock, after their initial resuscitation. Restricted intravenous fluid against standard care. Again, no difference in ninety-day mortality.

Notice that the two trials sit at different points in time. CLOVERS in the first hours, CLASSIC later, in the ICU.

[[Both found restrictive equal to liberal. Early or late, less fluid was not worse.]]

So the guideline says either strategy is acceptable after the first thirty per kilo. More fluid goes only to a patient who is both fluid-responsive and fluid-tolerant.

Now a way to hold all of this in one picture. Malbrain's ROSE model. Look at the screen if you'd like to see it.

{{pic}}

Four phases, each with its own job. Resuscitation: rescue, in minutes, fast boluses to save life. Optimisation: titrate to perfusion, over hours, smaller challenges, each one tested. Stabilisation: maintenance only, over days, no more boluses. And Evacuation: remove the excess.

[[Resuscitation, optimisation, stabilisation, evacuation. The fluid balance climbs, flattens, and must come back down.]]

The evacuation phase is de-resuscitation, now a guideline statement. Active fluid removal, once the patient is stable without hypoperfusion. Diuretics first, ultrafiltration if not enough.

What are you aiming for? A neutral, then a negative, fluid balance. A falling weight. Fewer B-lines, and better oxygenation. All while the perfusion stays normal: the capillary refill and the lactate.

And here's the caution.

[[Stop removing fluid if hypoperfusion returns: rising lactate, slow capillary refill, falling urine output, or hypotension.]]

Taking fluid off is a drug too, and it has its own overdose.

And remember the second ANDROMEDA-SHOCK trial from the line of trials. It is missing from this card's table, and it tells you the bedside perfusion check is a good way to steer.
lesson.cap: ROSE phases: fluid balance climbs, flattens in stabilisation, then falls in evacuation. Shape only, no scale.

spine: What it is: after the first 30 mL/kg, the question is whether to keep giving fluid or to switch early to vasopressors.
Evidence: **CLOVERS** gave about **2.1 L less fluid** with no difference in 90-day mortality; **CLASSIC** also found restricted fluid equal to standard care.
What I do: SSC 2026 accepts either strategy. I give further fluid only if a dynamic test is positive and the patient tolerates it.
De-resuscitation: I think in ROSE phases: resuscitation, optimisation, stabilisation, evacuation. Once stable without hypoperfusion, I remove fluid, diuretics first.
Caution: I stop removing fluid if perfusion worsens, such as rising lactate, slow capillary refill or falling urine output.

open.text:
Let me start with a puzzle.

For twenty-five years, intensive care has run big, expensive trials on how to resuscitate septic patients. More fluid against less. A strict protocol against usual care. One bedside target against another. And almost every one of them has come back with the same answer on mortality. No difference.

So does it not matter what we do? That's the wrong conclusion. And the panel asking this question wants to see whether you can read a neutral trial properly.

Here's the real question underneath. After the first thirty per kilo, do you keep giving fluid, or do you switch early to a vasopressor and hold back? For years, the reflex was to keep pouring. The trials have slowly taken that reflex apart.

[[A neutral trial of less fluid doesn't mean nothing matters. It means less fluid is safe.]]

What is the professor really checking? First, do you know the trials by name, and what each one actually compared. Second, do you know what the guideline does with them. Third, can you describe fluid as a series of phases over days, not one decision in the first hour. And fourth, do you know when to stop taking fluid off.

The trap is to say restriction saves lives. No trial has shown that.

So here's the plan. First, the line of resuscitation trials, in order. Then CLOVERS in a little more detail. Then the newest guideline step, fluid removal. And finally CLASSIC, the ROSE model, and the targets for de-resuscitation.

close.text:
So let's bring it together.

After the first thirty per kilo, the question is whether to keep giving fluid, or switch early to a vasopressor.

The evidence. CLOVERS gave about two litres less fluid, with no difference in ninety-day mortality. CLASSIC also found restricted fluid equal to standard care.

[[So the guideline accepts either strategy, and I give further fluid only if a dynamic test is positive and the patient tolerates it.]]

Then I think in ROSE phases. Resuscitation, optimisation, stabilisation, evacuation. Once the patient is stable without hypoperfusion, I remove fluid, diuretics first.

And the caution. I stop removing fluid if perfusion worsens: a rising lactate, a slow capillary refill, or a falling urine output.

That's your answer. The question, the evidence, what I do, de-resuscitation, and the caution.

But here's something to carry forward. Today we argued about how much fluid. We haven't asked what's in the bag. One bag carries far more chloride than your plasma does, and the other doesn't. Does that matter to the kidney? And why would you still choose the high-chloride bag for one particular patient?

That's next. Balanced crystalloid or normal saline.

questions.text: Balanced crystalloid or normal saline in the ICU?

steps.bridge: Crystalloid first; balanced preferred, but saline in TBI. Next: why does saline cause trouble →

lesson.text:
You met this card with septic shock fluids. Crystalloid is first line, a strong recommendation. Within crystalloids, balanced is preferred over saline, but only conditionally. And saline is preferred in traumatic brain injury.

[[Crystalloid first, strongly. Balanced over saline, conditionally. Saline in brain injury.]]

Keep those three grades apart, because the panel often asks for them together. Now see what happens when a patient needs enormous volumes.

steps.bridge: Ringer's lactate avoids hyperchloraemic acidosis but can drop sodium. Next: what trauma guidance says about saline →

lesson.text:
A major burn is the ultimate fluid stress test.

Why does a burn need so much fluid? Two reasons. Fluid is lost from the burned surface. And far more is lost inside the body. The burn triggers a capillary leak, not only in the burned skin but throughout the body, and plasma sequesters into the tissues. The goal isn't a number. It's euvolaemia and perfusion.

When do you start formal resuscitation? Burns over twenty percent of the body surface in adults, and over fifteen percent in children. And with what? A balanced crystalloid, Ringer's lactate. Why not saline? Because at these volumes, saline's chloride would produce a hyperchloraemic acidosis. But watch the sodium, because Ringer's lactate carries less sodium than plasma, and large volumes can lower it.

[[Ringer's lactate avoids the chloride acidosis, at the cost of a falling sodium.]]

Now the formulas. Parkland: four millilitres, times the percent of body surface burned, times the weight in kilos, of Ringer's lactate, over twenty-four hours. Half in the first eight hours, half over the next sixteen. And the eight hours are counted from the time of the burn, not from arrival. A patient who reaches you three hours late has five hours left for that first half.

So a seventy-kilo man with a forty percent burn. Four times forty times seventy. Eleven point two litres in the day, and five point six of them in the first eight hours.

{{**Parkland** = 4 mL × %TBSA × kg (RL, 24 h)
½ in first 8 h from **time of burn**, ½ over next 16 h
70 kg, 40% → 11.2 L; 5.6 L in first 8 h
**Modified Brooke**: 2–4 mL × %TBSA × kg (notes); classic 2 mL adults, 3 mL children
**Target**: urine 0.5 mL/kg/h adults, 1 mL/kg/h children}}

The modified Brooke formula is lower. Your notes give two to four millilitres. The classic version is two for adults and three for children.

And here's the most important line on this card.

[[The formula only starts the fluid. The urine output steers it: half a millilitre per kilo per hour in adults, one in children.]]

Formulas are a starting point. The urine tells you whether you're right.

Now, the bleeding trauma patient. What does his guideline say about saline?

steps.bridge: Avoid excess saline in bleeding trauma, yet protect perfusion in TBI. Next: the trials and the TBI exception →

lesson.text:
The European guideline on major bleeding after trauma. This card is its targets, and every line has a reason.

Start with blood pressure. Until the bleeding is controlled, and with no brain injury, the guideline accepts a restricted volume strategy, a systolic of eighty to ninety. That's permissive hypotension, roughly a mean pressure of fifty to sixty. Why accept a low pressure? Because a higher pressure pushes blood out of the wound faster and blows off fresh clot, and the fluid needed to reach it dilutes the clotting factors that are left.

But in severe brain injury, a GCS of eight or less, it flips. A mean pressure of eighty or more. Because the injured brain often loses its autoregulation, so its blood flow follows the pressure. Permissive hypotension starves it.

[[In bleeding trauma, accept a low pressure until the bleeding is stopped. In severe brain injury, never.]]

Vasopressors go in alongside fluid for life-threatening hypotension. The fluid is isotonic crystalloid, and the guideline says avoid excess saline. That's the line for our question. Large volumes of saline bring the chloride acidosis, and acidosis worsens the coagulopathy.

Then the blood. A haemoglobin target of seven to nine. To start coagulation support, plasma to red cells of at least one to two, or fibrinogen concentrate with red cells. Tranexamic acid, one gram over ten minutes, then one gram over eight hours, started within three hours of injury. Platelets above fifty, and above a hundred with ongoing bleeding or brain injury.

{{**Bleeding trauma targets**
SBP 80–90 (no TBI) until bleeding controlled
MAP ≥80 in severe TBI (GCS ≤8)
Isotonic crystalloid; avoid excess 0.9% saline
Hb 7–9 g/dL · plasma:RBC ≥1:2, or fibrinogen + RBC
TXA 1 g/10 min + 1 g/8 h, within 3 h
Platelets >50; >100 if bleeding or TBI}}

And one aside the panel may test. A pelvis still unstable despite a binder needs early preperitoneal packing, embolisation or surgery.

So the trauma guideline steers away from saline in bleeding, yet protects the pressure in the brain. Now let's see why the brain is the one place saline wins.

Now the full argument: the mechanism, the trials, and the exception.

The mechanism first. Saline has far more chloride than plasma. Give large volumes, and plasma chloride rises. The strong ion difference narrows, bicarbonate falls, and you get a hyperchloraemic metabolic acidosis.

And the kidney? The proposed harm runs through the macula densa. High chloride arriving there triggers tubuloglomerular feedback. The afferent arteriole constricts, renal blood flow falls, the filtration rate drops, and acute kidney injury may follow. Notice the word proposed. It's a plausible mechanism, not a proven one.

[[High chloride may constrict the kidney's own arterioles. That's the case against saline.]]

Now the trials. SMART, in twenty eighteen. Fifteen thousand eight hundred and two ICU adults, a cluster crossover design, open label. The outcome was major adverse kidney events at thirty days: death, new dialysis, or persistent renal dysfunction. Fourteen point three percent with balanced fluid, against fifteen point four with saline. An odds ratio of zero point nine one. Small, but it favoured balanced fluid.

Then three trials that found nothing. SPLIT in twenty fifteen, BaSICS in twenty twenty-one, and PLUS in twenty twenty-two. No significant difference in kidney injury or mortality.

So how do you weigh one positive open-label trial against three neutral ones? Pool them. The Hammond meta-analysis in twenty twenty-two found a mortality risk ratio of about zero point nine six. A probable small benefit.

[[The guideline suggests balanced over saline, conditional, moderate certainty. A small likely benefit, not a large proven one.]]

{{**SMART** 2018 (n 15,802): MAKE30 14.3 vs 15.4%, OR 0.91, balanced better
**SPLIT** 2015 · **BaSICS** 2021 · **PLUS** 2022: no difference
**Hammond** 2022 meta-analysis: mortality RR ≈0.96
**SSC 2026**: balanced > saline, conditional, moderate}}

Now the exception. Traumatic brain injury. Balanced solutions are slightly hypotonic, Ringer's lactate most of all. Give a lot of a hypotonic fluid, and plasma osmolality falls. Water then moves into the injured brain, and cerebral oedema worsens. A subgroup of BaSICS suggested harm with balanced fluid in brain injury.

[[In brain injury, use saline. The brain cares about osmolality more than the kidney cares about chloride.]]

And one last practical point. With large volumes of Ringer's lactate, watch the sodium. It can fall.

spine: What it is: saline carries more chloride than plasma; balanced solutions are closer to plasma.
Why it matters: large volumes of saline cause hyperchloraemic acidosis, and high chloride may reduce renal blood flow and raise AKI.
Evidence: **SMART** showed fewer major kidney events with balanced fluid; SPLIT, BaSICS and PLUS were neutral. SSC 2026 suggests balanced over saline, conditional.
What I do: balanced crystalloid by default for resuscitation, watching sodium with large volumes of Ringer's lactate.
Caution: in traumatic brain injury I use saline, because balanced fluids, especially Ringer's lactate, are slightly hypotonic and may worsen cerebral oedema.

open.text:
Let me start with a bag of saline.

We call it normal saline. But think about what's in it. Sodium and chloride, about one hundred and fifty-four of each, per litre. Your plasma has about one hundred and forty of sodium, and only about a hundred of chloride. So that bag carries roughly half as much chloride again as your blood does. There's nothing normal about it.

Give one litre, and the kidney copes. Give six litres to a septic patient, and his chloride climbs, his bicarbonate falls, and he develops a metabolic acidosis that you caused.

Balanced solutions, Ringer's lactate and Plasma-Lyte, replace part of that chloride with a buffer, so they look more like plasma.

[[The difference between the two fluids is the chloride.]]

So the question looks simple. Balanced or saline? But what the professor is really checking is three things. Do you know why chloride might hurt? Do you know the trials, including the neutral ones, and can you weigh them honestly? And do you know the one patient where saline is still the right answer?

The trap is to say balanced fluids save lives. The evidence is closer than that.

So here's the plan. First, where the guideline puts each fluid. Then Ringer's lactate in the burned patient, where huge volumes test the choice. Then what the trauma guideline says about saline. And finally, the mechanism, the trials, and the brain-injured exception.

close.text:
So let's bring it together.

Saline carries more chloride than plasma. Balanced solutions are closer to plasma.

Why it matters. Large volumes of saline cause a hyperchloraemic acidosis, and high chloride may reduce renal blood flow and raise the risk of kidney injury.

The evidence. SMART showed fewer major kidney events with balanced fluid. SPLIT, BaSICS and PLUS were neutral.

[[The guideline suggests balanced over saline, a conditional recommendation. So balanced crystalloid is my default for resuscitation, and I watch the sodium with large volumes of Ringer's lactate.]]

And the caution. In traumatic brain injury I use saline, because balanced fluids, especially Ringer's lactate, are slightly hypotonic and may worsen cerebral oedema.

That's your answer. What it is, why it matters, the evidence, what I do, and the exception.

But here's something to carry forward. Today we compared two kinds of salt water. There's a third option, a fluid your own liver makes, that should stay inside the vessels far longer. For decades it was the fluid of choice for the sickest patients, then a famous meta-analysis accused it of harm, and a very large trial was run to settle the argument.

That's next. Albumin, the trials and the indications.

questions.text: Albumin — the trials and the indications.

steps.bridge: Crystalloid alone is preferred; albumin only after large volumes or in cirrhosis. Next: which trials put albumin there →

lesson.text:
You met this card with septic shock fluids. Crystalloid is first line, strongly. And for albumin, the twenty twenty-six guideline prefers crystalloid alone, conditionally, with albumin left for case-by-case use after large crystalloid volumes or in cirrhosis.

[[Albumin is no longer a routine add-on. It's an exception you have to justify.]]

So which trials pushed it there?

steps.bridge: SAFE: albumin equals saline; SAFE-TBI: albumin harms. Next: how did the guideline wording change →

lesson.text:
Five trials, and between them they settle the colloid argument.

SAFE, in twenty oh four, in the ICU. Saline against four percent albumin. Twenty-eight-day mortality was similar. That was the trial that answered the alarm. Albumin did not kill. But it didn't save lives either.

Then the follow-up in the brain-injured patients from SAFE, called SAFE-TBI, in twenty oh seven. Here albumin had a higher mortality at twenty-four months.

[[SAFE: albumin equals saline. SAFE-TBI: albumin harms the injured brain.]]

Then the starches. FIRST, in twenty eleven, in trauma. Saline against a modern starch. Starch needed less volume, and gave a lower lactate in penetrating injury. Mortality was similar. Your notes say kidney injury was less with starch in that trial. Be careful. The larger trials, CHEST and the Scandinavian starch trial, showed more kidney injury with starch, and those are the ones that count.

CHEST, in twenty twelve. Saline against six percent starch. Mortality similar, and more renal replacement therapy with starch. That's why starch now has a strong recommendation against.

And CRYSTAL, in twenty thirteen, in shock. Crystalloid against colloid. Twenty-eight-day mortality similar.

{{TRIAL | COMPARISON | RESULT
**SAFE** 2004 | Saline vs 4% albumin | Mortality similar
**SAFE-TBI** 2007 | Saline vs albumin in TBI | **Albumin: higher mortality** (24 mo)
**FIRST** 2011 | Saline vs HES 130/0.4 | Less volume; mortality similar
**CHEST** 2012 | Saline vs 6% HES | Mortality similar; **more RRT** with HES
**CRYSTAL** 2013 | Crystalloid vs colloid | Mortality similar}}

So across five trials, no colloid beat crystalloid on survival. Starch hurt the kidney. And albumin hurt the injured brain.

How has the guideline wording followed this?

steps.bridge: 2026 moved from albumin after large volumes to crystalloid alone. Next: is albumin any better in burns →

lesson.text:
This card is a list of what changed between the twenty twenty-one and twenty twenty-six guidelines. Albumin is one line, but learn the whole card, because the panel loves old against new.

Thirty per kilo: suggested in both, and twenty twenty-six adds adjusted or ideal weight when the body mass index is above thirty. Prolonged infusion of beta-lactams: conditional, now strong. Source control: no time given before, now within six hours. The MAP target in older patients: sixty-five, now sixty to sixty-five. The oxygen target: insufficient evidence, now either strategy, with ninety to ninety-six percent the taught range. Blood purification: no recommendation, now suggested against. Peripheral vasopressors: suggested, now with stronger emphasis. Dynamic measures: very low certainty, now low.

And albumin.

[[In twenty twenty-one, albumin was suggested after large crystalloid volumes. In twenty twenty-six, crystalloid alone is preferred.]]

{{ITEM | 2021 | 2026
Albumin | After large volumes | **Crystalloid alone**
β-lactam infusion | Conditional | **Strong**
Source control | No time | **6 h**
MAP if old | 65 | **60–65**
Blood purification | None | **Against**
Dynamic measures | Very low | **Low**}}

One honest caution. In a transition year, an exam key may hold either answer. Read whether the question says latest, or names a year.

Now, is albumin any better where the leak is worst, in burns?

steps.bridge: In burns albumin may cut crystalloid but has no proven outcome benefit. Next: ALBIOS, the grade and the real indications →

lesson.text:
A burn patient who gets more fluid than the formula predicts is said to have fluid creep. Why does it happen? Over-titration, chasing every dip in urine output with more fluid. And opioids, which may raise fluid needs.

And what does creep do? Oedema everywhere. Compartment syndrome of the abdomen and of the limbs. Pulmonary oedema. And a burn that was partial thickness can deepen, because the swollen tissue around it loses its blood supply.

So there's one practical trigger to remember.

[[Once more than two hundred and fifty millilitres per kilo has been given, measure the intra-abdominal pressure.]]

That two hundred and fifty mark is known as the Ivy index. And once fluid overload is definite, remove fluid.

Now the colloid question. In the first hours, the burn capillaries leak, and colloid molecules leak out with the water, and can worsen the oedema. Albumin may reduce the total crystalloid a patient needs. But it has no definite outcome benefit.

[[Even in burns, albumin can save crystalloid volume, but it hasn't been shown to save lives.]]

The pattern is the same as in sepsis. Albumin changes the fluid chart. It hasn't changed survival.

So let's put the evidence, the grade and the real indications together.

Here is the albumin answer in full.

SAFE, twenty oh four, in the ICU. Four percent albumin against saline. Twenty-eight-day mortality the same. Albumin is safe, but not better.

SAFE-TBI. In the brain-injured patients, albumin raised twenty-four-month mortality, thirty-three percent against twenty. In severe injury the gap was wider still, about forty-two against twenty-two. Why would a natural protein hurt the brain? The proposed reason is that the four percent albumin used was slightly hypotonic. A hypotonic fluid lets water into the injured brain, and the intracranial pressure rises.

[[Avoid albumin in traumatic brain injury.]]

ALBIOS, twenty fourteen, in severe sepsis. Albumin added to crystalloid. No mortality benefit. There was a signal of benefit in the septic shock subgroup, but it was post-hoc. A post-hoc signal raises a question. It doesn't answer one.

So the twenty twenty-six guideline says this.

[[Crystalloids alone are suggested over crystalloid plus albumin, conditional, moderate certainty. Albumin is case by case, after large crystalloid volumes or in cirrhosis.]]

Remember that twenty twenty-one had suggested albumin with large volumes. That's the change.

{{**SAFE** 2004: 4% albumin = saline
**SAFE-TBI**: albumin ↑ 24-month mortality, 33 vs 20% (GCS 3–8: 42 vs 22%)
**ALBIOS** 2014: no mortality benefit; post-hoc signal in shock
**SSC 2026**: crystalloid alone > + albumin (conditional, moderate)
**Indications**: SBP · paracentesis >5 L · HRS with terlipressin}}

So where does albumin have real evidence? Three places, all in liver disease. Spontaneous bacterial peritonitis. Large-volume paracentesis, over five litres. And hepatorenal syndrome, with terlipressin.

Go back to our woman after six litres, with an albumin of eighteen. In twenty twenty-six, you can consider albumin for her, case by case. But you are not treating the number. You're asking whether more crystalloid is doing harm. And if she had a head injury, the answer would be no albumin at all.

Let me start with a patient.

A woman with septic shock from a perforated bowel. She's back from theatre, and over the last day she has had six litres of crystalloid. She is puffy, her serum albumin is eighteen grams per litre, and she still needs noradrenaline. The surgeon says, give her albumin. It's the natural colloid. It stays in the vessels. It's her own protein.

It sounds obviously right. And for decades, that's exactly what we did.

Then, in the late nineteen nineties, a meta-analysis suggested albumin might actually increase deaths in critically ill patients. Practice split. So the question had to be settled with a proper trial, and that's where today's story starts.

[[Albumin sounds right in theory. In the trials, it has mostly been safe, but not better.]]

What is the professor really checking? First, do you know SAFE, and its brain-injury warning. Second, ALBIOS, and how to read its septic shock signal. Third, the twenty twenty-six guideline wording, which has changed. And fourth, the few places where albumin genuinely has evidence.

The trap is to treat a low albumin level as an indication. It isn't.

So here's the plan. First, where albumin sits among the fluids. Then the trials that put it there. Then how the guideline wording changed. Then albumin in burns. And finally ALBIOS, the grade and the real indications.
