They found profound but reversible myocardial depression, an ejection fraction below forty percent, in half of them. And those ventricles were dilated. In the survivors, the end-diastolic volume index was about a hundred and fifty-nine millilitres per square metre, against about eighty-one in those who died.

Then the paradox. [[The survivors had the lower ejection fraction, about thirty-two percent, against fifty-five in those who died.]]

Look at the picture on your screen.

{{pic}}

On the left, the survivors. A big ventricle. The dashed line, the chamber at the end of systole, is not much smaller than the outer line at the end of diastole, so the ejection fraction is low. But because the chamber is so big, the shaded ring between the two, the stroke volume, is still there. On the right, those who died. A small ventricle, with a normal-looking ejection fraction.

How can that be? Remember that the ejection fraction is a ratio. Stroke volume, divided by end-diastolic volume. [[A dilated ventricle can keep its stroke volume with a low ejection fraction, simply because it holds more blood.]] The dilatation is an adaptation. The weakened heart stretches, and the Frank-Starling mechanism lets it keep pumping a reasonable volume each beat.

And the normal ejection fraction on the right? It isn't a healthy heart. It's a heart squeezing against almost no resistance, because the vessels are profoundly dilated. An undilated ventricle ejecting into a vasoplegic circulation looks brisk, even when its muscle is weak.

So a hyperdynamic ejection fraction in septic shock is a bad sign. It points to profound vasoplegia, not to a strong heart.

One honest caution. This was twenty patients, with the methods of the nineteen eighties, and later studies have not consistently found that a low ejection fraction predicts survival. So learn the paradox as a lesson about load, not as a rule that a low ejection fraction is good news.

Which takes us straight to load.
lesson.cap: Survivors: dilated LV, low EF, stroke volume kept. Non-survivors: small LV, 'normal' EF from low afterload.

steps.bridge: Low afterload hides dysfunction until pressors unmask it. Next: what do I look for on echo →

lesson.text:
The ejection fraction is not a pure measure of the muscle. It measures how the muscle copes with its load. And in sepsis, the load is strange.

First, afterload. With a very low systemic vascular resistance, the ventricle does little work per beat, so the ejection fraction looks normal even when contractility is depressed. It's like judging a weightlifter's strength by watching him lift an empty bar.

[[Low afterload hides a weak ventricle. The ejection fraction looks normal because the heart is barely being asked to work.]]

Second, what unmasks it. Fluids and vasopressors. Once you give noradrenaline and the afterload is restored, the weight goes back on the bar, and the weakness shows. That's why the incidence depends on the day you look. In the first six hours, about eighteen to twenty-nine percent of patients have a low ejection fraction. By day one to three, about sixty percent. [[The noradrenaline doesn't cause the cardiomyopathy. It reveals it.]]

So when you scan a patient at the door of the emergency department, before any pressor, a normal ejection fraction tells you very little. Scan again once the pressure is restored.

Third, why are the filling pressures normal? You'd expect a failing ventricle to back up and raise the wedge pressure. Two things prevent that. The left ventricle dilates, a preload adaptation that lets it accept more volume without the pressure climbing. And the right ventricle is often failing too, in about thirty percent, so it can't deliver much blood across to fill the left. The wedge pressure sits around eleven to fourteen millimetres of mercury. Normal.

So in sepsis, two of your old reassurances fail together. A normal ejection fraction, and a normal wedge. Both can hide a heart that is struggling.

If those mislead, what should you look for on the echo?

steps.bridge: EF under 45%, poor strain, RV dysfunction; note TAPSE cut-off is <17 mm, not 16. Next: how do I treat it →

lesson.text:
So you put the probe on. Look at three things. The left ventricle squeezing. The left ventricle relaxing. And the right ventricle.

The squeeze. An ejection fraction below forty-five percent. But you know now that the ejection fraction can hide disease, so look at the long axis as well. The tissue Doppler velocity of the mitral annulus in systole, S prime, below seven point five centimetres a second. And global longitudinal strain worse than minus twenty percent, that is, less negative. [[Strain detects dysfunction that the ejection fraction hides.]] The longitudinal fibres, just under the endocardium, tend to suffer first, and the ejection fraction can stay normal while they fail. And, of course, a low output.

The relaxation. Look at the early diastolic velocity of the mitral annulus, e prime. Below seven at the septum, and below ten at the lateral wall. And the ratio of the mitral E wave to e prime: above thirteen laterally, or above fifteen at the septum, suggesting raised filling pressure. A trick for the sites. The septum is always the slower of the two. So the septum has the lower e prime cut-off, and the higher ratio.

The right ventricle. Often forgotten, often failing. A right-to-left ventricular size ratio above zero point six. A TAPSE, the tricuspid annular plane systolic excursion, below seventeen millimetres. A tricuspid S prime below ten centimetres a second. And a fractional area change below thirty-five percent. [[The TAPSE cut-off is below seventeen millimetres, not sixteen.]] Older notes, including yours, print sixteen.

{{Chamber | Findings
LV systolic | EF **<45%** · S′ <7.5 cm/s · GLS worse than −20% · low output
LV diastolic | e′ septal <7, lateral <10 cm/s · E/e′ lateral >13, septal >15
RV | RV/LV >0.6 · **TAPSE <17 mm** · S′ <10 cm/s · FAC <35%}}

Why does the right ventricle matter so much here? Because in sepsis it's hit from both sides. Its muscle is depressed, like the left. And its afterload often rises, from lung injury and from positive-pressure ventilation. A struggling right ventricle can't fill the left, which, as we said, is one reason the wedge stays normal.

One honest caution. Every one of these numbers depends on load and on timing. Read them with the vasopressor dose and the fluid state in mind, and repeat them.

So you've found it. How do you treat it?

steps.bridge: Cause, fluid, noradrenaline, dobutamine, then rescue. Next: do β-blockers help →

lesson.text: You climbed this ladder in the inotropes question, so just the rungs. Treat the cause, with antibiotics and source control. Fluids, guided by dynamic indices, because this heart tolerates excess volume poorly. Noradrenaline to restore the pressure. Dobutamine when hypoperfusion persists despite an adequate pressure. Then levosimendan and beta-blockers, which sit on the ladder as options, though the guideline suggests against both. And VA-ECMO at the top, as rescue. Which leaves the question everyone asks. If a racing heart is part of the problem, should we slow it?

Start with the rationale, because it's attractive.

A septic heart racing at a hundred and forty has very little time to fill, and it burns oxygen with every beat. Slow it, and three good things should follow. Myocardial oxygen demand falls. Diastole lengthens, so the ventricle fills better. And beta-blockade may damp the inflammatory response.

Then came Morelli, in twenty thirteen. Patients in septic shock with persistent tachycardia, given esmolol to bring the heart rate down. Twenty-eight day mortality was forty-nine point four percent with esmolol, against eighty point five percent in the controls.

[[Morelli's esmolol trial cut twenty-eight day mortality from about eighty to about forty-nine percent.]]

A huge effect. And that is exactly the problem. The criticism was the control group. A mortality of eighty percent is far higher than in most septic shock populations, so the result was hard to generalise.

Then STRESS-L, with landiolol, a beta-blocker about eight times more beta-one selective than esmolol. No fall in SOFA, and no mortality benefit. It was stopped early, with a signal pointing towards harm.

Ivabradine took a different route, slowing the sinus node without depressing contractility. In sixty patients, the haemodynamics improved, but thirty-day mortality was no different.

And pooled together, the trials give only a weak signal of benefit, a risk ratio of zero point seven eight.

{{**Heart-rate control in septic shock**
Morelli 2013 (esmolol): 28-day mortality **49.4% vs 80.5%**; very high control mortality
STRESS-L (landiolol): no fall in SOFA, no mortality benefit; stopped early
Ivabradine (n = 60): better haemodynamics, no 30-day mortality difference
Pooled: RR 0.78, weak signal}}

[[So the twenty twenty-six guideline suggests against beta-blockers in septic shock.]] It's one of the new statements.

Why might the dramatic early result not hold? Think about what the tachycardia is doing. In many septic patients, a fast heart is compensation. The stroke volume is limited, and the rate keeps the output up. Slow it in the wrong patient, and you take away the one thing holding the output together.

So in the viva. The esmolol trial was striking but flawed. STRESS-L was negative. The guideline suggests against.

spine: What it is: acute, reversible, global biventricular dysfunction in sepsis, with LV dilatation, poor response to fluid and catecholamines, and no coronary cause.
Why: mediators, nitric oxide, disturbed calcium handling and mitochondrial failure. Low afterload hides it, so EF can look normal until vasopressors restore pressure.
Echo: LVEF below **45%**, reduced strain, diastolic dysfunction, and RV dysfunction with TAPSE below **17 mm**. It usually recovers in **7–10 days**.
What I do: treat the source, give fluid by dynamic indices, noradrenaline, then dobutamine for persistent hypoperfusion; VA-ECMO for refractory cases.
Evidence: Morelli's esmolol trial cut 28-day mortality from **80.5% to 49.4%**, but STRESS-L with landiolol showed no benefit. SSC 2026 suggests against β-blockers.

open.text:
Let me start with a paradox.

Two patients in septic shock. You put an echo probe on both. Patient A's ventricle is big and sluggish, with an ejection fraction of about thirty percent. Patient B's ventricle is small and brisk, with an ejection fraction of fifty-five. Which heart is in better shape?

Every instinct says Patient B. And in nineteen eighty-four, Margaret Parker and her colleagues showed that the instinct can be wrong. In their patients, it was those with the low ejection fraction who survived.

That paradox is the heart of this question. Septic cardiomyopathy is common, it is reversible, and it hides. The panel wants the definition, the mechanisms, the echo findings and the treatment. But what the professor is really checking is whether you understand why the ejection fraction lies in sepsis. And then comes the follow-up. Do beta-blockers help? One trial said yes, another said no, and now the guideline has spoken.

So the plan. First, what septic cardiomyopathy is. Then what causes it. Then Parker's paradox, and why the ejection fraction misleads. Then the echo criteria. Then the treatment ladder. And finally, the heart-rate control trials.

close.text:
So let's bring it together.

[[Septic cardiomyopathy is an acute, reversible, global dysfunction of both ventricles in sepsis, with a dilated left ventricle, a poor response to fluid and catecholamines, and no coronary cause.]]

Why it happens: mediators, nitric oxide, disturbed calcium handling and mitochondrial failure. And the low afterload hides it, so the ejection fraction can look normal until vasopressors restore the pressure.

On echo: an ejection fraction below forty-five percent, reduced strain, diastolic dysfunction, and right ventricular dysfunction with a TAPSE below seventeen millimetres. It usually recovers in seven to ten days.

What you do: treat the source, give fluid by dynamic indices, then noradrenaline, then dobutamine for persistent hypoperfusion, and VA-ECMO for refractory cases.

The evidence on rate control. Morelli's esmolol trial cut twenty-eight day mortality from eighty point five to forty-nine point four percent. But STRESS-L, with landiolol, showed no benefit. And the guideline suggests against beta-blockers.

That's your answer. What it is, why it happens, what you see, what you do, and the trials.

But here's something to carry forward. Everything we did with sepsis rested on knowing what normal looks like. A heart rate, a blood pressure, a creatinine. Now imagine a patient whose normal values have all moved. Her heart is faster, her pressure lower, her PaCO2 lower and her creatinine lower, all by design. She has a fever, and she's pregnant. How do you spot sepsis in a body that already looks a little like it? That's next.

questions.text: Sepsis in pregnancy — which scores, and how is it different from non-pregnant sepsis?

steps.bridge: Cardiac output and heart rate rise, SVR falls. Next: how does the blood gas change →

lesson.text:
Start with the circulation, because every sign of shock lives there.

Pregnancy builds a high-flow, low-resistance circulation, to feed the placenta. The intravascular volume rises by about forty-five percent. The cardiac output rises by forty to fifty percent. Stroke volume rises first, by about thirty percent, and the heart rate keeps climbing towards term, up by fifteen to twenty-five percent. And the systemic vascular resistance falls by about twenty percent, as hormones relax the vessels and the placenta adds a low-resistance bed.

[[So pregnancy already looks a little like early sepsis: a fast heart, a high output and a low resistance.]]

Now the pressures. The systolic changes little. The diastolic falls by about twenty percent in mid-pregnancy, and returns to baseline at term. The CVP is unchanged. And oxygen consumption rises by thirty to forty percent, so she has less reserve when something goes wrong.

{{**Cardiovascular changes in pregnancy**
CO ↑40–50% · SV ↑30% · HR ↑15–25% · intravascular volume ↑45%
SVR ↓20% · SBP minimal change · DBP ↓20% mid-pregnancy, baseline at term · CVP unchanged
O₂ consumption ↑30–40%}}

What does this mean at the bedside? Two things, and they cut in opposite directions.

First, the familiar signs of sepsis, a fast heart and a low resistance, are partly there already. So tachycardia must go further before it alarms you, and that is exactly what the adapted scores build in.

Second, the trap that cuts the other way. [[A blood pressure of a hundred and twenty over eighty in the second trimester is relatively high for her.]] So a reading that looks normal may hide a change from where she was. Always compare her with her own earlier numbers.

So the circulation has shifted. And so has the blood gas.

steps.bridge: A compensated respiratory alkalosis with PaCO2 about 30. Next: what changes in blood and kidney →

lesson.text:
The blood gas of pregnancy is a compensated respiratory alkalosis. And it's worth knowing why.

Progesterone stimulates breathing. She breathes more, so the PaCO2 falls to about thirty millimetres of mercury, against thirty-five to forty outside pregnancy. The kidney compensates by excreting bicarbonate, which falls to eighteen to twenty-two. So the pH sits slightly alkaline, seven point four to seven point four seven. The PaO2 is a touch higher, a hundred to a hundred and four. The base excess doesn't change.

{{ | Pregnant | Non-pregnant
pH | **7.40–7.47** | 7.35–7.45
PaCO₂ (mmHg) | **about 30** | 35–40
PaO₂ (mmHg) | 100–104 | 90–100
HCO₃⁻ (mmol/L) | **18–22** | 20–28
Base excess | no change | −2 to +2}}

Now the two clinical traps.

[[A PaCO2 of forty in a breathless pregnant woman is not normal. It means she is tiring.]] On a non-pregnant chart, forty looks perfect. In her, it's a rise of ten from her baseline, and a warning that her breathing is failing.

The second trap is the buffer. With her bicarbonate already low, she has less reserve to absorb an acid load. So in a septic mother, a metabolic acidosis develops faster.

So her blood gas reads differently. And so do her blood count and her kidneys.

steps.bridge: Dilutional anaemia and a lower creatinine, so normal values mislead. Next: how is qSOFA adapted →

lesson.text:
Three more systems, and each one shifts a number you rely on.

The blood. The plasma volume rises more than the red cell mass, so the haemoglobin falls. That's a dilutional anaemia. Physiological, not a sign of bleeding. And pregnancy is hypercoagulable, with fibrinogen and clotting factors rising.

The kidney. Glomerular filtration and renal plasma flow rise by about half. So the creatinine falls, to roughly zero point four to zero point eight milligrams per decilitre. [[A creatinine of one milligram per decilitre is abnormal in pregnancy.]] On a non-pregnant scale it looks fine. In her, it may already be kidney injury. Go back to our woman on the labour ward, with a creatinine of zero point nine. That number should make you look harder.

The gut. Progesterone relaxes the lower oesophageal sphincter, transit slows, and constipation is common. Put that together with a full abdomen, and the risk you know well as an anaesthetist is aspiration.

And nutrition. She's in a high-calorie state, with needs that rise in labour and peak in lactation.

{{**Blood:** dilutional anaemia · hypercoagulable
**Kidney:** GFR and renal plasma flow ↑ about 50% · creatinine about 0.4–0.8 mg/dL · **1.0 is abnormal**
**Gut:** lax lower oesophageal sphincter, slow transit → **aspiration**}}

Now put the last three cards together. A faster heart, a lower resistance, a lower PaCO2, a lower creatinine. [[Normal non-pregnant values mislead in pregnancy. A number that looks normal may already be abnormal for her.]]

So how do the scores adapt?

steps.bridge: omqSOFA: SBP 90, RR 25, anything but alert. Next: which ward score tracks the mother →

lesson.text:
The obstetrically modified qSOFA, omqSOFA, keeps the three parts of qSOFA and moves the thresholds.

The systolic pressure: ninety or less, instead of a hundred or less. The respiratory rate: twenty-five or more, instead of twenty-two or more. And mentation: anything other than alert, instead of a Glasgow score below fifteen.

{{Criterion | Pregnant (omqSOFA) | Non-pregnant (qSOFA)
Systolic BP | **≤90** | ≤100
Respiratory rate | **≥25** | ≥22
Mentation | anything other than alert | GCS <15}}

[[Both numbers shift because normal pregnancy already has a lower blood pressure and faster breathing.]] Pressure down by ten. Breathing up by three.

And remember what qSOFA is, from earlier. A risk prompt, built to predict a bad outcome, not a diagnostic test. The pregnant version inherits that. A positive omqSOFA says this mother is at risk, so escalate. A negative one doesn't reassure.

For tracking her hour by hour on the ward, you need something with more parameters. That's MEOWS.

steps.bridge: MEOWS triggers on yellow and red bands. Next: what is obstetric SOFA →

lesson.text:
MEOWS, the modified early obstetric warning score, is the ward chart of pregnancy. Like NEWS, it tracks many vital signs over time, but with bands set for pregnant physiology. And instead of adding points, it colours them. Each observation falls in a normal, a yellow or a red band.

Hold the red bands, because they're the ones that drive action. A respiratory rate below ten or above thirty. A temperature below thirty-five or above thirty-eight. A systolic pressure above one hundred and eighty, or below ninety. A heart rate above one hundred and twenty, or below forty. And neurologically, responding only to pain, or unresponsive. Oxygen saturation is scored too, with ninety-six to a hundred percent as normal.

{{Parameter | Normal | Yellow | Red
RR | 10–20 | 21–30 | <10 or >30
Temp °C | 36–37.4 | 35–36 or 37.5–38 | <35 or >38
SBP | 100–139 | 150–180 or 90–100 | >180 or <90
HR | 50–99 | 100–120 or 40–50 | >120 or <40
Neuro | alert | voice | pain or unresponsive}}

[[The usual trigger is one red, or two yellows, and either calls for urgent review.]]

Notice what the chart is built to catch. It flags both ends, because in pregnancy the dangers come from both ends. A low pressure, for sepsis or haemorrhage. A high pressure, for pre-eclampsia. One chart, watching for all three.

One honest caution. The systolic bands on your card leave a gap. Normal stops at one hundred and thirty-nine, and yellow starts at one hundred and fifty. Charts differ between hospitals, so learn the red bands and the trigger, and use your own unit's chart for the rest.

So the ward chart flags her. Once she's in the ICU, how do you measure her organ dysfunction?

steps.bridge: Obstetric SOFA adjusts oxygenation and creatinine for pregnancy. Next: which sources are specific to pregnancy →

lesson.text:
Here's where the whole question comes together.

Why do the scores need adapting at all? Because, as we've built over the last few cards, pregnancy raises the heart rate and the cardiac output, lowers the blood pressure, gives a compensated respiratory alkalosis with a low PaCO2, and lowers the creatinine. [[So a normal-looking creatinine or PaCO2 may already be abnormal, and a fast heart or a low pressure may be wrongly dismissed as pregnancy.]] The error cuts both ways.

Obstetric SOFA takes the same organ systems as SOFA and adjusts them for pregnancy. The respiratory score uses modified PaO2 to FiO2 bands. The kidney scores from a lower creatinine, ninety micromoles per litre or more, which is about one milligram per decilitre, the very number we called abnormal in pregnancy. The nervous system uses a simple alert, voice or pain score, rather than the full Glasgow scale. And the cardiovascular system scores a mean pressure below seventy, or the need for vasopressors.

And one structural difference the panel may probe. Each system in obstetric SOFA scores only zero to two, not zero to four.

{{**omqSOFA** (bedside flag): RR ≥25 · SBP ≤90 · any altered mentation
**Obstetric SOFA** (ICU, organ dysfunction): same systems, adjusted
Resp: modified PaO₂/FiO₂ bands · Renal: from **≥90 µmol/L** · CNS: alert/voice/pain · CVS: MAP <70 or vasopressors
Each system scores **0–2**, not 0–4}}

Now see how the three scores fit together, because they mirror the non-pregnant story exactly. omqSOFA is the bedside flag, like qSOFA. MEOWS is the ward tracking chart, like NEWS. And obstetric SOFA is the ICU's measure of organ dysfunction, like SOFA. [[Flag with omqSOFA, track with MEOWS, quantify with obstetric SOFA.]]

That parallel is the best way to answer an X versus Y question. Show the panel that the structure is the same, then name exactly which numbers move, and why.

And in every one of these patients, remember there are two. Consider the fetus, and the timing of delivery.

So where is the infection coming from?

steps.bridge: Chorioamnionitis, pyelonephritis, endometritis, pneumonia. Next: how resuscitation and delivery are decided →

lesson.text:
This card carries two subjects. The first is amniotic fluid embolism, which belongs to another conversation, so only the outline. Aggressive multi-organ support, and correction of the coagulopathy, often with a massive transfusion protocol. Emergency delivery, and if the bleeding won't stop, caesarean with ligation of the uterine or internal iliac arteries, even hysterectomy. VA-ECMO as rescue, which has reduced mortality. And if she arrests, a perimortem caesarean within five minutes.

Now the part that belongs to this question. The sources of sepsis that come with pregnancy. Four of them, and each has a reason.

Chorioamnionitis, infection of the membranes and the amniotic fluid. Your card links it with an altered vaginal pH, and with amniocentesis.

Pyelonephritis. And here's why it's so common. Progesterone relaxes smooth muscle, including the ureters, so they lose their tone. The growing uterus presses on them too, and urine stagnates. Add Gram-negative colonisation, and a lower urinary infection climbs easily to the kidney. [[In pregnancy, progesterone slackens the ureters, so a simple urinary infection can rise to pyelonephritis.]]

Endometritis, after delivery, linked with instrumentation.

And pneumonia, in a woman who has less respiratory reserve and a higher oxygen demand than before.

{{**Pregnancy-specific sources of sepsis**
Chorioamnionitis (altered vaginal pH, amniocentesis)
Pyelonephritis (progesterone → ureteric tone lost; Gram-negative colonisation)
Endometritis (instrumentation)
Pneumonia}}

A way to hold them, through time. Before delivery, the membranes and the kidney. After delivery, the uterus. And throughout, the lung.

[[So in a septic pregnant or recently delivered woman, look at the uterus, the kidney and the lung.]]

Now, how do you resuscitate her, and when do you deliver?

The principle first. [[Resuscitate her as you would any patient: crystalloids, vasopressors and inotropes, by the same rules.]] Pregnancy doesn't change the drugs of sepsis care. It changes the position, the access, and the decisions around them.

Access. Two large-bore peripheral cannulae. And avoid the femoral route. Why? Because the gravid uterus compresses the inferior vena cava. Fluid and drugs given below that compression reach the heart slowly and unreliably. So the lines go above the diaphragm.

That same compression is why you place her in left uterine displacement. Lying flat on her back, the uterus sits on the vena cava, cutting the venous return and with it the cardiac output. Tilt her, or push the uterus to the left, and the return opens again. Without it, your fluids and pressors are working against a clamp.

Then the fetus. If preterm delivery is likely, steroids for fetal lung maturity: two doses of betamethasone, twenty-four hours apart. Mind the name, because your notes print beclomethasone, which is an inhaled steroid. The drug is betamethasone, twelve milligrams intramuscularly, two doses. And fetal well-being is followed with a biophysical profile.

And the decision to deliver. It's multidisciplinary, the obstetricians, the intensivists and the anaesthetists together. Correct the coagulopathy first, because an operative delivery in a septic, coagulopathic mother is dangerous.

{{**Circulation and delivery**
Access: 2 large-bore peripheral · **avoid femoral** (IVC compression) · left uterine displacement
Resuscitation: as in any patient
Fetal lung: **betamethasone** 12 mg IM × 2, 24 h apart
Fetal monitoring: biophysical profile
Delivery: multidisciplinary; correct coagulopathy first}}

[[Involve the obstetricians early, and decide delivery jointly, with the fetus in mind.]]

spine: What it is: sepsis in pregnancy is hard to spot, because pregnancy itself raises heart rate and cardiac output and lowers blood pressure.
Why it differs: a compensated respiratory alkalosis with PaCO2 about **30** and a lower creatinine, so normal non-pregnant values mislead.
Scores: omqSOFA uses RR **25** or more, systolic BP **90** or less and any altered mentation. Obstetric SOFA adjusts PaO2/FiO2 and scores creatinine from **90 µmol/L**.
Sources: chorioamnionitis, endometritis, pyelonephritis and pneumonia. On the ward I screen with MEOWS.
What I do: resuscitate as in any patient, with left uterine displacement; involve obstetrics early, and decide delivery jointly with the fetus in mind.

open.text:
Let me start with a woman on the labour ward.

She's thirty weeks pregnant, with a fever. Her heart rate is a hundred and five. Her blood pressure is ninety-eight over fifty-five. She's breathing twenty-two times a minute. Her creatinine is zero point nine milligrams per decilitre. In a non-pregnant woman, you'd be worried. Here, someone says, it's just pregnancy.

Some of it may be. But some of it may be sepsis. And sepsis remains one of the leading causes of maternal death worldwide, and its signs hide inside normal pregnancy.

This is an X versus Y question. How is sepsis in pregnancy different? The panel wants three things. Do you know how pregnancy shifts the normal values, so that the usual thresholds mislead? Do you know the adapted scores, the obstetrically modified qSOFA, MEOWS on the ward, and obstetric SOFA? And do you know what stays the same, and what changes, when you treat her?

So the plan. First, the circulation of pregnancy. Then the blood gas. Then the blood and the kidney. Then the three scores. Then the sources of sepsis that only pregnancy brings. And finally, resuscitation, and the decision to deliver.

close.text:
So let's bring it together.

[[Sepsis in pregnancy is hard to spot, because pregnancy itself raises the heart rate and cardiac output and lowers the blood pressure.]]

Why it differs: a compensated respiratory alkalosis, with a PaCO2 of about thirty, and a lower creatinine. So normal non-pregnant values mislead.

The scores. omqSOFA uses a respiratory rate of twenty-five or more, a systolic pressure of ninety or less, and any altered mentation. Obstetric SOFA adjusts the PaO2 to FiO2 bands, and scores creatinine from ninety micromoles per litre.

The sources: chorioamnionitis, endometritis, pyelonephritis and pneumonia. And on the ward, I screen with MEOWS.

What I do: resuscitate as in any patient, with left uterine displacement. Involve obstetrics early, and decide delivery jointly, with the fetus in mind.

That's your answer. Why it's different, the scores, the sources, and what you do.

But here's something to carry forward. Over these last questions, we kept reaching for the echo. To check a heart behind a high NT-proBNP. To find septic cardiomyopathy, with its strain and a TAPSE below seventeen millimetres. But how do you actually get those numbers at the bedside? Which windows do you open, and what do TAPSE and its left-sided cousin, MAPSE, really measure? That's next. Echo views, TAPSE and MAPSE.

questions.text: Echo views, TAPSE and MAPSE.

steps.bridge: The basic FATE sequence gives five windows on the heart and pleura. Next: what the parasternal long axis shows →

lesson.text:
Start with a simple protocol, built for exactly this patient. It's called FATE, focus assessed transthoracic echo, and it was developed in Denmark by Erik Sloth and his colleagues for the sick, the ventilated and the hurried.

The basic FATE set has five views, in a fixed order. The subcostal four-chamber. The apical four-chamber. The parasternal long axis. The parasternal short axis, at the level of the papillary muscles. And pleural scanning, on both sides.

Why start subcostal? Because in a ventilated patient, inflated lungs often hide the parasternal windows, while the liver gives you a clear path to the heart from below. And from that same position you see a pericardial effusion and the IVC.

Why the short axis at the papillary muscles? Because at that level you see the left ventricle as a ring, with walls supplied by all three coronary arteries, and you see the shape of the septum.

[[And notice the fifth view. FATE is a heart and pleura protocol by design. Pleural scanning is part of the basic set, not an extra.]] In a breathless, shocked patient, the effusion beside the heart may be as important as the heart itself.

{{**Basic FATE, in order:** 1 Subcostal 4-chamber · 2 Apical 4-chamber · 3 PLAX · 4 PSAX (papillary muscle level) · 5 Pleural scanning, both sides}}

Now let's open the view you'll use most for left ventricular function.

steps.bridge: PLAX gives contractility, EF and LVOT size. Next: which view measures the annular excursions →

lesson.text:
The parasternal long axis. You place the probe at the left sternal edge, in the second to fourth intercostal space, with the marker dot pointing to the right shoulder. It's the only basic view where the marker points to the right shoulder, and that's the detail an examiner likes to catch.

What do you see? The heart cut along its length. The right ventricle at the top, nearest the probe. Below it the septum, the left ventricular cavity and its back wall. And to one side the aortic root, the mitral valve and the left atrium.

The card gives four uses. You judge contractility. You estimate the ejection fraction. You look for regional wall motion abnormalities. And you measure the diameter of the left ventricular outflow tract.

Why is the outflow tract diameter measured here and nowhere else? Because ultrasound draws a boundary most sharply when the beam hits it at right angles. In this view the walls of the outflow tract lie across the beam, so their edges are crisp.

[[Measure the outflow tract diameter in the long axis. But measure the blood velocity in an apical view, where the beam runs along the flow.]]

That split matters, because stroke volume is the area of the outflow tract multiplied by the velocity time integral. And the area comes from the radius squared. So a small error in that one diameter becomes a large error in the stroke volume. You met this when we used VTI to test fluid responsiveness.

{{**Stroke volume = LVOT area × LVOT VTI**
LVOT diameter: PLAX · LVOT VTI: apical 5-chamber or 3-chamber}}

Keep one more thing from this view for later. Behind the left atrium, you'll often see a small circle, the descending aorta. It becomes the landmark that tells a pericardial effusion from a pleural one.

Now move to the apex, where the two annuli live.

steps.bridge: Apical 4-chamber shows both ventricles and their annuli. Next: the normal and abnormal bands for TAPSE and MAPSE →

lesson.text:
The apical four-chamber view. The probe sits over the apex of the heart, and the marker dot points to the left shoulder.

Now you're looking up the heart from its tip. All four chambers at once, both ventricles side by side, both atria beyond them, and between them the mitral and tricuspid valves.

The card gives four uses. Chamber enlargement. Regurgitant and stenotic valve lesions. The contractility of both ventricles. And the inflow patterns across the mitral and tricuspid valves.

Why is this the view for chamber size? [[Because it's the one basic view where you can put the right ventricle directly beside the left.]] Normally the right is clearly the smaller. When it becomes as large as the left, it's in trouble. You'll use that comparison again and again.

And here's why TAPSE and MAPSE belong to this view. As each ventricle contracts, its valve ring, the annulus, is pulled down towards the apex. From the apex, that movement runs straight along the ultrasound beam, towards the probe.

So you drop an M-mode cursor through the lateral edge of the tricuspid annulus, and you get a trace of that point rising and falling over time. The height of that excursion is TAPSE, tricuspid annular plane systolic excursion. Do the same at the mitral annulus, and you have MAPSE.

[[TAPSE and MAPSE are the same measurement on two sides. How far the valve ring travels towards the apex in systole.]]

Think of it as a ruler laid along the length of the heart. The beam is the ruler, and the annulus is the point that slides along it.

So what counts as normal, and what counts as failure?

steps.bridge: MAPSE below about 10 mm is abnormal; for TAPSE the true cut-off is under 17 mm. Next: the other signs of RV overload →

lesson.text:
This card gives the bands for five measures of systolic function. Don't learn it as a grid of numbers. Learn the two you'll use, and the one that runs backwards.

Start with the ejection fraction. Normal is fifty-five percent or more. Mildly reduced, forty-five to fifty-four. Moderate, thirty to forty-four. Severe, below thirty. Fractional shortening follows the same direction, normal at twenty-five percent or more.

Now the two annular excursions.

MAPSE. Normal is eleven millimetres or more. Nine to ten is mild. Six to eight is moderate. Below six is severe. So, in round terms, [[MAPSE below about ten millimetres means left ventricular long-axis dysfunction.]]

TAPSE. Normal is seventeen millimetres or more. Eleven to sixteen is mild. Six to ten is moderate. Below six is severe. [[TAPSE below seventeen millimetres means right ventricular systolic dysfunction.]]

{{ | Normal | Mild | Moderate | Severe
EF (%) | ≥55 | 45–54 | 30–44 | <30
FS (%) | ≥25 | 20–24 | 15–19 | <15
MSS (mm) | <10 | 7–12 | 13–24 | >24
MAPSE (mm) | ≥11 | 9–10 | 6–8 | <6
TAPSE (mm) | ≥17 | 11–16 | 6–10 | <6}}

A trap on the printed card. It once gave the normal TAPSE as sixteen to twenty. The current chamber guideline from the American and European echo societies sets the cut-off at seventeen, with no upper limit. A healthy TAPSE is often around twenty-four.

Why does TAPSE work so well for the right ventricle? Because the right ventricle ejects mostly by shortening along its length. So one point on its annulus captures much of its pump. The left ventricle also twists and squeezes inwards, so MAPSE tells only part of its story. But it's the part that often fails first, and in sepsis a low MAPSE carries prognostic weight.

And the row that runs backwards is MSS, the mitral to septal separation. It's the gap between the opening mitral leaflet and the septum. In a good heart the leaflet nearly touches the septum, so low is normal and high is bad. It's also called E-point septal separation. Its printed normal and mild bands overlap, so keep the direction, not the digits. The wider the gap, the weaker the ventricle.

The ejection fraction, fractional shortening and MSS come from the long axis. MAPSE and TAPSE come from the apical four-chamber.

So TAPSE is one number. What else tells you the right ventricle is overloaded?

steps.bridge: TAPSE under 17 mm sits with a dilated RV and plethoric IVC. Next: why TAPSE alone can mislead →

lesson.text:
You met these seven signs in the lesson on ultrasound in undifferentiated shock. Size, function and pressure. A right ventricle as big as the left. A TAPSE below seventeen, a fractional area change below thirty-five percent, and free-wall strain below twenty percent. A fast tricuspid jet, a distended IVC, and a thick wall that dates it as chronic.

Here's why it matters today. [[TAPSE is one sign among seven. Read it with the size of the ventricle and the IVC, never alone.]] A low TAPSE beside a small right ventricle and a collapsing IVC tells a very different story.

Why never alone? Look at its limits.

steps.bridge: TAPSE is load and angle dependent, so it reflects afterload too. Next: how ventilation loads the RV in ARDS →

lesson.text:
Every measure of right ventricular function has a weakness. The panel won't ask for all seven. But it will ask about TAPSE, so start there.

[[TAPSE is load and angle dependent.]] Take those one at a time.

Angle first. TAPSE is the distance one point travels along the beam. If the cursor doesn't line up with the direction the annulus moves, you measure only part of that travel, and the TAPSE reads low.

Load second, and this is the one that matters in intensive care. TAPSE measures how far the ventricle shortens against whatever it's pushing into right now. Raise the pulmonary vascular resistance, and a perfectly healthy muscle shortens less.

Think of judging an engine by how far the car travels in a minute. On the flat, it's a fair guide. On a steep hill, a good engine covers less ground. TAPSE is the distance travelled. The afterload is the hill.

So the number on its own can't tell you whether the muscle is weak or the hill is steep.

Now the others, briefly. Fractional area change needs the endocardial border traced accurately, and the right ventricle's border is hard to trace. RIMP, the right ventricular index of myocardial performance, is unreliable when the right atrial pressure is high, or the rhythm is irregular, as in atrial fibrillation. Notice the irony. Those are exactly the patients who need it. The pulsed tissue Doppler S prime is angle dependent, and assumes every segment behaves like the one you sampled. IVA, the isovolumic acceleration, is load and angle dependent and varies with age and heart rate. The ejection fraction on two-dimensional echo is unreliable, because the right ventricle isn't a simple shape. And three-dimensional echo is accurate but rarely at hand.

{{Measure | Limitation
RVEF 2D | unreliable
FAC | needs accurate border tracing
**TAPSE** | **load and angle dependent**
RIMP | unreliable with high RA pressure or AF
IVA | load and angle dependent; varies with age, HR
S′ | angle dependent; assumes uniform segments
RVEF 3D | not readily available}}

[[Four of the seven depend on the angle. And the measures the ICU uses most depend on the load.]]

So what puts the steepest hill in front of the right ventricle in your ICU? Very often, the ventilator.

steps.bridge: PEEP and high plateau raise PVR and strain the RV. Next: how to read a low TAPSE on the ventilator →

lesson.text:
In ARDS, right ventricular dysfunction is common. It's found in twenty-two to fifty-five percent of patients, depending on how it's defined and looked for. And it matters. [[Survival is much higher in ARDS without right ventricular dysfunction.]]

Why is the right ventricle so vulnerable here? Because it's a thin-walled chamber, built to push into a low-pressure circuit. It copes well with more volume, and badly with more pressure. Raise its afterload suddenly, and it dilates and fails.

And in ARDS, almost everything raises that afterload. The card lists five factors. Hypoxia, which constricts the pulmonary vessels. Hypercarbia, and the respiratory acidosis that comes with it, which constrict them further. High PEEP. And positive pressure ventilation itself.

How does positive pressure do it? The small vessels around the alveoli run through the lung tissue. When you inflate the alveoli with a high pressure, those vessels are squeezed and stretched thin. [[So high PEEP and high plateau pressures raise the pulmonary vascular resistance, and the right ventricle feels it with every breath.]]

Now look at that list again. Four of the five are things the ventilator either causes or can correct. That's the good news.

So the response is right ventricle protective ventilation, and it has three parts. Minimise the plateau and driving pressures. Lower the pulmonary vascular resistance by improving the PaO2 and the PaCO2. And prone the patient.

{{**RV-protective ventilation**
Minimise plateau and driving pressure · Correct PaO₂ and PaCO₂ to lower PVR · Prone positioning}}

Why prone? You learned it as an oxygenation manoeuvre. But turning the patient opens the collapsed dorsal lung, so the same breath spreads more evenly, plateau pressure often falls, and the CO2 clears better. [[Prone positioning appears here as a right ventricular manoeuvre, not only an oxygenation one.]]

And you'll recognise the first part from the ventilation lessons. The driving pressure you keep low to protect the lung also protects the right ventricle. One setting, two organs.

So now bring it back to the bedside. You find a low TAPSE in a ventilated patient. What do you do with it?

This is the question the panel really wants answered. What do TAPSE and MAPSE tell you, and what does a low TAPSE mean on a ventilator?

Start with the two measurements, cleanly. TAPSE is the long-axis movement of the tricuspid annulus, on M-mode, in the apical four-chamber view. Below seventeen millimetres is right ventricular systolic dysfunction. MAPSE is the same movement at the mitral annulus. Below about ten is left ventricular long-axis dysfunction, and in sepsis a low MAPSE carries prognostic weight.

Now the core idea. [[Both measure shortening against the current load, not pure contractility.]] So on the ventilator, a low TAPSE may be the ventilator, not the myocardium.

Take Patient A. Severe ARDS, a plateau of thirty-two, a PaCO2 of seventy, and a TAPSE of thirteen. Is his right ventricle weak? Perhaps. But his afterload is very high. So before you call it failure, look for the picture of acute cor pulmonale.

What is that picture? A right ventricle that has dilated, with an end-diastolic area more than about six-tenths of the left. When it equals or exceeds the left, that's severe. A septum that flattens, or moves the wrong way, because the right ventricular pressure is pushing it into the left. And a full, plethoric IVC.

{{**Acute cor pulmonale:** RV/LV end-diastolic area >0.6 (severe ≥1) + septal flattening or dyskinesia + plethoric IVC}}

If Patient A has that picture, your first treatment isn't a drug. It's the ventilator. Lower the plateau and driving pressures. Correct the hypoxia and the CO2, to bring the pulmonary vascular resistance down. And prone him.

Then look again. If the TAPSE recovers as the load falls, the muscle was never the problem.

[[A low TAPSE in a ventilated patient is a question about load, before it's a verdict on the muscle.]]

One honest caution. These numbers are simple and repeatable, which is why we love them. But they are still single numbers. Always pair TAPSE with the size of the right ventricle, the shape of the septum and the IVC. And pair MAPSE with the whole look of the left ventricle.

spine: What it is: the core views are subcostal, apical 4-chamber, parasternal long and short axis, and pleural scanning, as in the FATE sequence; I add the IVC from subcostal.
TAPSE and MAPSE: both are measured on M-mode in apical 4-chamber. **TAPSE under 17 mm** means RV systolic dysfunction; **MAPSE under about 10 mm** means LV long-axis dysfunction.
Why it matters: both are simple and repeatable. In sepsis a low MAPSE carries prognostic weight.
On the ventilator: a low TAPSE may reflect afterload, because PEEP and plateau pressure raise PVR. RV dysfunction affects **22–55%** of ARDS and worsens survival.
What I do: look for acute cor pulmonale, then protect the RV: lower plateau and driving pressure, correct PaCO2 and hypoxia, and prone.
Caution: both are load and angle dependent. I never read one number alone; I pair it with RV size, septal shape and the IVC.

open.text:
Let me start where the last lesson left us, with a probe in your hand.

Your patient is on the second day of septic shock. Ventilated, on noradrenaline, and the lactate isn't clearing. Someone at the bedside asks the question that decides the next hour. Is it the vessels, or is it the pump? And if it's the pump, which side?

Over the sepsis lessons, we kept reaching for the echo. A TAPSE below seventeen. A low MAPSE in septic cardiomyopathy. Today we learn where those numbers come from. Which windows you open, in what order, and what each one is for.

This question opens a new block, the failing pump. First, how to see the heart. Then cardiogenic shock and how to treat it. Then the machines that support it, and the trials behind them. Then a heart that fails in pregnancy. And finally, a heart that is squeezed from outside, in tamponade.

So what is the professor really checking here? Three things. Do you know the basic windows, and why each one earns its place? Do you know what TAPSE and MAPSE physically measure, and their cut-offs? And do you know the trap? [[A low TAPSE on a ventilator may be the ventilator, not the muscle.]] The resident who calls that right ventricular failure, and reaches for an inotrope, has missed the load.

So here's the plan. First, the five basic views. Then the long axis, and the apical four-chamber, where TAPSE and MAPSE live. Then the normal and abnormal bands. Then the limits of these numbers. And finally, the right ventricle on the ventilator.

close.text:
So let's bring it together.

The core views are the subcostal, the apical four-chamber, the parasternal long and short axis, and pleural scanning. That's the FATE sequence. And from the subcostal window, I add the IVC.

[[TAPSE and MAPSE are measured on M-mode in the apical four-chamber view. TAPSE below seventeen millimetres means right ventricular dysfunction. MAPSE below about ten means left ventricular long-axis dysfunction.]]

Why they matter: both are simple and repeatable, and in sepsis a low MAPSE carries prognostic weight.

On the ventilator: a low TAPSE may reflect afterload, because PEEP and plateau pressure raise the pulmonary vascular resistance. Right ventricular dysfunction affects twenty-two to fifty-five percent of ARDS, and worsens survival.

What I do: look for acute cor pulmonale, then protect the right ventricle. Lower plateau and driving pressure, correct the CO2 and the hypoxia, and prone.

And the caution: both are load and angle dependent. I never read one number alone.

That's your answer. The views, the measurements, why they matter, the ventilator, and the caution.

But here's something to carry forward. Today the pump was mostly loaded from outside. Now picture a man with a large anterior infarct. Cold hands, a falling pressure, crackles to his shoulders. This time the muscle itself has failed. How do you stage that shock, how do you tell its types apart, and which type gets a diuretic and which a vasopressor? That's next. Cardiogenic shock.

questions.text: Cardiogenic shock — types, SCAI staging, treatment. Which phenotype gets diuretics, which gets vasopressors?

steps.bridge: SCAI runs from at risk to extremis; stage C is hypoperfusion needing more than fluid. Next: how to phenotype the shock at the bedside →

lesson.text:
Start with severity. Cardiogenic shock isn't one thing. It's a spectrum, from a patient who might crash to one who is crashing. In twenty nineteen, the Society for Cardiovascular Angiography and Interventions, SCAI, gave that spectrum a common language, and refined it in twenty twenty-two. Five stages, A to E.

Stage A is at risk. Risk factors for shock, such as a large infarct or acute heart failure, but no signs of it yet.

Stage B is beginning. Relative hypotension or a tachycardia, but no hypoperfusion. The pressure is slipping, but the tissues are still being fed.

Stage C is classic. [[Hypoperfusion that needs more than volume. An inotrope, a vasopressor, or mechanical support.]] Usually with a relative hypotension.

Stage D is deteriorating. Like C, but failing to respond to the first interventions, and getting worse.

Stage E is extremis. Supported by several interventions at once, and perhaps in cardiac arrest, with CPR or ECMO running.

And across all of them sits a modifier, the letter A, for arrest. It marks a patient who has needed CPR, including defibrillation.

{{**SCAI stages**
A At risk · B Beginning (hypotension or tachycardia, no hypoperfusion) · **C Classic (hypoperfusion needing more than volume)** · D Deteriorating · E Extremis
Modifier **A** = cardiac arrest}}

Now here's the point of the whole scale. [[The boundary between B and C is hypoperfusion.]] Stage B has a low pressure with normal tissues. Stage C has tissues that are starving, and volume alone won't fix them. That's where the drugs, and perhaps the machines, begin.

Why does staging matter? Because it gives the team a shared word for how sick the patient is, and risk climbs with each stage. Patient A, cold and wet with a lactate of four, is at least stage C. Patient B is hypoperfused too. If fluid alone doesn't fix her, she's stage C as well.

So we know how sick they are. Now, what kind of shock is it?

steps.bridge: Cold or warm is perfusion; wet or dry is congestion. Next: which treatment each profile gets →

lesson.text:
In the nineteen seventies, James Forrester and his colleagues, using the new pulmonary artery catheter in patients after myocardial infarction, sorted them by two numbers. The cardiac index, for flow. And the wedge pressure, for congestion. The cut-offs were a cardiac index of two point two litres per minute per square metre, and a wedge pressure of eighteen millimetres of mercury. Four groups fell out, and their outlook differed sharply.

Today we use the same grid with words you can find at the bedside. Two questions. Is he warm or cold? That's perfusion. Is he wet or dry? That's congestion.

{{pic}}

Cold and wet is classic cardiogenic shock. The cardiac index is low, the systemic resistance is high as the body clamps down, and the wedge pressure is high. That's Patient A.

Cold and dry is euvolaemic cardiogenic shock. A low cardiac index and a high resistance, but a normal wedge pressure. That's Patient B, who has been vomiting.

Warm and wet is vasodilatory cardiogenic shock, or mixed shock. The cardiac index is low, but the resistance is low or normal, and the wedge pressure is high. Think of the infarct patient who also has sepsis, or a big inflammatory response after the infarct.

And warm and dry. A high cardiac index, a low resistance, a low wedge pressure. That's vasodilatory shock, and it is not cardiogenic shock at all.

[[Warm and dry is the only quadrant with a raised cardiac index. Three of the four have a low index, and that is what makes them cardiogenic.]]

One honest caution about the words. In Forrester's grid, warm meant a cardiac index above two point two. In the shock grid, warm means the vessels are dilated. So a warm and wet patient in shock still has a low index.

How do you tell at the bedside? Cold means cool, mottled extremities, a slow capillary refill, a narrow pulse pressure, confusion, and a falling urine output. Wet means orthopnoea, crackles, a raised JVP, oedema, and B-lines on lung ultrasound.

So the grid is two questions, and each answer points to a different treatment. Let's see which.
lesson.cap: Cold or warm is perfusion; wet or dry is congestion. Warm and dry is not cardiogenic shock.

steps.bridge: Wet gets diuretic, but cold and wet needs perfusion restored first. Next: which vasoactive drug fits each subtype →

lesson.text:
This card is the ESC bedside algorithm for acute heart failure. It uses the same two questions, warm or cold, wet or dry, and gives a treatment for each profile.

First, a sense of proportion. [[About ninety-five percent of patients with acute heart failure are wet. Only five percent are dry.]] Congestion is the rule. So the real decision is usually about perfusion.

Wet and warm. Congested but perfused. If the problem is mainly a high blood pressure, the vascular type, give a vasodilator with a diuretic. If the problem is mainly fluid, the cardiac type, give a diuretic with a vasodilator, and ultrafiltration if the diuretic fails.

Wet and cold is where the danger is, and the card splits it at a systolic pressure of ninety.

With a systolic below ninety, give an inotropic agent, and add a vasopressor if the pressure stays refractory. That's the order in this heart failure algorithm. Hold it lightly. The next card puts noradrenaline first, and I'll show you why both are right. Go to mechanical support if the drugs don't work. And the diuretic? Only once perfusion is corrected.

Why wait? Because a diuretic lowers preload. In a heart that is already failing to deliver flow, taking away filling can drop the output further. And a kidney with poor blood flow responds poorly to a diuretic anyway.

[[In cold and wet, restore perfusion first. The diuretic comes once the patient is warm.]] Give it first, and you can deepen the shock.

With a systolic of ninety or more, a cold and wet patient can usually take a vasodilator and a diuretic, with an inotrope only if he's refractory.

Dry and warm is compensated. Adjust the oral therapy.

And dry and cold is hypoperfused and hypovolaemic. Give a fluid challenge, and an inotrope if he's still hypoperfused.

{{Profile | Treatment
Wet & warm, vascular | vasodilator + diuretic
Wet & warm, cardiac | diuretic + vasodilator; UF if resistant
**Wet & cold, SBP <90** | **inotrope; vasopressor if refractory; diuretic once perfused; MCS if no response**
Wet & cold, SBP ≥90 | vasodilator + diuretic
Dry & warm | adjust oral therapy
Dry & cold | fluid challenge; inotrope if still hypoperfused}}

So back to our patients. Patient A, cold and wet with a pressure of eighty-five, gets perfusion restored first, and his diuretic later. Patient B, cold and dry, gets a careful fluid challenge.

But which vasoactive drug, exactly?

steps.bridge: Noradrenaline is the vasopressor of choice; dopamine is not an equal option. Next: where each treatment sits on the escalation ladder →

lesson.text:
This card matches a vasoactive drug to each subtype of shock. And it carries a correction worth knowing.

Classic, cold and wet. The cardiac index is low and the resistance is high. [[Noradrenaline is the vasopressor of first choice, with an inotrope added once the patient is stable, and after revascularisation.]]

Why noradrenaline? Its alpha effect raises the perfusion pressure, including the pressure that drives blood into the coronary arteries, and its modest beta-one effect supports the heart without driving the rate too hard.

So the last card said inotrope first, and this one says noradrenaline first. Is that a contradiction? No. The heart failure algorithm is written for acute heart failure as a whole, where many patients have a low output with a pressure that is only just holding. There, an inotrope to raise the flow is the first move. Established cardiogenic shock is usually more hypotensive, and below a certain pressure nothing is perfused, the heart included. So restore the pressure first, then add the inotrope for flow. [[Let the pressure choose the order. If the pressure is too low, noradrenaline first. If it holds but the flow is low, an inotrope first.]] And both cards agree on the diuretic. It waits until perfusion is back.

Now the correction. An older American statement listed noradrenaline or dopamine side by side. That's out of date. In the SOAP two trial, De Backer and colleagues compared dopamine with noradrenaline in patients with shock. Dopamine caused more arrhythmias across the trial. And in the cardiogenic shock subgroup, it was linked with more deaths. [[Dopamine is not an equal option in cardiogenic shock.]]

Euvolaemic, cold and dry. The same drugs, plus small fluid boluses, because the left ventricular filling pressure may be low, and these patients may tolerate fluid.

Vasodilatory, warm and wet, or mixed. This subtype has a low systemic resistance. So noradrenaline, guided by the haemodynamics.

Right ventricular shock. Here the goals change. Keep the preload up with fluid boluses. Lower the right ventricular afterload with inhaled pulmonary vasodilators. Treat bradycardia and keep atrioventricular synchrony. And for pressure, noradrenaline or vasopressin. [[Vasopressin raises the systemic resistance with a neutral effect on the pulmonary resistance.]] That's why it's singled out when the right ventricle is the weak side.

And normotensive shock. Hypoperfused, but the systolic is above ninety, with a high resistance. Here an inotrope first may be enough.

{{Subtype | Vasoactive
Cold & wet (classic) | **noradrenaline** first; add inotrope once stable, after revascularisation
Cold & dry | as above + small fluid boluses
Warm & wet / mixed | noradrenaline, haemodynamics-guided
RV shock | fluids; NA or **vasopressin**; inotropes; inhaled pulmonary vasodilators
Normotensive (SBP >90) | inotrope or vasopressor}}

So the drugs are matched. But drugs are only the first rung of a ladder.

steps.bridge: Drugs and reperfusion come before temporary support. Next: what the IABP trial showed →

lesson.text:
This card is the management ladder for cardiogenic shock. And it starts with a place, not a drug.

The patient often starts in a spoke hospital. The ladder points him to a cardiogenic shock hub, a centre that can offer every rung.

Rung one is resuscitation and medical therapy. Inotropes and vasopressors. Mechanical ventilation if needed. And therapy for the specific cause.

Rung two is reperfusion, PCI, CABG or fibrinolysis. [[But reperfusion is for acute coronary syndromes only. It's not a universal rung.]] In an infarct, opening the culprit vessel early is the single most important step.

Rung three is temporary mechanical support. An intra-aortic balloon pump, a percutaneous ventricular assist device, ECMO, or an implantable assist device.

Rung four is the durable destination. A heart transplant, or a permanent ventricular assist device.

{{**Spoke → shock hub**
1 Resuscitation + medical therapy · 2 Reperfusion (**ACS only**) · 3 Temporary MCS · 4 Durable: transplant or destination VAD
**Recovery** and **palliation**: exits at every rung}}

And here's the part residents miss. [[Recovery and palliation are exits at every rung, in both directions.]] A patient can recover and step down from any level. And palliation isn't the end of the ladder. It runs alongside the whole of it.

So drugs and reperfusion come before machines. And the first machine most of us reach for is the balloon pump. Did it work?

steps.bridge: IABP gave no mortality benefit, so it is not routine. Next: does any device improve survival →

lesson.text:
The intra-aortic balloon pump inflates in diastole, to push blood back into the coronary arteries, and deflates just before systole, to lower the afterload. For decades, it was the reflex in infarct shock.

Then came IABP-SHOCK two, published in twenty twelve. Patients with cardiogenic shock after myocardial infarction were randomised to a balloon pump or no balloon pump. [[At thirty days, there was no difference in mortality.]]

So the recommendation followed. The balloon pump is not routinely recommended in cardiogenic shock. The twenty twenty-three ESC guideline on acute coronary syndromes makes routine use a class three. It keeps a place in the mechanical complications, such as a ruptured septum, which you'll meet later in this block.

But know the limitation, because a sharp panel will ask. The trial included only mild to moderate cases of shock. The most severe end was never tested. [[A negative trial in a restricted population is not the same as saying the device never works.]]

So what about stronger machines?

Is there a role for mechanical circulatory support in cardiogenic shock? Here's the evidence in one sweep. We'll take each trial apart in the next question.

The balloon pump first. IABP-SHOCK two found no thirty-day mortality benefit. So it's not routine.

Then ECMO. ECLS-SHOCK, in the New England Journal in twenty twenty-three, gave routine early VA-ECMO in infarct shock. Thirty-day mortality was forty-seven point eight percent against forty-nine percent. No difference. And there was more bleeding, and more vascular complications such as limb ischaemia. Remember why it might fail. ECMO pumps blood back up the aorta, and that raises the afterload on the left ventricle.

Then the microaxial pump, the Impella. DanGer Shock, in the same journal in twenty twenty-four. Three hundred and sixty patients with ST elevation infarct shock, a lactate of two point five or more, and an ejection fraction below forty-five percent. Comatose patients after an out of hospital arrest were excluded. [[At one hundred and eighty days, mortality was forty-five point eight percent against fifty-eight point five. A number needed to treat of eight.]] The pump draws blood out of the left ventricle into the aorta. It unloads the ventricle.

{{**IABP-SHOCK II:** no 30-day benefit
**ECLS-SHOCK (2023):** 30-day 47.8% vs 49.0%; more bleeding, vascular complications
**DanGer Shock (2024):** 180-day **45.8% vs 58.5%**, HR 0.74, **NNT 8**
Harms: complications 24% vs 6%; RRT 42% vs 27%}}

But that benefit had a price. Composite complications, meaning bleeding, limb ischaemia and haemolysis, were twenty-four percent against six. And renal replacement therapy, forty-two percent against twenty-seven.

The twenty twenty-five American guideline on acute coronary syndromes reflects this. The microaxial flow pump gets a two-a recommendation for selected patients with ST elevation infarct shock. Routine balloon pumps and routine VA-ECMO get a class three, no benefit.

So what's your answer to the panel? [[Yes, for a selected patient. Infarct shock, a low ejection fraction, not comatose, in a hub centre, as rung three after drugs and reperfusion. Not routine for all.]]

spine: What it is: low output with hypoperfusion. SCAI stages it from **A (at risk)** to **E (extremis)**; stage C needs more than fluid.
Phenotype: cold and wet is classic shock; cold and dry is euvolaemic; warm and wet is vasodilatory or mixed.
What I do: cold and wet gets **noradrenaline plus an inotrope**, then a diuretic once perfused. Cold and dry gets cautious fluid. Warm and wet needs a vasopressor.
Caution: noradrenaline, not dopamine; in SOAP II dopamine gave more arrhythmias overall and more deaths in the cardiogenic shock subgroup. Reperfuse the culprit early.
Evidence: IABP-SHOCK II and ECLS-SHOCK (VA-ECMO) showed no benefit. **DanGer Shock** (Impella in STEMI shock, n=360) cut 180-day mortality **45.8% vs 58.5%**, NNT 8.
Trade-off: that benefit cost more bleeding, vascular complications needing intervention and renal replacement, so the device is for selected patients in a hub centre.

open.text:
Let me start with two patients, both with cardiogenic shock after a heart attack.

Patient A is cold to the knees and grey. His blood pressure is eighty-five systolic, he's breathless at forty-five degrees, and there are crackles to both mid-zones. His lactate is four.

Patient B also has cold hands and a lactate of four. But her chest is clear, her neck veins are flat, and she's been vomiting for a day.

Both are failing pumps. But one is drowning, and the other is dry. And if you give them the same treatment, you'll hurt one of them.

This is a scenario question with a sting in its tail. Which phenotype gets diuretics, and which gets vasopressors? What the professor is really checking is whether you can classify before you treat. Stage the severity. Then read the profile at the bedside, warm or cold, wet or dry. Then match the drug to the profile.

And there are two traps. [[The first is the diuretic given too early, in a patient who is cold and wet.]] The second is dopamine offered as an equal choice to noradrenaline.

So here's the plan. First, the SCAI stages. Then the four profiles. Then the treatment for each. Then the right vasoactive drug for each subtype. Then where machines sit on the ladder. And finally, the trial evidence for those machines.

close.text:
So let's bring it together.

Cardiogenic shock is low output with hypoperfusion. SCAI stages it from A, at risk, to E, extremis. [[Stage C is hypoperfusion that needs more than fluid.]]

The phenotype. Cold and wet is classic shock. Cold and dry is euvolaemic. Warm and wet is vasodilatory or mixed. And warm and dry is not cardiogenic at all.

What I do. Cold and wet gets noradrenaline plus an inotrope, and a diuretic once perfused. Cold and dry gets cautious fluid. Warm and wet needs a vasopressor.

The cautions. [[Noradrenaline, not dopamine, which causes more arrhythmias in cardiogenic shock. And in infarct shock, reperfuse the culprit vessel early.]]

The evidence. The balloon pump and routine VA-ECMO showed no benefit. DanGer Shock, with the Impella in infarct shock, cut one hundred and eighty day mortality from fifty-eight point five to forty-five point eight percent, a number needed to treat of eight. But at the cost of more bleeding, limb ischaemia and dialysis. So the device is for selected patients, in a hub centre.

That's your answer. The stages, the phenotypes, the drugs, the ladder and the evidence.

But here's a puzzle to carry forward. ECMO gives full flow and full gas exchange. The Impella gives less flow, and no gas exchange. Yet in the trials, the smaller machine won. Same disease, opposite verdicts. Why? That's the next question. The evidence for mechanical circulatory support, trial by trial.

questions.text: What is the evidence for mechanical circulatory support in cardiogenic shock?

steps.bridge: Routine early VA-ECMO did not lower 30-day mortality and doubled bleeding. Next: did an LV-unloading pump do better →

lesson.text:
ECLS-SHOCK was published in the New England Journal in twenty twenty-three.

The population. Four hundred and twenty patients with cardiogenic shock from an infarct, a lactate above three, and early revascularisation planned. And notice one detail, because it matters later. [[About seventy-eight percent had been resuscitated from cardiac arrest.]]

The arms. Early, routine VA-ECMO, started before the PCI, on top of standard care. Against PCI and standard care alone.

The result. Death at thirty days was forty-seven point eight percent with ECMO, against forty-nine percent without. A relative risk of zero point nine eight. No difference.

And the harms. Moderate or severe bleeding, twenty-three point four percent against nine point six. More than double. Limb ischaemia and other vascular complications needing an intervention, eleven percent against three point eight, nearly three times as common.

{{**ECLS-SHOCK (NEJM 2023)** · n = 420 · infarct CS, lactate >3 · ~78% post-arrest
30-day death **47.8% vs 49.0%** (RR 0.98)
Bleeding **23.4% vs 9.6%** · vascular complications **11.0% vs 3.8%**}}

[[So routine early VA-ECMO did not lower thirty-day mortality, and it doubled bleeding.]] An earlier and smaller trial, ECMO-CS, in twenty twenty-two, was also negative.

Why would the most powerful support fail? Hold that question. First, let's see the trial that went the other way.

steps.bridge: Impella in selected STEMI shock cut 180-day mortality, NNT 8, at a cost in complications. Next: why the two devices diverged →

lesson.text:
DanGer Shock was published in the New England Journal in twenty twenty-four.

The population was chosen with care. Cardiogenic shock from an ST elevation infarct, a lactate of two point five or more, and a left ventricular ejection fraction below forty-five percent. [[And comatose patients after an out of hospital arrest were excluded.]] Hold on to that. It's the sharpest contrast with ECLS-SHOCK.

The arms. A microaxial flow pump, the Impella CP, with standard care, against standard care alone. Three hundred and sixty were randomised. One hundred and seventy-nine against one hundred and seventy-six were analysed.

The result. Death at one hundred and eighty days was forty-five point eight percent with the pump, against fifty-eight point five. A hazard ratio of zero point seven four. [[A number needed to treat of eight. Eight patients treated, one life saved.]]

And the harms. A composite of severe bleeding, limb ischaemia, haemolysis, device failure and worsening aortic regurgitation, twenty-four percent against six point two. A relative risk of four point seven four. And renal replacement therapy, forty-one point nine percent against twenty-six point seven.

{{**DanGer Shock (NEJM 2024)** · STEMI-CS, lactate ≥2.5, LVEF <45% · comatose OHCA excluded · 360 randomised, 179 vs 176 analysed
180-day death **45.8% vs 58.5%** · HR 0.74 · **NNT 8**
Complications **24.0% vs 6.2%** (RR 4.74) · RRT **41.9% vs 26.7%**}}

So it saved lives, and it hurt people. Both at once. Your notes add two points. The benefit seems greatest when the pump goes in before an arrest. And this work belongs in centres that see many of these patients.

So why did the two trials diverge?

Same disease, opposite verdicts. There are three explanations, and a good answer gives all three.

The first is what each device does to the left ventricle.

Think about where VA-ECMO returns its blood. Through a cannula in the femoral artery, pumping up the aorta, against the direction the heart ejects. So the failing ventricle now has to open its aortic valve against that pressure. [[ECMO supports the circulation, but it raises the afterload on the left ventricle.]] A weak ventricle may fail to eject at all. It distends, its filling pressure rises, and the lungs flood. In ECLS-SHOCK, only a small minority had the ventricle vented.

The Impella does the opposite. It sits across the aortic valve, draws blood from inside the left ventricle, and pushes it into the aorta. [[The Impella unloads the left ventricle. It lowers its volume, its pressure and its work.]]

You can see it on a pressure-volume loop.

{{pic}}

With peripheral ECMO, the loop moves right and up. A bigger, higher-pressure ventricle, ejecting less. With the Impella, the loop shrinks and moves left. A smaller, less stretched ventricle, doing far less work.

The second explanation is the patients. ECLS-SHOCK was mostly patients after cardiac arrest, many of whom die of brain injury whatever the heart does. DanGer Shock excluded comatose arrests. So it studied patients whose outcome the heart could still decide.

The third is time. ECLS-SHOCK measured death at thirty days. DanGer Shock at one hundred and eighty.

{{ | ECLS-SHOCK | DanGer Shock
Device | VA-ECMO | Impella CP
LV | afterload ↑ | **unloaded**
Mortality | 30 d: 47.8 vs 49.0% | 180 d: **45.8 vs 58.5%**
Verdict | negative | positive, NNT 8
Harms | bleeding, limb ischaemia | more complications too}}

[[So these were not head-to-head trials. Different devices, different patients, different follow-up.]] Never say the Impella beat ECMO.

And the guideline. The twenty twenty-five American guideline on acute coronary syndromes gives the microaxial flow pump a two-a recommendation in selected ST elevation infarct shock. Routine balloon pumps and routine VA-ECMO get a class three, no benefit.

One honest caution. The Impella roughly quadrupled complications, and raised dialysis from twenty-seven to forty-two percent. So the device is for chosen patients. Non-comatose infarct shock, a low ejection fraction, in a centre that does this often. Not a routine for all.
lesson.cap: Peripheral VA-ECMO raises LV afterload and shifts the loop right; Impella unloads it and shifts it left.

spine: What it is: three trials frame it. **IABP-SHOCK II** found no 30-day mortality benefit, so IABP is not routine.
ECLS-SHOCK (NEJM 2023): routine early VA-ECMO in infarct shock, n=420. 30-day mortality **47.8% vs 49.0%**, with more bleeding and vascular complications (limb ischaemia).
Why ECMO may have failed: it raises LV afterload and few were vented; most were post-arrest; complications offset gain. Patients and follow-up differ, so not head-to-head.
DanGer Shock (NEJM 2024): Impella CP in STEMI shock, lactate ≥2.5 and LVEF <45%, comatose arrests excluded. 180-day mortality **45.8% vs 58.5%**, NNT 8.
Who benefits: selected non-comatose STEMI shock with low EF; the pump unloads the LV. 2025 ACC/AHA: microaxial pump **2a**; routine IABP and VA-ECMO **class 3**.
Caution: Impella raised complications about four-fold (**24% vs 6%**) and renal replacement **42% vs 27%**. Device support is for chosen patients, not a routine for all.

open.text:
Let me start with a paradox.

Two machines for the same failing heart. The first is the most powerful support we have. It takes over the whole circulation and the lungs as well, and can pump four or five litres a minute. The second is a thin pump on a catheter, sitting across the aortic valve, and it gives less flow.

Both were tested in infarct shock, in large randomised trials, in the same journal, a year apart. And the big machine lost. The small one won.

This is a trial question. The panel wants the three trials by name, their populations, their results and their harms. But what the professor is really checking is the step after that. [[Can you explain why the two devices diverged? And can you say who should get one?]] The resident who says ECMO failed, so machines don't work, or Impella won, so put one in everybody, has missed the point of both trials.

You already have the balloon pump from the last lesson. IABP-SHOCK two, no thirty-day benefit, so not routine.

So here's the plan. First, ECLS-SHOCK, for ECMO. Then DanGer Shock, for the Impella. And finally, the two side by side, and why they came out opposite.

close.text:
So let's bring it together.

Three trials frame the answer. IABP-SHOCK two found no thirty-day mortality benefit, so the balloon pump is not routine.

ECLS-SHOCK, twenty twenty-three. Routine early VA-ECMO in infarct shock, four hundred and twenty patients. Thirty-day mortality forty-seven point eight against forty-nine percent, with more bleeding and limb ischaemia.

Why ECMO may have failed. It raises the afterload on the left ventricle, and few were vented. Most patients were after an arrest. And the complications offset any gain.

DanGer Shock, twenty twenty-four. The Impella in infarct shock with a lactate of two point five or more and an ejection fraction below forty-five, with comatose arrests excluded. [[One hundred and eighty day mortality forty-five point eight against fifty-eight point five percent. A number needed to treat of eight.]]

Who benefits. Selected, non-comatose patients with infarct shock and a low ejection fraction. The pump unloads the ventricle. The twenty twenty-five guideline: microaxial pump two-a, routine balloon pump and routine ECMO class three.

And the caution. [[The Impella quadrupled complications and raised dialysis. Device support is for chosen patients, not a routine for all.]]

That's your answer. The three trials, why they diverged, who benefits, and the price.

But ECMO hasn't left the stage. It failed as a routine in infarct shock. Yet for the patient who can't come off bypass, or the massive PE, or the arrest that won't respond, it's still the only machine that can take over both the heart and the lungs. So when do you use it, what does it cost the patient, and how do you protect the left ventricle it loads? That's next. VA-ECMO.

questions.text: VA-ECMO - what are the indications and complications?

steps.bridge: VA-ECMO drains venous blood, oxygenates it and pumps it arterially. Next: the circuit and what it bypasses →

lesson.text:
The circuit is simple to say. [[Blood is drawn from the venous system, oxygenated, and pumped into the arterial circulation.]]

So it gives two things at once. Partial or complete support for the heart, because it supplies flow. And oxygenation, because the blood passes through a membrane lung on the way.

That second property is what sets it apart. A balloon pump, an Impella or a surgical assist device can add flow. Only VA-ECMO also does the work of the lungs. So when the heart and the lungs have both failed, or when you don't yet know which has failed, it's the only device that covers both.

steps.bridge: It bypasses both the RV and the lungs, centrally or peripherally. Next: the listed indications and contraindications →

lesson.text:
Now look at the circuit as the right ventricle sees it.

VA-ECMO uses a centrifugal pump. It draws deoxygenated blood from the right atrium, passes it through the oxygenator, and returns it to the arterial system.

So which parts of the patient does that blood skip? [[It bypasses the right ventricle and the pulmonary circulation altogether.]]

That's why it works in right ventricular failure whatever the pulmonary vascular resistance. Compare the Impella RP, a right-sided pump. It has to push blood into the pulmonary artery, so it's limited by the very afterload it's trying to overcome. ECMO simply goes around it.

It can be placed in two ways. Centrally, through a sternotomy, with cannulae in the right atrium and the aorta. That's typical after cardiac surgery, when the chest is already open. Or peripherally, through the femoral vessels, which you can do at the bedside, or even during CPR.

And remember the word peripheral. When the arterial cannula sits in the femoral artery, the blood travels up the aorta against the heart. That's where both of the big complications of this lesson start.

So who should get it?

steps.bridge: Graft failure, post-cardiotomy, RV infarct and PE lead the list. Next: does it help septic cardiomyopathy →

lesson.text:
