This card gives the indications for mechanical support from the right ventricular chapter, and they're worth learning as a group.

Five indications. Primary graft failure after a heart transplant. Right ventricular failure after an LVAD. An inferior myocardial infarction. Cardiogenic shock after cardiac surgery. And pulmonary embolism.

Why inferior, and not anterior? [[Because in most people the right coronary artery supplies both the inferior wall and the right ventricle.]] So an inferior infarct is the classic way to lose the right ventricle.

And notice the second entry. An LVAD supports the left side, but it can unmask a weak right ventricle, which then can't keep up with the flow the LVAD demands.

Three contraindications. Advanced age. Multiple co-morbidities. And irreversible organ injury.

{{**Indications:** primary graft failure · RV failure after LVAD · inferior MI · post-cardiotomy shock · PE
**Contraindications:** advanced age · multiple co-morbidities · irreversible organ injury}}

Here's the logic behind those contraindications. [[ECMO is a bridge. It needs somewhere to go.]] Recovery, a durable device, or a transplant. If the destination doesn't exist, the bridge leads nowhere.

So is there a place for ECMO in septic shock?

steps.bridge: Observational data suggest benefit in septic shock mainly when the EF is very low. Next: what ECMO does to the left ventricle →

lesson.text:
You met septic cardiomyopathy in the sepsis block. A heart stunned by sepsis, usually reversible, if the patient survives long enough. So can ECMO buy that time?

First, what VA-ECMO does to the haemodynamics. It lowers the preload, because it drains the right atrium. It raises the afterload, because it pumps into the arteries. It maintains the mean pressure. And the heart's own output falls.

Now the evidence. It's observational. In one cohort with a cardiac index of three litres per minute per square metre or less, or an ejection fraction of thirty-five percent or less, survival was fifty-one percent with ECMO, against fourteen percent without. And lactate and catecholamine doses fell faster.

A meta-analysis of fourteen studies, four hundred and sixty-eight patients, found overall survival of thirty-six percent. But it depended heavily on the heart. Sixty-two percent with an ejection fraction below twenty percent. Thirty-two percent with an ejection fraction above thirty-five.

{{**VA-ECMO in septic shock (observational)**
CI ≤3 or EF ≤35%: survival **51% vs 14%**
Meta-analysis, 14 studies, 468 pts: overall 36% · **EF <20%: 62%** · EF >35%: 32%}}

[[So ECMO helps cardiogenic septic shock, not purely distributive shock.]] The lower the ejection fraction, the better it does. If the vessels are the problem, not the pump, more flow from a machine adds little.

One honest caution. These are observational data, not randomised trials. They point to who might benefit. They don't prove it.

Now back to that afterload. What does ECMO do to the left ventricle itself?

steps.bridge: Peripheral ECMO fails to unload the LV and raises stroke work. Next: how that played out in the trial →

lesson.text:
The clearest way to see what a device does to the left ventricle is the pressure-volume loop. One loop is one heartbeat. Volume along the bottom, pressure up the side. The width is the stroke volume. And the area inside the loop is the stroke work, a large part of what sets the heart's oxygen use.

This card compares three devices.

The balloon pump makes the loop wider. It lowers the afterload in systole, so the ventricle ejects more. [[The balloon pump buys stroke volume.]]

The Impella and the TandemHeart make the loop smaller. They draw blood out of the left heart and return it to the arteries, so the ventricle fills less and pushes less. Stroke work falls sharply, and so does myocardial oxygen consumption. [[A percutaneous ventricular assist device buys unloading.]]

Peripheral ECMO does neither.

{{pic}}

Look at the left panel. The dashed loop is the shocked ventricle. The red loop is the same ventricle on femoral ECMO. Blood is being pumped up the aorta against it, so the arterial elastance rises, which means the effective afterload rises. The ventricle has to generate more pressure to open its valve. So the loop moves right and up. A bigger, more stretched ventricle, doing more stroke work, with oxygen consumption unchanged, or even higher.

[[Peripheral ECMO fails to unload the left ventricle.]] It supports the body while the ventricle itself works harder.

Now the right panel. The Impella loop shrinks and moves left, and loses its square shape, because the pump is emptying the ventricle all through the cycle.

This is the physiology behind the trials. ECMO rescues the circulation and loads the ventricle. The Impella rescues the ventricle. And it's why the two are sometimes put together.

So how did that afterload play out in infarct shock?
lesson.cap: Peripheral ECMO: loop shifts right and up, LV not unloaded. Impella: loop shrinks and shifts left.

steps.bridge: Routine ECMO in infarct shock did not cut mortality and doubled bleeding. Next: the full complication list and how to vent →

lesson.text:
You met this trial in the last question. ECLS-SHOCK gave routine early VA-ECMO to four hundred and twenty patients with infarct shock, most of them after an arrest. Thirty-day mortality was forty-seven point eight against forty-nine percent. And bleeding more than doubled, twenty-three point four against nine point six, with limb ischaemia eleven against three point eight.

Here's why it matters today. [[Those two harms are the complications you'll list first.]] And the afterload you just saw on the loop is one reason the benefit didn't appear. So let's put the whole picture together.

Here's the full answer, indications, complications, and the one complication you must be able to manage.

The indications. Refractory cardiogenic shock of any cause, beyond drugs, as a bridge to recovery, to a decision, to a durable device or to a transplant. Also shock after cardiac surgery, massive PE, and cardiac arrest, as ECPR. [[It's the only device that gives full biventricular support and gas exchange together.]]

The contraindications. A heart that can't recover with no option of a device or a transplant. Severe aortic regurgitation, because the returning flow would pour back into the ventricle. Aortic dissection. Inability to anticoagulate. And severe peripheral arterial disease, if you plan femoral access.

The complications. Bleeding and limb ischaemia lead the list, as ECLS-SHOCK showed. Then stroke, haemolysis and infection.

And differential hypoxia, also called Harlequin, or north-south, syndrome. Here's how it happens. With femoral cannulation, well-oxygenated blood from the circuit goes up the aorta. If the heart is recovering and ejecting, but the lungs are still poor, the heart sends its own poorly oxygenated blood into the first branches of the aorta, the coronaries and the arteries to the head and right arm. So the lower body is pink and the brain and heart get the dark blood. That's why you monitor oxygen saturation, or a blood gas, from the right arm.

{{**Complications:** bleeding (ECLS-SHOCK 23.4% vs 9.6%) · limb ischaemia (11.0% vs 3.8%) · stroke · haemolysis · infection · **differential (Harlequin) hypoxia**
**LV distension signs:** AV closed · loss of pulsatility · rising PA or wedge pressure · worsening pulmonary oedema}}

Now the one that kills quietly. Left ventricular distension. Retrograde flow raises the afterload. A weak ventricle can't open its aortic valve. So it fills and doesn't empty. It dilates, the left atrial pressure climbs, the lungs flood, and blood sitting still in the ventricle can clot.

[[Watch for it: an aortic valve that stays shut on echo, a flat arterial trace with no pulsatility, a rising wedge pressure, and worsening pulmonary oedema.]]

And how do you vent? Step by step. First, lower the ECMO flow, to reduce the afterload, and add an inotrope to help the ventricle eject. If that fails, unload it mechanically. A balloon pump, or an Impella, which together with ECMO is sometimes called ECPELLA. Or decompress the left atrium, with an atrial septostomy or a surgical vent.

One honest caution. Every step you add to protect the ventricle adds its own bleeding and vascular risk. So vent when the signs appear, not by reflex.

spine: What it is: venous blood drained, oxygenated and pumped back into the arteries. It is the only device giving full biventricular and gas-exchange support.
Indications: refractory cardiogenic shock as a bridge, post-cardiotomy shock, graft failure, massive PE and arrest. In septic cardiomyopathy, observational data favour a **very low EF**.
Complications: bleeding (**23.4% vs 9.6%** in ECLS-SHOCK), limb ischaemia, stroke, haemolysis, infection, and Harlequin hypoxia with femoral cannulation.
Contraindications: no exit (no recovery, VAD or transplant), severe AR, aortic dissection, no anticoagulation, severe PAD. **ECLS-SHOCK**: no routine 30-day benefit.
Why: retrograde flow raises LV afterload. A weak LV distends, the aortic valve stays shut, and pulmonary oedema follows.
What I do: watch pulsatility and the aortic valve on echo. If distended, lower flow and add an inotrope, then vent with IABP, Impella or atrial septostomy.

open.text:
Let me start in the cardiac theatre.

The valve is in. The surgeon tries to come off bypass, and the heart won't take over. The pressure sags, the ventricles look stunned, and two attempts later the anaesthetist is running adrenaline and noradrenaline at doses that frighten everyone. The heart might recover in a few days. But not in the next five minutes.

That's one of the classic reasons to reach for VA-ECMO. A machine that can take over the heart and the lungs together, while the heart rests.

This is a direct question. Indications and complications. But what the professor is really checking is whether you understand what the machine does to the heart it supports. [[VA-ECMO rescues the circulation, but it loads the left ventricle.]] The resident who lists complications and forgets left ventricular distension has missed the one that kills quietly.

So here's the plan. First, the circuit, and what it bypasses. Then the indications and contraindications. Then a special case, septic cardiomyopathy. Then what ECMO does to the left ventricle. Then the trial in infarct shock. And finally, the complications, and how you vent a distended ventricle.

close.text:
So let's bring it together.

VA-ECMO drains venous blood, oxygenates it and pumps it back into the arteries. [[It's the only device that gives full biventricular support and gas exchange.]]

The indications. Refractory cardiogenic shock as a bridge, shock after cardiac surgery, graft failure, massive PE and arrest. In septic cardiomyopathy, observational data favour a very low ejection fraction.

The complications. Bleeding, twenty-three point four against nine point six percent in ECLS-SHOCK. Limb ischaemia, stroke, haemolysis, infection, and Harlequin hypoxia with femoral cannulation.

The contraindications. No exit, meaning no recovery, device or transplant. Severe aortic regurgitation, dissection, no anticoagulation, and severe peripheral arterial disease. And ECLS-SHOCK showed no routine thirty-day benefit.

Why the ventricle suffers. [[Retrograde flow raises the left ventricular afterload. A weak ventricle distends, the aortic valve stays shut, and pulmonary oedema follows.]]

What I do. Watch the pulsatility and the aortic valve on echo. If the ventricle distends, lower the flow and add an inotrope, then vent with a balloon pump, an Impella, or an atrial septostomy.

That's your answer. What it is, the indications, the complications, why the ventricle suffers, and what you do.

Now carry this forward. Picture a woman of twenty-eight, three weeks after the birth of her first child, breathless when she lies flat, with an ejection fraction of twenty-five percent. The pump has failed, but the cause, the drugs, and even the bromocriptine on the chart belong to her alone. That's next. Peripartum cardiomyopathy.

questions.text: What is peripartum cardiomyopathy?

steps.bridge: Peripartum cardiomyopathy is a pregnancy-associated myocardial cause of shock. Next: its definition and drug limits →

lesson.text:
Start by placing it. This card lists the myocardial causes of cardiogenic shock, the causes where the muscle itself fails.

Acute decompensated heart failure comes in two forms. Chronic heart failure of known cause that has decompensated. Or acute heart failure as the first presentation.

Then four other myocardial causes. Chronic ischaemia. Dilated cardiomyopathy. Myocarditis. And stress-induced cardiomyopathy, Takotsubo.

Then two endocrine causes. Thyroid disease, too little or too much. And phaeochromocytoma.

And two that belong to pregnancy. [[Peripartum cardiomyopathy, and coronary artery dissection.]] So in a pregnant or newly delivered woman with a failing heart, these are the two to think of first. One is a disease of the muscle. The other tears a coronary artery and causes an infarct in a young woman, often with no risk factors.

{{**Myocardial causes of CS:** ADHF (decompensated chronic, or first presentation) · chronic ischaemia · DCM · myocarditis · Takotsubo
**Pregnancy:** peripartum cardiomyopathy · coronary artery dissection
**Endocrine:** hypo/hyperthyroidism · phaeochromocytoma}}

So what exactly is peripartum cardiomyopathy?

steps.bridge: EF under 45% around delivery, no other cause; ACE inhibitors wait until after birth. Next: the full drug plan and bromocriptine →

lesson.text:
The definition has three parts, and each one is tested.

The timing. It arises towards the end of pregnancy or in the months after delivery. Your card gives the classic window, the last month of pregnancy to the first five months after birth.

The echo criterion. [[An ejection fraction under forty-five percent.]]

And no other cause. It's a diagnosis of exclusion. You've looked for valve disease, ischaemia, myocarditis, and a cardiomyopathy that was there before the pregnancy, and found none.

Your notes put its frequency at about one in three and a half thousand pregnancies.

Now the drugs, and here's the trap. Before delivery, you avoid the ACE inhibitors and angiotensin receptor blockers. Why? Because, especially in the second and third trimesters, they injure the fetal kidney. After delivery, they're allowed again.

So what do you use before delivery? Beta-blockers. Diuretics, for the congestion. Hydralazine with a nitrate, which take the place of the ACE inhibitor by lowering the afterload and the preload. And digoxin.

{{**PPCM:** end of pregnancy to 5 months postpartum · **EF <45%** · no other cause
**Avoid before delivery:** ACE inhibitors, ARBs (allowed postpartum)
**Use:** β-blocker · diuretic · hydralazine + nitrate · digoxin}}

The prognosis. [[Persistent left ventricular dysfunction means a poor prognosis. And it can recur in a later pregnancy.]] So she needs counselling about contraception and about any future pregnancy.

That's the core. Now the full plan, with the newer drugs and bromocriptine.

Here's the full answer, before delivery, after delivery, and the one drug that belongs to this disease alone.

Start with the definition, cleanly. Heart failure with an ejection fraction below forty-five percent, from late pregnancy to five months after delivery, mostly in the month after delivery, with no other cause.

Before delivery. A beta-blocker, usually metoprolol. Hydralazine with a nitrate, for the afterload. And a loop diuretic, for the congestion. [[Avoid the ACE inhibitor, the ARB, the ARNI, the mineralocorticoid antagonist and the SGLT2 inhibitor, because of fetal harm or too little safety data.]] Your patient's whole modern heart failure toolkit is locked away until the baby is born.

After delivery, the lock comes off. Full guideline-directed therapy. And if she's breastfeeding, enalapril or captopril are acceptable.

Now bromocriptine, and the idea behind it. Prolactin, the hormone of lactation, can be cut into a smaller sixteen kilodalton fragment under oxidative stress. That fragment is thought to injure the small vessels and the heart muscle. Bromocriptine stops the pituitary releasing prolactin. So it's an attempt to remove the toxin at its source.

The dose. If uncomplicated, two point five milligrams once daily for one week. If the ejection fraction is below twenty-five percent, or she's in shock, two point five milligrams twice daily for two weeks, then once daily for six weeks. [[And always with at least prophylactic anticoagulation.]] Why? Because bromocriptine has been linked to thrombotic events, the weeks after delivery are a hypercoagulable time, and a dilated, poorly contracting heart is itself prone to clot. If there's a thrombus in the heart, or the ejection fraction is very low, the dose becomes therapeutic.

{{**Bromocriptine** (16-kDa prolactin hypothesis)
Uncomplicated: 2.5 mg once daily × 1 week
EF <25% or shock: 2.5 mg twice daily × 2 weeks, then once daily × 6 weeks
Always with anticoagulation (at least prophylactic) · ESC 2018 class **IIb**}}

And the honest caution. The evidence is limited. The one randomised trial, by Hilfiker-Kleiner in twenty seventeen, compared one week with eight weeks of the drug in sixty-three women. It had no placebo arm, so it speaks to the length of the course, not to whether the drug works at all. The twenty eighteen ESC pregnancy guideline gives it a class two-b. And it stops lactation, so she can't breastfeed. Discuss that with her first.

Now the patient in shock. Three points. Avoid dobutamine where you can, and prefer levosimendan. Why? Because work in this disease suggests that beta-adrenergic stimulation harms this particular myocardium, and levosimendan supports contraction by a different route, by sensitising the muscle to calcium. Second, go early to mechanical support. You know from the last lessons how fast cardiogenic shock moves through its stages. And third, plan urgent delivery, with the heart team, the obstetricians and the anaesthetists together.

[[In peripartum shock, prefer levosimendan, go early to mechanical support, and deliver with the heart team.]]

spine: What it is: heart failure with **LVEF under 45%**, from late pregnancy to 5 months postpartum, mostly in the month after delivery, with no other cause.
What I do before delivery: beta-blocker, hydralazine with nitrate, and a loop diuretic. I avoid ACE inhibitors, ARBs, ARNI, MRA and SGLT2 inhibitors.
After delivery: full heart failure therapy; enalapril or captopril if she breastfeeds. Bromocriptine stops lactation.
Bromocriptine (16-kDa prolactin theory): 2.5 mg daily for 1 week, or twice daily 2 weeks then daily 6 weeks if EF <25% or shock; with anticoagulation; ESC 2018 **IIb**.
In shock: avoid dobutamine where possible, prefer levosimendan, go early to mechanical support, and plan urgent delivery with the heart team.
Caution: persistent LV dysfunction means a poor prognosis, and it can recur, so counsel on future pregnancy.

open.text:
Let me start with the woman from the end of the last lesson.

She's twenty-eight. Three weeks ago she had her first baby, and it went well. Now she can't lie flat. Her ankles are swollen, she's tired all the time, and her heart rate is a hundred and ten. Everyone around her says the same thing. That's what having a new baby feels like.

Then someone does an echo. The ejection fraction is twenty-five percent.

Peripartum cardiomyopathy hides in plain sight, because its early symptoms look like the ordinary tiredness and swelling of late pregnancy and new motherhood. And when it's missed, it can end in cardiogenic shock.

This is a direct question, but it reaches into three different worlds. Cardiology, obstetrics and pharmacology. What the professor is really checking is three things. Can you define it precisely, with its timing and its ejection fraction? Do you know which drugs are safe before delivery, and which are not? And do you know where bromocriptine fits, and how weak its evidence is?

[[The trap is the drug chart. Most heart failure drugs you would reach for are unsafe before delivery.]]

So here's the plan. First, where it sits among the causes of cardiogenic shock. Then the definition and the basic drug plan. And finally, the full plan before and after delivery, bromocriptine, and the patient in shock.

close.text:
So let's bring it together.

[[Peripartum cardiomyopathy is heart failure with an ejection fraction under forty-five percent, from late pregnancy to five months after delivery, mostly in the month after delivery, with no other cause.]]

Before delivery: a beta-blocker, hydralazine with a nitrate, and a loop diuretic. I avoid the ACE inhibitors, ARBs, ARNI, mineralocorticoid antagonists and SGLT2 inhibitors.

After delivery: full heart failure therapy, with enalapril or captopril if she breastfeeds. And bromocriptine stops lactation.

Bromocriptine, for the sixteen kilodalton prolactin theory. Two point five milligrams daily for a week, or twice daily for two weeks then daily for six, if the ejection fraction is below twenty-five or she's in shock. Always with anticoagulation. ESC class two-b.

In shock: avoid dobutamine where possible, prefer levosimendan, go early to mechanical support, and plan urgent delivery with the heart team.

And the caution: persistent dysfunction means a poor prognosis, and it can recur. So I counsel her on future pregnancy.

That's your answer. The definition, the drugs before and after delivery, bromocriptine, shock, and the prognosis.

So far in this block, the muscle itself has failed. But a strong, healthy heart can fail too, if something squeezes it from the outside. A young man, stabbed in the chest, with a falling pressure and distended neck veins. Or a patient on the second day after cardiac surgery, slowly becoming hypotensive. How do you diagnose it at the bedside, before it's too late? That's next. Cardiac tamponade.

questions.text: Diagnose cardiac tamponade at the bedside.

steps.bridge: Tamponade is compression, not volume; rate of filling matters. Next: why a small fast effusion can kill →

lesson.text:
Start with the definition. [[Tamponade is the haemodynamic decompensation that occurs when the pressure in the pericardial cavity compresses the heart.]] It's a medical emergency, and it needs emergency decompression.

Notice what that definition does not say. It says nothing about the size of the effusion. Tamponade is a pressure problem, not a volume problem.

So what decides whether an effusion causes it? Three things. The volume of the fluid. The rate at which it collects. And the compliance of the pericardium, how much it can stretch.

And the pericardium has a reserve. About two hundred to two hundred and fifty millilitres can enter it before the pressure starts to climb steeply. That's the pericardial reserve volume.

{{**Tamponade depends on:** volume · **rate** · pericardial compliance
Pericardial reserve volume: **200–250 mL**}}

One small trap. You'll meet that same number, two hundred to two hundred and fifty millilitres, in a different place. It's also roughly the fluid needed before the cardiac silhouette enlarges on a chest X-ray. Same number, different meaning.

So why does the rate matter so much? Let's look at the pericardium's pressure-volume curve.

steps.bridge: The acute pericardium has little reserve and the septum shifts into the LV. Next: what I find at the bedside →

lesson.text:
The pericardium is a tough, fibrous sac. It stretches, but slowly. So what matters is whether it has time.

{{pic}}

Look at the red curve. That's an acute effusion. A small reserve, and then the curve turns sharply upwards. [[In an acute effusion, a small volume quickly exceeds the limit of pericardial stretch.]] That's Patient B, with blood collecting after a pacing wire. A thin rim, and the pressure is already high.

Now the dark curve. That's a chronic effusion. Over weeks, the pericardium has stretched. So the curve stays flat for much longer, and a far larger volume is tolerated before tamponade. That's Patient A.

Now look at the steep end of either curve. That's where the last drop effect lives. The final small increment of fluid produces the critical compression. And the reverse is just as true. [[The first small volume drained produces the largest relief.]] Take off a few tens of millilitres, and the patient can be transformed. That's why a needle can save a life before you've drained much at all.

Now, why does the pressure crash? Through ventricular interdependence. The two ventricles share the septum, and they share the pericardium. With the sac full, the heart's total volume is fixed. The right ventricle can't take in the venous return. So it pushes the septum towards the left ventricle. The left ventricle gets smaller, it fills less, its output falls, and the pressure drops.

[[In tamponade, the two ventricles compete for a fixed space. When one fills, the other has to give way.]]

Think of two people sharing a sleeping bag that can't stretch. When one breathes in, the other gets squeezed.

Hold on to that picture. Every bedside sign and every echo sign of tamponade comes from it.

So what do you find at the bedside?
lesson.cap: Acute: steep early. Chronic: the pericardium has stretched. On the steep part, small volumes matter most.

steps.bridge: Beck's triad and pulsus paradoxus raise the suspicion. Next: which chamber collapse confirms it on echo →

lesson.text:
The classic signs come in a triad, described by the surgeon Claude Beck in the nineteen thirties. [[Beck's triad is hypotension, a raised JVP and muffled heart sounds.]]

Each one is the physiology you just learned. The pressure falls because the left ventricle can't fill. The JVP rises because the blood can't get into the right heart. And the heart sounds are muffled because fluid lies between the heart and your stethoscope.

But don't wait for all three. The full triad is often absent, especially when the effusion collects fast.

The card gives four other features. Breathlessness. Tachycardia, which is the body's attempt to keep up the output when each beat is small. Electrical alternans, the QRS height alternating from beat to beat, as the heart swings back and forth in a large effusion. And pulsus paradoxus.

Pulsus paradoxus means an inspiratory drop in the cardiac output and the blood pressure. In practice, a fall in systolic pressure of more than ten millimetres of mercury on breathing in. Adolf Kussmaul named it paradoxical in the eighteen seventies, because the pulse faded at the wrist while the heart could still be heard beating.

Why does it happen? Go back to the sleeping bag. When the patient breathes in, more blood returns to the right ventricle. In a tight pericardium, the right ventricle can only expand by pushing the septum into the left. So the left ventricle fills less, and the systolic pressure falls with each breath in. [[Pulsus paradoxus is ventricular interdependence that you can feel with your fingers.]]

{{**Beck's triad:** hypotension · ↑JVP · muffled heart sounds
**Also:** breathlessness · tachycardia · electrical alternans · **pulsus paradoxus** (inspiratory SBP fall >10 mmHg)}}

One honest caution. Pulsus paradoxus depends on spontaneous breathing. On a ventilator the pattern changes. And it can be absent with severe aortic regurgitation, an atrial septal defect, or a very stiff left ventricle.

The signs raise the suspicion. The echo confirms it.

steps.bridge: RA systolic and RV diastolic collapse; the RV sign is more specific. Next: the Doppler signs of interdependence →

lesson.text: You met this card in the lesson on echo in shock. The pericardial pressure squeezes whichever chamber has the lowest pressure at that moment, so the right side collapses first. The right atrium collapses in late diastole and early systole. The right ventricle collapses in early diastole, best seen in expiration. [[Right ventricular diastolic collapse is the more specific sign, above ninety percent.]] And a plethoric IVC is very sensitive but non-specific. Here, those signs are your confirmation. Now the Doppler signs, which show interdependence beat by beat.

steps.bridge: Mitral inflow falls more than 25% in inspiration. Next: is the diagnosis clinical or echo, and how to bridge →

lesson.text:
The Doppler signs of tamponade are ventricular interdependence, measured.

Put the pulsed Doppler sample across the tricuspid valve, and watch the E wave, the early filling velocity, as the patient breathes. In inspiration, more blood returns to the right heart. [[The tricuspid E wave rises by more than forty percent in inspiration.]]

Now move to the mitral valve. At the same moment, the septum has pushed into the left ventricle, so the left side fills less. [[The mitral E wave falls by more than twenty-five percent in inspiration.]]

Right side up, left side down. With different cut-offs, forty and twenty-five. That's the sleeping bag, written in velocities.

The card adds a ten percent fall in the velocity time integral. And it gives the outflow signs. In inspiration, the left ventricular outflow VTI falls by more than ten percent, and the right ventricular outflow VTI rises by more than ten. But these are neither sensitive nor specific. And a septal bounce, the septum flicking towards the left ventricle in inspiration, is not specific either.

{{**Doppler in tamponade (inspiration)**
Tricuspid E **↑ >40%** · Mitral E **↓ >25%** · VTI ↓ 10%
LVOT VTI ↓ >10%, RVOT VTI ↑ >10%: neither sensitive nor specific
Septal bounce: not specific}}

So which do you trust most? The mitral inflow variation, with the chamber collapse. Then put them together with the patient.

steps.bridge: Clinical diagnosis confirmed by echo; fluids only buy time and PPV can kill. Next: the vasoactive bridge →

lesson.text:
This is the follow-up the panel almost always asks. Is tamponade a clinical diagnosis or an echo diagnosis? And how do you keep the patient alive until it's drained?

[[Tamponade is a clinical diagnosis, confirmed by echo.]] The clinical picture is Beck's triad, tachycardia and pulsus paradoxus, in a patient with an effusion. The echo confirms it, with right atrial systolic collapse, right ventricular diastolic collapse, which is the more specific, a plethoric IVC, and mitral inflow varying by more than twenty-five percent with breathing.

Why insist on the clinical part? Because an effusion alone is not tamponade. Patient A has a huge effusion and a normal pressure. Patient B has a thin rim and is dying. The echo shows you fluid. Only the patient tells you whether it's compressing the heart.

Now the bridge. Fluids only temporise. A bolus pushes the venous pressure up, so the right heart can fill against the pericardial pressure, for a while. Noradrenaline can hold the pressure. Neither treats the cause.

And here's the warning that every anaesthetist must carry. [[Avoid positive pressure ventilation and induction before drainage, if you possibly can.]] Why? Because this patient is alive on two things. A high venous pressure pushing blood into the heart, and a sympathetic system clamping every vessel. Positive pressure raises the pressure in the chest and cuts the venous return. Induction removes the sympathetic tone. Do both at once, and the patient can arrest on the table.

If intubation truly can't be avoided, have the drainage ready first, with the surgeon or the needle scrubbed. Keep the vasopressor running. And use the lowest airway pressures you can.

{{**Bridge to drainage:** fluid bolus (temporises) · noradrenaline · avoid PPV and induction before drainage
**If intubation unavoidable:** drainage ready first · vasopressor running · lowest airway pressures}}

And the definitive treatment is pericardiocentesis, or a surgical window.

So, the vasoactive bridge, and how it compares with the other mechanical causes of shock.

steps.bridge: A fluid bolus and noradrenaline hold the pressure while drainage is arranged. Next: how and where to drain →

lesson.text:
This card covers the mechanical and electrical causes of cardiogenic shock, and the drugs for each. Tamponade is the last row, but the others are worth knowing beside it.

Pericardial tamponade. A fluid bolus, and noradrenaline. [[But pericardiocentesis or a surgical pericardial window is the definitive therapy.]] The drugs only hold the line.

A ventricular septal defect after an infarct. Treat it like classic cold and wet shock, with temporary mechanical support, including a balloon pump. Why the balloon? Because it lowers the systemic afterload, so less blood crosses the defect from left to right, and more goes forwards. Then surgical repair or percutaneous closure.

Dynamic left ventricular outflow obstruction. This is the one where the usual rules reverse. Give fluid, and phenylephrine or vasopressin. Avoid inotropes and avoid vasodilators. Use esmolol or amiodarone, and consider pacing. Why? Because the obstruction gets worse when the ventricle is small and squeezing hard. So you fill it, raise the afterload, and slow it down. [[In dynamic outflow obstruction, inotropes are contraindicated. Almost everywhere else in this chapter, they're part of the answer.]]

Bradycardia. Chronotropic agents, atropine, isoprenaline, dopamine, dobutamine or adrenaline, and temporary pacing. And treat the cause.

{{Cause | Vasoactive | Definitive
Tamponade | fluid bolus + noradrenaline | **pericardiocentesis or window**
Post-MI VSD | as cold & wet; IABP | surgery or umbrella closure
Dynamic LVOTO | fluid, phenylephrine or vasopressin; **no inotropes or vasodilators**; esmolol | —
Bradycardia | atropine, isoprenaline, dopamine, dobutamine, adrenaline | pacing}}

Notice a theme. In each of these, the drugs buy time while you fix a mechanical problem. In tamponade, that fix is a needle or a knife. So how and where do you drain?

Pericardiocentesis. Start with who needs it.

In an unstable patient, the indication is one word. Tamponade. Drain now.

In a stable patient, there are four indications. A large effusion, more than twenty millimetres. A chronic effusion, present for more than three months. A symptomatic moderate to large effusion that hasn't responded to medical treatment. And even a small effusion, if you suspect tuberculosis, bacterial infection or a cancer, because you need the fluid for diagnosis.

The three puncture sites. Subcostal, parasternal and apical. The subcostal route is the classic blind approach. Today, use echo to choose the site where the fluid is deepest and closest to the skin.

Now the contraindications, and the logic behind them. There are only two true absolute ones. Aortic dissection, and free wall rupture after an infarct. [[In dissection or free wall rupture, the fluid is blood under arterial pressure. Draining it with a needle can restart the bleeding. These patients go to surgery, not a needle.]]

Your card adds severe pulmonary hypertension to the absolute list. Treat it as a strong caution instead. A right ventricle already struggling against a high pulmonary pressure can collapse when the effusion comes off, so drain only for a clear reason, slowly, and with a plan. But in true tamponade, it doesn't stop you.

The relative ones are platelets below fifty thousand, a coagulopathy, and anticoagulant therapy.

{{**Unstable:** tamponade → drain
**Stable:** >20 mm · >3 months · symptomatic despite therapy · small if TB, bacterial or malignant
**Sites:** subcostal · parasternal · apical
**Absolute C/I:** aortic dissection · post-MI free wall rupture
**Caution:** severe PAH (card lists it as absolute)
**Relative:** platelets <50,000 · coagulopathy · anticoagulants}}

And one complication you must know. [[Pericardial decompression syndrome: a paradoxical haemodynamic deterioration after a successful drainage.]] The patient who was saved by the needle can collapse minutes or hours later, often with pulmonary oedema or ventricular failure. So don't relax the moment the fluid comes out. Watch closely afterwards. It's rare. But it's one reason a large effusion is often drained in stages, rather than all at once.

spine: What it is: haemodynamic collapse from pericardial pressure compressing the heart. The rate of filling matters more than the volume.
How I diagnose: it is a **clinical diagnosis confirmed by echo**. Beck's triad, tachycardia and pulsus paradoxus raise it.
Echo: RA systolic collapse, RV diastolic collapse, a plethoric IVC, and mitral inflow falling **more than 25%** in inspiration.
Why: with a tight pericardium, inspiration fills the RV, the septum shifts left, and LV output falls.
What I do: fluid bolus and noradrenaline only to temporise, then urgent **pericardiocentesis** or a surgical window.
Caution: avoid positive pressure ventilation and induction before drainage; both cut venous return. In dissection, free-wall rupture or trauma, go to surgery, not a needle.

open.text:
Let me start with two patients and two effusions.

Patient A has had a pericardial effusion from a cancer for weeks. On the echo it's huge, more than two centimetres all round. She's a little breathless, but her pressure is fine.

Patient B had a pacing wire placed this morning. Now he's grey, his pressure is seventy, and his neck veins are full. On the echo, there's only a thin rim of fluid.

The big effusion is coping. The small one is killing. Why?

That's the heart of tamponade. It's not about how much fluid there is. It's about the pressure that fluid creates, and how fast it got there.

This is a scenario question. Diagnose tamponade at the bedside. What the professor is really checking is three things. Do you understand why rate matters more than volume? Do you know the clinical signs, and the echo signs that confirm them? And do you know how to keep the patient alive until the fluid is drained?

[[The trap is induction and positive pressure ventilation before drainage. They can turn a patient in tamponade into a cardiac arrest.]]

So here's the plan. First, what tamponade is, and why a small effusion can kill. Then the bedside signs. Then the echo, chamber collapse and Doppler. Then whether the diagnosis is clinical or echo. Then the bridge to drainage. And finally, the drainage itself.

close.text:
So let's bring it together.

[[Tamponade is haemodynamic collapse from pericardial pressure compressing the heart. The rate of filling matters more than the volume.]]

How I diagnose it. It's a clinical diagnosis confirmed by echo. Beck's triad, tachycardia and pulsus paradoxus raise it.

The echo. Right atrial systolic collapse, right ventricular diastolic collapse, a plethoric IVC, and mitral inflow falling by more than twenty-five percent in inspiration.

Why. With a tight pericardium, inspiration fills the right ventricle, the septum shifts left, and the left ventricular output falls.

What I do. A fluid bolus and noradrenaline, only to temporise. Then urgent pericardiocentesis, or a surgical window.

And the caution. [[Avoid positive pressure ventilation and induction before drainage. Both cut the venous return.]] And in dissection, free wall rupture or trauma, go to surgery, not a needle.

That's your answer. What it is, how you diagnose it, the echo, why, what you do, and the caution.

But now the examiner turns a screen towards you. A parasternal long axis clip, with a black space behind the heart. Before tamponade, there's a simpler question. Is that fluid around the heart, or around the lung? And how big is it? That's next. The echo spotter.

questions.text: Spotter - echo clip showing pericardial effusion. What is it and what next?

steps.bridge: PLAX shows the LV, LA and the descending aorta behind them. Next: how pleural fluid looks in its own window →

lesson.text: You met this view at the start of the block. The parasternal long axis, with the probe at the left sternal edge and the marker to the right shoulder, used for contractility, ejection fraction, wall motion and the outflow tract diameter. Here, one more structure matters. Behind the left atrium sits a small circle, the descending thoracic aorta, cut across. [[That circle is your landmark for telling pericardial fluid from pleural fluid.]] Find it before you say a word.

steps.bridge: Pleural fluid is anechoic in the mid-axillary view. Next: how to tell the two apart on PLAX →

lesson.text:
Before the landmark rule, look at pleural fluid in its own window.

The pleura is seen in the mid-axillary lines, on both sides. Place the probe there, above the diaphragm, and look for fluid sitting between the lung and the chest wall.

A transudate is anechoic. Simply black, with no echoes in it.

And if the fluid has specks in it? [[The plankton sign is debris appearing as swirling, punctiform echoes within an effusion.]] Depending on the clinical context, it may mean infection, an empyema, or blood, a haemothorax.

{{**Pleural view:** mid-axillary lines, both sides · transudate = **anechoic**
**Plankton sign:** swirling punctiform echoes → infection or haemothorax}}

So this is how pleural fluid looks from the side. Now, how do you tell it from pericardial fluid on the long axis?

steps.bridge: Pericardial fluid is in front of the descending aorta, pleural behind it. Next: how big is the effusion →

lesson.text:
This is the heart of the spotter, and it rests on one rule.

First, find the descending thoracic aorta. On the long axis view it's a small circle, behind the left atrium, near the back of the heart.

[[Pericardial fluid lies in front of the descending aorta. Pleural fluid lies behind it.]]

{{pic}}

Look at the left panel. Pericardial fluid sits between the back wall of the left ventricle and the bright pericardial line. And it can track towards the left atrium, between the atrium and the descending aorta.

Now the right panel. Pleural fluid sits below and behind the descending aorta, deeper on the screen. It doesn't track in front of it.

Why does this work? Because of anatomy. The descending aorta lies outside the pericardial sac, behind it. So fluid inside the sac is stopped by the pericardium in front of the aorta. Fluid in the left pleural space lies further back, beside the spine, so it appears behind the aorta.

So when your examiner shows you that black space, your first sentence is the landmark. I find the descending aorta. The fluid lies in front of it, so it's pericardial.

Then confirm in other windows. Pericardial fluid wraps around the heart in the subcostal view. Pleural fluid sits above the diaphragm in the mid-axillary view.

Then size it, at end-diastole. That has its own card, next.

And watch for a mimic. [[An echo-free space in front of the heart only may be an epicardial fat pad, not fluid.]] Fat often has a faint speckled texture, and it moves with the heart.

Then look for tamponade. Right atrial and right ventricular collapse, a plethoric IVC, and respiratory variation in the mitral inflow. And always match it to the patient.

What do you do? If there's tamponade, or the patient is unstable, drain now. If he's stable, drain when it's symptomatic despite treatment, large and chronic, or you suspect bacterial, tuberculous or malignant fluid. Otherwise, treat the cause and repeat the echo.
lesson.cap: PLAX: pericardial fluid lies in front of the descending aorta; pleural fluid lies behind it.

steps.bridge: Under 10 mm is mild, over 20 mm is large. Next: when it needs draining →

lesson.text:
The sizing, on its own, because it's the number the examiner asks for next.

You measure the echo-free space at end-diastole. [[Mild is under ten millimetres. Moderate is ten to twenty. Large is over twenty.]] And you describe its distribution, circumferential, all the way round, or loculated, in one pocket.

{{Size | End-diastolic space
Mild | <10 mm
Moderate | 10–20 mm
Large | >20 mm
Distribution: circumferential or loculated}}

Why does loculation matter? Because a loculated effusion can compress a single chamber, often after cardiac surgery, and cause tamponade with a small, localised collection that is easy to miss.

You learned the indications for drainage in the tamponade lesson. If unstable with tamponade, drain. If stable, drain for a large effusion over twenty millimetres, a chronic one over three months, a symptomatic one despite treatment, or even a small one if you suspect tuberculosis, bacteria or a cancer. And not with a needle in dissection or free wall rupture. Here it closes the spotter, with one rule. [[Size does not equal tamponade.]] A small fast effusion can compress the heart, while a large slow one may not.

spine: What it is: an echo-free space around the heart. On PLAX I find the descending aorta behind the left atrium.
How I tell: pericardial fluid lies **in front of** the descending aorta; pleural fluid lies **behind** it. I confirm in subcostal and pleural views.
Size at end-diastole: mild under **10 mm**, moderate 10–20 mm, large over **20 mm**; circumferential or loculated. An anterior-only space may be a fat pad.
What next: look for tamponade, meaning RA and RV collapse, a plethoric IVC and respiratory mitral inflow variation, and match it to the clinical picture.
What I do: drain if tamponade. If stable, drain when symptomatic despite treatment, large (>20 mm) and chronic (>3 months), or suspected bacterial, TB or malignant.
Caution: size does not equal tamponade. A small fast effusion can compress; a large slow one may not.

open.text:
Let me start with the clip.

The examiner presses play. A parasternal long axis view. The heart is beating, and behind it, at the bottom of the screen, there's a black, echo-free space. He says nothing. He waits.

This is a spotter. You have a few seconds to say what it is, and then he'll ask what you'll do. What the professor is really checking is a single landmark, and a sequence. [[Can you tell pericardial fluid from pleural fluid on one view? Then can you size it, look for tamponade, and decide whether to drain?]]

The resident who says effusion, needs draining, has made two mistakes. He hasn't said which effusion. And he's treated size as if it were tamponade.

So here's the plan. First, the long axis view again, and its landmark. Then the pleural window. Then the landmark rule, pericardial against pleural. Then sizing. And finally, when to drain.

close.text:
So let's bring it together.

It's an echo-free space around the heart. On the long axis view, I find the descending aorta behind the left atrium.

[[Pericardial fluid lies in front of the descending aorta. Pleural fluid lies behind it.]] I confirm in the subcostal and pleural views.

The size, at end-diastole. Mild under ten millimetres, moderate ten to twenty, large over twenty. Circumferential or loculated. And an echo-free space only in front may be a fat pad.

What next. I look for tamponade, meaning right atrial and right ventricular collapse, a plethoric IVC and respiratory variation in the mitral inflow, and I match it to the patient.

What I do. Drain if there's tamponade. If stable, drain when it's symptomatic despite treatment, large and chronic, or suspected bacterial, tuberculous or malignant.

And the caution. [[Size does not equal tamponade.]] A small fast effusion can compress the heart, and a large slow one may not.

That's your answer. What it is, how you tell, the size, what next, and what you do.

And that closes the failing pump. We've seen the heart fail from within, and from outside. But there's another way the circulation empties, and it's the most common in trauma. Not the pump, but the blood itself, pouring out. How much blood can a patient lose before his pressure falls, and why does the pressure fall so late? That's the next block, bleeding and trauma, starting with the classes of haemorrhagic shock.

questions.text: What are the classes of haemorrhagic shock?

steps.bridge: Four classes by blood lost; BP holds until Class III. Next: how do I spot shock before the pressure falls →

lesson.text:
ATLS grades haemorrhage by one thing: the share of the blood volume that has been lost. In a seventy kilo adult, the blood volume is about five litres. So fifteen percent is about seven hundred and fifty millilitres.

[[Class one is under fifteen percent. Class two is fifteen to thirty. Class three is thirty to forty. Class four is over forty.]]

Now, don't learn the rest of the table as columns. Learn it as a story of compensation, because that's what it is.

When blood is lost, the stretch on the baroreceptors falls. The sympathetic system fires. It does three things. It squeezes the veins, pushing the blood that was sitting in them back towards the heart. You met that idea as the stressed volume. It speeds the heart. And it tightens the arterioles, which holds the diastolic pressure up.

Now think about what that does to the pulse pressure. The stroke volume is smaller, so the systolic would like to fall. But the arteries are clamped, so the diastolic rises. The gap between them closes.

[[In class two, the systolic is still normal. Only the pulse pressure narrows. That narrow pulse pressure is the first sign in the blood pressure itself.]]

{{pic}}

Look at the picture if you'd like to see it. The systolic line runs flat across class one and class two, while the heart rate climbs. The diastolic rises to meet it. Then, at about thirty percent, the systolic finally turns down.

{{Class | Loss | Pulse | BP | Urine mL/h
I | <15% | <100 | normal | >30
II | 15–30% | 100–120 | **normal**, narrow PP | 20–30
III | 30–40% | 120–140 | **falls** | 5–15
IV | >40% | >140 | low | negligible}}

Let me walk you up the ladder once. Class one: a pulse under a hundred, a normal pressure, a slightly anxious patient. Class two: pulse a hundred to a hundred and twenty, breathing twenty to thirty, urine twenty to thirty millilitres an hour, mildly anxious, and that narrow pulse pressure. Class three is where compensation runs out. The pulse is a hundred and twenty to a hundred and forty, the breathing thirty to forty, the urine five to fifteen, and he's anxious and confused. [[The first fall in systolic pressure marks class three. By then he has lost thirty percent or more.]] Class four: a pulse over a hundred and forty, almost no urine, confused and lethargic.

Now go back to Patient A. A heart rate of one hundred and fifteen, a pulse pressure of only twenty-four, breathing fast, a little confused. He's class two, maybe early class three. The normal systolic was never reassurance. It was compensation, working flat out.

You've seen this in theatre. The young patient who bleeds holds his pressure for a long time, and then falls off a cliff. And the induction drug that removes his sympathetic tone pushes him off that cliff in a single minute.

One honest caution. The classes are a teaching ladder, and real patients don't always climb it in order. The elderly and those on beta-blockers may never mount the tachycardia. The fit young patient compensates so well that he looks fine until late. So the table guides you. It does not clear anyone.
lesson.cap: Systolic holds through class II while pulse rises and pulse pressure narrows; it first falls at about 30% loss.

steps.bridge: Occult shock shows as tachycardia, shock index over 1, lactate and base deficit. Next: which of these facts are exam traps →

lesson.text: You met this card in the shock index lesson, so just the thread. In the bleeding patient, control the massive external bleeding first, and intubate only after you've filled the tank, with a quarter to half the usual induction dose. And actively hunt for occult shock: a systolic under one hundred and ten, a shock index over one, a lactate over four or a base deficit over six, cold limbs. Why does it matter here? [[Those flags are how you catch class two, while the systolic is still normal.]]

Now a quick sweep. Eight statements, the kind the panel fires one after another. Some you know already. Some we'll build properly in the next lessons. Say true or false in your head before I answer.

First. The blood pressure first falls in class two shock. False. It first falls in class three, at thirty to forty percent.

Second. A shock index over one predicts mortality. True.

Third. Permissive hypotension suits severe head injury. False. [[Permissive hypotension is contraindicated in TBI.]] The injured brain needs its perfusion pressure, and a low pressure adds a second injury to the first. We'll come to the targets soon.

Fourth. Tranexamic acid helps if given up to eight hours after injury. False. [[The window is three hours. Eight hours is the length of the infusion, not the window.]] That confusion sits in many notes.

Fifth. Fibrinogen is the first factor to fall critically. True. Hold that. It will matter when we reach coagulopathy.

Sixth. Albumin is the preferred fluid in head injury. False. In the head injury group of the SAFE trial, albumin was linked to higher mortality.

Seventh. The Berlin definition of polytrauma needs an abbreviated injury score of three or more in two or more body regions, plus a physiological factor. True.

And eighth. The injury severity score sums the three worst injuries, whatever region they're in. False. The injury severity score takes only the worst injury in each of three different body regions, squares each one, and adds them. Taking the three worst injuries regardless of region is the new injury severity score.

You don't need to dwell on the last two. The ones that will come back again and again are the class three fall, the three-hour window, and no permissive hypotension in TBI.

spine: What it is: ATLS grades haemorrhage by blood lost. Class I under 15%, II 15–30%, III 30–40%, IV over 40%.
Why BP misleads: vasoconstriction and tachycardia hold the pressure. In Class II the BP is still normal; only the pulse pressure narrows. BP first falls in **Class III**.
What I look for early: heart rate, narrow pulse pressure, breathing rate, urine output, mental state, and lactate or base deficit.
Shock index: heart rate divided by systolic BP. **Over 1** means occult shock and predicts mortality. SBP under 110 is already a warning.
Caution: a normal BP after injury does not exclude major bleeding. I treat hypotension after injury as bleeding until proven otherwise.

open.text:
In the last block, the pump was failing. Now the pump is strong. It's the tank that's draining.

Let me start with a patient. Patient A is twenty-four. His motorbike went under a truck. He arrives talking. His blood pressure is one hundred and twelve over eighty-eight, and the junior says, he's stable. But his heart rate is one hundred and fifteen. He's breathing fast. And he keeps asking the same question twice.

Is he stable?

He isn't. He may already have lost up to a litre and a half of blood. And the number everyone trusts, the systolic pressure, will be the last one to tell you.

This opens a new block, bleeding and trauma. Over the next lessons we'll go from recognising the bleeding, to resuscitating it, to the clotting that fails, to the drugs and devices, and finally to the new ATLS order that ties it all together.

This first question sounds like a table to recite. Four classes, four columns. And yes, the panel wants the table. But what the professor is really checking is whether you understand why the blood pressure holds for so long, and what you look at instead.

[[The trap is to think that a bleeding patient becomes hypotensive early. He doesn't. The pressure is the last thing to fall.]]

So here's the plan. First, the four classes and the physiology that shapes them. Then the early flags that catch shock before the pressure falls. And then a quick sweep of the true or false traps the panel likes to set.

close.text:
So let's bring it together.

ATLS grades haemorrhage by blood lost. Class one under fifteen percent, class two fifteen to thirty, class three thirty to forty, class four over forty.

[[The blood pressure misleads because compensation holds it. In class two the systolic is still normal, and only the pulse pressure narrows. The systolic first falls in class three.]]

So I look earlier. The heart rate, a narrow pulse pressure, the breathing rate, the urine output, the mental state, and the lactate or base deficit.

And the shock index, heart rate divided by systolic. Over one means occult shock, and it predicts death. A systolic under one hundred and ten is already a warning.

The caution: a normal pressure after injury does not exclude major bleeding. [[I treat hypotension after injury as bleeding until proven otherwise.]]

That's your answer. What it is, why the pressure misleads, what I look for, the shock index, and the caution.

But here's something to carry forward. You've recognised that Patient A is bleeding. Now what? For years, the reflex was two large cannulas and two litres of warm crystalloid, then the operating theatre to fix everything. ATLS itself cut that first bolus to one litre in its tenth edition. Why was the old reflex making patients worse? And what replaced it? That's next.

questions.text: What is damage control resuscitation and damage control surgery?

steps.bridge: Cold, acid and coagulopathy feed each other and kill. Next: how resuscitation is changed to break that cycle →

lesson.text:
Three things kill the bleeding patient together. Hypothermia, a core temperature under thirty-four degrees. Acidosis, a pH under seven point two. And coagulopathy.

[[The lethal triad is a loop. Each limb worsens the other two, so all three together carry a very high mortality.]]

Let's build the loop, one link at a time.

Start with the clotting itself. Clotting is a chain of enzymes, and enzymes are fussy. They need the right temperature and the right pH.

Now the cold. Why does the trauma patient get cold so fast? He's exposed, at the roadside and in the resuscitation room. He's lost his thermoregulation, and he isn't shivering. His metabolism is low, so he makes little heat. And we pour cold fluid into him. In the cold, the clotting enzymes slow down and the platelets work poorly.

Then the acid. Poor perfusion makes lactate. And saline, given in large volume, adds a chloride acidosis on top. [[In acid, factor seven a, the ten a and five a complex, and the platelets all fail.]] And acid depresses the heart, so perfusion falls further, and more acid is made.

Now close the loop. The coagulopathy means more bleeding. More bleeding means more shock, so more acid. And more transfusion of cold fluid, so more cold. Round and round.

How strong is each limb? The classic numbers come from massively transfused trauma patients, and notice what they predict. Not death itself, but life-threatening coagulopathy. A pH under seven point one carried an odds ratio of about twelve. A temperature under thirty-four, about nine. An injury severity score over twenty-five, about eight. And a systolic under seventy. With all four together, ninety-eight percent became severely coagulopathic.

{{**Predictors of life-threatening coagulopathy (odds ratio)**
pH <7.1 → 12.3
Temperature <34 °C → 8.7
ISS >25 → 7.7
SBP <70 mmHg
All four → 98% became coagulopathic
(Cosgriff 1997)}}

And one number to remember on its own. [[A core temperature under thirty-two degrees in trauma carries close to a hundred percent mortality.]] Notice the words in trauma. You've cooled patients deliberately in theatre and in the ICU. That is controlled cooling in a patient who isn't bleeding. Here, the cold arrives together with bleeding and acid.

As an anaesthetist, you know how hard it is to rewarm a patient once he's cold. That's why the warming starts at the door, not in the ICU.

So the question becomes, how do you break a loop with three limbs? You attack all three at once. That's damage control resuscitation.

steps.bridge: Low BP target, little crystalloid, blood first; the SBP target is 80–90, not 70. Next: how much blood, and in what ratio →

lesson.text:
Damage control resuscitation has three pillars. A lower pressure target, very little crystalloid, and blood first.

The first pillar, permissive hypotension. [[Until the bleeding is controlled, I target a systolic of eighty to ninety, a MAP of fifty to sixty, with normal mentation and palpable pulses.]] I follow the lactate and the central venous saturation to check the tissues are coping.

Why accept a lower pressure? Think of what's happening at the bleeding vessel. A fresh clot is soft and fragile. Raise the pressure behind it, and you can blow it off. Then the bleeding starts again, and the new blood that comes out has fewer clotting factors in it, because you've diluted them. So a normal pressure in a patient who's still bleeding often buys more bleeding, not more perfusion.

Here's the trap. Some notes give seventy to ninety, or a MAP of fifty. [[Say eighty to ninety. Seventy is too low.]]

And the big exception, which the panel will always test. [[No permissive hypotension in head injury or spinal cord injury. In severe TBI, with a GCS of eight or less, keep the MAP at eighty or more.]] The injured brain has lost its autoregulation. Its blood flow now follows the pressure, and a low pressure means a second, ischaemic injury on top of the first.

The second pillar, restrict crystalloid. Large volumes worsen bleeding. They dilute the clotting factors and disrupt the clot. They cause oedema, and they injure the liver cells. Crystalloid is a bridge until blood arrives, not a treatment.

The third pillar, haemostatic resuscitation. Blood products come first, red cells, plasma and platelets, in a ratio of about one to one to one. You are giving back what was lost, not something that only looks like it.

And what about colloids? [[Blood is the only colloid used in trauma.]] Starch raises kidney injury and mortality. Gelatin causes anaphylaxis. Hypertonic saline has a place only for raised intracranial pressure.

So three pillars. A target of eighty to ninety, except in the head. Crystalloid only as a bridge. And blood first. Now the obvious next question. How much blood, and in what ratio?

steps.bridge: Ratio matters: PROPPR 1:1:1 cut deaths from exsanguination. Next: which drug I add early to stop clot breakdown →

lesson.text:
First, what counts as a massive transfusion? The classic definition is ten or more units of red cells in twenty-four hours. But think about that for a moment. The patient who bleeds to death in the first hour never reaches ten units. So the definition only counts the survivors, and only in hindsight.

So newer definitions look at speed. More than four units in one hour with ongoing need. Or more than half the blood volume replaced in three hours. [[A massive transfusion is defined by the rate of bleeding, not only the total.]]

Second, emergency blood, before you know the group. Group O red cells, because they carry no A or B antigens for the patient's antibodies to attack. And group AB plasma, because it carries no anti-A or anti-B antibodies to attack the patient's cells. Each is the universal donor for its own part.

Third, the ratio, and the trial behind it. Why a ratio at all? Because whole blood is red cells, plasma and platelets together. If you give red cells alone, you carry oxygen but you dilute the clotting. [[The ratio is an attempt to rebuild whole blood from its parts.]]

PROMMTT was an observational study. Patients who got higher plasma and platelet ratios had lower early mortality. But observational data has a problem. The patient who lives long enough to receive plasma is already a survivor. So PROPPR randomised it. One to one to one, against one to one to two.

[[PROPPR found no difference in twenty-four-hour or thirty-day mortality. But one to one to one gave fewer deaths from exsanguination, and more patients achieved haemostasis.]] That's why one to one to one is the standard. Say the result honestly: no mortality difference on the primary outcome, but fewer bleeding deaths.

Fourth, predicting who needs it, so the blood arrives before the crisis. The ABC score has four points, each worth one. A systolic under ninety. A heart rate over a hundred and twenty. A penetrating mechanism. And a positive FAST. Two or more, activate the protocol. TASH is the longer score, with seven variables. You need only its name.

So the ratio rebuilds whole blood. Now the drug that protects the clot you're trying to build.

steps.bridge: TXA within 3 h, 1 g then 1 g over 8 h. Next: which electrolyte falls with every unit and must be replaced →

lesson.text:
Tranexamic acid. Four facts, and one trap.

The trial is CRASH two. [[The dose is one gram over ten minutes, then one gram over eight hours. It cut bleeding deaths by about fifteen percent.]]

The window. [[Within three hours of injury.]] After three hours, it increased bleeding deaths.

The trap. Many notes say benefit if given within eight hours. That's wrong. Eight hours is the length of the infusion, not the window.

The head injury result belongs to a different trial, CRASH three. Benefit in mild to moderate TBI when given early, and none in severe TBI.

And the European guidance. Give it as early as possible to anyone bleeding or at risk of bleeding, with the first dose before hospital if you can.

Why three hours, and why late tranexamic acid harms, has its own lesson in the CRASH trials. For now, early, one plus one, never after three hours.

steps.bridge: Calcium is needed for clotting and contractility; keep ionised calcium normal. Next: what the surgeon does in parallel →

lesson.text:
Four other drugs. One matters a great deal. The other three you need only briefly.

The one that matters is calcium. Calcium is a cofactor in the clotting cascade. It's also what makes the heart contract, and what gives the vessels their tone. So in a bleeding patient, low calcium hits him three ways at once. He clots worse, his heart squeezes less, and his vessels relax.

And massive transfusion drives it down. Why that happens, and the trap in measuring it, we'll build in the next question. For now, the rule.

[[Keep the ionised calcium in the normal range, about one point one to one point three millimoles per litre. Check it every ten units transfused, and more often in practice.]]

The trap is an old number. [[Some notes say keep the ionised calcium above nought point nine. That threshold is outdated.]] The European trauma guideline asks for the normal range.

Now the three you need only briefly.

Recombinant factor seven a. Off-label in trauma. No outcome benefit, and a risk of thrombosis. A last resort only, if at all.

Steroids in spinal cord injury. This is a history question. In NASCIS two, the patients given high-dose methylprednisolone within eight hours seemed to recover more motor function, but that was a subgroup finding. NASCIS three found forty-eight hours of it better than twenty-four, if started between three and eight hours. But the benefits didn't hold up, and the harms did. [[High-dose steroids in acute spinal cord injury are now not recommended.]]

And antioxidants. Vitamins A, C and E may lessen inflammation, and vitamin C may protect the kidneys. You don't need more than that.

So calcium in the normal range. Now, while you resuscitate, what is the surgeon doing?

steps.bridge: Damage control surgery: stop bleeding and soiling, then ICU, then repair. Next: how the two halves fit into one strategy →

lesson.text:
Damage control surgery is the temporary sacrifice of anatomy to save physiology. Go back to the warship. Keep it afloat now, repair it in dry dock later.

[[It has three stages. An abbreviated operation to control bleeding and contamination. Then resuscitation in the ICU. Then a planned return to theatre for the definitive repair.]]

Stage one is short and focused. Stop the bleeding, by packing, clamping or tying. Stop the soiling, by closing or stapling off the holes in the bowel. Don't join it. Don't reconstruct. Get out.

Stage two is yours. In the ICU, you break the triad. Rewarm him, correct the acid, correct the clotting, replace the calcium, restore the perfusion.

Stage three is the real operation, done when the physiology can survive it. That's usually at twenty-four to forty-eight hours.

Now the rewarming, because you'll be asked how. There are three levels. Passive external: blankets and a warm room. Active external: forced warm air. And active internal: warmed intravenous fluids, and in the extreme case, warm peritoneal lavage. Start at the door, and use all of them in the bleeding patient.

Then the methods of bleeding control, from the simplest. A pelvic binder. Compressive dressings. Tourniquets on the limbs. Surgery is the gold standard. Interventional radiology, which can embolise a bleeding vessel. And if the pelvis is still bleeding and the patient is unstable despite a binder, pelvic packing or embolisation.

[[The aim is control of the source, by whichever route is fastest.]]

And there's one more tool on this list, a balloon placed inside the aorta. It's called REBOA. Zone three, below the kidneys, for pelvic bleeding. Zone one, in the chest, for abdominal bleeding. It has its own question, with a trial that surprised many people, so we'll keep it for then.

Now let's put the two halves together.

Here is the whole answer, in one piece.

Damage control resuscitation restores perfusion and clotting before definitive repair. A systolic of eighty to ninety, a MAP of fifty to sixty, until the bleeding is controlled. Not in TBI or spinal cord injury, where in severe TBI the MAP stays at eighty or more. Blood products first, one to one to one. Minimal crystalloid. Early tranexamic acid. And calcium.

Now, why calcium in that list? Because the triad has grown a fourth limb.

[[Add hypocalcaemia to hypothermia, acidosis and coagulopathy, and the lethal triad becomes the lethal diamond. Each limb worsens the others.]]

{{pic}}

Look at the picture if you like. Four corners, and every corner linked to every other. Low calcium weakens the clot, so the coagulopathy deepens. It weakens the heart and the vessels, so the shock and the acid deepen. And the more blood you give to treat all that, the lower the calcium goes.

Damage control surgery is the other half. Abbreviated surgery to control bleeding and contamination. Then the ICU. Then definitive repair at twenty-four to forty-eight hours.

And why stage it at all? This is the sentence the professor wants. [[A long operation in a cold, acidotic, coagulopathic patient deepens all four limbs. The ICU fixes the physiology, so that the repair can be survived.]]

Go back to the surgeon in the opening. His repairs were perfect. But every hour of them made the diamond worse. Damage control would have given him a shorter operation and a living patient.
lesson.cap: Hypothermia, acidosis, coagulopathy and hypocalcaemia: each worsens the others.

spine: What it is: damage control resuscitation and surgery treat physiology first. Stop the bleeding, restore perfusion and clotting, and repair anatomy later.
Why: hypothermia, acidosis and coagulopathy, plus **hypocalcaemia** (the lethal diamond), each worsen the others. Long surgery in that state kills.
What I do (DCR): permissive hypotension, **SBP 80–90 (MAP 50–60)** until bleeding is controlled, not in TBI; minimal crystalloid; blood products **1:1:1**; early TXA; calcium.
What the surgeon does (DCS): abbreviated surgery to control bleeding and contamination, ICU resuscitation, then definitive repair at **24–48 h**.
Evidence: **PROPPR**, 1:1:1 vs 1:1:2: no difference in 24-h or 30-day mortality, but fewer deaths from exsanguination. **CRASH-2** supports early TXA.
Caution: no permissive hypotension in TBI or spinal cord injury. There I keep MAP 80 or more.

open.text:
Let me start with an operation. Picture it, because it's the classic story.

A surgeon opens the abdomen of a young man who was stabbed. The liver is torn, the bowel is holed, and blood is everywhere. He's a superb surgeon. He spends four hours. He repairs the liver, joins the bowel, closes beautifully. Every repair is perfect. And the patient dies in the recovery room, cold, acidotic, oozing from every needle hole.

The operation was a success. The patient died.

What killed him wasn't his anatomy. It was his physiology. And the surgery, however good, made the physiology worse with every hour it went on.

The name for the answer comes from the navy. When a warship is hit, the crew don't try to repair it at sea. They stop the flooding, put out the fires, keep it afloat, and get it to port. The real repair comes later, in dry dock. That's damage control.

[[Damage control means physiology first. Stop the bleeding, restore perfusion and clotting, and repair the anatomy later.]]

There are two halves. Damage control resuscitation is what you do, the anaesthetist and the intensivist. Damage control surgery is what the surgeon does. What the professor is really checking is whether you see them as one strategy, and whether you know the reason for it, the lethal triad.

So here's the plan. First, the lethal triad, the reason for everything. Then how resuscitation changed: the pressure target, the fluid, the blood and its ratio, tranexamic acid, and calcium. Then the surgery. And finally, how the two halves fit together.

close.text:
So let's bring it all together.

[[Damage control resuscitation and surgery treat physiology first. Stop the bleeding, restore perfusion and clotting, and repair the anatomy later.]]

Why? Because hypothermia, acidosis and coagulopathy, and now hypocalcaemia, the lethal diamond, each worsen the others. A long operation in that state kills.

What I do, the resuscitation. Permissive hypotension, a systolic of eighty to ninety, a MAP of fifty to sixty, until the bleeding is controlled, and not in TBI. Minimal crystalloid. Blood products one to one to one. Early tranexamic acid. And calcium.

What the surgeon does. An abbreviated operation to control bleeding and contamination, resuscitation in the ICU, then definitive repair at twenty-four to forty-eight hours.

The evidence. PROPPR, one to one to one against one to one to two: no difference in twenty-four-hour or thirty-day mortality, but fewer deaths from exsanguination. And CRASH two supports early tranexamic acid.

The caution. [[No permissive hypotension in TBI or spinal cord injury. There I keep the MAP at eighty or more.]]

That's your answer. What it is, why, what I do, what the surgeon does, the evidence, and the caution.

But here's a puzzle to carry forward. Coagulopathy sits in the triad, and we've talked as if we cause it, with cold fluid and dilution. Yet about a quarter of major trauma patients are already coagulopathic when they arrive, before a single bag of fluid has gone in. How can that be? That's next.

questions.text: What is trauma-induced coagulopathy?

steps.bridge: TIC starts early from shock and protein C, before fluids; fibrinogen falls first. Next: what makes it worse once it starts →

lesson.text:
Trauma-induced coagulopathy has two phases. An early one the body makes, and a late one we add.

The early phase has several names. Acute traumatic coagulopathy, or ACoTS. Whatever you call it, it needs two ingredients together, tissue injury and shock. The Royal London group showed that the injury alone wasn't enough. The early coagulopathy appeared when the injury came with hypoperfusion.

Here's how it works. The tissue injury exposes the endothelium and starts the clotting. The shock does something more surprising. In the poorly perfused vessel wall, thrombin binds to a receptor called thrombomodulin, and that complex switches on protein C. Activated protein C is an anticoagulant. It breaks down activated factors five and eight. And it uses up plasminogen activator inhibitor, the body's brake on fibrinolysis, so clots that do form are broken down too fast.

[[Shock activates protein C, which anticoagulates, and drives hyperfibrinolysis. And fibrinogen is the first factor to fall.]]

So the early lesion isn't simply a shortage of everything. It's a system tipped towards anticoagulation and clot breakdown, with fibrinogen running out first.

Then the late phase, the one we add. Consumption, as factors are used up at the bleeding sites. Dilution, with clot-free fluids. And hypothermia and acidosis.

{{**Six drivers of TIC**
Tissue damage · shock · inflammation · hypothermia · acidosis · haemodilution}}

Now see what follows for treatment, because this is where the mechanism pays off. If the coagulopathy is already there on arrival, you can't wait for a lab result to start correcting it. [[Hence early plasma, early fibrinogen and early tranexamic acid.]] Tranexamic acid blocks exactly the hyperfibrinolysis that protein C has unleashed. That's one reason it has to be early, and we'll see the other reason in the CRASH lesson.

So the body lights the fire. Now let's see what fans it.

steps.bridge: Cold and acid stop the clotting enzymes and platelets working. Next: how I replace the fibrinogen that falls first →

lesson.text: You met the lethal triad in the damage control lesson. Clotting is a chain of enzymes, and they need warmth and a normal pH. Below thirty-four degrees, or below a pH of seven point two, the enzymes slow, the factor ten a and five a complex fails, and the platelets fail. [[The early coagulopathy is the spark. Cold and acid are the fuel.]] That's why warming and perfusion are part of treating the clotting, not separate from it.

steps.bridge: Concentrate is fast; cryoprecipitate also gives VIII, vWF and XIII. Next: does giving fibrinogen early save lives →

lesson.text:
Fibrinogen falls first and falls furthest in the bleeding trauma patient. Normally it's about two to four grams per litre. So why does it matter so much?

Think of a wall. The platelets are the bricks, and fibrin is the mortar that binds them together. Fibrinogen is what becomes the fibrin. Without enough of it, the platelets pile up, but nothing holds them, and the clot crumbles.

You have two ways to replace it.

[[Fibrinogen concentrate is a pathogen-reduced powder that contains fibrinogen only. Cryoprecipitate comes from controlled thawing of plasma, and contains fibrinogen, factor eight, von Willebrand factor and factor thirteen.]]

Each has its strengths. The concentrate is fast. It needs no thawing and no blood group matching, and you know exactly how much you're giving. Cryoprecipitate carries more than fibrinogen, which can help in some bleeding. But it has to be thawed, it has to be group-matched, it may not be available, and it's an allogeneic product, usually pooled from several donors.

{{| **Concentrate** | **Cryoprecipitate**
Source | lyophilised powder | thawed FFP
Contains | fibrinogen only | fibrinogen, VIII, vWF, XIII
Dose | (target − measured, mg/dL) ÷ 1.7 mg/kg; often ~70 mg/kg | 1 unit per 5–10 kg
For | fast, no matching | more factors}}

[[Cryoprecipitate is dosed at about one unit per five to ten kilos.]] The concentrate has a formula on your screen, but you don't need to recite it. Know that it's calculated from the gap between the target and the measured level.

And the early studies were encouraging. CRYOSTAT one showed that early cryoprecipitate was feasible, and restored fibrinogen levels quickly.

So the obvious next question. If fibrinogen falls first, and early cryoprecipitate restores it, does giving it early to everyone save lives?

steps.bridge: CRYOSTAT-2: early cryoprecipitate gave no mortality benefit, harm signal in penetrating injury. Next: why transfusion itself drops calcium →

lesson.text:
That's exactly what CRYOSTAT two asked, published in JAMA in twenty twenty-three.

The patients were major trauma haemorrhage, with the major haemorrhage protocol activated, in UK and US major trauma centres.
