A tear lets blood into the wall of the aorta, it forms a second channel, and that channel can squeeze the true one shut. The question is a CT spotter. Aortic dissection.

questions.text: Spotter: CT — aortic dissection.

steps.bridge: An intimal tear lets blood split the media into a false lumen; the flap is what I see on CT. Next: which scan proves it →

lesson.text:
The aortic wall has three layers. The intima on the inside, a thin lining. The media in the middle, thick, muscular and elastic. And the adventitia outside.

A dissection starts with a tear in the intima. Through that tear, blood under arterial pressure is driven into the media, and it splits the media apart, tracking along the vessel. It doesn't split it just anywhere. It runs in the outer third of the media, where the vasa vasorum run, the small vessels that feed the aortic wall itself.

So now the aorta has two channels. The true lumen, the real one, still lined by intima. And a new one inside the wall, the false lumen. Between them, a thin sheet of torn intima and inner media. That's the intimal flap.

{{pic}}

[[On CT, the flap splits the aorta into a true and a false lumen. A double-barrelled aorta.]]

And here's why it kills, beyond rupture. The false lumen is under pressure, and it's often the bigger of the two. It can bulge and press on the true lumen, narrowing it. Any branch that comes off the true lumen, a renal artery, a mesenteric artery, an artery to the legs, can be starved.

[[The false lumen can compress the true lumen, and that causes malperfusion.]]

So when you see the flap, look at the branches too. A kidney that doesn't enhance, or a bowel that looks ischaemic, tells you the dissection is already starving an organ.
lesson.cap: The intimal flap splits the aorta into a true and a false lumen; the false lumen can squeeze the true one.

steps.bridge: ECG-gated CT aortogram from neck to pelvis is the definitive test. Next: how I classify what I see →

lesson.text:
Which scan proves it? Four candidates, each with a role and a limit.

Transthoracic echo may show severe aortic regurgitation, or blood around the heart, if the root is involved. But it can easily miss the dissection itself.

Transoesophageal echo is far better than transthoracic, and it can be done at the bedside, in theatre, or when the patient can't travel or can't have contrast. And it guides the surgeon in theatre. One honest caution: the air-filled trachea lies between the oesophagus and the aorta higher up, so there's a small blind spot at the top of the ascending aorta and the start of the arch.

MR angiography is detailed but slow, and unsuitable for an unstable patient.

[[The CT aortogram is the definitive test. The twenty twenty-four ESC guideline makes ECG-gated contrast CT, from the neck to the pelvis, the first-line imaging.]]

Why ECG-gated? Because the aortic root moves with every heartbeat, and gating freezes that movement, so a moving root isn't mistaken for a flap. Why neck to pelvis? Because you need the whole length of the tear, and every branch it might be starving.

steps.bridge: Ascending aorta involved means type A; otherwise type B. Next: what each type needs →

lesson.text:
Now classify what you see. The Stanford system is the one that decides management, and it rests on a single question.

[[Is the ascending aorta involved? If yes, it's Stanford type A. If not, it's type B.]]

{{pic}}

The card defines type A as involving the aorta before the left subclavian origin, and type B as beyond it. That's the usual way it's taught. But be precise in the viva. Strictly, type A means any involvement of the ascending aorta, wherever the tear began. And a dissection confined to the arch, sparing the ascending aorta, fits neither neatly. The twenty twenty-four ESC system calls that non-A, non-B.

And the older DeBakey system maps onto it simply. DeBakey one involves the ascending and the descending aorta. DeBakey two, the ascending only. Both are Stanford A. DeBakey three, the descending only, is Stanford B.

{{DeBakey | Stanford
I: ascending + descending | A
II: ascending only | A
III: descending only | B}}

So when the professor asks which type, don't describe the whole aorta. Answer one question. Is the ascending aorta involved?
lesson.cap: Stanford turns on one question: is the ascending aorta involved? Yes is type A, no is type B.

steps.bridge: Type A goes to surgery; type B is managed medically. Next: which type B patients need intervention →

lesson.text:
And that single question decides the treatment, because the numbers invert.

[[Type A goes to surgery. Type B is managed medically.]]

In type A, medical management carries a mortality of about fifty percent. Surgery brings it down to fifteen to twenty percent. In type B, it's the other way round. Medical management carries about fifteen percent. Surgery about thirty.

{{ | Type A | Type B
Preferred | **surgery** | **medical**
Medical mortality | ~50% | ~15%
Surgical mortality | 15–20% | ~30%}}

So surgery cuts the risk of death in type A, but doubles it in type B. Why the difference? The ascending aorta sits inside the pericardium, close to the aortic valve and the coronary arteries. A dissection there can rupture into the pericardium, or tear the valve open. The descending aorta has no such neighbours, and the operation is the bigger danger.

But medical is not the answer for every type B.

steps.bridge: Rupture, malperfusion, refractory pain or hypertension, or rapid expansion make type B complicated. Next: how I stabilise while I decide →

lesson.text:
A dissection becomes complicated when it starts to do damage. The card lists five features. Rupture, or impending rupture. Pain you can't control. Malperfusion syndrome, the starved organ we met on the CT. Cardiac tamponade. And severe aortic regurgitation.

[[Rupture, intractable pain and malperfusion make a dissection complicated.]] The last two, tamponade and regurgitation, come from the ascending aorta, so they're type A problems.

For type B, add two more that the guidelines list. Hypertension that won't come down despite full treatment. And an aorta that is expanding fast on repeat scans. [[A complicated type B dissection goes for intervention, usually endovascular repair, called TEVAR.]]

So while you decide, you stabilise.

steps.bridge: Opioid, then heart rate under 60 and systolic pressure lowered, with an arterial line. Next: which drugs, in what order →

lesson.text:
Every patient with an acute dissection needs the same first hour, whatever the type. And the whole of it follows from one idea.

What tears the aorta further isn't only how high the pressure is. It's how steeply the pressure rises with each beat. That's the rate of rise of pressure, dP by dt. Each heartbeat sends a pressure wave that jolts the flap. A faster heart means more jolts every minute. A steeper upstroke means a harder jolt each time. [[So you lower both the heart rate and the force of each beat, not just the blood pressure.]]

Now the steps.

First, the analgesia. An opioid, usually morphine. Pain drives the sympathetic system, which drives the rate and the force. So the opioid is not comfort alone. It's treatment.

Then the targets.

[[A heart rate under sixty, and a systolic pressure under one hundred and twenty, usually one hundred to one hundred and twenty.]]

{{**Targets in acute dissection**
HR <60 bpm (ACC/AHA 2022: 60–80)
SBP <120 mmHg, or the lowest that keeps end-organ perfusion (about 100–120)
Arterial line, central line}}

One honest caution. The twenty twenty-two ACC and AHA guideline puts it slightly differently: a systolic under one hundred and twenty, or the lowest pressure that keeps the organs perfused, and a heart rate of sixty to eighty. Know both, and say which you're quoting.

And the lines. An arterial line, so you see every beat, and a central line for the infusions. The aim is to avoid swings in pressure, up or down.

So which drugs, and in what order?

The order is the whole answer.

[[First line is an intravenous beta-blocker.]] It lowers the heart rate and the force of each beat together, which is exactly what you want. Three agents. Labetalol, which blocks alpha one as well as beta receptors, so it lowers the pressure too. Esmolol, short-acting and beta one selective, given as an infusion, so you can switch it off if the pressure falls too far. And metoprolol, in small boluses.

If he can't have a beta-blocker, use a non-dihydropyridine calcium channel blocker, such as diltiazem. An ACE inhibitor can also be considered.

And here's a trap in the card's source. The notes gave nicardipine as the non-dihydropyridine choice. Nicardipine is a dihydropyridine. It dilates the arteries and can make the heart race. The non-dihydropyridine alternative is diltiazem.

Then, if the pressure is still high despite the beta-blocker, add a vasodilator: nitroglycerin or sodium nitroprusside.

[[Never give the vasodilator before the beta-blocker.]]

Why? Because a vasodilator on its own drops the pressure, and the body answers with a reflex tachycardia. A faster heart, with a stronger kick, means a steeper rise of pressure. That's exactly the force that drives the tear further. You've lowered the number on the monitor and made the dissection worse.

As anaesthetists, we reach for nitroglycerin to treat a hypertensive spike. Here, it only comes after the heart rate is controlled.

spine: What I see: an **intimal flap** splitting the aorta into a **true and a false lumen**, a double-barrelled aorta. The false lumen can compress the true lumen and cause malperfusion.
Classify: if the **ascending aorta** is involved it is **Stanford A**; if not, **Stanford B**.
What next: type A goes to **emergency surgery**. Type B is treated **medically** unless complicated by rupture, malperfusion, refractory pain or hypertension, or rapid expansion; then TEVAR.
Medical control: opioid, then IV beta-blocker first. Target **HR under 60** (ACC/AHA 2022: 60–80) and **SBP under 120** (or lowest that keeps perfusion), with an arterial line.
Caution: never give a vasodilator before the beta-blocker. Reflex tachycardia raises shear stress (dP/dt) and extends the tear.

open.text:
The panel puts a CT on the screen. A slice through the chest. And in the aorta, where you'd expect a round white circle of contrast, there's a thin line running across it, splitting it into two.

That line is the whole diagnosis. And the questions that follow come in a fixed order. What is it? Which scan proves it? What type is it? And what do you do in the next hour?

Why does this matter so much? Because aortic dissection is an emergency where the right answer depends almost entirely on one anatomical question: is the ascending aorta involved? Get that right, and you know whether the patient needs a surgeon tonight or a beta-blocker and a bed in the ICU.

And there's a drug trap, the kind anaesthetists walk into. Most of us reach for a vasodilator to bring a high pressure down. Here, used first, a vasodilator can make the dissection worse.

So here's the plan. First, how a dissection forms, which is what you see on the CT. Then the scan that proves it. Then the classification. Then what each type needs, and when type B becomes complicated. And finally, how you control the pressure, with which drugs, in what order.

close.text:
So let's bring it together.

What you see on the CT is an intimal flap, splitting the aorta into a true and a false lumen. A double-barrelled aorta. And the false lumen can squeeze the true lumen, starving the organs downstream.

The scan that proves it is the ECG-gated CT aortogram, from the neck to the pelvis.

[[Then classify. If the ascending aorta is involved, it's Stanford A. If not, Stanford B.]]

Type A goes to emergency surgery. Type B is treated medically, unless it's complicated by rupture, malperfusion, pain or hypertension you can't control, or rapid expansion. Then it goes for TEVAR.

And the medical control. An opioid, then an intravenous beta-blocker first. A heart rate under sixty, and a systolic under one hundred and twenty, or the lowest that keeps the organs perfused, with an arterial line.

[[The caution. Never give a vasodilator before the beta-blocker. The reflex tachycardia steepens each pressure upstroke, and extends the tear.]]

That's your answer to the spotter. What you see, how you classify it, what comes next, how you control it, and the caution.

Now, we've seen what happens when blood tears into the wall of a vessel. The next question is about something else entering the circulation, something that has no business being there. A bubble of air. A droplet of fat. Or fluid from around a baby. Three emboli that look alike at the bedside, and differ mainly in their timing.

questions.text: Emboli — air, fat and amniotic fluid.

steps.bridge: Air causes sudden collapse with a fall in ETCO2; fat comes 24–72 h after a long-bone fracture. Next: why ETCO2 falls →

lesson.text:
Start with air.

Air gets into the circulation when a vein is open to the air, and the pressure in that vein is lower than atmospheric. So think of where that happens. Central lines, during insertion or removal. Neurosurgery, especially in the sitting position, where the operative site is well above the heart, and the veins in the bone can't collapse. Any open vein above the level of the heart.

Then the air travels to the right heart and the pulmonary arteries. A large bubble can block the right ventricular outflow like an air lock. Smaller bubbles lodge in the lung vessels. Either way, blood stops reaching the lung. The patient collapses. You may hear a mill-wheel murmur, a churning, splashing sound over the heart as blood and air are beaten together. And the end-tidal carbon dioxide falls suddenly. We'll see why on the next card.

[[Air embolism is sudden collapse during a procedure, with a mill-wheel murmur and a sudden fall in end-tidal carbon dioxide.]]

Now treat it. Every step has a reason.

Stop the entry. Tell the surgeon, and flood the field with saline, so no more air can be drawn in. Then position the patient left side down, head down. That lets the air float up into the apex of the right ventricle, away from the outflow tract, so blood can get past it. Aspirate the air through a central line, if one is in. And give a hundred percent oxygen. Oxygen treats the hypoxia, and it also washes out the nitrogen, so the bubble shrinks. And for the same reason, switch off any nitrous oxide, because it diffuses into the bubble and makes it bigger.

[[Stop entry, flood the field, left side down and head down, aspirate, and a hundred percent oxygen.]]

Now fat.

Fat embolism comes later. It typically appears twenty-four to seventy-two hours after a long-bone fracture. Fat droplets from the marrow enter the circulation, and the illness that follows is hypoxia, petechiae and confusion. Those three are the heart of Gurd's criteria. The petechiae are the clue that gives it away: look across the chest, the armpits, and inside the conjunctivae. Treatment is mainly supportive.

{{| Air | Fat | Amniotic fluid
**When** | instant, during a procedure | 24–72 h after long-bone fracture | labour, delivery, or just after
**Clue** | mill-wheel murmur, ETCO2 falls | petechiae, confusion | seizures, then DIC}}

So the setting tells you what it is. But what ties all three together is what happens to the end-tidal carbon dioxide.

steps.bridge: Emboli create dead space, so ETCO2 drops and the arterial–end-tidal gap widens. Next: how amniotic fluid embolism presents →

lesson.text:
Here's the physiology under every embolus.

Carbon dioxide reaches the lung in the blood. To appear in the breath, it has to be carried to an alveolus that is also being ventilated. Normally the end-tidal value sits just below the arterial value, about three to five millimetres of mercury below it.

Now block a pulmonary artery, with air, fat, a clot, or anything else. The alveoli downstream are still being ventilated. The ventilator keeps pushing gas in and out of them. But no blood reaches them, so they carry no carbon dioxide. They breathe out gas that is almost free of it, and that dilutes the gas from the rest of the lung. That's dead space: lung that is ventilated but not perfused.

{{pic}}

[[Dead space lowers the end-tidal carbon dioxide and widens the gap to the arterial value.]]

And here's the sign that tells you what kind of problem it is. [[A sudden fall in end-tidal carbon dioxide, with a stable or rising PaCO2, means pulmonary blood flow has fallen.]] It isn't a ventilation problem. The carbon dioxide is still in the blood. It simply isn't reaching the lung.

And the same pattern appears whenever the lung is poorly perfused. Pulmonary embolism, fat embolism, cardiogenic shock, right ventricular failure. You've seen it in theatre a hundred times, every time the cardiac output fell suddenly and the capnograph followed it down.

Now let's go to the most dramatic of the three emboli.
lesson.cap: An embolus stops flow to ventilated lung: end-tidal CO2 falls, PaCO2 does not, and the gap widens.

steps.bridge: AFE is sudden hypoxia and collapse in labour, then DIC; half die in the first hour. Next: why it behaves this way →

lesson.text:
Amniotic fluid embolism. The facts first.

It's rare, about three point three per hundred thousand deliveries. But the mortality is high, anywhere from fifteen to eighty-five percent. And of those who die, half die in the first hour.

The sequence is classic. Sudden hypoxia, respiratory failure. Then hypotension, or cardiac arrest. Seizures. And then DIC, with bleeding.

It happens during labour, at delivery, or within about thirty minutes after.

[[Amniotic fluid embolism is sudden hypoxia and collapse in labour, then DIC. And it's a clinical diagnosis, made by exclusion.]]

There's no test that confirms it in time. So you act on the picture, and you don't wait.

steps.bridge: AFE is an anaphylactoid reaction, not a plug: RV failure first, then LV failure and DIC. Next: how I treat it →

lesson.text:
Now the mechanism. And this is where the trap lies.

The old view was mechanical. Debris from the amniotic fluid, things like fetal hair and skin cells, entered the mother's circulation through a torn uterine vein, travelled to the lung, and physically blocked the pulmonary vessels. Like a clot.

The current view, and the exam answer, is different.

[[Amniotic fluid embolism is not a plug. It's a maternal systemic inflammatory response to fetal material, an anaphylactoid reaction.]]

The fetal material enters the maternal circulation. And the mother's body reacts to it, with a sudden, overwhelming inflammatory response.

And it runs in two phases.

The first phase is in the lung and the right heart. The pulmonary vessels go into spasm. The right ventricle suddenly faces a huge afterload, and fails. Blood stops crossing the lung, so the mother becomes profoundly hypoxic.

The second phase follows. The left ventricle fails too. And DIC sets in, with bleeding.

[[Right ventricular failure and hypoxia first. Then left ventricular failure, and DIC.]]

Now three wrong answers that a question writer likes to offer. Mechanical blockage of the pulmonary vessels: that's the old view. An IgE-mediated allergy: it isn't. That's why the word is anaphylactoid, not anaphylactic. And tissue factor: it does explain the DIC, but only the DIC, not the whole syndrome.

So if a question asks for the mechanism, the answer is systemic inflammatory activation by fetal material.

Which leads directly to how you treat her.

You met this card with sepsis in pregnancy, so just the treatment. Aggressive support of every failing organ, and correct the coagulopathy early with the massive transfusion protocol. Deliver the baby as an emergency, by caesarean if needed, with arterial ligation or even hysterectomy for the bleeding. And VA-ECMO as the rescue for refractory collapse. [[If she arrests, deliver the baby by perimortem caesarean within five minutes.]] Emptying the uterus takes its weight off the great vessels, so it helps her resuscitation as well as the baby.

spine: What it is: three emboli that look alike but differ in timing. Air is sudden and procedural; fat comes 24–72 h after a long-bone fracture; amniotic fluid strikes in labour.
Air: sudden collapse, a **mill-wheel murmur** and a **sudden fall in ETCO2** from dead space. I stop entry, flood the field, tilt left lateral head-down, aspirate, and give **100% oxygen**.
Fat: hypoxia, **petechiae** and confusion after a long-bone fracture (Gurd criteria).
Amniotic fluid: sudden hypoxia, hypotension or arrest, seizures, then **DIC**. It is an anaphylactoid reaction: RV failure first, then LV failure and bleeding.
What I do for AFE: organ support, massive transfusion protocol, emergency delivery, and VA-ECMO as rescue.
Caution: AFE is a clinical diagnosis of exclusion. Mortality is high and **half die in the first hour**, so I act before any test confirms it.

open.text:
Three patients. All three suddenly can't oxygenate, and their pressure falls.

Patient A is in the sitting position for a posterior fossa craniotomy. You're watching the capnograph, and the end-tidal carbon dioxide drops off a cliff.

Patient B is a young man who broke his femur two days ago. Tonight he's confused, breathless, and there's a rash of tiny spots across his chest.

Patient C is a woman in labour. She suddenly gasps, goes blue, has a seizure, and an hour later she's bleeding from every cannula site.

Three emboli. Air, fat and amniotic fluid. At the bedside, in the first few minutes, they can look the same. Sudden hypoxia, sudden collapse.

So how do you tell them apart? [[Mostly by timing. Air is instant and procedural. Fat comes a day or more after a long-bone fracture. Amniotic fluid strikes in labour.]]

What is the professor really checking? First, can you recognise each one from its setting. Second, do you understand why the end-tidal carbon dioxide falls, because that's the physiology under all three. Third, do you know the modern view of amniotic fluid embolism, because the old one is the trap. And fourth, can you act, because in amniotic fluid embolism, half the patients who die, die in the first hour.

So here's the plan. First, air and fat, side by side. Then the capnograph, and why it falls. Then amniotic fluid embolism: the facts, the mechanism, and the treatment.

close.text:
So let's bring it together.

Three emboli that look alike, and differ in their timing. Air is sudden and procedural. Fat comes twenty-four to seventy-two hours after a long-bone fracture. Amniotic fluid strikes in labour.

Air gives sudden collapse, a mill-wheel murmur, and a sudden fall in end-tidal carbon dioxide from dead space. [[Stop the entry, flood the field, left side down and head down, aspirate, and give a hundred percent oxygen.]]

Fat gives hypoxia, petechiae and confusion after a long-bone fracture. Those are Gurd's criteria.

Amniotic fluid gives sudden hypoxia, hypotension or arrest, seizures, and then DIC. It's an anaphylactoid reaction. Right ventricular failure first, then left ventricular failure, and bleeding.

What you do for amniotic fluid embolism. Organ support, the massive transfusion protocol, emergency delivery, and VA-ECMO as a rescue.

And the caution. [[It's a clinical diagnosis of exclusion. Half of those who die, die in the first hour, so you act before any test confirms it.]]

That's your answer. The timing, air, fat, amniotic fluid, what you do, and the caution.

Now, amniotic fluid embolism ended in bleeding. But it's rare. The commonest way a mother bleeds to death is far more ordinary. A uterus that won't contract after the baby is born. And because pregnancy hides blood loss so well, she can look fine until very late. That's the next question. Postpartum haemorrhage.

questions.text: Postpartum haemorrhage in the ICU — how do you resuscitate?

steps.bridge: PPH is over 500 mL; find which of the four Ts is the cause. Next: why the bleeding is so easily under-estimated →

lesson.text:
Postpartum haemorrhage is blood loss over five hundred millilitres. Massive haemorrhage is over a thousand to fifteen hundred.

Primary haemorrhage is within twenty-four hours of birth. Secondary is from twenty-four hours up to six weeks.

To find the cause, think of four Ts.

{{T | Finding | Treatment
**Tone** | soft, boggy uterus | massage, uterotonics
**Trauma** | tear, haematoma, inversion | suture; drain haematoma >3 cm; replace uterus
**Tissue** | retained placenta | manual removal, curettage
**Thrombin** | blood not clotting | plasma, platelets, factors; rFVIIa}}

Tone. A soft, boggy uterus that won't contract. You treat it with massage and uterotonics. Trauma. A tear, a haematoma, or an inverted uterus. You suture the tear, drain a large haematoma, and put the uterus back. Tissue. A retained placenta, which keeps the uterus from contracting. You remove it. And thrombin. Blood that won't clot. You give plasma, platelets and factors.

[[Atony, a uterus that won't contract, is the commonest cause.]] So feel the uterus first. If it's firm and she's still bleeding, look for the other Ts.

steps.bridge: Shock appears late, and fibrinogen under 2 g/L is already dangerous. Next: what order I resuscitate and stop it in →

lesson.text:
Now the heart of this question. Why is obstetric haemorrhage so easily missed?

Start with the physiology. By the end of pregnancy, her blood volume has risen by about forty-five percent. She has a big reserve. So she can lose a lot before her pressure falls.

[[In pregnancy, shock appears late. She can lose one to one and a half litres before her blood pressure falls.]]

So the pressure on the monitor is reassuring you about the wrong thing. Watch the heart rate, the colour, the mental state, the urine. Go back to our patient. A heart rate of a hundred and fifteen, with a normal pressure, is already a warning.

Then the measurement. Visual estimates of blood loss are unreliable. Blood soaks into drapes, pads and the bed, and some of it stays hidden inside, in the uterus or a haematoma. Our eyes tend to underestimate it.

And now the laboratory warning, which is the clever part. In pregnancy, fibrinogen is normally high, about four to six grams per litre. So a fibrinogen that would look acceptable in another patient is already a sign of serious consumption here.

[[A fibrinogen under two grams per litre in postpartum haemorrhage is already dangerous.]]

Exam stems like to hide this clue. A fibrinogen of a hundred and thirty milligrams per decilitre is one point three grams per litre. In anyone, that's low. In a bleeding mother, whose normal is three to four times higher, it's an alarm.

So what follows? Replace fibrinogen early, and start the massive transfusion protocol early, without waiting for the pressure to fall.

Now the order in which you stop the bleeding.

steps.bridge: Climb the ladder: uterotonics, then transfusion, then tamponade, sutures, embolisation, hysterectomy. Next: which uterotonic, and who must avoid it →

lesson.text:
Think of postpartum haemorrhage as a ladder. You climb one rung at a time, and you keep resuscitating on every rung.

The first rung is prevention. Active management of the third stage: oxytocin at delivery, controlled cord traction, and uterine massage.

Then, when she bleeds, resuscitate. Two large cannulae, oxygen, monitoring, bloods and a cross-match.

Then bimanual massage and oxytocin, and find which T it is.

If the uterus still won't contract, add a second uterotonic: carboprost, methylergonovine or misoprostol.

If the bleeding is massive, transfuse red cells, platelets and factors, with vasopressors as needed.

Then the mechanical rungs. Balloon tamponade or packing. Compression sutures, such as the B-Lynch. Ligation of vessels, or embolisation.

And the last rung, hysterectomy.

[[Uterotonics first, then transfusion, then tamponade, compression sutures, embolisation, and hysterectomy.]] And uterotonics come before the balloon.

Now two pieces of evidence the panel wants.

The WOMAN trial. Tranexamic acid, one gram intravenously, within three hours of birth, reduced deaths from bleeding: one point five against one point nine percent. Notice what it did not change. All-cause mortality. [[WOMAN cut deaths from bleeding, not deaths from all causes. And the drug works best given early.]]

And E-MOTIVE, published in twenty twenty-three. The idea was simple: detect bleeding early, by measuring it rather than guessing, and then give a bundle of first steps together, not one at a time. That cut the combined outcome of severe haemorrhage, surgery or death by about sixty percent.

So which uterotonic, and who must avoid it?

steps.bridge: Oxytocin first; no ergometrine in hypertension, no carboprost in asthma. Next: which fibrinogen product to give →

lesson.text:
Four drugs. Learn each one with the patient who must not have it.

{{Drug | Dose | Avoid in
**Oxytocin** (first) | 20 IU in 1 L saline; up to 500 mL over 10 min | rapid bolus: hypotension
**Methylergonovine** | 0.2 mg IM | **hypertension, pre-eclampsia**
**Carboprost** (PGF2α) | 0.25 mg IM | **asthma**
**Misoprostol** (PGE1) | 1,000 µg rectally | few; slower}}

Oxytocin comes first, as an infusion. Avoid a rapid bolus, which causes hypotension.

Methylergonovine, an ergot, nought point two milligrams intramuscularly. It constricts vessels, so avoid it in hypertension and pre-eclampsia.

Carboprost, a prostaglandin, nought point two five milligrams intramuscularly. It can cause bronchospasm, so avoid it in asthma.

Misoprostol, a thousand micrograms rectally. Few contraindications, but slower to act.

[[No methylergonovine, or any ergot, in hypertension or pre-eclampsia. No carboprost in asthma.]] A question stem that says no asthma is telling you the answer is carboprost.

You met fibrinogen concentrate and cryoprecipitate in the trauma lessons. The concentrate is fibrinogen alone, fast, with no matching. Cryoprecipitate also carries factor eight, von Willebrand factor and factor thirteen, but needs thawing and group matching. Now apply it to this mother. [[Give fibrinogen when it's under two grams per litre, or the FIBTEM A five is under twelve millimetres, with ongoing bleeding.]] Giving it empirically above that level didn't help, in the OBS two and FIB-PPH trials. So measure, then replace.

spine: What it is: postpartum haemorrhage is blood loss over 500 mL; massive is over 1,000–1,500 mL. I find the cause with the four Ts: tone, trauma, tissue, thrombin.
Why it is missed: blood volume rises by 45% in pregnancy, so shock appears late, after 1–1.5 L lost. Visual estimates are unreliable.
What I do: two large cannulae, massive transfusion protocol, oxytocin then a second uterotonic, then balloon tamponade, compression sutures, embolisation, and hysterectomy if needed.
Fibrinogen: normal in pregnancy is 4–6 g/L. I give it when **under 2 g/L** (or FIBTEM A5 under 12 mm) with ongoing bleeding; empirical fibrinogen above that did not help (OBS2, FIB-PPH).
Evidence: **WOMAN**: TXA 1 g within 3 h of birth cut bleeding deaths (1.5% vs 1.9%), not all-cause. **E-MOTIVE** (2023): early detection plus a bundle cut severe PPH, surgery or death by ~60%.
Caution: no methylergonovine in hypertension or pre-eclampsia; no carboprost in asthma.

open.text:
You're called to the labour ward. A woman delivered an hour ago. The midwife says she's lost some blood, but her blood pressure is a hundred and ten over seventy. Her heart rate is a hundred and fifteen. And she's quiet, a little pale.

The trap is the blood pressure. In most patients, a normal pressure buys you time. In this one, it may be the last thing to go.

Postpartum haemorrhage is one of the leading causes of maternal death worldwide. And it's one of the few obstetric emergencies that lands squarely in the ICU and the theatre. You're the one asked to resuscitate her.

What is the professor really checking? First, do you know the definition, and the four causes. Second, do you understand why the bleeding is so easily under-estimated, and what the early warning really is. Third, can you climb the treatment ladder in the right order. Fourth, do you know which drug to give, and which to avoid in whom. And finally, the evidence: tranexamic acid, and fibrinogen.

So here's the plan. First, the definition and the four Ts. Then why the loss is hidden. Then the ladder. Then the uterotonics. And finally, fibrinogen.

close.text:
So let's bring it together.

Postpartum haemorrhage is blood loss over five hundred millilitres. Massive is over a thousand to fifteen hundred. You find the cause with the four Ts: tone, trauma, tissue and thrombin.

Why it's missed. Blood volume rises by forty-five percent in pregnancy, so shock appears late, after one to one and a half litres. And visual estimates are unreliable.

What you do. Two large cannulae, the massive transfusion protocol, oxytocin, then a second uterotonic. Then balloon tamponade, compression sutures, embolisation, and hysterectomy if you need it.

[[Fibrinogen is normally four to six in pregnancy. Give it when it's under two, or the FIBTEM A five is under twelve, with ongoing bleeding.]]

The evidence. WOMAN: tranexamic acid within three hours of birth cut deaths from bleeding, though not all-cause deaths. And E-MOTIVE: early detection plus a bundle cut severe haemorrhage, surgery or death by about sixty percent.

[[And the caution. No methylergonovine in hypertension or pre-eclampsia. No carboprost in asthma.]]

That's your answer. What it is, why it's missed, what you do, fibrinogen, the evidence, and the caution.

And that closes our block on bleeding and trauma. We've followed blood out of the vessels, into cavities, into the pelvis, into the wall of the aorta.

The next block is about a different kind of loss. Not blood, but plasma, pouring out through burned skin, hour after hour. And every decision in a burn, the fluid, the transfer, the prognosis, starts from one number. How much of the body is burned? And how do you estimate it, in a child as well as an adult? That's where we go next. Burns.

questions.text: How do you estimate burn surface area?

steps.bridge: TBSA and depth are estimated in the survey, after ABCDE. Next: the adult rule of nines →

lesson.text:
Before you count anything, you treat the patient. A burn is a trauma patient first.

So the primary survey is the one you already know. ABCDE. Airway, breathing, circulation, disability, exposure. And look for associated trauma, because a man escaping a fire may have jumped, fallen, or been thrown. [[The burn is the obvious injury. It isn't always the one that kills him first.]]

Two burn points sit inside that survey. First, avoid putting your IV line into a limb with a circumferential burn. Second, check the distal pulses in any circumferential burn. Why? Because the burned skin becomes a stiff, tight sleeve. As the tissue underneath swells over the coming hours, that sleeve can choke the circulation beyond it. We'll meet the treatment for that, the escharotomy, in a later lesson.

Then the history. In trauma you learned AMPLE. Burns adds one letter, AMPLET. Allergies, medications, past history, last meal, events. And the T, tetanus status, because a burn is an open, contaminated wound.

Now listen to the events, because two of them carry red flags.

A closed-space fire, a room, a car, a burning building, means think of carbon monoxide and cyanide, before you see a single sign. An electrical injury means think of arrhythmia, compartment syndrome and rhabdomyolysis, because the current travels through tissue the skin doesn't show. Each of those gets its own lesson in this group.

Only after all that do you estimate the extent and the depth of the burn. And here's the rule that trips people up.

[[Only partial-thickness and full-thickness burns count towards the burned surface area. Simple redness, erythema, does not.]]

Why leave it out? Because a superficial burn damages only the outer layer of the skin. The barrier is still intact, so it doesn't pour out plasma, and it doesn't drive the fluid need. Count it, and you overestimate the burn, and then the fluid.

Go back to our man. His red, unblistered face hurts, and it needs care. But it adds nothing to his number.

So how do you put a number on the rest? In an adult, you start with nines.

steps.bridge: Head and arms 9% each, trunk and legs 18% each, perineum 1%. Next: how a child differs →

lesson.text:
The rule of nines divides the adult body into regions of nine percent, or multiples of nine.

The head and neck, nine. Each whole arm, nine. The front of the trunk, eighteen. The back of the trunk, eighteen. Each whole leg, eighteen. And the perineum, the last one percent.

{{**Rule of nines (adult)**
Head and neck 9% · each arm 9%
Anterior trunk 18% · posterior trunk 18%
Each leg 18% (9% front, 9% back)
Perineum 1% · total 100%}}

[[Head nine, each arm nine, each leg eighteen, the trunk eighteen at the front and eighteen at the back, and one for the perineum.]]

When only part of a leg is burned, split it. The front of the leg is nine, the back is nine.

Now count our man. The front of the trunk, eighteen. Both arms, nine and nine, another eighteen. That's thirty-six already. And the face, remember, doesn't count. What about those scattered patches on his legs? They don't fill a region, so the nines can't measure them. For that, you need another tool.

steps.bridge: Lund-Browder enlarges the head and shrinks the legs in children. Next: why the proportions change →

lesson.text:
The rule of nines is quick. But it was built for an adult body, and for burns that cover whole regions. Real burns are rarely so tidy, and real patients aren't all adults. So you need two more tools.

The first is for patchy, scattered burns. Use the patient's own hand.

[[The patient's palm, with the fingers included, is about one percent of his body surface.]]

His palm, not yours. It scales with his body, so a child's hand measures a child. Our man has four patches on his legs, each about the size of his palm. Four percent. Add that to the thirty-six. [[Our man has a forty percent burn.]] Not sixty, not thirty. Forty.

The second tool is the Lund and Browder chart. It's a drawing of the body, front and back, divided into smaller regions. You shade the burn region by region, and the percentage given to the head and the legs changes with the patient's age.

{{Area | Adult (rule of nines) | Child (Lund-Browder)
Head | **9%** | **larger**, about 19% in infants, shrinking with age
Each arm | 9% | similar
Front / back trunk | 18% / 18% | similar
Each leg | **18%** | **smaller** in infants, growing with age
Perineum | 1% | 1%}}

Look at the two rows that move. The head, about nineteen percent in an infant, against nine in an adult, and shrinking as the child grows. The legs, smaller in the infant, and growing with age. The arms, the trunk and the perineum barely change.

[[Lund-Browder is the most accurate chart at any age, and the one you must use in a child.]]

So when the panel asks which method you use, don't say the rule of nines and stop. Say this. The rule of nines for a quick adult estimate. The palm for patchy burns. And Lund-Browder whenever accuracy matters, and always in a child.

But why should a child's head carry so much more of the body?

Think of how a body grows. A newborn's head is large, because the brain grows early and fast. The legs come later. Through childhood, the legs lengthen far more than the head grows. So, year by year, the share of the surface shifts away from the head and towards the legs.

Look at the two figures on your screen.

{{pic}}

On the left, the adult. Head nine, each leg eighteen. On the right, the infant. The head is roughly eighteen percent, double the adult figure. Each leg is roughly fourteen, against the adult eighteen. The arms, the trunk and the perineum stay close to adult proportions. And the adult pattern isn't reached until adolescence.

[[In a young child, the head counts double, and each leg counts less.]]

So what happens if you use the adult rule in a child? Two errors, in opposite directions.

[[The adult rule of nines underestimates a head burn in a child, and overestimates a leg burn.]]

Picture a toddler who pulls a pan of boiling water down over his head. By the adult rule, his whole head is nine percent. By his own chart, it's nearer eighteen. And that matters, because in children, formal fluid resuscitation starts above fifteen percent. One chart says no drip. The other says start one.

Now, what the examiner is really testing here is not the exact figure for a five-year-old. It's the principle. A head burn weighs far more in a small child. Say that, name Lund-Browder, and you've answered the question he's asking.
lesson.cap: Infant vs adult: the infant head is about 18%, double the adult 9%; each leg about 14%, not 18%.

spine: What it is: TBSA is the percentage of body surface with partial- or full-thickness burn. Superficial burns are not counted.
Adults: rule of nines. Head and neck **9%**, each arm 9%, front and back of trunk 18% each, each leg **18%**, perineum 1%.
Children: the head is larger and the legs smaller. In an infant the head is about **18–19%** and each leg about **14%**.
What I do: **Lund-Browder** is the most accurate chart at any age and essential in children. For patchy burns, the patient's palm with fingers is about 1%.
Why it matters: TBSA drives the fluid estimate and transfer decisions, so errors spread into resuscitation.
Caution: the rule of nines overestimates leg burns and underestimates head burns in a child.

open.text:
Picture a man carried in from a factory fire.

His face is red, like a bad sunburn, but it isn't blistered. The whole front of his chest and abdomen is blistered. Both arms are blistered, from the shoulder to the fingertips. And there are a few scattered patches on his legs. Someone at the door says sixty percent. Someone else says thirty. And that difference is not academic.

In the last group, the fluid was leaving through a hole you could find and close, a bleeding vessel. In a burn, it leaves through millions of holes you can't see. The capillaries leak. And how much fluid you give him over the next day begins with one number, the percentage of his body surface that is burned. [[Get that number wrong, and every calculation built on it is wrong too.]] Overcall it, and you drown him in oedema. Undercall it, and his kidneys pay.

This question sounds like a chart you learned as a student. The rule of nines. But what the professor is really checking is three things. Do you know which burns you count, and which you leave out? Do you know why a child is different, and which chart to use? And do you know where the estimate sits, inside a proper survey, rather than as the first thing you do?

So the plan. First, the survey, and where the estimate fits in it. Then the adult rule of nines. Then the tools for patchy burns and for every age. And finally, why a child's body changes the numbers.

close.text:
So let's bring it together.

[[The burned surface area is the percentage of the body with partial-thickness or full-thickness burn. Superficial redness is not counted.]]

In an adult, the rule of nines. Head and neck nine, each arm nine, the front and back of the trunk eighteen each, each leg eighteen, and one for the perineum.

In a child, the head is larger and the legs smaller. In an infant, the head is about eighteen to nineteen percent, and each leg about fourteen.

What do you do? Lund-Browder is the most accurate chart at any age, and essential in a child. For patchy burns, the patient's own palm with the fingers is about one percent.

Why does it matter? [[Because the burned surface area drives the fluid estimate and the decision to transfer. An error here spreads into everything that follows.]]

And the caution. In a child, the rule of nines overestimates a leg burn and underestimates a head burn.

That's your answer to the panel. What it is, the adult rule, the child, what you use, why it matters, and the caution.

But here's where this number leads. Our man has a forty percent burn, and he weighs seventy kilos. How many litres does that buy him, and how fast? How will you know you're giving too much? And once he survives the first day, his burn will start consuming his own muscle, unless you feed him. That's next.

questions.text: How do you manage burns — fluids and feeding?

steps.bridge: Capillary leak drives the need; Parkland gives 4 mL, half in 8 h. Next: the current lower starting rule →

lesson.text: You met this card with the fluid lessons, so here is the short version. A burn loses plasma from the wound, and far more through a capillary leak across the whole body. So formal fluids start above twenty percent in adults, and above fifteen percent in children, with Ringer's lactate. Parkland gives four millilitres per kilo per percent over the day, with half in the first eight hours from the time of the burn. Hold on to that four. It's the historic figure. Today's starting rule is lower.

steps.bridge: ABLS starts at 2 mL adults, 3 children, 4 electrical, and titrates hourly. Next: the exact urine targets →

lesson.text:
The American Burn Association's life support course, ABLS, now teaches a lower start.

[[Start at two millilitres per kilo per percent burn in adults, three in children, and four in electrical injury.]]

Why lower? Because when units gave the full Parkland volume regardless of response, and then added more, patients drowned in oedema. Fluid that leaks into the tissues can't be taken back quickly. So the safer path is to start lower, and let the patient's response pull the rate up if he needs it. Parkland's four is now the historic upper figure, not the place to begin.

The timing doesn't change. Half in the first eight hours, counted from the time of the burn, not from arrival. The other half over the next sixteen. And the fluid is Ringer's lactate.

Now our man. Look at the timeline on your screen.

{{pic}}

Two, times seventy kilos, times forty percent. Five thousand six hundred millilitres for the day. Half of that, two thousand eight hundred, in the first eight hours. That's three hundred and fifty millilitres an hour to start. Then a hundred and seventy-five an hour for the next sixteen. And notice. That's exactly half of what Parkland would have given him.

{{**ABLS start**: adults 2 · children 3 · electrical 4 mL/kg/%TBSA
70 kg, 40%: 2 × 70 × 40 = **5,600 mL**/24 h
**2,800 mL** in first 8 h from burn = **350 mL/h**
Children ≤30 kg: add maintenance with dextrose (D5LR)}}

But here's the line that matters more than the arithmetic. [[The formula sets only the first rate. From then on, the urine output sets every rate after it.]] You titrate every hour. Half a millilitre per kilo per hour in adults, roughly thirty to fifty millilitres. One millilitre per kilo per hour in children under thirty kilos. And seventy-five to a hundred millilitres an hour in electrical injury, until the urine clears. We'll unpack those targets on the next card.

Two more details the panel likes. In a child of thirty kilos or less, add maintenance fluid containing dextrose, five percent dextrose in Ringer's lactate, on top of the resuscitation rate, and watch the glucose. Small children have little stored glycogen, so a long fast in a stressed child brings hypoglycaemia.

And the titration works in both directions. [[When the urine is above target, turn the drip down.]] That's the half of the rule people forget, and forgetting it is how fluid creep begins.

So what exactly are you aiming for, and which burns do you leave out of the sum?
lesson.cap: ABLS start for 70 kg, 40%: 5,600 mL in 24 h; half in 8 h from the burn, 350 mL/h. Then titrate.

steps.bridge: Urine 0.5 mL/kg/h in adults and 1 in small children; superficial burns are not counted. Next: what happens if I overshoot →

lesson.text:
The urine target first.

[[In adults, half a millilitre per kilo per hour, roughly thirty to fifty millilitres. In children under thirty kilos, one millilitre per kilo per hour.]]

Why the urine? Because it's the perfusion gauge you can read every hour. The kidney is sensitive to under-filling, and with a catheter in the bladder, each hour gives you a fresh reading. And why more per kilo in a small child? Because a small child normally makes more urine for his weight than an adult does.

{{**Urine target** adults 0.5 mL/kg/h (≈30–50 mL/h) · children <30 kg 1 mL/kg/h
**Counted in %TBSA**: partial- and full-thickness only
**Not counted**: superficial (first-degree) burns}}

And remember what the target protects against. Both directions. The calculated volume is only a starting point. The rate is adjusted hourly to keep the urine at target, which guards against under-resuscitation and over-resuscitation alike.

Now the second half of this card, which links back to the survey. Only partial-thickness and full-thickness burns go into the sum. Superficial, first-degree burns are left out of the percentage used for the formula, even though they hurt and still need care. Our man's red face, again. Painful, treated, and not in his number.

[[A formula fed a wrong percentage gives a wrong start. The urine is what catches the error.]]

So what happens when the drip runs ahead of the patient?

steps.bridge: Over-titration causes compartment syndromes; measure bladder pressure. Next: how to feed the hypermetabolic patient →

lesson.text:
You met fluid creep with the albumin lessons. Giving more than the formula, chasing every low hour of urine with more fluid, brings oedema, abdominal and limb compartment syndrome, pulmonary oedema, and burns that deepen. So once more than two hundred and fifty millilitres per kilo has gone in, measure the intra-abdominal pressure, through the bladder. For our seventy-kilo man, that's seventeen and a half litres.

[[The urine target guards against too little. The bladder pressure guards against too much.]]

So the fluid is set. Now, how do you feed him?

A major burn turns the body's metabolism up, hard, and keeps it there. Stress hormones surge, catecholamines, cortisol and glucagon, and inflammation runs high. The result is a hypercatabolic state. Insulin resistance, so the sugar runs high. Lipolysis, breaking down fat. And proteolysis, breaking down muscle, to supply the amino acids the wound and the liver demand. The cost is poor wound healing and a suppressed immune system. And this state can last for months, well after the wounds have closed.

[[A big burn burns through the patient's own muscle as fuel, unless you feed it.]]

So the first rule is timing. Feed early, through the gut, ideally within about twelve hours. Why so early? Early enteral feeding helps prevent stress ulcers, reduces infection, and boosts immunoglobulins. Feed through a nasogastric tube. In burns over forty percent, place the feeding tube pre-emptively, because these patients can't eat enough on their own. Parenteral nutrition is kept for selected cases.

How much energy? Estimate the resting energy expenditure, then multiply it by a factor that rises with the burn size.

{{**Energy** = REE × factor by TBSA
<10% **1.2** · 10–20% **1.3** · 20–40% **1.5** · 40–60% **1.7** · >60% **2.0**
**Protein**: adults **1.5–2 g/kg/day** · children 2–4 (ESPEN 2.5–4)
**Fat** low, under about 25% of calories
Micronutrients: Zn, Cu, Se, Ca, vitamins B1, C, D, E}}

The factor runs from one point two in a small burn up to two in a burn over sixty percent. So the largest burns can double the energy need.

Protein matters even more than calories, because protein is what the body is stealing from its muscle. [[Protein one and a half to two grams per kilo per day in adults.]] More in children, two to four on your notes, and two and a half to four in the European guideline.

Keep the fat low, under about a quarter of the calories, because a high fat load leads to fatty infiltration of the organs. And replace the micronutrients the wound loses: zinc, copper, selenium, calcium, thiamine, and vitamins C, D and E.

Your card also lists glutamine. Leave it out of your answer. The largest trial, RE-ENERGIZE, published in two thousand twenty-two, gave enteral glutamine to about twelve hundred burned patients, and found no benefit in time to discharge or in survival. [[Glutamine is out. The largest trial found no benefit.]]

Then you can blunt the hypermetabolism itself, with two drugs. Propranolol, a beta-blocker, damps the catecholamine drive. In burned children, Herndon's group in Galveston showed that it lowered the resting energy expenditure and reduced muscle protein breakdown. And oxandrolone, an anabolic steroid, helps preserve lean mass.

[[Feed early, feed protein, and blunt the hypermetabolism with propranolol and oxandrolone.]]

One honest caution. A starved, catabolic patient who is suddenly fed can develop refeeding syndrome. Watch the phosphate and the magnesium in the first days of feeding.

spine: Why: burns cause capillary leak and sequestration. Fluids are needed above **20% TBSA** in adults and **15%** in children.
What I do: Ringer's lactate at **2 mL/kg/%TBSA** in adults, 3 in children, 4 in electrical injury, half in the first 8 h from the time of burn.
Target: urine **0.5 mL/kg/h** in adults, 1 mL/kg/h in children under 30 kg. The formula is only a start; I titrate every hour.
Caution: fluid creep. Over-resuscitation causes abdominal and limb compartment syndrome and pulmonary oedema, so I measure bladder pressure in big resuscitations.
Feeding: early enteral, ideally within **12 h**, protein **1.5–2 g/kg/day**, and propranolol or oxandrolone for hypermetabolism.
Also: think of inhalation injury, carbon monoxide and cyanide in any closed-space fire.

open.text:
Let me start with our man from the factory. Seventy kilos, a forty percent burn, and the clock started the moment the fire touched him.

For decades, the answer to how much fluid came from one formula. In the late nineteen sixties, Charles Baxter, working at Parkland Hospital in Dallas, set out four millilitres per kilo for every percent burned, over the first day. It saved lives. Before formal resuscitation, many patients with large burns died of burn shock in the first days.

But then something odd happened. Burn units kept giving more than the formula. Not less. More. And their patients swelled. Abdomens tightened, limbs needed decompressing, lungs filled. In two thousand, Basil Pruitt gave this a name. Fluid creep.

So the panel's question has two halves, and both are traps for the confident resident. The fluid half. Why does a burn need fluid at all? What rate do you start, and why is it lower than Parkland now? What do you titrate to, every hour? And what goes wrong when you overshoot? Then the feeding half. Because a big burn drives one of the most intense hypermetabolic states in medicine, and a patient you resuscitate perfectly can still waste away.

So the plan. First, the classic formula and why fluid is needed. Then today's starting rule, worked through for our man. Then the urine targets. Then fluid creep. And finally, feeding.

close.text:
So let's bring it together.

Why fluid? A burn causes a capillary leak and sequestration of plasma. Formal fluids are needed above twenty percent in adults, and fifteen in children.

What do you do? [[Ringer's lactate at two millilitres per kilo per percent in adults, three in children, four in electrical injury.]] Half in the first eight hours from the time of the burn.

The target is urine, half a millilitre per kilo per hour in adults, one in children under thirty kilos. And the formula is only the start. You titrate every hour, down as well as up.

The caution is fluid creep. Over-resuscitation causes abdominal and limb compartment syndrome and pulmonary oedema, so in a big resuscitation, you measure the bladder pressure.

[[Feeding: early enteral, ideally within twelve hours, protein one and a half to two grams per kilo per day, with propranolol or oxandrolone for the hypermetabolism.]]

And in any closed-space fire, you think of inhalation injury, carbon monoxide and cyanide.

That's your answer to the panel. Why, what you do, the target, the caution, feeding, and the fire.

But notice what every number today assumed. That the burn you can see on the skin is the burn that's there. Now picture a lineman who touched a high-voltage cable. A small black mark on his hand. Another on his foot. By the skin, a tiny burn. And an hour later, his urine is the colour of cola. That's next.

questions.text: Fluid management in electrical burns. How is it different from thermal burns?

steps.bridge: Skin hides deep muscle injury, so the formula underestimates need. Next: what else the survey must catch →

lesson.text:
This card has its full lesson with compartment syndrome. Here's what you need for this question. The skin underestimates the muscle damage, so the burned-surface formulas are unreliable. Look for rhabdomyolysis: a high CK, and a dipstick positive for myoglobin. Start at four millilitres per kilo per percent, and aim for seventy-five to a hundred millilitres of urine an hour in an adult, about one to one and a half per kilo, until the pigment clears.

[[Electrical injury: start at four, and push the urine to seventy-five to a hundred millilitres an hour until it runs clear.]]

steps.bridge: Electrical injury brings arrhythmia, compartment syndrome and rhabdomyolysis. Next: how wounds and compartments are handled →

lesson.text: Go back to the survey from the first burns lesson. ABCDE, then AMPLET, and the events carry the red flags. For electricity, the card names three: arrhythmia, compartment syndrome and rhabdomyolysis. So put him on an ECG monitor after a high-voltage injury, or if his first ECG is abnormal. And a high-voltage victim is often thrown, or falls from a height, so look for spinal and blunt injuries too.

steps.bridge: Electrical injury may need fasciotomy, not just escharotomy. Next: test the key differences →

lesson.text:
The full wound lesson sits with compartment syndrome. For electricity, the point is depth. A circumferential burn of a limb, the neck or the chest that compromises circulation or breathing needs an escharotomy, a cut through the stiff burned skin. But in electrical injury, the swelling is in the muscle, under the fascia. Cutting the skin won't free it.

[[Escharotomy releases the skin. Fasciotomy releases the muscle. Electrical injury often needs the second.]]

Eight quick statements. Answer each in your head before I do.

Parkland gives half the volume in the first sixteen hours. False. Half in the first eight hours, from the time of the burn.

The revised Baux score adds seventeen for inhalation injury. True. The Baux score is the age plus the percent burned, and the revised version adds seventeen points when there's an inhalation injury.

Pulse oximetry detects carbon monoxide poisoning. False. It reads falsely normal. We'll see why in the next lessons.

Sodium nitrite is preferred for cyanide in smoke inhalation. False. Hydroxocobalamin is.

Full-thickness burns are painless, and hair plucks out easily. True. The nerve endings and the hair follicles have been destroyed.

Early burns cause anaemia that needs transfusion. False. Early on, the blood is concentrated, because plasma leaks out and the red cells stay behind.

A circumferential chest burn is treated by fasciotomy. False. Escharotomy. Fasciotomy is for deep muscle compartments.

And electrical burns need a higher urine target than thermal burns. True. And here's why. Myoglobin from the dead muscle is filtered by the kidney, and in the tubules it forms casts that block them and injure the cells. [[A high urine flow keeps the myoglobin moving, and washes it out before it can cast.]]

One honest caution on the extras. Alkalinising the urine with isotonic bicarbonate is often added, but the evidence for it is weak. And watch the calcium. Bicarbonate lowers the ionised calcium, and so does calcium being laid down in damaged muscle.

spine: What differs: the skin burn underestimates deep muscle damage, so TBSA formulas are unreliable in electrical injury.
What I do: start at **4 mL/kg/%TBSA** (thermal adults start at 2) and titrate to urine **75–100 mL/h**, about 1–1.5 mL/kg/h, until the urine clears.
Why the higher target: myoglobin from damaged muscle forms tubular casts and causes AKI. A high urine flow washes it out.
Also: consider alkalinising the urine (weak evidence) and watch calcium. ECG monitoring for high voltage or an abnormal ECG.
Caution: check compartments often; deep injury may need **fasciotomy**, not just escharotomy.

open.text:
Let me start with that lineman.

He touched a high-voltage cable. There's a small charred wound on his hand, where the current went in, and another on his foot, where it came out. Add up the skin, and it's a few percent. By the thermal rules you've just learned, he's under twenty percent, so no formal fluids at all. Yet within the hour, his urine is dark, like cola, and his forearm is getting hard.

So what happened between the hand and the foot?

The current has to travel through him, and each tissue resists it differently. Where the resistance is high, the current makes heat. Bone resists the current most, so bone heats the most, and it cooks the muscle wrapped around it, from the inside. Meanwhile the skin over the limb may look almost normal.

Look at the cross-section on your screen.

{{pic}}

A small wound on the skin. A white ring of bone at the centre. And around the bone, a thick band of cooked, dying muscle that nobody can see.

[[An electrical burn is an iceberg. The skin shows you the tip. The damage is in the muscle underneath.]]

And just as an iceberg sinks a ship below the waterline, this hidden muscle does its harm out of sight. Dead muscle releases myoglobin, which attacks the kidney. It swells inside its tight fascia, which causes compartment syndrome. And if the current crossed the chest, from hand to foot, it can disturb the heart's rhythm.

This is an X versus Y question, so the panel wants the differences, cleanly. Why the formulas fail. The starting rate. The urine target, and why it's higher. The extras, the bicarbonate, the calcium and the ECG. And what you do for the compartments.

So the plan. First, the electrical burn card. Then the survey red flags. Then the wound and the compartments. And finally, a quick test of the differences.
open.cap: Electrical injury: a small skin wound, but bone heats most and cooks the deep muscle around it.

close.text:
So let's bring it together.

What differs? [[In electrical injury, the skin burn underestimates the deep muscle damage. So the burned-surface formulas are unreliable.]]

What do you do? Start at four millilitres per kilo per percent, where a thermal burn in an adult starts at two. Then titrate to a urine output of seventy-five to a hundred millilitres an hour, about one to one and a half per kilo, until the urine clears.

Why the higher target? Myoglobin from damaged muscle forms casts in the tubules and causes acute kidney injury. A high urine flow washes it out.

Also, consider alkalinising the urine, knowing the evidence is weak, and watch the calcium. Monitor the ECG after a high-voltage injury, or if the first ECG is abnormal.

[[And the caution: check the compartments often. Deep injury may need a fasciotomy, not just an escharotomy.]]

That's your answer to the panel. What differs, what you do, why, the extras, and the caution.

But notice a pattern. In both lessons, thermal and electrical, the answer to how much came back to the same word. Titrate. To what, exactly? Is the urine the only endpoint? How far do you turn the drip, and when do you stop trusting crystalloid alone? That's next.

questions.text: What are the endpoints of burn resuscitation?

steps.bridge: The formula only starts the drip; urine output steers it. Next: why the lower starting rule is now preferred →

lesson.text: Look at the formula card one more time, and read only its last line. The formula only starts the drip. Parkland's four, or today's two, are guesses about an average patient with a burn of that size. The urine output, half a millilitre per kilo per hour in adults and one in children, tells you about this patient. [[The formula is where you start. The urine is where you steer.]]

steps.bridge: Starting at 2 mL/kg avoids fluid creep; electrical injury starts at 4, not 3. Next: the exact urine targets →

lesson.text:
The modified Parkland formula is two millilitres, times the weight in kilos, times the percent burned, titrated to the urine output. Current trauma and burns guidance favours starting there, rather than infusing the classic four regardless of response. For a high-voltage electrical injury, it rises to four, with a urine target of seventy-five to a hundred millilitres an hour until the urine clears.

Why is the lower start safer? Think about which mistake you can undo. If you start low and he needs more, the urine tells you within an hour or two, and you turn the rate up. But if you start high, the extra fluid doesn't stay in his vessels. It leaks into his tissues, and you can't call it back. [[Under-resuscitation shows itself early and can be corrected. Over-resuscitation hides in the tissues and stays.]]

That's the reason for the change. Concern about fluid creep. Over-resuscitation with the classic formula drove massive oedema, abdominal compartment syndrome and worse breathing.

{{**Modified Parkland** = 2 mL × kg × %TBSA (adults), titrated to urine
Electrical: **4 mL**, urine 75–100 mL/h until clear
Adjust the **rate** in steps (about **20–33%**, by protocol), not boluses
Projected 24-h volume > ~**6 mL/kg/%TBSA** → consider **albumin rescue**; measure bladder pressure}}

Now go back to the sixth hour. What should the junior have done? Not a bolus. Change the rate, in steps of about a fifth to a third, depending on your unit's protocol, up or down, and watch the next hours. A bolus pours fluid into a leaking capillary bed all at once, and much of it ends up as oedema. A rate change is gentler, and it lets the trend tell you whether you were right.

And when do you stop trusting crystalloid alone? When the projected volume for the day passes about six millilitres per kilo per percent, think of albumin as a rescue, and measure the bladder pressure. You met albumin in burns already. It may cut the crystalloid needed, though it has no proven survival benefit.

[[Either formula's volume is only a starting estimate. The real rate is set, hour by hour, by the patient.]]

steps.bridge: Urine 0.5 mL/kg/h in adults, 1 in children under 30 kg. Next: how the target changes in electrical injury →

lesson.text: The targets you met with fluids and feeding, once more. Half a millilitre per kilo per hour in adults, roughly thirty to fifty millilitres. One per kilo per hour in children under thirty kilos. Read them as a trend over several hours, not one reading at a time. And alongside the urine, keep watching perfusion and lactate, the signs we built at the very start of this package. [[One hour of low urine is a question. A trend is an answer.]]

One patient breaks the half-millilitre rule. The electrical injury. Dead muscle releases myoglobin, so the target rises to seventy-five to a hundred millilitres an hour, about one to one and a half per kilo, until the urine clears. [[In electrical injury, the endpoint isn't just a volume. It's a colour.]] When the dark urine runs clear, you can bring the target back down.

spine: What it is: the formula only gives a starting rate. Hourly urine output is the main endpoint.
Adults: **0.5 mL/kg/h**, about 30–50 mL/h. Children under 30 kg: **1 mL/kg/h**.
Electrical injury: **75–100 mL/h**, about 1–1.5 mL/kg/h, until the pigment clears, to protect the kidney from myoglobin.
Also: I follow perfusion and lactate, and the urine trend, not one reading.
Caution: change the rate in steps of about 20–33% (protocols vary), not boluses. If projected volume passes about 6 mL/kg/%TBSA, consider albumin rescue and bladder pressure.

open.text:
Let me start at the sixth hour.

Our man from the factory is on his fluids. Last hour his urine was twenty millilitres. The junior gives a litre bolus. The next hour, it's ninety, and everyone relaxes. The hour after, it's fifteen again, and another bolus goes in. By the next morning, he has had far more than any formula predicted, and his abdomen is tight.

Nobody did anything outrageous. Each decision chased one number. And that's the problem this question is about.

The panel asks, what are the endpoints of burn resuscitation? What the professor is really checking is whether you know that the formula is not the endpoint. That the urine is the main one, with a different number for an adult, a child and an electrical injury. That you read trends, not single readings. And that you know how to adjust the rate, and when to call for help beyond crystalloid.

So the plan. First, the formula, seen from the angle of endpoints. Then why the lower starting rule is safer. Then the urine targets. And finally, the patient whose endpoint is a colour.
